title: Prompt-to-Paper: Agentic AI System for Bioinformatics
summary: While recent advances in large language models have enabled end-to-end automated manuscript generation, existing systems suffer from three critical deficiencies: (i) generated claims are not deterministically grounded in verifiable literature, (ii) experimental results are frequently fabricated rather than executed, and (iii) there exists no standardized, multi-dimensional framework to assess whether AI-generated manuscripts meet the quality and rigor required for real-world publication. We present Prompt-to-Paper, a multi-agent framework that directly addresses this evaluation gap through three integrated innovations. First, a deterministic retrieval-augmented generation pipeline with section-aware relevance scoring and snowball citation expansion grounds every claim in a verifiable corpus of 60--100 papers. Second, an autonomous coding agent executes real computational biology experiments replacing synthetic outputs with genuine numerical results. Third, an eight-dimensional automated quality scorer, benchmarked with approximate reference statistics from published papers and augmented with explicit hallucination penalties, provides standardized, reproducible quality assessments. The quality-driven improvement loop uses a context-rich reviser that routes each iteration to one of three researcher actions and fires a deep research cycle every ten iterations to re-run experiments and re-manuscript from stronger outputs. We validate the system on five bioinformatics case studies; all five cases compiled submission-formatted PDFs with zero out-of-range citations. The improvement loop raises manuscript quality by an average of +17.96 points on a 0--100 scale (maximum +26.04. As partial external checks, a human reviewer scored the five manuscripts at an average of 7.0 out of 10. Complete manuscripts are produced at approximately 0.31 USD per paper.

AI.tldr: Prompt-to-Paper: a multi-agent system for deterministic, verifiable, end-to-end AI-generated manuscripts with grounding, autonomous experiments, and multi-dimensional quality scoring.
AI.motivation: Address three critical deficiencies in AI-generated manuscripts: (i) lack of deterministic grounding in verifiable literature, (ii) fabrication of experimental results, and (iii) absence of a standardized, multi-dimensional quality framework for publication readiness.
AI.method: Three integrated innovations: (1) deterministic retrieval-augmented generation with section-aware relevance scoring and snowball citation expansion grounding claims in a corpus of 60–100 papers; (2) autonomous coding agent executes real computational biology experiments producing genuine numerical results; (3) an eight-dimensional automated quality scorer, benchmarked with approximate reference statistics and augmented with hallucination penalties, plus a context-rich reviser directing iterations among three researcher actions; a deep research cycle every ten iterations that re-runs experiments and re-writes the manuscript. Validation on five bioinformatics case studies, with all five producing submission-form PDFs and zero out-of-range citations. Improvement loop reports +17.96/100 on average (max +26.04); human reviewer average 7.0/10; cost ~$0.31 per paper.
AI.result: Five manuscript-quality improvements demonstrated; all papers are submission-ready with verifiable grounding and no invalid citations; average objective quality gain quantified; human evaluation provided for external validity; cost-efficiency demonstrated for automated manuscript production.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides verifiably grounded, experimentally validated, and quality-assessed AI-generated manuscripts, showing substantial quality gains and cost-effectiveness, though real-world adoption requires careful alignment with publication standards and thorough external validation.

title: From Graphs to Gradients: Physics-Inspired Structural Attribution for Cyber-Physical IoT Systems and Beyond
summary: Interpretable explanation methods in Artificial Intelligence aim to uncover the underlying causes and their effects, enabling a deeper understanding of why a system behaves in a certain way under different inputs. Unlike traditional explainability methods, which mainly highlight correlations between input and output variables, causal explanation focuses on interventional questions. By doing so, it provides more robust insights, helping users understand automated decisions, especially in high-risk domains. Recovering an explicit directed causal structure, however, is often impractical in large-scale, hybrid cyber-physical systems with feedback loops and partial observability. This paper introduces a novel framework inspired by statistical mechanics that instead models variable dependencies through an undirected, energy-based representation of cyber-physical IoT systems. Our approach enables rigorous dependency-aware attribution by analysing how variations in the energy landscape reflect the influence of individual components, without recovering a directed causal graph. It also supports reasoning about perturbation effects across hybrid interactions, providing reliable explanations of abnormal behaviours. We empirically examined our framework through simulations on an industrial IoT testbed with hybrid continuous and discrete variables, demonstrating higher attribution accuracy, improved robustness and better scalability than state-of-the-art graph-based approaches. While the attributions are not intended to fully recover the system's generative dynamics, they provide valuable, dependency-aware explanations supporting both human interpretation and downstream predictive and diagnostic tasks. Although demonstrated in industrial IoT security, our framework also applies to other high-dimensional cyber-physical and socio-technical systems requiring principled, structural explanations.

AI.tldr: Energy-based, undirected dependency modeling for explanations in cyber-physical IoT systems, enabling dependency-aware attribution without recovering directed causal graphs; shows improved attribution accuracy, robustness, and scalability over graph-based methods, with applicability to CPS and IoT security.
AI.motivation: In large-scale CPS with feedback, partial observability, and hybrid variables, recovering explicit directed causal structures is impractical. A robust, scalable explanation method that captures dependencies without full causal graphs is needed to support interpretation and downstream tasks.
AI.method: Proposes a framework inspired by statistical mechanics that uses an undirected energy-based representation to model variable dependencies. Explanations are derived by analyzing how variations in the energy landscape reflect influence of components, enabling perturbation reasoning across hybrid interactions. Evaluated on a simulated industrial IoT testbed with hybrid continuous/discrete variables, and compared to state-of-the-art graph-based approaches.
AI.result: Empirical results show higher attribution accuracy, improved robustness, and better scalability than graph-based methods. Attributions provide dependable explanations suitable for human interpretation and downstream predictive/diagnostic tasks; not intended to fully recover the system's generative dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers principled, dependency-aware explanations for high-dimensional CPS, with potential applicability beyond industrial IoT security to other CPS and socio-technical systems requiring structurally informed explanations.

title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
summary: Large language models are increasingly explored as AI tutors, yet deploying them in K-12 settings raises concerns around privacy, cost, and reliance on proprietary models. Small language models (SLMs) offer a promising alternative, but selecting the right model for a specific educational context remains difficult, particularly when the target domain, such as block-based programming, is largely absent from model training data. We introduce CSTutorBench, a benchmark for evaluating language models as CS tutors in VEX VR, a block-based robotics environment. The benchmark comprises 17 scenario-based questions scored against a pedagogical rubric grounded in established tutoring and feedback research, with a human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge pipeline for evaluation. Preliminary findings across 11 models (4B-120B parameters) reveal that models perform well on surface-level criteria such as vocabulary and tone but struggle with deeper pedagogical behaviors, particularly avoiding answer leakage and engaging with student debugging histories. In our sample, model family and instruction-tuning approach appear to be better predictors of tutoring quality than parameter count alone, though the small number of models limits the strength of this conclusion. A targeted prompt revision grounded in recent educational prompt engineering research improved scores for 10 of 11 models. These results underscore the value of context-specific, pedagogically grounded benchmarks for SLM selection in educational deployment.

AI.tldr: Introduces CSTutorBench, a domain-specific benchmark evaluating small language models as CS tutors in VEX VR; finds instruction-tuning and model family better predict tutoring quality than size alone; prompt engineering improves performance; highlights need for pedagogically grounded, context-specific evaluation for SLM use in education.
AI.motivation: tackle privacy, cost, and reliance issues with LLM-based tutors in K-12 and address the difficulty of choosing suitable SLMs for niche domains with little training data; provide a benchmarking framework to assess pedagogical tutoring capabilities.
AI.method: 17 scenario-based questions in VEX VR evaluated with a pedagogical rubric; human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge pipeline; tested 11 models ranging from 4B to 120B parameters; analyzed surface-level vs deeper pedagogical behaviors; applied targeted prompt revision informed by educational prompt engineering.
AI.result: Surface criteria (vocabulary, tone) were met, but deeper pedagogy (avoiding answer leakage, engaging with debugging histories) lagged; model family and instruction-tuning better predicted tutoring quality than parameter count; prompt revisions improved scores for 10 of 11 models.
AI.conclusion: Context-specific, pedagogically grounded benchmarks are valuable for selecting SLMs for education; results advocate focusing on domain alignment and prompt engineering over sheer parameter counts, while acknowledging limited model samples and the need for broader validation.

title: Foundation Models for Automatic CAD Generation
comment: Accepted as a book chapter in "Advances in Global Applied Artificial Intelligence" (G. A. Tsihrintzis, M. Virvou, N. G. Bourbakis, L. C. Jain, Eds.), authenticated version will be published in Springer series: Learning and Analytics in Intelligent Systems
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable the automatic generation of parametric 3D designs from natural-language specifications. This chapter presents an empirical study of foundation models for automatic Computer-Aided Design (CAD) generation of mechanical parts, using a unified evaluation pipeline and a curated benchmark of 97 engineering design problems. We introduce LLMForge, a multi-model text-to-CAD framework integrating JSON-schema validation, analytic feature scoring, mesh synthesis, and multi-round iterative refinement, studied under two critique regimes. IterTracer uses a Phong-shaded ray-trace renderer with analytic visual metrics (silhouette IoU, hole visibility, edge clearance, aspect-ratio conformance) for lightweight geometry-aware feedback across rounds. IterVision replaces the analytic scorer with a VLM semantic critic (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) that evaluates rendered views via chain-of-thought visual reasoning, assessing spatial coherence and design intent. On a benchmark spanning four canonical geometry families (plates with holes and bolt circles, multi-feature boxes, flanged cylinders, and L-brackets), we evaluate seven foundation models: DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-3-27B, GLM-4.5, MiniMax-M2.1, and INTELLECT. Under IterTracer, the four highest-ranked models form a tight cluster (overall mean in [0.885, 0.890]) with 98.97% mesh success, showing that compact instruction-tuned models can match substantially larger systems. VLM-based critique in IterVision yields 100% watertight mesh generation on the leading model while surfacing systematic difficulty on rotationally symmetric geometries such as cylinders, where visual and semantic scoring diverge most. We discuss benchmark design, failure modes, CAD-oriented prompting, and implications for industrial workflows and scalable automated mechanical design.

AI.tldr: A multi-model text-to-CAD pipeline (LMMForge) with two critique regimes (IterTracer: analytic geometry feedback; IterVision: VLM semantic critique) evaluated on 97 problems across four geometry families. Seven foundation models show competitive performance, with compact models matching larger systems under analytic feedback; VLM critique achieves perfect mesh watertightness for the leading model but reveals symmetry-related challenges.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, automated CAD generation from natural language using foundation models, and to establish a unified evaluation pipeline and benchmark for parametric mechanical designs, addressing geometry-aware feedback, mesh quality, and design intent.
AI.method: Develop LLMForge, a text-to-CAD framework integrating JSON-schema validation, analytic feature scoring, mesh synthesis, and iterative refinement. Two critique regimes: IterTracer uses a Phong-shaded ray-trace renderer and analytic metrics (silhouette IoU, hole visibility, edge clearance, aspect-ratio conformance); IterVision uses a VLM-based semantic critic (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) with chain-of-thought visual reasoning to assess spatial coherence and design intent. Benchmark spans four geometry families (plates with holes/bolt circles, multi-feature boxes, flanged cylinders, L-brackets) and seven foundation models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-3-27B, GLM-4.5, MiniMax-M2.1, INTELLECT).
AI.result: Under IterTracer, the top four models form a tight cluster (overall mean in [0.885,0.890]) with 98.97% mesh success, indicating compact instruction-tuned models can match larger systems. Under IterVision, the leading model achieves 100% watertight meshes but shows systematic difficulty on rotationally symmetric geometries (e.g., cylinders) where visual and semantic scoring diverge.
AI.conclusion: The study informs benchmark design, failure modes, CAD-oriented prompting, and implications for industrial workflows and scalable automated mechanical design; highlights the complementary strengths of analytic feedback and semantic critique in enabling robust CAD generation with foundation models.

title: Quaternion-Averaging-Based Adaptive Complementary Filter for Pedestrian Dead Reckoning With a Foot-Mounted AHRS
summary: Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR) can be applied to indoor navigation systems. GPS suffers from signal degradation due to roofs and high-rise buildings, whereas PDR can estimate positions without being affected by such signal degradation. The accuracy of a foot-mounted AHRS(Attitude and Heading Reference System)-based PDR depends on the accuracy of the attitude estimation algorithm used in the AHRS. In this article, a Quaternion-Averaging-Based Adaptive Complementary Filter (QAACF) for PDR with a foot-mounted AHRS is proposed to improve estimation accuracy while reducing computational cost. QAACF fuses a quaternion derived from angular velocity with quaternions derived from acceleration and magnetic field measurements using Markley's quaternion averaging, which combines two quaternions more rigorously than linear interpolation. In addition, QAACF adaptively adjusts the weights of angular velocity, acceleration, and magnetic field measurements according to gait phases and the level of magnetic disturbances. Experimental results showed that the proposed QAACF achieves low Root Mean Square Errors (RMSEs) compared to existing attitude estimation filters while requiring lower computational cost than Kalman filters.

AI.tldr: QAACF: a quaternion-averaging adaptive complementary filter for foot-mounted AHRS in PDR that fuses quaternions from angular velocity, acceleration, and magnetic field via Markley averaging, with gait-phase and disturbance-aware adaptive weighting; achieves lower RMSE than existing filters and lower computational cost than Kalman filters.
AI.motivation: Attitude estimation errors in PDR degrade indoor navigation accuracy; existing filters either underperform in dynamic gait or are too computationally intensive. A robust, efficient fusion scheme is needed to handle gait dynamics and magnetic disturbances.
AI.method: Propose QAACF that uses Markley quaternion averaging to fuse quaternions derived from angular velocity, acceleration, and magnetic field. The filter adaptively weights these quaternions based on gait phase and magnetic disturbances, combining them within a complementary filtering framework to produce attitude estimates.
AI.result: Experimental results show QAACF achieves lower RMSE than existing attitude estimation filters and requires lower computational cost than Kalman filters.
AI.conclusion: QAACF improves attitude estimation accuracy for foot-mounted AHRS in PDR while reducing computational burden, enhancing indoor navigation performance.

title: Statistically Meaningful Geometry and Gauge Symmetry Breaking: A Geometric Foundation for Scientific Discovery and Intelligence Emergence
summary: The rapid scaling of over-parameterized machine learning architectures, particularly LLMs, raises a profound crisis: do these systems exhibit genuine intelligence, or are they merely sophisticated statistical pattern matchers? Classical flat Euclidean statistics cannot differentiate continuous interpolation from the autonomous discovery of novel causal laws. To resolve this, we introduce Statistically Meaningful Geometry (SMG), a framework modeling over-parameterized learning systems as infinite-dimensional non-parametric Orlicz fiber bundles. We prove that under persistent out-of-distribution (OOD) stimuli governed by unmodeled causal mechanisms, continuous optimization fails. Unmodeled variance is rejected by the visible horizontal base manifold, leaking into the unobservable vertical fiber space and generating an accumulation of Active Acausal Tension. Driven by the statistical manifold's non-linear curvature, this tension inevitably strikes a conjugate focal boundary ($T_{\text{crit}} = π^2 / K_{\text{max}}$), triggering localized volumetric collapse and a catastrophic matrix singularity ($[G_f]^{-1} \to \infty$). We demonstrate this geometric breakdown acts as the strict non-equilibrium trigger for a Gauge Symmetry Break (GSB). The system purges hidden tension from unobservable gauge redundancies, spontaneously crystallizing a new, mathematically independent horizontal coordinate axis. This non-parametric phase transition registers as a discrete $+1.0$ integer step-jump in observable Structural G-Entropy. By decoupling parameter charts and subjecting emergent axes to a Minimal Energy Path Criterion and a Causal Invariance Filter, we distinguish genuine discovery from malignant hallucinations. Ultimately, SMG provides a parameter-free, falsifiable dashboard to mathematically certify true intelligence, transforming AI for Science into an engine of autonomous paradigm shifts.

AI.tldr: Proposes Statistically Meaningful Geometry (SMG) to diagnose genuine intelligence in over-parameterized systems by modeling learning dynamics as infinite-dimensional fiber bundles; identifies a geometric non-equilibrium transition (Gauge Symmetry Break) that yields observable axes and a discrete entropy jump, offering a parameter-free falsifiable dashboard to certify genuine discovery vs hallucination.
AI.motivation: Address the inability of classical flat Euclidean statistics to distinguish autonomous discovery of novel causal laws from mere interpolation in large, over-parameterized models (e.g., LLMs).
AI.method: Model learning systems as non-parametric Orlicz fiber bundles with a curved statistical manifold. Analyze persistent out-of-distribution (OOD) stimuli driven by unmodeled causal mechanisms. Show that continuous optimization fails and unmodeled variance leaks into unobservable vertical space, causing Active Acausal Tension. Use curvature-driven dynamics to reach a conjugate focal boundary T_crit = π^2 / K_max, leading to volumetric collapse and singularity [G_f]^-1 → ∞. Interpret as non-equilibrium trigger for Gauge Symmetry Break (GSB), purging hidden tension and crystallizing a new horizontal axis. Quantify via a +1.0 step in observable Structural G-Entropy and apply a Minimal Energy Path Criterion and a Causal Invariance Filter to separate genuine discovery from hallucination.
AI.result: Demonstrates a geometric breakdown acting as the trigger for a GSB, yielding emergent horizontal coordinates and a discrete entropy change. Proposes a parameter-free, falsifiable dashboard to certify true intelligence and to transform AI-for-science into drivers of paradigm shifts.
AI.conclusion: SMG presents a rigorous, parameter-free framework to certify genuine intelligence in AI systems by linking geometric non-equilibrium phenomena to observable entropy changes; intended as a diagnostic tool separating true causal discovery from hallucinations and enabling autonomous scientific paradigm shifts.

title: CanvasAgent: Enabling Complex Image Creation and Editing via Visual Tool Orchestration
summary:
Complex image creation and editing often require more than a single generation or editing model. A user request may involve synthesizing images, localizing objects, segmenting regions, editing selected content, compositing intermediate assets, reading text, and enhancing the final result. Such tasks shift multimodal agents from perception-augmented reasoning to manipulation-centered visual creation, where tools must actively transform visual states rather than merely inspect them. However, existing multimodal tool-use agents are mostly optimized for perception, search, or domain-specific editing, and lack large-scale supervision for executable image-creation trajectories. In this paper, we introduce CanvasCraft, a large-scale multimodal tool-use dataset for complex image creation and editing, and \textbf{CanvasAgent}, a tool-augmented multimodal agent that learns to orchestrate heterogeneous visual tools through multi-turn interaction. CanvasCraft contains 140K fully annotated executable trajectories and 10K
  RL task specifications. CanvasAgent is first trained with SFT to learn executable reasoning-action trajectories, and is then optimized with GRPO using a hybrid reward that combines outcome- and process-level signals. During rollout, CanvasAgent inspects intermediate results, tracks visual assets, and adapts tool decisions to the evolving visual state. Experiments evaluate both final image quality and trajectory behavior, demonstrating the effectiveness of CanvasAgent and the proposed dataset for complex multi-tool image creation workflows.

AI.tldr: Proposes CanvasCraft dataset and CanvasAgent—a large-scale, tool-augmented multimodal system for complex image creation/editing that orchestrates multiple visual tools via multi-turn interaction, trained with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO RL fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap in multimodal agents that are primarily perception-focused and lack scalable supervision for executable, multi-tool image-creation trajectories; aims to enable manipulation-centered visual creation.
AI.method: Introduce CanvasCraft with 140K fully annotated executable trajectories and 10K RL task specs; develop CanvasAgent to orchestrate heterogeneous tools; train with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn reasoning-action trajectories, then optimize with GRPO using a hybrid outcome- and process-level reward; during rollout the agent inspects intermediate results, tracks assets, and adapts tool decisions to evolving visual states.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on final image quality and trajectory behavior shows CanvasAgent effectively orchestrates multiple tools and improves complex image-creation workflows.
AI.conclusion: CanvasCraft and CanvasAgent establish a scalable framework for tool-driven image creation, enabling complex, multi-step editing tasks through iterative tool use and adaptive state-aware decision making.

title: Shifting is Optimal under Gap-ETH: A Lower Bound Framework for Geometric Approximation Schemes
summary:
The shifting technique of Hochbaum and Maass [J.ACM'85] produces PTASes with the fastest known running times $n^{O(1/\varepsilon^{d-1})}$ for several $d$-dimensional geometric problems. However, it is only known, due to Marx [FOCS'07], that these algorithms are indeed optimal for dimension $d=2$.
  We show that these running times are optimal under Gap-ETH for every constant dimension. More precisely, we develop a framework that enables us to prove the conditional optimality of the shifting algorithms for several problems on unit ball graphs, such as maximum independent set, maximum induced forest, and others, as well as for the problem of piercing unit balls.
  Our framework is built using the cube wiring theorem of De Berg et al. [SICOMP'20] and the reduction steps of Marx and Sidiropoulos [SoCG'14] to create a convenient maximization version of geometric CSP that can be used as a basis for reductions.

AI.tldr: Conditional lower bounds (under Gap-ETH) extend the optimality of Hochbaum–Maass shifting PTAS from 2D to any fixed dimension for problems on unit-ball graphs (e.g., MIS, maximum induced forest, piercing unit balls).
AI.motivation: To determine whether the fast PTAS running times achieved by the shifting technique are near-optimal in higher dimensions and for a broader set of problems, by establishing conditional hardness results.
AI.method: Introduce a maximization version of geometric CSP built from the cube wiring theorem and Marx–Sidiropoulos reductions to enable reductions to unit-ball-graph problems, yielding Gap-ETH-based lower bounds for the shifting framework.
AI.result: Under Gap-ETH, the n^{O(1/ε^{d−1})} running times of the shifting technique are optimal for every fixed dimension d, for a range of problems on unit-ball graphs (including MIS, maximum induced forest, and piercing unit balls).
AI.conclusion: The shifting technique PTAS is essentially optimal in fixed dimension under Gap-ETH; the authors supply a general reduction-based framework to transfer conditional optimality to a broad class of unit-ball-graph problems.

title: Narrative World Model: Narratology-Grounded Writer Memory for Long-Form Fiction
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures; 9-page main text plus appendix. Preprint
summary: Long-form fiction writers need memory that answers multi-hop questions about evolving story state: who knows a secret and when they learned it, whether an event preceded the narration that revealed it, whether a setup paid off, and how a relationship shifted. General-purpose retrieval and agent-memory systems represent entities and facts but not the narratological structure these questions turn on, so they surface the wrong evidence or none at all. We introduce the Narrative World Model (NWM), a writer-memory system that pairs a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval. To measure memory rather than the answerer, we read every system through a single held-constant Opus 4.8 reader over only that system's chapter-safe evidence, on a reproducible public corpus and a validated multi-hop benchmark, and we compare against the strongest existing temporal-knowledge-graph agent-memory framework, Graphiti/Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025). NWM substantially and significantly outperforms this baseline on multi-hop narratological QA across both corpora, and far exceeds GraphRAG and flat retrieval. The advantage is representational rather than an artifact of extraction: it survives rebuilding the baseline with NWM's own extractor, and traces to its narratology-grounded structure and query-conditioned retrieval, not to graph size or extractor quality.

AI.tldr: NWM introduces a narratology-grounded temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval to support memory for long-form fiction, achieving superior multi-hop narratological QA over Graphiti/Zep and GraphRAG in a reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose retrieval and agent-memory systems fail to capture narratological structure needed to track evolving story state (who knows what when, prior events, setups, relationship shifts). A memory system grounded in narratology could improve long-form fiction QA by representing temporal states and dependencies; evaluation is performed via a fixed reader on a controlled corpus to isolate memory quality.
AI.method: Develop Narrative World Model (NWM): a typed temporal-state graph grounded in narratology combined with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval. Evaluation uses a single Opus 4.8 reader restricted to chapter-safe evidence, across reproducible public corpora, comparing against Graphiti/Zep and baselines like GraphRAG. Also tests robustness by rebuilding the baseline using NWM’s extractor.
AI.result: NWM substantially and significantly outperforms Graphiti/Zep on multi-hop narratological QA across both corpora, and far exceeds GraphRAG and flat retrieval. The advantage is representational, surviving reconstruction with NWM’s extractor, and traces to the narratology-grounded structure and query-conditioned retrieval rather than graph size or extractor quality.
AI.conclusion: A narratology-grounded memory design with query-conditioned retrieval yields superior performance for narratological reasoning in long-form fiction, indicating representational structure—not just data scale or extraction quality—is key for memory-based QA in narrative domains.

title: Learning 4D Geometric Priors for Inference-Efficient World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual future dynamics and executable action sequences. However, existing video-action co-training methods primarily optimize appearance-oriented video latents, which may insufficiently capture the temporally evolving geometry required for precise manipulation. We propose MECo-WAM, a Multi-Expert Co-Training World Action Model that injects action-relevant 4D geometric priors into video-action representations while preserving the original lightweight inference graph. During training, MECo-WAM combines video and action experts with a lightweight 4D expert supervised by relational targets from a frozen VGGT encoder. Asymmetric expert visibility prevents non-causal shortcuts from auxiliary geometry to action generation. To transfer geometric knowledge into the deployed video-action pathway, we introduce decayed 4D read-mask attention, which provides restricted current-frame geometric guidance early in training and progressively removes this dependency. We further propose action-aware temporal geometric distillation, which aligns within-frame geometric relations and their temporal evolution while emphasizing visual regions most relevant to robot actions. At deployment, all auxiliary 4D components are removed. Experiments on LIBERO (98.2%), RoboTwin 2.0 (92.6%), and challenging real-world manipulation tasks show that MECo-WAM improves manipulation performance without increasing inference cost.

AI.tldr: MECo-WAM injects 4D geometric priors into video-action models via multi-expert co-training, decayed geometric guidance, and action-aware distillation; deployed with no extra inference cost and improved manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Video-action co-training tends to optimize appearance in video latents, missing temporally evolving geometry critical for manipulation; need geometry-aware representations without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: Three experts: video, action, and a lightweight 4D geometric expert supervised by frozen VGGT; asymmetric visibility; decayed 4D read-mask attention to transfer geometry early and gradually detach; action-aware temporal geometric distillation aligning spatial relations and their temporal evolution; deploy with 4D components removed.
AI.result: Improved manipulation performance on LIBERO (98.2%) and RoboTwin 2.0 (92.6%) and real-world tasks; no inference cost increase.
AI.conclusion: MECo-WAM validates geometry-informed co-training as effective for WAMs, preserving lightweight deployment while enhancing manipulation; the approach enables better geometry capture without runtime penalties.

title: Design-CP: Context Parallelism for Design of Protein Nanoparticles
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Workshop on Generative and Agentic AI for Biology (ICML 2026)
summary: Many all-atom generative protein models can in principle design large multimeric complexes by jointly modelling all chains, but their quadratic token- and atom-pair representations quickly exceed single-GPU memory as the number of chains and residues modelled grows. We introduce Design-CP, two context-parallel (CP) inference strategies for RFdiffusion 3 (1D row-sharding and 2D grid sharding with ring attention) that distribute the quadratic activations across a multi-GPU mesh while preserving pretrained weights. We characterise their scaling when sampling icosahedral assemblies, showing that the maximum feasible asymmetric subunit (ASU) size grows with the expected square-root trend in GPU count and that 2D sharding achieves better wall-clock scaling. Moreover, we show how strong point-group symmetry constraints make CP usable out of the box for end-to-end, all-atom design of icosahedral nanoparticles, yielding favourable in silico structural and interface metrics. Finally, we demonstrate octahedral nanoparticle design on a small cluster of workstation-grade 16GB GPUs, illustrating how Design-CP can be a practical path towards democratising large-assembly protein design.

AI.tldr: Design-CP introduces context-parallel inference for RFdiffusion 3 to scale all-atom multimer design across multiple GPUs. It presents 1D row-sharding and 2D grid sharding with ring attention to distribute quadratic activations, showing sqrt(GPU_count) scaling in ASU size and superior wall-clock performance for 2D sharding. It leverages symmetry constraints for end-to-end icosahedral nanoparticle design and demonstrates feasibility on small GPU clusters, aiming to democratize large-assembly protein design.
AI.motivation: All-atom generative protein models face memory and compute bottlenecks due to quadratic activations when modelling many chains and residues. There is a need for distributed inference strategies that preserve pretrained weights to enable large-assembly design on multi-GPU hardware.
AI.method: Two context-parallel inference strategies (1D row-sharding and 2D grid sharding with ring attention) are proposed for RFdiffusion 3 to distribute quadratic activations across a multi-GPU mesh while preserving pretrained weights. The authors characterize scaling for sampling icosahedral assemblies, evaluate subunit size growth with GPU count, compare wall-clock performance between sharding strategies, and apply strong point-group symmetry constraints to enable end-to-end, all-atom design of icosahedral nanoparticles. They also demonstrate octahedral nanoparticle design on a small cluster of workstation GPUs.
AI.result: 2D sharding achieves better wall-clock scaling than 1D row-sharding. Maximum feasible asymmetric subunit (ASU) size grows with the square root of GPU count. Strong symmetry constraints enable usable end-to-end all-atom design of icosahedral nanoparticles, with favorable in silico structural and interface metrics. The approach is demonstrated on a small cluster of 16GB GPUs, indicating practicality and potential democratization of large-assembly protein design.
AI.conclusion: Design-CP provides practical, scalable distributed inference for large-assembly protein design by offloading activations across GPUs without retraining, with 2D grid sharding preferred for scaling. Symmetry constraints enable out-of-the-box end-to-end design of symmetric nanoparticles, making large multimer design more accessible on commodity hardware.

title: A Task-Driven Evaluation of UAV Detection and Tracking under Synthetic Fog
summary: Fog severely degrades the visibility of small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in skydominant, long-range imagery, reducing the reliability of downstream detection and tracking. This paper presents a task-driven evaluation framework that links depth-aware synthetic fog generation, image restoration, object detection, and tracking within a unified pipeline. Given the practical difficulty of collecting and annotating foggy UAV scenes, synthetic fog is generated from real clear-weather outdoor images containing UAV targets using monocular depth estimation and the atmospheric scattering model. Representative restoration methods from classical, convolutional neural network (CNN)-based, and transformer-based families are first compared, after which the selected restoration model is integrated into the downstream perception pipeline. Detection is evaluated under both clean-only and fog-inclusive training regimes using multiple detector variants, while tracking-by-detection is assessed on clean, foggy, and restored video sequences. Beyond image-level restoration metrics, the study evaluates how fog and restoration affect detection robustness and tracking performance. The results show that fog substantially degrades both detection and tracking, primarily through increased missed detections. Fog-inclusive training provides the most consistent improvement in robustness, whereas test-time restoration is most beneficial when the detector has been trained only on clean imagery. These findings show that restoration quality does not necessarily translate into proportional gains in downstream perception and therefore should be evaluated jointly with detection and tracking performance.

AI.tldr: Synthetic fog generation from clear UAV imagery using monocular depth and atmospheric scattering, evaluating restoration methods in a joint detection/tracking pipeline; fog-trained detectors gain robustness; restoration helps mainly when detectors are trained on clear data; emphasizes joint evaluation over restoration quality alone.
AI.motivation: Fog severely degrades UAV visibility in long-range imagery; collecting labeled foggy data is difficult, necessitating synthetic fog and task-driven evaluation of restoration in downstream perception tasks.
AI.method: Generate synthetic fog from real clear-weather UAV images via monocular depth estimation and the atmospheric scattering model. Compare restoration methods across classical, CNN-based, and transformer-based families and integrate the chosen restoration into a downstream perception pipeline. Evaluate detectors under clean-only and fog-inclusive training regimes; assess tracking-by-detection on clean, foggy, and restored sequences; analyze image-level restoration metrics alongside effect on detection and tracking robustness.
AI.result: Fog substantially degrades detection and tracking, mainly by increasing missed detections. Fog-inclusive training provides the most robust improvements in detection/tracking robustness; test-time restoration benefits are greatest when detectors are trained only on clean imagery. Restoration quality does not directly translate to proportional gains in downstream perception, underscoring the need for joint evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A task-driven evaluation framework with synthetic fog is viable and informative: training with fog improves robustness; restoration alone does not guarantee downstream gains and should be evaluated together with detection/tracking performance.

title: Generalized altitudes and their bounds
summary: We introduce generalized altitudes of a simplex, extending the usual vertex-to-opposite-face altitude to arbitrary pairs of opposite faces. These quantities encode the relative position of the affine spans of such faces and yield a uniform formula for the angle between them. We also derive an equivalent algebraic expression in terms of generalized cross products and Gram determinants, linking the construction to standard determinant-based tools. Finally, we prove that every generalized altitude is bounded below by a quantity controlled by the ordinary height of the simplex. Thus, classical height or thickness assumptions imply control over this broader family of geometric quantities. The results provide a compact framework for studying simplex quality and are motivated by applications to triangulation criteria for Riemannian manifolds.

AI.tldr: Generalized altitudes for a simplex between opposite faces are introduced, yielding a uniform angle formula; an algebraic expression via generalized cross products and Gram determinants links the construction to determinant-based tools; every generalized altitude is bounded below by a quantity controlled by the ordinary height, ensuring existing height/thickness assumptions imply control over these quantities; applied framework supports simplex quality assessments and triangulation criteria for Riemannian manifolds.
AI.motivation: Extend the vertex-to-opposite-face altitude concept to all pairs of opposite faces to obtain a uniform, robust measure of simplex quality and to facilitate triangulation criteria in Riemannian geometry.
AI.method: Define generalized altitudes using the affine spans of opposite faces, derive a uniform formula for the angle between these spans, provide an algebraic expression using generalized cross products and Gram determinants, and prove a lower bound in terms of the usual height.
AI.result: A cohesive framework of generalized altitudes with a uniform angle formula, an explicit algebraic representation, and a guaranteed lower bound tied to ordinary height, enabling a compact approach to assessing simplex quality.
AI.conclusion: Generalized altitudes are controlled by standard height, making classical height-thickness conditions sufficient to bound this broader family; the framework is well-suited for applications in triangulation criteria for Riemannian manifolds.

title: FirstResearch: Auditable Question Formation for LLM Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: LLM systems for scientific discovery increasingly assist with ideation, literature synthesis, experiment planning, and report generation, but the first research question they propose can remain difficult to audit: it may sound plausible without exposing the mechanism, falsifier, or assumption that a scientist should inspect. We introduce FirstResearch, a first-principles research-question formation framework for scientific LLM agents whose core artifact is a structured Research Question Certificate. The certificate records primitive definitions, assumptions, a mechanism model, a tension or contradiction, a falsifiable hypothesis, a minimal decisive test, and a failure update rule, making the proposed question inspectable before downstream execution. On ten LLM-agent research topics, FirstResearch outperforms controlled prompt-level baselines inspired by AI co-scientist, Agent Laboratory, and AI Scientist-v2 under a primary DeepSeek-blind-judge protocol. A Gemini-2.5-Flash independent-judge rescore of the same 40 baseline packages preserves the system-level ranking, with FirstResearch scoring 4.86/5 versus 4.38/5 for the strongest baseline and Pearson agreement of 0.865 on average score. A one-repeat ablation checkpoint further suggests that the certificate-centered core is the strongest component: certificate-only scoring reaches 4.90/5 under DeepSeek and 4.88/5 under Gemini, while removing certificates drops below 1/5 under both judges. These results are preliminary and use LLM judges rather than human domain experts, but they support a narrow scientific-discovery claim: explicit derivation constraints are a promising mechanism for making LLM-generated scientific questions more auditable. Code, prompts, saved outputs, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/louiswang524/FirstResearch.

AI.tldr: Introduces FirstResearch, a first-principles framework for auditable LLM-generated research questions via a Research Question Certificate (primitive definitions, assumptions, mechanism model, tension, falsifiable hypothesis, minimal test, failure update). Evaluated on ten topics; outperforms baselines under DeepSeek and Gemini rescoring; certificate-centric core strong; removing certificates cripples performance; results are preliminary and judge-based (not domain experts). Code available.
AI.motivation: Address the auditability gap in LLM-assisted scientific ideation by making the derivation of research questions explicit and inspectable, ensuring mechanisms, assumptions, and falsifiability are exposed before execution.
AI.method: Propose FirstResearch framework and a structured Research Question Certificate comprising primitive definitions, assumptions, a mechanism model, a tension/contradiction, a falsifiable hypothesis, a minimal decisive test, and a failure update rule. Evaluate on ten LLM-agent research topics against prompt-based baselines inspired by AI co-scientist, Agent Laboratory, and AI Scientist-v2 using DeepSeek blind-judge protocol; independent Gemini-2.5-Flash rescoring; perform a one-repeat ablation showing certificates are essential.
AI.result: FirstResearch achieves higher scores than baselines (4.86/5 vs 4.38/5) with Pearson agreement ~0.865. Certificate-only scoring is near or equal to full framework (4.90/5 and 4.88/5). Removing certificates drops scores below 1/5. Code, prompts, outputs, and scripts available at GitHub. Results are preliminary, judged by LLMs rather than domain experts.
AI.conclusion: Explicit derivation constraints via the Research Question Certificate improve auditable quality of LLM-generated scientific questions. The certificate-centered core appears to drive performance. Further validation with domain experts and broader tasks is warranted to establish generalizability and real-world utility.

title: GEM-Occ: From Visual Geometry Evidence to Embodied Semantic Occupancy Memory
summary: Semantic occupancy provides a structured spatial memory for embodied indoor agents by jointly representing occupied regions, observed free space, unknown areas, and object semantics. However, existing indoor occupancy benchmarks and methods mainly focus on single-view prediction or room-level online perception, leaving long-horizon semantic mapping across connected indoor spaces underexplored. We introduce HIOcc, a hierarchical indoor occupancy benchmark that unifies ScanNet, ScanNet++, and Matterport3D under a common sparse semantic occupancy format while preserving their native observation geometries, including perspective RGB-D frames and pano-centric observation groups. HIOcc supports three complementary evaluation regimes: local semantic occupancy prediction, room-level online occupancy mapping, and building-level mapping across connected panoramic environments. We further propose GEM-Occ, a Gaussian Evidence Memory framework for semantic occupancy mapping. Rather than using pointmaps as persistent map states, GEM-Occ treats local visual geometry predictions as transient evidence, converts them into semantic Gaussian occupancy evidence and free-space ray evidence, and fuses them into a persistent hierarchical memory through visibility- and uncertainty-aware causal updates. The memory is organized into local caches, room-level submaps, and a building-level graph, and can be queried at any time through Gaussian-to-occupancy splatting. Experiments on HIOcc show that GEM-Occ improves local occupancy prediction, online map stability, free-space reasoning, revisit consistency, and building-level scalability over prior indoor occupancy and Gaussian-based mapping baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes HIOcc benchmark for hierarchical semantic occupancy mapping and GEM-Occ Gaussian Evidence Memory for long-horizon indoor mapping; shows performance gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of single-view/room-level benchmarks to enable cross-space, long-horizon semantic occupancy mapping with uncertainty-aware memory.
AI.method: Unify ScanNet, ScanNet++, and Matterport3D into a common sparse semantic occupancy format while preserving observation geometries (perspective RGB-D and pano groups). Define three evaluation regimes: local semantic occupancy prediction, room-level online occupancy mapping, and building-level mapping across panoramic spaces. Propose GEM-Occ, a Gaussian Evidence Memory that treats local predictions as transient evidence, converts them into semantic Gaussian occupancy and free-space evidence, and fuses them into a persistent hierarchical memory (local caches, room-level submaps, building-level graph) with visibility- and uncertainty-aware causal updates and Gaussian-to-occupancy splatting for queries.
AI.result: Experiments on HIOcc show GEM-Occ improves local occupancy prediction, online map stability, free-space reasoning, revisit consistency, and building-level scalability over prior indoor occupancy and Gaussian-based mapping baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical memory with probabilistic evidence fusion enables robust long-horizon semantic occupancy mapping across connected indoor environments, with better local predictions, map stability, and scalability than prior baselines.

title: Geometry-Aware Infrastructure-Anchored Denoiser for UWB Sensing and Work-Zone Reconstruction
summary: Accurate work-zone geometry perception is critical for intelligent transportation systems, and ultra-wideband sensing offers a low-cost approach for infrastructure-aided reconstruction. However, outdoor UWB ranging is often degraded by non-line-of-sight propagation, burst noise, and long-tail errors, which can distort downstream spatial reconstruction. We present GAIA, a geometry-aware, infrastructure-anchored learning framework that couples temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection. GAIA preserves range denoising as the supervised task while orienting the learned distances toward boundary-consistent reconstruction. We evaluate GAIA on a real-world outdoor UWB dataset with synchronized UWB, GNSS, and IMU measurements, and further test robustness using a real-data-calibrated stress-test simulator. GAIA achieves the lowest overall range MSE and highest polygon IoU among evaluated filtering-based and learning-based baselines, reducing MSE by 18.4% and improving polygon IoU by 15.5% over PoseMLP. These results show that geometry-aware range denoising provides an effective path toward spatially coherent work-zone reconstruction.

AI.tldr: GAIA is a geometry-aware, infrastructure-anchored learning framework for outdoor UWB-based work-zone geometry reconstruction, combining temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection to denoise range while enforcing boundary-consistent reconstruction; it achieves state-of-the-art performance on real outdoor data (lower MSE, higher IoU) against baselines including PoseMLP.
AI.motivation: Outdoor UWB ranging suffers from non-line-of-sight, burst noise, and long-tail errors, which distort spatial reconstruction; a method that denoises range while aligning estimates with boundary geometry is needed for accurate work-zone geometry.
AI.method: GAIA couples temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection. Range denoising remains the supervised task, while the learned distances are oriented toward boundary-consistent reconstruction through geometry-aware objectives. Evaluation uses real UWB data with synchronized GNSS and IMU, plus a stress-test simulator.
AI.result: GAIA achieves the lowest overall range MSE and highest polygon IoU among evaluated filtering-based and learning-based baselines, reducing MSE by 18.4% and improving polygon IoU by 15.5% over PoseMLP.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware range denoising facilitates spatially coherent work-zone reconstruction. GAIA demonstrates improved reconstruction quality and robustness in outdoor UWB settings, suggesting a promising direction that integrates denoising with geometry-driven reconstruction.

title: Binocular Gaze Estimation with Single Camera and Single Light Source
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2019 International Conference on Video, Signal and Image Processing (VSIP 2019), Wuhan, China, October 29-31, 2019; published in VSIP '19: Proceedings of the 2019 International Conference on Video, Signal and Image Processing, pp. 10-14, ACM, 2020; 4 figures, 1 table; ACM Proceedings ISBN: 978-1-4503-7148-3
summary: According to commonly consented theories, the minimum hardware requirement for gaze tracker is one camera and two light sources to realize gaze estimation with free head movements. However, in some scenarios such as eye tracking on mobile devices, it is preferable to use less components, especially light sources. We propose a gaze estimation method with one camera and one light source. A "virtual light source" is introduced, which is geometrically placed symmetrically to the real light source with respect to the camera, and generates a "virtual glint" in the acquired image. We estimate the "virtual glint" by exploiting the relationship between the distance between two pupils and two glints in the captured image, and estimate the gaze with polynomial regression assuming two light sources are available. A new normalization factor for regression method is verified, which turns out to be practical for one-glint system. The performance is proved to be acceptable, while degradation is noticed compared to system with two actual light sources.

AI.tldr: Gaze estimation with one camera and one light source using a virtual light source to simulate a second glint; introduces a normalization factor for regression in one-glint systems; achieves acceptable performance but degrades relative to two-light setups.
AI.motivation: Reduce hardware complexity for gaze tracking, especially on mobile devices, by using a single light source while maintaining gaze estimation capabilities.
AI.method: Introduce a virtual light source symmetric to the real light w.r.t. the camera to produce a virtual glint. Estimate the virtual glint from the pupil-glint geometry and apply polynomial regression under the assumption of two light sources. Propose a normalization factor to improve regression performance in one-glint scenarios.
AI.result: Performance deemed acceptable with observable degradation compared to a system using two actual light sources.
AI.conclusion: A practical one-light gaze estimation approach using a virtual glint is feasible but trades off accuracy for hardware simplification; normalization enhances regression robustness in this setting.

title: Deciding monotonicity of simple drawings of the complete graph
summary: A drawing of a graph is {\em $x$-monotone} if every vertical line intersects each edge of the graph at most once. We present an $O(n^5)$ time algorithm for deciding whether a simple drawing of the complete graph $K_n$ is weakly isomorphic to an $x$-monotone drawing. We note that this algorithm can also decide whether a drawing of $K_n$ is strongly isomorphic to an $x$-monotone drawing.

AI.tldr: Polynomial-time algorithm to decide weak/strong isomorphism to x-monotone drawings for K_n (O(n^5)).
AI.motivation: To recognize whether a given simple drawing of the complete graph K_n can be represented as an x-monotone drawing, up to weak or strong isomorphism.
AI.method: An O(n^5) time algorithm that tests (weak/strong) isomorphism to an x-monotone drawing for simple drawings of K_n.
AI.result: The algorithm runs in O(n^5) time and correctly decides weak (and, as noted, strong) isomorphism to an x-monotone drawing.
AI.conclusion: Provides a polynomial-time recognizer for x-monotone drawings of the complete graph, applicable to both weak and strong isomorphism.

title: Memory in the Loop: In-Process Retrieval as ExtendedWorking Memory for Language Agents
summary: Language agents run a loop - observe, reason, act - but the memory they reason over sits outside it: a store queried at most once per turn. We study the regime where memory moves inside the loop, read and written on every step. The obstacle has always been latency: networked stores answer in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and in-loop retrieval can inflate end-to-end latency by up to 83x when retrieval is expensive. Prior work manages that cost rather than questioning it: serving-layer scheduling hides it, "memory-first" designs ration retrieval to once per turn. We argue latency is a property of where the store lives, not the in-loop pattern: an in-process store answers in ~100us, three orders of magnitude below the network regime, and at that speed the per-step tax collapses. By the extended-mind thesis's parity principle, a store fast enough to be constantly and directly available becomes extended working memory, not a tool the agent merely consults. The premise is causal: holding a fixed per-turn memory-latency budget and varying only the store's answer speed, redundant actions rise monotonically with latency - 0.0 of 12 at in-process speed, 7.2 of 12 at a 110ms cloud round trip (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-mini; exact permutation p=0.0079). We demonstrate the regime end-to-end: across four GPT-5-class models under a bounded window, recall improves from 0/5 to 3.6-4.8/5 with in-loop memory, store ops at p50 80-165us - though an instructed restate-every-reply baseline also solves it perfectly, at a token cost that grows with the working set. The store never lost a fact in any run (244 of 244 writes kept); every miss traces to the agent's read policy, not the store. Our measurements also relocate the bottleneck: the dominant per-step cost is embedding (~200-400ms over the network); pairing the in-process store with a small local embedder returns the complete operation to a measured ~40us.

AI.tldr: In-loop, in-process memory dramatically reduces latency and enables extended working memory in language agents, yielding substantial recall gains and lower per-step cost when combined with a local embedder.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that networked or off-path stores are necessary for memory in agents, and to quantify how store latency and location affect per-step recall and overall latency.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation across four GPT-5-class models with an in-process memory store (read/write ~100 µs) embedded in the reasoning loop; compare against networked stores; measure per-step latency, recall (0/5 to 3.6–4.8/5), and the effect of a local embedder; analyze read policies and bottlenecks.
AI.result: End-to-end recall improves from near zero to near-perfect (3.6–4.8/5) with in-loop memory; per-step store latency ~80–165 µs; instruction-based restate-every-reply baseline solves but at higher token costs; no writes were lost; embedding later becomes the dominant cost (200–400 ms network) unless mitigated by local embedder (~40 µs total).
AI.conclusion: Store locality determines latency regime; a fast in-process store effectively becomes extended working memory; the optimization shifts from memory retrieval strategies to memory locality and embedding throughput; system design should favor in-process memory and lightweight local encoding to maximize recall with minimal latency.

title: Dynamic Evaluation of Classical and Control-Aware Optimal Trajectory Planning in Robot Manipulators
comment: Accepted at MERCon 2026. To be presented at MERCon 2026. 7 pages, 7 figures
summary: Trajectory planning strongly influences tracking accuracy, actuator demand, and overall execution behavior in robotic manipulators. Classical planners such as cubic, quintic, and trapezoidal profiles are widely used for their simplicity and smoothness, yet they remain purely kinematic and ignore system dynamics and control effort during trajectory generation. As a result, nominally smooth trajectories can lead to inefficient nonlinear execution and increased corrective control action. This paper presents a control-aware optimal trajectory planning framework that explicitly incorporates manipulator dynamics and actuator effort within a finite-horizon formulation. A midpoint linearization strategy is introduced to improve approximation accuracy for large point-to-point motions. In contrast to prior comparisons, the proposed approach enables fair, isolated evaluation of trajectory generation effects under identical closed-loop nonlinear execution conditions. To this end, a unified evaluation framework is developed in which all planners are executed under identical nonlinear dynamics, controller structure, and actuator constraints. Simulations on a nonlinear simplified UR5 manipulator show that the proposed approach consistently reduces tracking error, corrective torque, and closed-loop execution cost compared to classical methods, achieving substantial reductions in actuator effort and execution cost across all evaluated scenarios, demonstrating that kinematic smoothness alone does not ensure dynamically efficient execution.

AI.tldr: A dynamics-aware, finite-horizon trajectory planner that includes actuator effort and manipulator dynamics, using midpoint linearization and a unified, fair evaluation; achieves lower tracking error and actuator cost versus classical kinematic profiles on a nonlinear UR5 model.
AI.motivation: Kinematic trajectory planners ignore system dynamics and control effort, leading to inefficient execution and larger corrective action; a fair evaluation framework is needed to compare planners under identical nonlinear dynamics and constraints.
AI.method: Formulate a finite-horizon optimal control problem that embeds full manipulator dynamics and actuator constraints; introduce a midpoint linearization to improve approximation for large motions; establish a unified evaluation framework to compare planners under identical nonlinear dynamics and controller structure.
AI.result: Simulation with a nonlinear UR5-like manipulator shows the proposed method reduces tracking error, corrective torque, and overall execution cost, with substantial reductions in actuator effort across scenarios compared with classical methods.
AI.conclusion: Dynamics-aware trajectory planning yields dynamically efficient trajectories that outpace purely kinematic smoothness; fair, unified evaluation is crucial to isolate planning effects.

title: The Granularity Paradox: How Temporal Disaggregation Inflates In-Sample Fit and Compounds Out-of-Sample Error
summary: This paper explores the "Granularity Paradox" in time-series forecasting, wherein finer temporal disaggregation (e.g., Monthly to Weekly/Daily) improves in-sample diagnostics and dataset size (N), but degrades out-of-sample accuracy due to recursive error compounding over longer horizons (H). Conversely, coarse aggregation (Annual) eliminates recursive error propagation but reduces data available to estimators. We formalize this trade-off and benchmark 10 models - spanning naïve, statistical, machine learning, and deep learning architectures - across six granularities using a 13-year public procurement dataset. The empirical results reveal a non-monotonic threshold structure: recursive autoregressive and seasonal models degrade substantially under high-frequency forecasting (e.g., Holt-Winters reaches a Test R-squared of -151 and TPFE of 425.85% at the Daily grain), while the LSTM traces a U-shaped error curve, worsening from Monthly (19.66%) through Bi-Weekly (35.94%) before overcoming the error propagation penalty at Daily (TPFE of 4.35%, R-squared of 0.66). Linear Regression remains stable across all granularities (16.3-17.0% TPFE), confirming that the paradox is driven by recursive feedback topology, not model complexity. The results demonstrate that standard pointwise metrics (RMSE, MAE) systematically mask cumulative error propagation, and that evaluating forecasts without goal-dependent cumulative metrics produces misleading assessments of model adequacy. We introduce a consensus-dissensus diagnostic comparing the directional behaviour of pointwise metrics against cumulative TPFE across granularities, enabling the identification of models whose standard diagnostics mask systematic error propagation.

AI.tldr: Finer temporal disaggregation in time-series forecasting can improve in-sample diagnostics and data size but harms out-of-sample accuracy due to recursive error propagation; coarse aggregation avoids propagation but reduces data. The paper formalizes this Granularity Paradox, benchmarks 10 models across six granularities on a 13-year dataset, and shows non-monotonic thresholds in performance, revealing that standard pointwise metrics mask cumulative error. It also proposes a consensus-dissensus diagnostic to detect propagation effects.
AI.motivation: To resolve a fundamental trade-off in temporal forecasting between granularity (data per series) and error accumulation over recursive forecasts, and to show that standard metrics fail to capture cumulative propagation, potentially misleading model adequacy.
AI.method: Benchmark 10 models (naïve, statistical, ML, deep learning) over six granularities on a 13-year public procurement dataset. Evaluate with cumulative metrics (e.g., TPFE, R-squared) and standard metrics (RMSE/MAE). Analyze recursive topology effects (autoregressive/seasonal vs. non-recursive models) and introduce a consensus-dissensus diagnostic comparing directional behavior of pointwise metrics to cumulative TPFE across granularities.
AI.result: Found a non-monotonic threshold structure: recursive autoregressive/seasonal models degrade under high-frequency forecasting (Holt-Winters: Test R-squared ≈ -151; TPFE ≈ 425.85% at Daily). LSTM exhibits a U-shaped error: deteriorates Monthly→Bi-Weekly, then improves at Daily (TPFE ≈ 4.35%, R-squared ≈ 0.66). Linear Regression remains stable across granularities (TPFE ≈ 16.3–17.0%). Paradox driven by recursive feedback topology, not model complexity. Standard pointwise metrics mask cumulative error; consensus-dissensus diagnostic can flag propagation effects across granularities.
AI.conclusion: The Granularity Paradox arises from recursive feedback in forecasts; evaluate with cumulative, goal-dependent metrics rather than solely pointwise errors. The proposed consensus-dissensus diagnostic helps identify models whose standard diagnostics mask systematic error propagation, guiding granularity-aware model selection.

title: Ground3D-LMM: Fine-Grained 3D Point Grounding and Spatial Reasoning with LMM
summary: Natural-language queries about 3D environments become actionable when responses are verifiable and metric. Verifiability requires explicit grounding to the referred 3D region, while metric answers report physical measurements in real-world units (e.g., size, thickness, clearance, and distance). Existing 3D large multimodal models (LMMs) approaches remain limited: conversational systems typically respond without explicit 3D grounding, while 3D grounding models are not designed for interactive, metric-aware dialogue. In this paper, we present Ground3D-LMM, a unified model that takes a point cloud and an optional RGB image as input and supports 3D spatial conversation with (i) point-grounded responses and (ii) metric numeric outputs at both object and part granularity, including multi-object queries. To evaluate this intersection of grounding and measurement, we define the 3D Grounded Measurement task, which requires predicting the referred 3D region and the corresponding metric quantities in real-world units. We introduce a large-scale dataset built on ScanNet and ScanNet++ datasets with dense object and part annotations and roughly 2.5M question-answer pairs spanning eight tasks, along with a manually verified test set. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets and tasks show that our proposed Ground3D-LMM model provides a strong baseline for grounded, metric-aware 3D conversational understanding. Our dataset and model are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Ground3D-LMM integrates 3D grounding and metric-aware responses for 3D conversational QA by taking a point cloud (and optional RGB) to produce point-grounded answers and real-world metric outputs, defines a 3D Grounded Measurement task, and introduces a 2.5M QA dataset on ScanNet/ScanNet++; results show strong baselines; dataset and model are public.
AI.motivation: Current 3D LMMs lack explicit 3D grounding and metric-aware dialogue; existing grounding models aren't interactive or metric-aware; need verifiability and real-world units for 3D NL queries.
AI.method: A unified Ground3D-LMM that accepts point cloud (+ optional image), performs 3D spatial conversation with point-grounded responses and metric outputs at object/part granularity, supports multi-object queries; defines 3D Grounded Measurement task; builds a large-scale dataset with dense annotations and 2.5M QA pairs; provides test set; public release.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across datasets/tasks show Ground3D-LMM provides a strong baseline for grounded, metric-aware 3D conversational understanding.
AI.conclusion: Public release of dataset and model; demonstrates feasibility of joint grounding and measurement in 3D LMMs; lays groundwork for future research in metric-grounded 3D NL interactions.

title: The Minimum Dominating Set Problem on Bipartite Circle Graphs: Complexity and Approximation
summary:
A circle graph is the intersection graph of a set of chords in a circle. A dominating set of a graph $G=(V,E)$ is a subset $D\subseteq V$ such that every vertex in $V\setminus D$ is adjacent to at least one vertex of $D$. Computing a minimum dominating set is known to be NP-hard on circle graphs.
  In this paper, we study the minimum dominating set problem on bipartite circle graphs, namely, circle graphs admitting a chord representation in which the chords can be partitioned into two color classes such that no two chords of the same color intersect. We prove that the problem remains NP-hard for this restricted graph class by a reduction from Planar Monotone 3-SAT. On the positive side, we present a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm and develop a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) based on local search.

AI.tldr: Minimum dominating set on bipartite circle graphs is NP-hard, but there exist efficient approximations: a polynomial-time 2-approximation and a PTAS via local search.
AI.motivation: Understand the complexity of the minimum dominating set problem on a restricted subclass of circle graphs (bipartite circle graphs) and assess whether the restriction yields tractable algorithms or remains hard, while providing approximation guarantees.
AI.method: Hardness proof via a reduction from Planar Monotone 3-SAT. For algorithms, design a polynomial-time 2-approximation and develop a PTAS based on local search techniques.
AI.result: Proves NP-hardness for bipartite circle graphs. Provides a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm and a PTAS for the problem via local search.
AI.conclusion: The minimum dominating set problem remains NP-hard on bipartite circle graphs, but effective approximations are achievable: a guaranteed 2-approximation and a PTAS, indicating practical usefulness despite intractability.

title: Akashic: A Low-Overhead LLM Inference Service with MemAttention
summary: Recent LLM-based agent systems continuously accumulate context across multi-turn interactions, tool invocations, and cross-session workflows. Replaying the full history for every request quickly becomes impractical: long contexts increase prefill cost, may exceed context limits, and often bury task-relevant evidence in irrelevant content, degrading both serving efficiency and output quality. We propose Akashic, a low-overhead memory system built around MemAttention, which organizes context into bounded chunks and models semantic relationships across chunks, preserving cross-chunk evidence without repeatedly rewriting the full history. Akashic further applies hardware-software co-designed memory placement to co-locate likely co-retrieved chunks, reducing retrieval fragmentation and I/O overhead. Across four representative workloads and three model sizes, Akashic improves task accuracy by up to 10.2 points, throughput by up to 1.21x, and sustainable request rate by up to 1.88x over strong prior memory baselines.

AI.tldr: Akashic is a low-overhead memory system for LLM agents that uses MemAttention with bounded chunks and cross-chunk semantics, plus hardware-software co-designed memory placement, to avoid full-history replay while preserving evidence.
AI.motivation: Long, multi-turn, cross-session histories in LLM-based agents cause high cost, context-limit violations, and degraded output due to noisy/history bloat; there is a need for compact, semantically connected memory.
AI.method: Organize context into bounded chunks, model semantic relationships across chunks with MemAttention, and co-locate likely co-retrieved chunks through hardware-software memory placement to reduce retrieval fragmentation and I/O.
AI.result: Across four workloads and three model sizes, Akashic yields up to 10.2 points of accuracy gain, up to 1.21x throughput, and up to 1.88x sustainable request rate over strong prior memory baselines.
AI.conclusion: Akashic demonstrates that structured, cross-chunk memory with co-designed placement can preserve cross-chunk evidence, reduce full-history replay, and improve efficiency and quality for LLM agents.

title: Physics-Regularized Machine Learning for Proprioceptive Vehicle Localization Using Onboard Sensors
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Accurate and robust localization is essential for autonomous mobility systems in real-world environments. While fusing Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) data with satellite-based correction signals provides precise vehicle pose estimates, performance degrades substantially during outages. Recent studies indicate that Machine Learning (ML) can improve IMU-based proprioceptive localization, highlighting untapped potential for onboard sensors readily available in production vehicles. This paper introduces Physics-Regularized Machine Learning for Localization (PRML2), a hybrid framework that combines the complementary strengths of Kalman filtering and data-driven learning to estimate vehicle pose directly from onboard sensors. A key aspect of PRML2 is its physics-regularized learning, enabled by end-to-end training of an ML model through a differentiable Kalman filter. This improves consistency with vehicle motion models, thereby enhancing both localization accuracy and generalization across driving conditions. We evaluate the performance limits of ML-enhanced onboard odometry on a publicly available dataset and show that PRML2 achieves superior localization accuracy and demonstrates real-time capability. This work also introduces a novel dataset to support vehicle localization research under low-friction conditions. The proposed framework provides a robust and cost-effective solution for vehicle localization under degraded sensing conditions by integrating learning with physics-based priors.

AI.tldr: PRML2 fuses Kalman filtering with physics-regularized ML to produce onboard odometry from sensors, via a differentiable Kalman filter for end-to-end training; shows improved accuracy, real-time performance, and a new low-friction dataset.
AI.motivation: Localization for autonomous mobility systems remains vulnerable during sensor outages; leveraging physics priors with data-driven learning can enhance robustness and cost-effectiveness using onboard sensors.
AI.method: Hybrid framework: a Kalman filter provides motion/prior dynamics; a neural network estimates pose from onboard sensing; a differentiable Kalman filter enables end-to-end training with physics-regularized loss to enforce consistency with vehicle dynamics; evaluation on public datasets and a newly introduced low-friction dataset.
AI.result: PRML2 achieves superior localization accuracy compared to baselines, demonstrates real-time capability, and generalizes across driving conditions; introduced a novel dataset for low-friction vehicle localization.
AI.conclusion: Physics-regularized learning via a differentiable Kalman filter effectively combines model-based priors with data-driven learning to improve robust onboard odometry under degraded sensing conditions.

title: Exogenous Dropout: A Simple, Strong Baseline for Corruption-Robust Time Series Forecasting with Covariates
summary: Time series forecasters that use exogenous covariates are fragile in deployment: when those covariates are noised, temporally misaligned, or missing, strong exogenous-fusion and exogenous-adapted models can degrade far above the endogenous-only floor. We study whether such robustness requires specialized architectures, or whether it can be obtained through a simple training intervention. We propose exogenous dropout, a model-agnostic method that randomly zeros whole exogenous channels during training. Across electricity-price forecasting, reservoir hydrology, and meteorology, exogenous dropout substantially improves robustness under Gaussian noise, temporal misalignment, and fully missing channels, while preserving clean accuracy. Applied to a dual-correlation network, it yields the most robust model in our experiments, outperforming a deliberately strong bounded architectural foil, BoundEx, which combines a learnable gate, a fallback residual to the endogenous backbone, and per-channel exogenous FiLM modulation. Architecture-by-dropout ablations, gate-behavior diagnostics, and a representation-level bound show that explicit architectural boundedness is not necessary for this robustness: an unbounded model trained with exogenous dropout is more robust than the bounded model in every domain. We release a corruption-robustness benchmark and recommend exogenous dropout as a simple, strong baseline for future work on time series forecasting with covariates.

AI.tldr: Exogenous dropout is a simple, model-agnostic training intervention that massively improves robustness of time-series forecasters that use covariates by randomly zeroing entire exogenous channels during training, outperforming bounded architectures across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Time-series models that incorporate exogenous covariates are fragile when covariates are noisy, misaligned, or missing. A simple training technique that reduces reliance on exogenous inputs could improve deployment robustness without sacrificing clean accuracy.
AI.method: Introduce exogenous dropout: during training, randomly zero out whole exogenous channels. Evaluate on electricity-price forecasting, reservoir hydrology, and meteorology. Compare to architecture-based bounded approaches like BoundEx. Conduct ablations (architecture-by-dropout, gate diagnostics) and assess representation-level bounds.
