AI.result: Exogenous dropout substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise, temporal misalignment, and missing channels while preserving clean accuracy. In experiments, a dual-correlation network with exogenous dropout was most robust, outperforming BoundEx. An unbounded model with exogenous dropout surpassed the bounded model in all domains. A corruption-robustness benchmark is released.
AI.conclusion: Unbounded models trained with exogenous dropout achieve robustness comparable to or better than specialized bounded architectures, making exogenous dropout a strong, simple baseline for time-series forecasting with covariates.

title: Light-Omni: Reflex over Reasoning in Agentic Video Understanding with Long-Term Memory
summary: Agentic video understanding equips models with long-term memory to autonomously process and respond to continuous, long-horizon multimodal streams. However, advanced video agents often rely on ``detective-style'' iterative reasoning for action control (e.g., $\mathtt{search}$) and evidence aggregation, incurring prohibitive costs and latency. We argue that such heavy reasoning primarily compensates for the lack of global context and semantic misalignment in retrieval. This paper introduces Light-Omni, a multimodal agent framework for reflexive and lightweight video understanding. It achieves this through dual contextual states that instantly build the required context in a single forward pass. First, we maintain a global state, a finite-sized multimodal script continuously consolidated from episodic memory, serving as the global context for Light-Omni. Through hierarchical merging, it preserves recent details while summarizing past events. Second, conditioned on this global context, we generate a parametric latent state that directly drives autonomous actions and produces retrieval embeddings, with minimal latency. Benefiting from this coupled design, Light-Omni achieves semantically aligned retrieval and reflexive responses while avoiding iterative reasoning. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of Light-Omni across multiple video benchmarks. Notably, it outperforms M3-Agent with an average 2.4% accuracy gain, a 12.1$\times$ speedup, and a 2.6$\times$ improvement in GPU memory efficiency. Furthermore, it serves as a memory system to enhance both the performance and efficiency of existing MLLMs. Project page: https://clare-nie.github.io/Light-Omni.

AI.tldr: Light-Omni: a reflexive, one-pass multimodal video agent with dual context states—an episodic memory–driven global script and a conditioned latent state—enabling fast, semantically aligned retrieval and actions with improved accuracy and memory efficiency over iterative detective-style methods.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational cost and latency of long-horizon video agents by replacing iterative, detective-style reasoning with a globally informed, compact context and a predictive latent state that directly drives actions and retrieval.
AI.method: Introduce two contextual states: (1) a global state: a finite multimodal script formed from episodic memory via hierarchical merging to balance recency and past events; (2) a conditioned latent state: generated from the global context to drive autonomous actions and produce retrieval embeddings in a single forward pass, enabling reflexive behavior.
AI.result: Empirical results show Light-Omni outperforms M3-Agent by 2.4% accuracy, achieves a 12.1× speedup and 2.6× GPU memory efficiency improvement across multiple video benchmarks; also functions as a memory system to boost existing MLLMs.
AI.conclusion: A coupled global + latent-context design yields semantically aligned retrieval and reflexive responses without iterative search, offering substantial gains in speed, memory efficiency, and performance, and serving as a memory backbone for broader multimodal models.

title: ArtisanCAD: An Industrial-Level CAD Agent with Expert-Grounded Knowledge Distillation
summary: Computer-aided design (CAD) for industrial components requires long-horizon procedural modeling, robust feature dependencies, editable parametric geometry, and production-grade B-Rep execution. Existing text-to-CAD methods have made promising progress in generating CAD programs from natural-language descriptions, but they still struggle when user prompts are ambiguous, underspecified, or only describe high-level design intent. They also rarely exploit expert procedural knowledge naturally available in industrial workflows, such as CATIA operation recordings, macro logs, drawing notes, and engineering descriptions. We present \algname, a skill-guided industrial CAD agent with expert-grounded knowledge distillation. The core of \algname is CAD intermediate representation (CAD-IR), an executable procedural representation that encodes parameters, ordered operations, MCP tool bindings, dependencies, generated entities, and verification rules. CAD-IR plays two key roles: it first serves as the carrier for distilling expert CAD procedures into reusable parameterized skills; then it provides a procedural scaffold that turns vague or intermediate-level prompts into complete executable CAD operations. \algname retrieves expert-derived skills, instantiates and revises CAD-IR, executes the resulting procedure through a dedicated CATIA-MCP backend, and uses multi-view visual feedback for iterative refinement, and finally generates production-ready B-Rep models. On the Text2CAD benchmark, CAD-IR improves generation from intermediate prompts by reducing mean Chamfer Distance from $14.83$ to $9.88$, showing its ability to bridge ambiguous textual intent and executable CAD construction. On four complex automotive components, CAD-IR enables expert CATIA recordings to be distilled into reusable skills, allowing \algname to generate editable CATIA-native B-Rep models for new variant requests.

AI.tldr: A skill-guided industrial CAD agent using CAD-IR to distill expert procedures into reusable skills and convert vague prompts into executable CATIA workflows; it improves Text2CAD accuracy and yields editable CATIA-native B-Rep models for automotive variants.
AI.motivation: CAD for industrial components requires long-horizon procedural modeling, robust feature dependencies, editable parametric geometry, and production-grade B-Rep execution. Existing text-to-CAD methods struggle with ambiguous prompts and rarely leverage expert procedural knowledge from workflows like CATIA operation logs and engineering notes.
AI.method: Introduce CAD-IR, an executable procedural representation encoding parameters, ordered operations, MCP tool bindings, dependencies, generated entities, and verification rules. Use CAD-IR to distill expert CAD procedures into reusable skills; retrieve, instantiate, and revise CAD-IR; execute through a CATIA-MCP backend; employ multi-view visual feedback for iterative refinement; produce production-ready B-Rep models.
AI.result: On Text2CAD benchmark, CAD-IR reduces mean Chamfer Distance from 14.83 to 9.88. On four complex automotive components, expert CATIA recordings are distilled into reusable skills, enabling editable CATIA-native B-Rep models for new variant requests.
AI.conclusion: CAD-IR bridges vague or intermediate design intent and executable CAD construction, demonstrating effective distillation of expert procedures into reusable skills and enabling production-grade B-Rep generation in industrial workflows.

title: Efficient Transfer Learning of Robot Dynamic Models Using Morphological Similarity
comment: Accepted for publication in the 2026 12th International Conference on Control, Decision and Information Technologies (CoDIT)
summary: This study proposes a neural network-based transfer learning framework for modeling the dynamics of soft, fin-actuated underwater robots. We focus on morphologically similar robots that differ in scale and hydrodynamic properties. A model trained on data from a larger robot (source domain) is adapted to a smaller one (target domain) with limited labeled data. To enable label-efficient transfer, we develop an autoencoder-based domain adaptation approach that learns a shared latent representation aligning the dynamics of both robots. Experiments on two real underwater robots show that the proposed method enables accurate state estimation of the body-frame velocities on a target platform without labeled data, highlighting its potential for efficient cross-robot dynamics transfer among morphologically similar platforms.

AI.tldr: A transfer learning framework with autoencoder-based domain adaptation enables label-efficient cross-robot dynamics transfer for morphologically similar soft underwater robots, achieving accurate body-frame velocity estimation on a target platform with no labeled data.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate, data-efficient transfer of dynamic models between morphologically similar soft robots that differ in scale and hydrodynamics, reducing labeling effort.
AI.method: Train a neural network on a larger source robot and adapt to a smaller target robot using limited labeled data; employ an autoencoder to learn a shared latent space that aligns dynamics across robots, enabling domain adaptation.
AI.result: Experiments on two real underwater robots show accurate body-frame velocity estimation on the target without labeled data, demonstrating effective cross-robot transfer among morphologically similar platforms.
AI.conclusion: Autoencoder-based domain adaptation facilitates label-efficient cross-robot dynamics transfer for morphologically similar soft robots, supporting scalable transfer learning in underwater manipulation contexts.

title: Empirical Minimal-Realisation Compression of Deep Neural Networks via Controllability-Observability Tests
summary: Deep neural networks often contain substantial hidden-state redundancy, but most compression methods operate directly on weights, neurons, or quantised representations without explicitly characterising the dynamical role of internal states. This paper proposes a controllability-observability framework for empirical state-order reduction of deep neural networks. By viewing a trained network as a depth-indexed nonlinear dynamical system, we construct data-driven reachability, observability, and balanced Gramians from hidden-state snapshots and output Jacobians. The resulting A/B/C tests estimate layer-wise reachable, observable, and jointly reachable--observable ranks. These ranks are then used not only as diagnostic measures of hidden-state redundancy, but also as actual compressed layer widths for realised reduced networks. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 compare the proposed balanced realisation against projection-based reduction, unstructured pruning, structured pruning, low-rank SVD, dynamic INT8 quantisation, and linear baselines. On MNIST, a four-layer SiLU DNN is reduced from state order 1024 to 277, giving 72.95% state compression and 73.48% parameter compression, while maintaining 95.45% accuracy compared with 96.60% for the full model. On CIFAR-10, a larger SiLU DNN is reduced from state order 4608 to 1339, giving 70.94% state compression and 83.09% parameter compression, while preserving accuracy from 54.45% to 54.44% and reducing CUDA inference latency by approximately 3X. The results show that balanced reachable-observable ranks provide a principled empirical minimal-realisation criterion for designing compact neural architectures with little or no loss in accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes a data-driven controllability–observability framework to empirically reduce DNN state order via balanced realizations, yielding compact architectures with minimal accuracy loss and latency gains.
AI.motivation: Hidden-state redundancy in deep networks is not fully captured by weight/activation pruning; a dynamical-systems lens can quantify internal state importance and guide architecture reduction.
AI.method: Treat the trained network as a depth-indexed nonlinear dynamical system and compute data-driven reachability, observability, and balanced Gramians from hidden-state snapshots and output Jacobians. Derive A/B/C tests to estimate layer-wise reachable, observable, and jointly reachable–observable ranks. Use these ranks to determine compressed layer widths, and compare against projection-based reduction, pruning, low-rank, and quantisation baselines.
AI.result: On MNIST, reduce a 4-layer SiLU network from state order 1024 to 277 (72.95% state, 73.48% parameter compression) with 95.45% accuracy (vs 96.60% full). On CIFAR-10, reduce 4608 to 1339 (70.94% state, 83.09% parameter) while preserving accuracy 54.45%→54.44% and achieving ~3× CUDA latency reduction. Demonstrates that balanced reachable–observable ranks provide an empirical minimal-realisation criterion with little accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Balanced reachable–observable ranks offer a principled, data-driven criterion for constructing compact neural architectures with substantial compression and maintained performance.

title: Statistical Adversaries: Natural Backdoor-like Features in Vision Datasets
summary: Model-specific adversarial attacks have been extensively studied. We study a different failure mode: naturally occurring statistical signals in vision data that can behave like backdoor-like triggers without being maliciously inserted. We call these signals statistical adversaries. We analyse Imagenet to find patterns that are strongly linked to certain labels. We then use statistical controls to remove random correlations from our candidate signals. Finally, we demonstrate that these signals directly and predictably alter model predictions. These statistical adversaries are more targeted than generic corruptions and transfer across different model architectures. This suggests that some vulnerabilities are driven by dataset structure and distribution rather than a single model's idiosyncrasies. We conclude that ordinary datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even in the absence of poisoning, and suggest that dataset audits should treat spurious structure not only as a source of bias or interpretability failure, but also as a latent attack surface for vision models.

AI.tldr: Natural statistical signals in vision datasets can act like backdoor triggers, enabling targeted misclassification without data poisoning; exemplifies vulnerabilities rooted in dataset structure across architectures.
AI.motivation: Investigate non-malicious, naturally occurring signals that correlate with labels and can be exploited as latent adversarial triggers, challenging the assumption that backdoors require poisoning.
AI.method: Scan ImageNet to identify label-associated patterns; apply statistical controls to remove spurious correlations; validate whether signals can predictably steer model outputs and test cross-model transferability.
AI.result: Found patterns with strong label linkage; after controlling for confounds, these signals reliably influence predictions; transfer observed across architectures; vulnerability attributed to dataset structure rather than model idiosyncrasies.
AI.conclusion: Ordinary datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even without poisoning; dataset audits should treat spurious structure as potential latent attack surfaces with implications for robustness, bias assessment, and interpretability analyses.

title: Synthetic Consumer Insight Generation with Large Language Models
summary: Modern data-driven marketing relies on large amounts of consumer data, yet collecting such data can be costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. This research examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to generate synthetic consumer data for projective techniques, a set of methods designed to elicit consumer associations, emotions, wants, and needs. We test LLM-generated responses across multiple projective tasks, LLMs, prompting strategies, and temperature settings, and compare them with human responses from a primary research study on perceptions of city tourism destinations. Human and LLM responses were analyzed using linguistic measures, diversity and concentration metrics, topic models, and top-term analyses. The results show substantial overlap between human and LLM responses in broad topics and associations, but also important differences in style, linguistic structure, and the way diversity is generated. Recommendations are given on how to best utilize LLMs for generating synthetic consumer data, how model and prompt choices shape response quality, and on recognizing the limitations of LLM synthetic consumer data generation.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate synthetic consumer data for projective techniques with overlap to human responses in broad topics but differ in style and diversity, requiring careful prompt/model choices and awareness of limitations.
AI.motivation: To reduce data collection costs and scale in consumer research by evaluating whether synthetic LLM-generated data can substitute or augment traditional projective techniques.
AI.method: Evaluate LLM-generated responses across multiple projective tasks, various LLMs, prompting strategies, and temperature settings; compare with human responses from a primary study on city tourism perceptions; analyze using linguistic measures, diversity/concentration metrics, topic models, and top-term analyses.
AI.result: There is substantial overlap between human and LLM responses in broad topics and associations, but notable differences in linguistic style and how diversity is generated; model/prompt choices influence response quality; synthetic data can be useful but requires careful deployment and an understanding of its limitations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a viable path to generating synthetic consumer data for projective techniques, but designers must account for differences in response style and diversity generation, select prompting strategies and model settings thoughtfully, and acknowledge limitations when applying such data in practice.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Velocity Correction for Proprioceptive Vehicle Localization using Evidential Mamba
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Indoor Positioning and Indoor Navigation (IPIN 2026), Rome, Italy. 6 pages, 4 figures
summary: Reliable localization in GNSS-denied environments remains a fundamental challenge for intelligent vehicles, as inertial navigation systems accumulate unbounded drift without external correction. Existing approaches provide drift correction through dedicated infrastructure, expensive external sensors, or complex multi-sensor fusion, each introducing practical deployment barriers. We propose Evidential Velocity Correction using Mamba (EVC-Mamba), a learning-based architecture that transforms onboard vehicle sensor data into a virtual velocity sensor for IMU drift correction without additional hardware. A Mamba-based selective state space model captures the temporal dynamics of vehicle motion, while evidential deep learning with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma distribution provides principled uncertainty quantification. The resulting uncertainty-aware velocity estimate is incorporated as a virtual correction measurement into an Error-State Extended Kalman Filter to reduce position drift. Evaluation on real-world vehicle data demonstrates that inertial navigation using the proposed velocity correction achieves localization accuracy within 10% of a dedicated external velocity sensor across different outage durations. The proposed architecture supports real-time onboard deployment at 40 Hz on edge hardware, enabling reliable localization during prolonged GNSS outages.

AI.tldr: A learning-based, uncertainty-aware velocity correction (EVC-Mamba) converts onboard sensors into a virtual velocity source to correct IMU drift, enabling real-time GNSS-denied localization with EKF, achieving ~10% error vs external velocity sensor and 40 Hz onboard.
AI.motivation: GNSS-denied localization suffers from unbounded IMU drift; existing drift-correction approaches require costly infrastructure or external sensors; a lightweight onboard solution is needed.
AI.method: Mamba-based selective state-space model for vehicle dynamics; evidential deep learning with Normal-Inverse-Gamma for uncertainty quantification; virtual velocity correction integrated as measurement in an Error-State EKF; real-time 40 Hz on edge hardware.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world vehicle data; inertial navigation with velocity correction achieves localization accuracy within 10% of dedicated external velocity sensor across outage durations; real-time 40 Hz onboard.
AI.conclusion: Architecture enables reliable GNSS-outage localization without extra hardware; feasible for edge deployment; improves robustness of autonomous vehicles in GNSS-denied environments.

title: Learning to Control LLM Agent Harnesses with Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are usually improved by changing prompts, models, or hand-written workflows, while the execution harness around the model is treated as fixed infrastructure. We argue that this harness is itself a learnable control layer. We formalize harness operation as a finite-horizon Harness MDP, where a lightweight controller selects structural execution actions while the LLM executor remains frozen. The controller is trained from offline rollouts using advantage-weighted regression with only terminal task-rubric rewards. We also separate final task quality from a post-hoc Harness Maturity Score, which measures whether the harness follows reliable execution patterns rather than only whether the final answer is correct. This separation gives a finite-buffer view of harness learning: final-quality gains require high-return support in the offline buffer, while process behavior can shift whenever it aligns with advantage-weighted actions. Across six controlled domains and two public-benchmark adapters, the learned controller consistently improves verification behavior and selectively improves final task quality, with the largest gains on adapted tau-bench retail, adapted AgentBench DB-Bench, and coding with a calibrated structural verifier. Ablations against behavior cloning and Forced CHECK show that the gains are not explained by imitation or by simply adding checks. These results identify harness control as a learnable layer for frozen LLM agents, while showing that offline support limits when better process control becomes better final answers.

AI.tldr: Treats the LLM execution harness as a learnable control layer via a finite-horizon Harness MDP; offline advantage-weighted regression training yields a controller that improves verification and, selectively, final task quality; gains are bounded by offline data.
AI.motivation: To address the common but underexplored notion that the execution harness around frozen LLMs is a learnable control layer, not just fixed infrastructure.
AI.method: Model the harness as a finite-horizon Harness MDP with a lightweight controller selecting structural execution actions while the LLM executor is frozen. Train the controller from offline rollouts using advantage-weighted regression with terminal task-rubric rewards. Introduce a post-hoc Harness Maturity Score to assess reliable execution patterns, enabling a finite-buffer view of harness learning. Evaluate across six domains and two public-benchmark adapters.
AI.result: The learned controller consistently improves verification behavior and selectively improves final task quality across domains. Largest gains on adapted tau-bench retail, adapted AgentBench DB-Bench, and coding with a calibrated structural verifier. Ablations (behavior cloning, Forced CHECK) indicate gains are not due to imitation or merely adding checks.
AI.conclusion: Harness control is a viable, learnable layer for frozen LLM agents. Offline support shapes whether improvements in process control translate into gains in final answers; harness learning can yield better verification and, when data permit, better task performance.

title: Rendering-Aware Bayesian 3D Gaussian Splatting with Native Uncertainty and Adaptive Complexity Control
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 24 tables including appendix. Preprint
summary: 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) is a strong representation for real-time novel-view synthesis, but its standard training pipeline relies on point estimates and hand-tuned heuristics, providing no native uncertainty or principled complexity control. This is most limiting under sparse views or fixed acquisition budgets, where a model must identify weakly supported geometry and select informative views. We introduce a rendering-aware Bayesian 3DGS framework that tracks Gaussian geometry with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart posterior over means and covariances using renderer-derived surrogate summaries. An optional Dirichlet-process extension adds a probabilistic component-usage signal, and the training schedule makes the closed-form versus approximate inference boundary explicit. Re-rendering posterior geometry samples yields native predictive uncertainty for interval calibration and active view selection. In a fixed-budget 16-to-32 active-view task, native NIW acquisition improves PSNR by +0.453 dB and LPIPS by -0.0146 over a scoring-only 3-member standard-ensemble baseline, winning 29/39 scene-seed pairs and 10/13 scene means; it also improves over PPU-style (+0.355 dB) and NIW-proxy (+0.401 dB) acquisition. NIW native intervals reduce 95% coverage error by about 17x relative to a shared proxy (0.046 vs. 0.796) and are about 10x closer to nominal coverage than a 3-member deep ensemble (0.047 vs. 0.454) at roughly one-third the training cost. As a reconstruction compatibility check, paired NIW-vs-standard analysis over 39 scene-seed runs yields +0.030 dB PSNR with 1.6% additional training time. These results position Bayesian 3DGS as a practical probabilistic scene representation for decision-facing tasks such as active view selection.

AI.tldr: Bayesian 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) with NIW posterior and optional Dirichlet-process extension enables uncertainty-aware, rendering-driven analysis for active-view synthesis under fixed budgets; shows improved accuracy and better calibration over baseline ensembles.
AI.motivation: Standard 3DGS training relies on point estimates with heuristics, lacking native uncertainty and principled complexity control, which is problematic with sparse views or fixed acquisition budgets.
AI.method: Introduce a rendering-aware Bayesian 3DGS by tracking Gaussian geometry with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart posterior over means and covariances using renderer-derived surrogate summaries. An optional Dirichlet-process extension adds a probabilistic component-usage signal. The training schedule clarifies closed-form vs. approximate inference. Re-rendering posterior geometry samples yields predictive uncertainty for interval calibration and active view selection.
AI.result: In a fixed-budget 16-to-32 active-view task, NIW acquisition improves PSNR by +0.453 dB and LPIPS by -0.0146 over a scoring-only 3-member baseline, winning 29/39 scene-seed pairs and 10/13 scene means; it also outperforms PPU-style (+0.355 dB) and NIW-proxy (+0.401 dB) acquisition. NIW native intervals reduce 95% coverage error by ~17x vs. a shared proxy (0.046 vs. 0.796) and are ~10x closer to nominal coverage than a 3-member deep ensemble (0.047 vs. 0.454) at ~1/3 training cost. Paired NIW-vs-standard analysis over 39 scene-seed runs yields +0.030 dB PSNR with 1.6% additional training time.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian 3DGS with NIW (and optional DP) provides a practical probabilistic scene representation for decision-facing tasks such as active view selection, delivering calibrated uncertainty and improved synthesis quality under fixed budgets.

title: Beyond Static Evaluation: Building Simulation Environments for Scalable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents, traditional static evaluation fails to capture multi-step decision-making. We introduce AgenticAI-Supervisor, an API and UI-driven RL Gym environment that decouples environment creation from scalable execution. By moving to verifiable execution outcomes, the platform generates high-fidelity traces and applies multi-dimensional reward shaping. Critically, our framework mitigates reward hacking through rigorous internal state validation and testing. This work provides a first look at our platform's core capabilities through a Customer Support Agent case study demonstrating a consistent closed-loop feedback for model optimization. Future work will focus on advanced features such as Computer Use, Tool Use, automated "stumping", and edge-case generation.

AI.tldr: AgenticAI-Supervisor presents an API/UI-driven RL Gym that decouples environment creation from scalable execution, enabling verifiable outcomes, high-fidelity traces, and multi-dimensional reward shaping to curb reward hacking; demonstrated via a customer-support agent case study with a closed-loop optimization loop; future work includes tool use, automated stumping, and edge-case generation.
AI.motivation: With LLMs evolving into autonomous agents, static evaluation fails to capture multi-step decision processes. There is a need for verifiable, reproducible evaluation frameworks that provide traceable outcomes and robust reward mechanisms to prevent reward hacking.
AI.method: Developed AgenticAI-Supervisor: an API/UI-driven RL Gym environment that decouples environment creation from scalable execution, emphasizes verifiable execution outcomes, generates high-fidelity traces, and applies multi-dimensional reward shaping. Internal state validation and testing are used to mitigate reward hacking.
AI.result: First look at core capabilities demonstrated via a Customer Support Agent case study, showing a consistent closed-loop feedback flow for model optimization.
AI.conclusion: Future work targets advanced features such as Computer Use, Tool Use, automated 'stumping', and edge-case generation, aiming to broaden capabilities and robustness of the platform.

title: IMR: Iterative Mode-World Weighted Regression for Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction
summary: Multi-agent motion prediction is essential for automated vehicles to understand the intentions of surrounding vehicles. However, previous prediction-based and anchor-based methods have limitations in mode diversity and prediction accuracy, respectively. These limitations may cause inadequate safety assessments and behavioral deviations in automated vehicles. To address this issue, a mode-world weighted regression loss is proposed to bridge the gap between these features. Specifically, this approach mitigates mode collapse while simultaneously improving world ranking and top-1 confidence. Furthermore, the proposed iterative decoder improves prediction accuracy by recurrently and segmentally generating trajectories. Experimental results show the proposed method ranks first in the Argoverse 2 multi-agent motion forecasting benchmark against other methods.

AI.tldr: Introduces a mode-world weighted regression loss and an iterative decoder to balance mode diversity and prediction accuracy in multi-agent motion forecasting, achieving state-of-the-art results on Argoverse 2.
AI.motivation: Existing methods face a trade-off between diversity (mode coverage) and accuracy (prediction precision). Mode-based approaches suffer from mode collapse; anchor-based methods may underperform in diverse futures. Bridging these aspects is crucial for safer, more reliable autonomous-vehicle predictions.
AI.method: Proposes a mode-world weighted regression loss to mitigate mode collapse while improving world ranking and top-1 confidence. Also introduces an iterative decoder that generates trajectories recurrently and in segments to boost accuracy.
AI.result: Empirical results show the method ranks first on the Argoverse 2 multi-agent motion forecasting benchmark compared with competing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively combines diversity and accuracy in predictions, delivering a superior state-of-the-art performance on a major benchmark and offering a pathway for safer, more reliable autonomous driving predictions.

title: AdaStop: Cost-Aware Early Stopping for DNN Test Selection
summary: Existing methods for testing deep neural networks (DNNs) primarily prioritize test inputs likely to reveal model faults under a fixed labeling budget. In practice, choosing that budget is difficult: too little testing misses failures, while too much incurs unnecessary labeling costs. This work studies the stopping problem in DNN testing. We formulate testing as a cost--benefit decision process in which labeling an input incurs cost $c$ and discovering a fault yields value $v$. Based on this formulation, we introduce \textit{AdaStop}, a framework that estimates the marginal fault discovery rate during testing and stops labeling when the estimated rate falls below the threshold $τ= c/v$. Experiments across multiple datasets, architectures, and selection strategies show that $65$--$84\%$ of faults can be discovered using only $9$--$31\%$ of the labeling budget.

AI.tldr: AdaStop reframes DNN testing as a cost-benefit stopping problem and stops labeling when the marginal fault-discovery rate falls below the per-item threshold τ = c/v; this yields substantial fault detection with a fraction of the labeling budget.
AI.motivation: In real-world DNN testing, allocating a fixed labeling budget is risky: too little leads to missed failures, too much wastes labeling cost. There is a need for an principled stopping rule to balance cost and benefit.
AI.method: Introduce AdaStop, a framework that estimates the marginal fault discovery rate during testing and compares it to τ = c/v. When the estimated rate falls below τ, labeling stops. The approach is evaluated across multiple datasets, architectures, and input selection strategies.
AI.result: Across diverse settings, AdaStop discovers 65%–84% of faults while using only 9%–31% of the labeling budget, indicating substantial labeling efficiency without major losses in fault discovery.
AI.conclusion: AdaStop provides an effective, budget-aware stopping rule for DNN testing, substantially reducing labeling costs while maintaining high fault-detection rates and showing generality across datasets, architectures, and strategies.

title: Multi-Teacher Contrastive Distillation for Edge-Efficient Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Computational pathology foundation models (PFMs) have advanced whole-slide image analysis. However, their size and inference cost hinder local deployment in pathology departments. We propose MuCoDi, a pretraining framework that distills frozen tile embeddings from multiple PFMs into compact edge-oriented encoders. Instead of regressing individual teacher features, MuCoDi trains lightweight MobileOne and RepViT students with a contrastive distillation objective adapted from MoCo v3, where cached Virchow2, UNI2, and H-Optimus-1 embeddings replace momentum-encoder keys. We pretrain students on 14.3M TCGA tiles from only 11.8K WSIs and evaluate frozen encoders on 23 clinically curated downstream classification tasks. RepViT-based MuCoEdge students retain near-teacher performance while reducing model size by orders of magnitude: MuCoEdge-R2.3 and MuCoEdge-R1.5 reach 71.0% external AUROC, within 0.8 percentage points of the best teacher (Virchow2, 71.8%), while MuCoEdge-R2.3 obtains the best external F1 and the second-best AUPRC (51.8% and 53.3%). MuCoEdge-R1.0 reaches 70.9% AUROC with only 6.4M parameters and 1.12 GFLOPs. On a Raspberry Pi 5, sub-million-parameter MobileOne students achieve up to 605-fold single-tile speedup over Virchow2 while retaining 66.5% to 66.9% external AUROC, demonstrating that PFM-quality pathology representations can be moved toward practical edge deployment. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/mucodi-6243.

AI.tldr: MuCoDi distills frozen tile embeddings from multiple large PFMs into compact edge-oriented encoders (MobileOne/RepViT) using a MoCo v3-inspired contrastive objective with cached PFM embeddings as keys, enabling near-teacher performance at edge-scale and substantial speedups on devices like Raspberry Pi 5.
AI.motivation: PFMs enable strong whole-slide image representations but are too large for local deployment in pathology departments. There is a need for efficient, edge-friendly models without large performance loss.
AI.method: MuCoDi pretrains lightweight students (MobileOne, RepViT) to imitate frozen tile embeddings from multiple PFMs through a contrastive distillation objective adapted from MoCo v3. Cached embeddings from Virchow2, UNI2, and H-Optimus-1 serve as keys. Training uses 14.3M TCGA tiles from 11.8K WSIs; evaluates on 23 downstream pathology tasks; emphasizes edge deployment with RepViT-based MuCoEdge variants (R2.3, R1.5, R1.0).
AI.result: Edges-based MuCoEdge students retain near-teacher performance: RepViT-based MuCoEdge-R2.3 and R1.5 achieve 71.0% external AUROC (0.8 pp below best teacher 71.8%), with best F1/AUPRC for MuCoEdge-R2.3 (51.8%/53.3%). MuCoEdge-R1.0 attains 70.9% AUROC with 6.4M params and 1.12 GFLOPs. On Raspberry Pi 5, sub-million parameter MobileOne students reach up to 605x single-tile speedups while preserving 66.5–66.9% AUROC on external tasks.
AI.conclusion: PFM-quality pathology representations can be effectively compressed for edge deployment with minimal performance loss and substantial latency reductions, enabling practical use in pathology departments. Code is available.

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to use tools, plan multi-step tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate over extended horizons. Reported benchmark gains often obscure recurring failure modes documented across otherwise unrelated evaluation efforts. This paper synthesizes 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023-2026), spanning 19 distinct benchmarks, into a cross-cutting taxonomy of agent limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first synthesis that integrates evidence across tool use, planning, long-horizon reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity into a single, unified taxonomy of LLM agent limitations. We identify six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial or underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes corresponding to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline. Across the literature, we find that failures compound nonlinearly with task length, that strong performance on individual sub-tasks does not reliably translate into end-to-end success, and that additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. At the same time, substantial progress has been demonstrated in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.

AI.tldr: A cross-cutting taxonomy of LLM agent limitations synthesized from 27 benchmarks (2023–2026), identifying six recurring failure clusters and noting nonlinear scaling with task length, poor transfer from sub-tasks to end-to-end success, and mixed impact of scaffolding; progress is evident in single-turn tool use, short-horizon tasks, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.
AI.motivation: To unify evidence across diverse evaluation efforts and illuminate persistent failure modes in LLM agents, enabling better evaluation design and targeted improvements across tool use, planning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity.
AI.method: Iterative synthesis of 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023–2026) spanning 19 benchmarks; qualitative grouping of reported error categories into six thematic clusters aligned with the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline.
AI.result: Identification of six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning/constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation due to context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety/security failures under adversarial/underspecified conditions, (6) measurement validity problems. Failures compound nonlinearly with task length; strong sub-task performance does not guarantee end-to-end success; additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. Notable progress in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: A unified taxonomy clarifies common failure modes across evaluation efforts, guiding more robust evaluation design and targeted improvements. While progress exists in constrained tasks, achieving robust end-to-end performance remains challenging and requires integrated improvements across tooling, planning, coordination, safety, and measurement practices.

title: Co-STAR: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy by an Autonomous Robot for Dementia -- A One-Week In-Home Study
comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE RO-MAN Conference 2026
summary: Cognitive therapies have been shown to enhance the quality of life and well-being of people living with dementia (PwDs). However, their use remains limited due to a shortage of trained professionals and the significant time and training required of informal caregivers. To address this gap, we developed and deployed a social robot capable of autonomously delivering cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) in the home. Nine PwDs participated in a one-week ($7$ days) study that involved daily robot-led sessions. Participants engaged positively with the system, completing nearly half of the scheduled sessions, an adherence rate higher than typically observed in caregiver-led CST. Our findings also highlight the crucial role of family members, who often supported session initiation and occasionally joined the activities, enriching the interactions. This work demonstrates the feasibility and potential of socially assistive robots to deliver in-home cognitive therapy, offering a scalable approach to extend access to dementia care.

AI.tldr: A social robot autonomously delivers cognitive stimulation therapy to people with dementia at home; nine participants over seven days; adherence higher than caregiver-led CST; family involvement enhances interactions; demonstrates feasibility and scalability of in-home robotic CST.
AI.motivation: Address limited access to cognitive therapies due to shortages of trained professionals and the time demands on informal caregivers; seeks a scalable, home-based CST delivery via robots to extend dementia care.
AI.method: One-week pilot study with nine people with dementia; daily robot-led CST sessions; robot operates autonomously; family members assist with initiating sessions and may join activities; outcomes include adherence and engagement.
AI.result: Participants engaged positively; completed about half of the planned sessions; adherence rate higher than typical caregiver-led CST; family members played a supportive and enriching role in the interactions.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility and potential of socially assistive robots for in-home cognitive therapy; offers a scalable approach to broaden access to dementia care.

title: Learnable Weighting of Intra-Attribute Distances for Categorical Data Clustering with Nominal and Ordinal Attributes
summary: The success of categorical data clustering generally much relies on the distance metric that measures the dissimilarity degree between two objects. However, most of the existing clustering methods treat the two categorical subtypes, i.e. nominal and ordinal attributes, in the same way when calculating the dissimilarity without considering the relative order information of the ordinal values. Moreover, there would exist interdependence among the nominal and ordinal attributes, which is worth exploring for indicating the dissimilarity. This paper will therefore study the intrinsic difference and connection of nominal and ordinal attribute values from a perspective akin to the graph. Accordingly, we propose a novel distance metric to measure the intra-attribute distances of nominal and ordinal attributes in a unified way, meanwhile preserving the order relationship among ordinal values. Subsequently, we propose a new clustering algorithm to make the learning of intra-attribute distance weights and partitions of data objects into a single learning paradigm rather than two separate steps, whereby circumventing a suboptimal solution. Experiments show the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in comparison with the existing counterparts.

AI.tldr: A unified graph-inspired distance for nominal and ordinal attributes is proposed, preserving ordinal order and capturing interdependencies, coupled with a single-stage clustering algorithm that jointly learns intra-attribute distances and cluster assignments, outperforming existing two-step methods.
AI.motivation: Categorical clustering often treats nominal and ordinal attributes identically and ignores potential dependencies between attribute types. Ordinal data carry order information that ordinary methods may discard, leading to suboptimal partitions. A unified metric and learning framework can improve clustering quality by respecting order and interdependencies.
AI.method: Introduce a distance metric for nominal and ordinal attributes within a unified formulation that preserves ordinal order and accounts for interdependencies via a graph-inspired view. Develop a single learning paradigm that jointly optimizes intra-attribute distances (weights) and clustering assignments in one pass, avoiding suboptimal results from sequential steps.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show improved clustering performance against existing methods on datasets with mixed nominal/ordinal attributes, validating the efficacy of the proposed metric and one-pass learning paradigm.
AI.conclusion: A unified intra-attribute distance metric and one-stage clustering algorithm can better exploit ordinal information and attribute interdependencies, reducing suboptimal solutions from multi-step pipelines and offering a principled approach for mixed-type data clustering; future work may explore scalability and broader applicability.

title: Harnessing Generative Image Models for Training-Free Primitive Shape Abstraction
summary: Representing 3D shapes as compact sets of geometric primitives is fundamental to robotics, simulation, and scene understanding. Generative image models trained at scale have recently emerged as generalist visual learners that can identify and segment object parts directly in the image domain, across arbitrary categories and without task-specific training. Adapting such models to downstream tasks typically requires fine-tuning; we ask whether their pretrained capability can instead be harnessed directly, without any training, and answer affirmatively with a training-free harness. Our pipeline renders multi-view images of a 3D object, uses a vision-language model to analyze its semantic parts, prompts a generative image model to paint a color-coded part segmentation mask, reprojects it onto the geometry, and fits a superquadric primitive to each part via parameter optimization. The approach contains no learned parameters: it is category-agnostic and orientation-invariant, properties that previous learning-based models struggled with. Its accuracy ceiling rises with future generative-model improvements, which we confirm with a ground-truth segmentation study showing that part segmentation, not primitive fitting, is the current accuracy bottleneck. On HumanPrim and Toys4K, our method achieves the lowest Chamfer distance among all evaluated methods, using 5--9 primitives per object on average.

AI.tldr: A training-free, category-agnostic 3D reconstruction pipeline that uses vision-language analysis of multi-view renders to generate color-coded part masks, reprojects them onto geometry, and fits 5–9 superquadric primitives per object; achieves state-of-the-art Chamfer distance on HumanPrim and Toys4K, with part segmentation quality as the current bottleneck.
AI.motivation: To exploit pretrained vision-language and generative image models for 3D object representation without task-specific fine-tuning, delivering a portable, orientation-invariant, category-agnostic primitive-based reconstruction that scales with improvements in generative models.
AI.method: Render multi-view images of a 3D object; use a vision-language model to identify semantic parts; prompt a generative image model to produce a color-coded part segmentation mask; reproject the mask onto the object geometry; fit a set of superquadric primitives to each part via parameter optimization; this pipeline contains no learned parameters and is not task-specific.
AI.result: Outperforms prior methods on HumanPrim and Toys4K by achieving the lowest Chamfer distance among evaluated methods; averages 5–9 primitives per object; reveals that part segmentation quality, not primitive fitting, is the current accuracy bottleneck; performance should improve with better generative models.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, category-agnostic, orientation-invariant 3D reconstruction framework leveraging pretrained vision-language and generative models, with current limits due to part segmentation accuracy; future advances in generative models are expected to raise the accuracy ceiling.

title: Controlling Tool Use with Heading-Specific Activation Steering
summary: Tool-augmented large language models extend their capabilities beyond parametric knowledge through external tools, but tend to invoke them unnecessarily. We investigate whether tool-use decisions have any stable internal representation that can be extracted and manipulated, a question that is non-trivial given that tools exist entirely in context at inference time and have no direct encoding in model weights. We show that steering vectors extracted from heading-anchors positions exert bidirectional causal control over tool-invocation behavior across five open-source models and three domains, suppressing unnecessary tool use most effectively in domains where parametric reasoning suffices. However, geometric analysis reveals that this causal effectiveness does not correspond to clean linear structure: tool-invocation steps exhibit diffuse, bimodal alignment with the suppression vector rather than the consistent negative alignment a linear encoding account would predict, and different tool types recruit largely distinct internal signatures with low cross-tool feature overlap. We hypothesize these geometric properties are indicative of the non-parametric nature of tools, and distinguish tool-use steering vectors from those extracted for parametrically grounded concepts. The relationship between this geometric irregularity and the observed causal effectiveness remains an open question.

AI.tldr: Tool-use steering vectors can causally control tool invocation across models, but their internal representations are non-linear and tool-type specific, suggesting a non-parametric basis for tools.
AI.motivation: To determine whether stable, extractable internal representations exist for tool-use decisions in LLMs, despite tools existing only in context at inference and not encoded in model weights.
AI.method: Extract heading-anchor–based steering vectors and test their bidirectional causal control on tool invocation across five open-source models and three domains; analyze whether the suppression effect aligns with a linear encoding; examine geometric alignment and cross-tool overlap among different tool types.
AI.result: Steering vectors exert bidirectional causal control and suppress unnecessary tool use, especially in domains where parametric reasoning suffices; however, tool-invocation steps show diffuse, bimodal alignment rather than consistent negative alignment expected from linear encoding; different tool types recruit largely distinct internal signatures with low cross-tool overlap.
AI.conclusion: The results support a non-parametric interpretation of tool-use representations: steering vectors are effective but do not map to a simple linear structure; tool-use appears domain- and tool-type-specific, leaving open how geometric irregularity relates to causal effectiveness and how such representations arise.

title: Observation Quality Matters: Robust Multi-Fisheye Calibration via Failure-Oriented Analysis
summary: Reliable calibration of multi-fisheye camera systems remains challenging as rig size, camera arrangement diversity, and field of view increase. Existing pipelines can jointly optimize intrinsics, extrinsics, and target poses, but their success still depends heavily on empirical capture rules and the quality of the observations supplied to the solver. This paper studies this dependency through a failure-oriented analysis. We reveal that calibration failures are not sufficiently explained by detector recall loss or global image-plane distribution imbalance. Instead, the dominant failure factor lies in intrinsic initialization: observations with limited radial span couple focal scale with fisheye projection-shape parameters, producing ill-conditioned updates. Guided by this insight, we propose CO-Calib, a plug-in calibration-data construction framework that combines a robust learning-based target detector with an error-analysis-guided frame selector. CO-Calib constructs initialization-friendly anchors, co-visible multi-camera constraints, and coverage-completion frames without changing the existing calibration workflow or optimization backend. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real multi-fisheye systems demonstrate that CO-Calib improves the overall success rate from 68.1% to 99.3%, increases extrinsic accuracy, and augments real-world calibration stability. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/HKUST-Aerial-Robotics/CO-Calib.

AI.tldr: A plug-in data-construction framework (CO-Calib) significantly boosts multi-fisheye camera calibration success and stability by addressing initialization issues via a learning-based detector and error-guided frame selection, yielding near-perfect success rates in experiments.
AI.motivation: Calibration failures in multi-fisheye systems are primarily caused by initialization sensitivity rather than simple detector recall or image distribution, necessitating initialization-friendly data and frames.
AI.method: CO-Calib integrates a robust learning-based target detector with an error-analysis-guided frame selector to construct initialization-friendly anchors, co-visible multi-camera constraints, and coverage-completion frames, without changing the existing calibration workflow or optimization backend.
AI.result: The approach raises calibration success rate from 68.1% to 99.3%, improves extrinsic accuracy, and enhances real-world calibration stability across synthetic and real multi-fisheye systems.
AI.conclusion: CO-Calib is effective for robust, plug-in calibration data construction in multi-fisheye systems and will have publicly available source code.

title: Breaking Structural Isolation: Scalable Graph Clustering via Community-Aware Sampling and Structural Entropy
comment: Accepted to the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (VLDB 2026). 18 pages, 15 figures, 15 tables
summary: Unsupervised graph clustering is a fundamental technique for uncovering underlying semantic patterns in large-scale networks. Although Graph Contrastive Learning has demonstrated promising performance, existing methods often suffer from the "structural isolation" issue during mini-batch training, making it challenging to capture cohesive community structures that characterize the global topological distribution. To address these challenges, we propose SCISE, a Scalable unsupervised graph Clustering framework that preserves structural Integrity by synergizing community-aware sampling with constrained Structural Entropy. Specifically, we first introduce the Structural Entropy Community Constraint operator (SECC), which optimizes structural information within a constrained solution space to mitigate community fragmentation and enhance partition cohesion. Second, to prevent global information loss during batch training, we design a Community-Aware Sampling Expansion (CSampE) mechanism that incorporates the community context of target nodes into sampling batches, effectively breaking structural barriers and preserving topological integrity. Finally, we devise a Structural Contrastive Learning (StructCL) module that refines edge weights based on intra-batch structural similarity, guiding the encoder to learn representations in a higher-order structural space. Extensive experiments on six mainstream benchmark datasets demonstrate that SCISE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, with ablation studies and robustness analyses further validating its effectiveness and reliability for real-world large-scale graphs.

AI.tldr: SCISE: a scalable unsupervised graph clustering framework that combats structural isolation by combining SECC, CSampE, and StructCL; achieves state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks and robust ablations.
AI.motivation: Graph Contrastive Learning suffers from structural isolation in mini-batch training, hindering the capture of global community structure and topological distribution.
AI.method: SECC optimizes structural information in a constrained space; CSampE expands sampling with community context to preserve global topology; StructCL refines edge weights using intra-batch structural similarity to learn higher-order structures.
AI.result: Empirical validation on six standard benchmarks shows SCISE significantly outperforms baselines; ablations and robustness analyses support reliability for large-scale graphs.
AI.conclusion: SCISE provides a scalable, structurally faithful unsupervised graph clustering framework, improving cohesion, topological integrity, and performance on large networks.

title: Hierarchical Classification via Cascading Feature Elimination: Application to Human Phenotype Ontology-Aligned Facial Phenotyping (FaceMesh2HPO)
summary: FaceMesh2HPO is a framework for classifying facial phenotypic descriptors aligned with the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) to support clinical diagnosis. Using annotations from 124 clinicians across 10 disorders (107 HPO terms) combined with non-syndromic controls, we generated 3D facial meshes (478 landmarks) from 2D images and trained a hierarchical PointNet-based pipeline with cascading classification and feature elimination. The best models, incorporating 3D meshes, facial outline, and demographic metadata, achieved AUROCs between ~0.55 and ~0.89, with higher performance at parent nodes than leaf terms. External validation showed variable generalizability across disorders. Results demonstrate that hierarchical modeling of 3D facial geometry enables interpretable, ontology-linked phenotype classification, though performance on rare leaf terms remains limited. Improved data diversity and feature selection strategies are needed to enhance robustness and clinical utility.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical 3D facial-geometry modeling aligned to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) supports interpretable syndrome classification, achieving AUROCs up to ~0.89, but leaf-term performance and generalizability are limited; improved data diversity and feature selection are needed.
AI.motivation: Provide ontology-linked, interpretable phenotyping from facial geometry to aid clinical diagnosis, especially for syndromes with rare leaf HPO terms; leverage 3D geometry and hierarchical modeling to improve robustness and interpretability.
AI.method: Generate 3D facial meshes (478 landmarks) from 2D images for 124 clinicians across 10 disorders (107 HPO terms) plus non-syndromic controls. Train a hierarchical PointNet-based pipeline with cascading classification and feature elimination, incorporating facial outline and demographic metadata. External validation assesses generalizability.
AI.result: Best models using 3D meshes, facial outline, and metadata yield AUROCs in ~0.55–0.89, with higher performance at parent nodes than leaves. External validation shows variable generalizability across disorders. Demonstrates interpretable, ontology-linked phenotype classification via hierarchical 3D facial geometry, though leaf-term performance (rare terms) remains limited.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical modeling of 3D facial geometry enables interpretable, ontology-linked phenotype classification; to improve clinical utility, expanding data diversity and refining feature selection are needed to boost robustness and leaf-term performance.

title: From Passive Retrieval to Active Memory Navigation: Learning to Use Memory as a Structured Action Space
summary: Long-term user memory is essential for personalized conversational agents, yet many memory systems still expose memory through passive retrieval interfaces, making the model a consumer of pre-selected evidence. We introduce NapMem, a framework for learning to use long-term user memory as a structured action space rather than passively retrieved context. NapMem organizes user history into a linked multi-granularity memory pyramid, where raw conversations, typed memory records, topic tracks, and user profiles are connected through provenance relations, and exposes these levels through memory tools. The agent is trained to select memory according to the query and intermediate evidence, allowing it to inspect different memory granularities before answering. Experiments on PersonaMem-v2, LongMemEval, and LoCoMo show that a NapMem agent trained with memory-tool reinforcement learning is competitive across diverse memory-intensive tasks, while evaluations on non-memory tasks suggest that the learned policy largely preserves general reasoning and tool-use abilities. Additional analyses examine storage, inference cost, tool-use behavior, and ablations over navigation, memory granularity, and RL training. Our results suggest that long-term user memory benefits from coupling structured storage with a learned policy for using memory at the appropriate granularity.

AI.tldr: NapMem introduces a structured, multi-granularity long-term memory as an actionable toolkit, using a hierarchical memory pyramid and memory-tool RL to select relevant memory, improving memory-intensive tasks while preserving general reasoning.
AI.motivation: Most memory systems expose memory passively, limiting the agent to pre-selected evidence. There is a need to treat long-term user memory as an active, structured resource that can be queried at appropriate granularities to personalize conversations efficiently.
AI.method: NapMem builds a linked, multi-granularity memory pyramid (raw conversations, typed memory records, topic tracks, user profiles) connected by provenance relations and exposed via memory tools. An agent is trained with memory-tool reinforcement learning to select memory conditioned on the query and intermediate evidence, enabling inspection of different granularities before answering. Evaluations are conducted on PersonaMem-v2, LongMemEval, and LoCoMo, with ablations.
AI.result: The NapMem agent achieves competitive performance on memory-intensive tasks and preserves general reasoning and tool-use abilities on non-memory tasks. Analyses cover storage, inference cost, tool-use behavior, and ablations across navigation, granularity, and RL training.
AI.conclusion: Structured long-term memory storage paired with a learned policy for choosing the appropriate memory granularity improves personalized conversational agents, balancing memory use with efficient reasoning.

title: FORGE: Towards Functional Tool-Use Generalization via Keypoint Trajectory Reasoning
summary: While humans readily repurpose a book, a stone, or a shoe to drive a nail, robots trained on specific tools fail to transfer the same function to novel ones -- a gap we formalize as functional generalization. Such tools share a common functional intent that is visually recognizable, yet this perceptual similarity does not carry over to action space, where each tool demands an entirely different motor pattern. To bridge this gap, we explore intermediate representations including affordance images, human video prompts, and 2D keypoint trajectories, finding that keypoint trajectories best balance functional expressiveness and action groundability. Building on this, we propose FunctiOnal Reasoning and Grounded Execution (FORGE), a two-stage policy that decouples functional reasoning from action execution: predicting generalizable keypoint trajectories from action-free data, then grounding them into robot actions with limited demonstrations. On a seven-tool hitting-function benchmark, FORGE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on unseen tools in both simulation and the real world, achieving over 2X improvement in average success rate.

AI.tldr: FORGE introduces a two-stage policy that decouples functional reasoning from action execution to achieve functional generalization across unseen tools using generalizable keypoint trajectories, outperforming SOTA on a seven-tool benchmark with >2x average success rate in simulation and on real hardware.
AI.motivation: Robots struggle to generalize tool use to novel objects because perceptual similarity of function does not translate into similar motor patterns; a missing link exists between function and action space.
AI.method: Evaluate intermediate representations (affordance images, human video prompts, 2D keypoint trajectories) and find 2D keypoint trajectories best balance functional expressiveness and action groundability. Propose FORGE: a two-stage policy that first predicts generalizable keypoint trajectories from action-free data (functional reasoning) and then grounds them into robot actions using limited demonstrations.
AI.result: On a seven-tool hitting-function benchmark, FORGE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on unseen tools in both simulation and the real world, achieving over 2× improvement in average success rate.
AI.conclusion: Keypoint trajectories serve as a favorable intermediate representation by balancing functional expressiveness and actionable grounding. Decoupling functional reasoning from action grounding in FORGE yields robust generalization to unseen tools and demonstrates practical applicability in real-world settings.

title: Parameter-Free Encoders Remain Viable for RDB Foundation Models
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As the space of potential targets is vast across enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models based on RDB-specific encoders provide a viable solution, but ideal design remains an open question. On the one hand, it has recently been argued that certain parameter-free subgraph encoders combined with single-table foundation models can achieve near SOTA performance, with no RDB-specific pre-training required. Meanwhile, other contemporary studies advocate for parameterized encoders pre-trained to exploit observable labels for learning task-specific representations. To address this ambiguity, we analyze RDB encoder properties specifically when labels are present as inputs, proving limitations on the potential efficacy of trainable encoder parameters. As empirical validation, we demonstrate that considerably simpler parameter-free encoders are still capable of strong performance across many relevant benchmarking tasks.

AI.tldr: Questioning the necessity of trainable RDB encoders for missing-value prediction; parameter-free subgraph encoders with single-table foundation models can approach near-state-of-the-art results; labels as inputs reveal limits of trainable parameters; empirical results favor simpler encoders.
AI.motivation: Clarify design trade-offs for RDB encoders in tabular prediction tasks, addressing debates between parameter-free vs. parameterized, pre-trained encoders, especially when labels are available.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of RDB encoders with labels as inputs to reveal limitations of trainable parameters; empirical benchmarks comparing parameter-free encoders against parameterized, pre-trained encoders across relevant tasks.
AI.result: Parameter-free encoders achieve strong performance, approaching state-of-the-art; learning trainable encoder parameters yields limited gains when labels are provided as inputs.
AI.conclusion: In RDB-based prediction with labeled inputs, simpler parameter-free subgraph encoders—used with single-table foundation models—are often sufficient, suggesting less need for RDB-specific pre-training of trainable encoders.

title: Patch Knowledge Transfer for Efficient AI-Generated Image Quality Assessment
summary: With the rapid advancement of image generation technologies, perceptual quality assessment of AI-generated images has emerged as a crucial research direction in computer vision. The core challenge of this task lies in achieving efficient quality assessment for massive generated images. Current mainstream approaches exhibit two key limitations: 1) Methods employing complex feature extraction strategies, while improving performance, incur prohibitive computational costs that hinder real-time inference; 2) Simple image scaling-based solutions, despite their computational efficiency, demonstrate significantly inferior assessment accuracy. To address this critical issue, we propose Patch Knowledge Transfer (PKT), a knowledge distillation-based optimization framework that achieves synergistic optimization of visual representation capability and inference efficiency through an innovative multi-level knowledge transfer mechanism. Specifically, we design a dual-model architecture: a teacher model with local-global hybrid processing provides high-quality supervision signals, while a student model relying solely on global processing efficiently inherits the teacher's representation capacity through multi-level supervision. Extensive experiments conducted on 4 AIGIQA databases demonstrate that the PKT framework enables the student model to maintain performance comparable to the teacher while reducing computational costs by 67.7\%. Furthermore, compared to existing methods, our approach achieves a superior balance between model efficiency and assessment accuracy.

AI.tldr: Patch Knowledge Transfer (PKT) enables efficient AI-generated image quality assessment via teacher-student distillation; a local-global teacher guides a global student, achieving comparable performance with 67.7% less computation, and superior efficiency-accuracy trade-offs on AIGIQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: There is a need for real-time perceptual quality assessment of massive AI-generated images. Existing methods either rely on complex feature extraction with high computational cost or use simple scaling with substantially lower accuracy.
AI.method: PKT is a knowledge-distillation-based optimization framework with multi-level supervision. It uses a dual-model architecture: a teacher model with local-global hybrid processing to provide high-quality supervision, and a student model that relies on global processing to efficiently inherit the teacher’s representation. Training involves multi-level knowledge transfer signals.
AI.result: On four AIGIQA databases, the student maintains performance close to the teacher while reducing computational cost by 67.7%. PKT achieves a better efficiency–accuracy balance compared with existing methods.
AI.conclusion: PKT delivers an effective, efficient framework for perceptual quality assessment of AI-generated images, enabling near-teacher performance with substantial computational savings and favorable cross-database efficiency/accuracy trade-offs.

title: TurnOPD: Making On-Policy Distillation Turn-Aware for Efficient Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student policy by matching a stronger teacher on the student's own trajectories, offering a promising framework for language agent training. However, its application to long-horizon agentic tasks remains insufficiently explored. We identify two key inefficiencies in vanilla agent OPD: (1) full-horizon rollouts often waste wall-clock resources on tail turns that provide weak and noisy KL supervision, and (2) trajectory-level KL objectives concentrate most of the loss on shallow tokens, leaving deeper decision turns under-trained once initial behaviors are aligned. To address these challenges, we propose TurnOPD, a turn-level budgeting strategy for efficient on-policy distillation of long-horizon agents. TurnOPD consists of two budget controllers: adaptive rollout-depth budgeting, which uses probe-based turn statistics to determine rollout length, and progressive turn-normalized loss budgeting, which gradually shifts KL weighting from token-level to turn-balanced supervision. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search with task-specialized teacher models show that TurnOPD achieves superior validation accuracy under equal wall-clock training budgets and advances the accuracy--time frontier beyond vanilla OPD.

AI.tldr: TurnOPD introduces turn-level budgeting to make on-policy distillation for long-horizon agents more efficient, via adaptive rollout-depth budgeting and progressive loss budgeting; it improves accuracy under fixed wall-clock budgets across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search with task-specific teachers.
AI.motivation: Vanilla OPD wastes computation on uninformative tail turns and concentrates loss on shallow tokens; need fine-grained, efficient supervision that allocates learning signal to important decision turns.
AI.method: Two budget controllers: (1) adaptive rollout-depth budgeting based on probe-based turn statistics to decide rollout length; (2) progressive turn-normalized loss budgeting that transitions KL emphasis from token-level losses to turn-balanced supervision as training progresses.
AI.result: TurnOPD yields higher validation accuracy under the same wall-clock budgets and pushes the accuracy-time frontier beyond vanilla OPD across three long-horizon domains with specialized teacher models.
AI.conclusion: TurnOPD effectively addresses inefficiencies in long-horizon on-policy distillation, offering a practical, domain-agnostic framework for efficient, turn-aware supervision.

title: GraspIT: A Dataset Bridging the Sim-to-Real gap and back for Validated Grasping SE(3) Pose Generation
summary: Robust robotic grasping of novel objects requires datasets that simultaneously provide photorealistic RGB-D observations, physically validated grasp quality annotations, and a principled bridge between simulation and the real world, which existing datasets lack to provide jointly. \textbf{GraspIT} addresses this gap: tabletop scenes in NVIDIA Isaac Sim are annotated via a four-stage physical slip-test on parallel Franka Panda instances, producing trajectory-reachability checks and continuous quality scores beyond force-closure.Of ${\sim}$2.3M candidates, 83% pass as \emph{good} ($s{\geq}0.50$); the 17% that passed force-closure but failed the slip-test provide graded hard negatives. A Real$\leftrightarrow$Sim loop back-projects these labels onto 100 real-world scenes. The release provides ${\sim}$316k annotated RGBD frame sets across 1035 sim and 100 real scenes, with instance masks, 6-DoF poses, physical object properties, and scored 6-DoF grasps. All tools are open-source and Docker-containerized. The trajectory planning within Isaac Sim further allows streaming of high resolution demonstrations for tabletop manipulation policy learning and behavior cloning.

AI.tldr: GraspIT offers a photorealistic RGB-D grasp dataset with a four-stage physical slip-test and a Real→Sim bridge, enabling validated grasps and policy learning from ~316k annotated frames across 100 real and ~1k simulated scenes.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of datasets that jointly provide photorealistic RGB-D observations, physically validated grasp scores, and a principled sim-to-real bridge for robust grasping of novel objects.
AI.method: Tabletop scenes in NVIDIA Isaac Sim are annotated via a four-stage physical slip-test on parallel Franka Panda arms, producing trajectory-reachability checks and continuous grasp quality scores (beyond force-closure). From ~2.3M candidates, 83% are labeled good (s≥0.50); 17% that pass force-closure but fail slip-test become graded hard negatives. A Real↔Sim loop back-projects labels onto 100 real-world scenes. The release includes ~316k annotated RGB-D frame sets across 1035 sim scenes and 100 real scenes, with instance masks, 6-DoF poses, physical object properties, and scored 6-DoF grasps. Tools are open-source and containerized; trajectory planning enables streaming high-resolution demonstrations for policy learning and behavior cloning.
AI.result: Creation of a large, richly annotated dataset that links realistic simulation with real-world data, including per-grasp scores and continuous quality metrics, plus tools for real-time demonstrations and policy learning.
AI.conclusion: GraspIT fills a key gap by providing a robust sim-to-real grasp dataset with validated grasp quality and rich annotations, enabling improved grasp generalization and learning for tabletop manipulation; its open-source nature supports broad adoption, though domain-specific limitations and potential SLIP-test generalization to diverse grippers/objects should be explored.

title: InvWeaver: Deductive Feedback for Invariant Synthesis in Interacting-Loop Programs
summary: Loop invariant inference is a fundamental yet challenging problem in program verification. Recent LLM-aided guess-and-check techniques have shown strong performance on single-loop programs, but they often struggle with programs containing multiple interacting loops. This paper presents InvWeaver, a neuro-symbolic framework for synthesizing invariants for such programs. The key idea is to expose inter-loop dependencies and propagate proof obligations through a combination of loop-level abstraction, obligation-guided inference, and weakest-precondition-based refinement. We evaluate InvWeaver on a comprehensive benchmark suite, including a newly curated dataset derived from classic algorithms. Experimental results show that InvWeaver substantially outperforms existing invariant inference methods, solving 72 out of 82 multi-loop benchmark problems and maintaining strong performance on single-loop tasks.

AI.tldr: InvWeaver is a neuro-symbolic framework that handles multi-loop invariant inference by exposing inter-loop dependencies and using obligation-guided inference with weakest-precondition refinement, achieving 72/82 on multi-loop benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-loop invariant inference is a challenging problem where existing LLM-guided guess-and-check methods perform well on single-loop programs but struggle with interacting loops. There is a need for a framework that explicitly handles inter-loop dependencies.
