AI.method: Introduce loop-level abstraction to reveal inter-loop dependencies, propagate proof obligations via obligation-guided inference, and refine invariants using weakest-precondition-based refinement. The framework is neuro-symbolic, leveraging learning-guided search and symbolic reasoning to synthesize invariants across multiple loops.
AI.result: InvWeaver solves 72 of 82 multi-loop benchmark problems, showing substantial improvement over existing invariant inference methods, while maintaining strong performance on single-loop tasks.
AI.conclusion: InvWeaver effectively addresses multi-loop invariant synthesis by explicitly modeling inter-loop dependencies and guiding invariant synthesis with obligations and weakest preconditions, achieving strong empirical results and introducing a new dataset derived from classic algorithms.

title: Cross-Contextual Vision-Language Adaptation with LoRA for Personalized Severe Adverse Event Detection in Clinical Wound Monitoring
summary: Wound monitoring is a critical yet underserved clinical challenge, where timely identification of severe adverse events (SAEs) such as infection, tissue deterioration, and delayed healing can significantly impact patient outcomes. While vision-language models (VLMs) show strong multimodal reasoning, they often lack domain-specific grounding to integrate wound imagery with heterogeneous clinical information, and provide limited mechanisms for detecting cases that diverge from the training distribution. We present a multimodal framework for automated wound monitoring and SAE detection. Our approach leverages paired clinical notes and wound descriptions capturing visual characteristics such as appearance, surrounding skin condition, color changes, and signs of inflammation or healing progression, encoded through a dual-stream Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) framework built on a frozen BiomedCLIP backbone. We introduce a cross-contextual LoRA fusion mechanism enabling information exchange between clinical semantics and visual wound descriptors, producing context-aware multimodal representations without full model fine-tuning. To identify personalized SAEs, we propose a wound-specific out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework combining semantic matching, visual typicality, caption-text alignment, and caption-visual alignment into a unified SAE (OOD) score. To capture healing dynamics, we incorporate covariate consistency and temporal drift penalties that leverage changes in wound characteristics across visits. Experiments on a longitudinal wound dataset collected through clinical visits show promising performance on both wound healing assessment and SAE detection, highlighting the potential of semantically enriched, temporally aware vision-language systems for clinical wound monitoring and early risk identification.

AI.tldr: Multimodal wound monitoring with LoRA-tuned BiomedCLIP and OOD-aware SAE detection using cross-context fusion for temporal wound dynamics.
AI.motivation: Wound monitoring requires integrating imagery with heterogeneous clinical data and robustly handling distribution shifts in clinical deployment.
AI.method: Frozen BiomedCLIP backbone with dual-stream LoRA; cross-contextual fusion between clinical semantics and visual wound descriptors; an SAE/OOD score combining semantic, visual, and alignment signals; covariate consistency and temporal drift penalties; longitudinal wound dataset.
AI.result: Demonstrates promising performance on wound healing assessment and SAE detection, indicating effectiveness of semantically enriched, temporally aware vision-language models for clinical monitoring.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances automated wound monitoring by grounding vision with clinical language and modeling temporal dynamics for early risk identification; further validation on larger datasets and in real-world deployment is warranted.

title: Onnes: A Physics-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Simulator for Cryogenic Fault Diagnosis in Quantum Computing Infrastructure
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 10 tables. Code, data, and released run logs: https://github.com/Onnes-Research/onnes
summary: Dilution refrigerators are the enabling infrastructure of superconducting quantum computers, yet their fault diagnosis is still dominated by threshold alarms that report that something is wrong, not what. We present Onnes, a physics-grounded digital-twin simulator of a dilution refrigerator (a forward physics model with a learned real-fridge noise fingerprint) that drives a live multi-agent LLM operations layer, and use it for a controlled head-to-head between a zero-shot LLM agent panel and a supervised ML classifier on cryogenic fault diagnosis. The twin couples a real dilution-cooling floor, a noise-and-correlation fingerprint learned from real BlueFors logs, and six physics-grounded fault classes, three engineered to overlap on temperature but separate on flow and pressure. Across a 1000-turn evaluation the zero-shot panel shows no significant difference from the classifier on detection but trails on classification, its errors concentrating on the confusable faults. Curated contrastive few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency voting then raise classification accuracy from 0.685 to 0.990, matching the supervised classifier (0.985) with no parameter updates and six labeled demonstrations; an ablation attributes the gain almost entirely to the demonstrations. Run as a continuous monitor across a nine-run fault-by-seed sweep, the agent catches every developing fault within one poll interval, and a confidence gate suppresses pre-onset false alarms whose rate is backend-dependent. As a first sim-to-real check, a detector trained purely on real BlueFors telemetry posts a real-hardware false-alarm rate of 6.4% and 100% recall on physics faults injected onto real held-out windows. All numbers are drawn verbatim from released run logs.

AI.tldr: A physics-grounded digital twin (Onnes) paired with a multi-agent LLM operations layer for cryogenic fault diagnosis in dilution refrigerators. Zero-shot LLM performance matches a supervised classifier in fault detection but lags in fine-grained classification; curated few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency boost classification accuracy to ~0.99, matching supervised results without retraining. Continuous monitoring achieves timely fault detection; a sim-to-real check shows a practical false-alarm rate with perfect recall on injected physics faults.
AI.motivation: Replace threshold-only alarms with actionable, physics-informed fault diagnosis for dilution refrigerators, reducing false alarms and enabling proactive maintenance by integrating a forward physics model with learned noise fingerprints and LLM-driven decision making.
AI.method: Construct Onnes, a forward-physics digital twin of a dilution refrigerator coupled to a real-floor and a learned BlueFors noise-and-correlation fingerprint, plus six physics-grounded fault classes (three that overlap on temperature but separate on flow/pressure). Evaluate in a 1000-turn trial comparing a zero-shot LLM agent panel against a supervised ML classifier. Enhance the zero-shot results with curated contrastive few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency voting; perform ablation to attribute gains; deploy as a continuous monitor across nine fault-by-seed sweeps with a confidence gate to suppress pre-onset false alarms. Validate with a sim-to-real check: detector trained on real telemetry tested on real hardware with injected physics faults.
AI.result: Zero-shot LLM achieves fault detection comparable to the classifier but inferior on fault classification; demonstration-driven few-shot learning raises classification accuracy from 0.685 to 0.990, aligning with the supervised classifier at 0.985 without parameter updates; ablation shows demonstrations drive the gain. In continuous monitoring, all faults are caught within one poll interval; confidence gating reduces pre-onset false alarms. In a real-hardware check, a detector trained on real telemetry shows a 6.4% false-alarm rate with 100% recall on injected physics faults.
AI.conclusion: A physics-grounded digital twin integrated with multi-agent LLMs can achieve near-supervised-level fault diagnosis in dilution refrigerators, with demonstrations and self-consistency providing the primary performance gains. The approach demonstrates effective sim-to-real transfer and practical control of false alarms, supporting proactive maintenance in cryogenic systems.

title: DexTele: A Dual-Arm Dexterous Teleoperation System Based on Motion Retargeting and Adaptive Force Control
summary: In dual-arm dexterous teleoperation, cross-platform generalization of motion retargeting and interactivity of grasping are crucial. However, the heterogeneity of robotic architectures and the wide variety of grasping objects pose significant challenges to achieving precise motion retargeting and compliant grasping in dual-arm dexterous teleoperation. To address these challenges, a dual-arm dexterous teleoperation system (DexTele) is proposed based on motion retargeting and adaptive force control. First, a vision-based motion retargeting module is designed to generate preliminary robot motions from human images. In this module, a motion-graph encoder and latent optimization are proposed for precise and convenient cross-platform motion retargeting. Second, an adaptive grasping module is designed to achieve compliant grasping. This module combines a vision-language model (VLM) with model predictive control (MPC), allowing the system to predict the required grasping force for a target object and perform gradient-based online optimization. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate that the DexTele achieves precise motion retargeting and compliant grasping with generalization across multiple robot platforms.

AI.tldr: A dual-arm dexterous teleoperation system (DexTele) enabling cross-platform motion retargeting and adaptive grasping via a vision-based motion-graph encoder with latent optimization and a vision-language model fused with MPC for compliant grasping, demonstrating cross-platform generalization.
AI.motivation: The heterogeneity of robotic architectures and the wide variety of grasping objects hinder precise motion retargeting and compliant grasping in dual-arm dexterous teleoperation, necessitating cross-platform generalization and adaptive interaction.
AI.method: Motion retargeting: a vision-based module using a motion-graph encoder and latent optimization to derive precise, cross-platform robot motions from human images. Grasping: an adaptive grasping module that combines a vision-language model with model predictive control to predict target-object grasping forces and perform gradient-based online optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show precise motion retargeting and compliant grasping with generalization across multiple robot platforms.
AI.conclusion: DexTele achieves cross-platform generalization in dual-arm dexterous teleoperation by integrating motion retargeting with adaptive force control; it presents a viable path toward generalizable teleoperation, with potential future work in robustness, real-time performance, and broader object/robot platform support.

title: PatchOptic for Shared-State LLM Workflows with Projected Views and Verified Structured Updates
summary: Agentic workflows often operate over shared, structured state. Because LLM context windows are limited, each model invocation is typically shown only the state fragment needed for the current workflow step, a pattern commonly known as progressive disclosure. Modern systems construct such model-facing views using grep-like keyword search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), abstract-syntax-tree (AST) queries, and task-specific agent skills. These methods make the read side manageable, but they do not define when a locally proposed rewrite is valid after it is applied back to the full state. The missing piece is a contract between local updates and global validity. We introduce PatchOptic, an optic-inspired interface for shared-state LLM workflows. Optics are compositional bidirectional accessors that describe how views of structured data are read and updated. PatchOptic borrows this view/update intuition and realizes it through projected reads and verified structured patches. Each workflow step declares a projected read view, an authorized write region, and a patch-source region. Beyond runtime enforcement, the same declaration yields a path-level footprint that supports delegation, sub-workflow composition, and static certificates for reordering independent steps within the same phase. We evaluate this design with PatchBench, a benchmark with 46 cases across domains. The results show that projected reads reduce reported leakage and token cost while preserving accepted-output quality under the strong actor. Runtime verification blocks declared workflow-contract violations before commit, and patch-read enforcement rejects compromised patch artifacts that use hidden sources.

AI.tldr: PatchOptic presents an optic-inspired, contract-based interface for shared-state LLM workflows. It uses projected reads and verified structured patches to ensure that local updates remain globally valid, enabling delegation, sub-workflow composition, and static reordering certificates, with runtime enforcement and patch-source validation.
AI.motivation: In progressive-disclosure workflows, local edits to a partial view can drift from the full state, causing invalid results if not reconciled with the global state. There's a lack of formal contracts between local updates and global validity, hindering composability and safety.
AI.method: Introduce PatchOptic, an optic-inspired interface that defines projected reads, authorized write regions, and patch-source regions for each workflow step. Implement runtime enforcement to block contract violations and patch-read checks to reject patches from hidden sources. Provide a Path-level footprint for delegation, sub-workflow composition, and static certificates to reorder independent steps. Evaluate with PatchBench (46 cases) across domains using projected reads and patch-based updates.
AI.result: Projected reads reduce leakage and token cost while preserving output quality under strong actor. Runtime verification blocks violations before commit; patch-read enforcement rejects compromised patch artifacts that rely on hidden sources.
AI.conclusion: PatchOptic offers a compositional, verifiable framework for shared-state LLM workflows, enabling safe delegation, modular sub-workflows, and reordering with static certificates. The PatchBench results suggest meaningful improvements in leakage, cost, and security without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Taxlifier: Leveraging Disease Taxonomy for Enhanced Multi-Label Classification in Chest Radiography
summary: Accurate and efficient classification of thoracic diseases in chest X-ray (CXR) images is crucial for timely diagnosis and treatment. However, the presence of multiple pathologies with overlapping visual characteristics poses significant challenges for automated classification systems. In this study, we propose two novel hierarchical multi-label classification techniques, namely the loss-based and logit-based methods, to address these challenges by leveraging the hierarchical relationships among different thoracic pathologies. The loss-based technique integrates hierarchical information directly into the optimization process, while the logit-based method adjusts the predicted probabilities of each class based on its parent class in the disease taxonomy. We evaluate the performance of both techniques using three large-scale CXR datasets: CheXpert (224,316 CXRs), PADCHEST (160,000 CXRs), and NIH (112,120 CXRs). The experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy, AUC, and F1 scores compared to the baseline method across various pathologies. The logit-based and loss-based methods improve accuracy by 12\% and 11\%, AUC by 13\% and 10\%, and F1 scores by 24\% and 12\%, respectively compared to the baseline. These results represent a substantial improvement over the baseline method. Furthermore, we conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis to validate the robustness and reliability of the proposed techniques. The integration of domain-specific hierarchical knowledge not only enhances the classification performance but also provides a more interpretable output for clinical decision support. Our findings highlight the potential of hierarchical multi-label classification in advancing computer-aided diagnosis systems for chest radiography.

AI.tldr: Two hierarchical multi-label classification methods (loss-based and logit-based) for thoracic disease classification in chest X-rays, leveraging disease hierarchies to improve performance across three large datasets.
AI.motivation: Chest X-ray datasets contain co-occurring pathologies with hierarchical relationships; exploiting taxonomy can improve accuracy and interpretability in automated diagnosis.
AI.method: Proposes two techniques: (1) loss-based method that embeds hierarchical information into the optimization objective; (2) logit-based method that revises predicted probabilities using parent-child relationships in the disease taxonomy. Evaluated on CheXpert (224k), PADCHEST (160k), and NIH (112k) CXRs.
AI.result: Both methods outperform a baseline: logit-based gains in accuracy +12%, AUC +13%, F1 +24%; loss-based gains in accuracy +11%, AUC +10%, F1 +12% across datasets and pathologies. Robust statistical validation reported; improvements observed across pathologies.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain-specific hierarchical knowledge improves classification performance and interpretability in chest radiography, indicating strong potential for hierarchical MLC in computer-aided diagnosis of thoracic diseases.

title: StateFuse: Deterministic Conflict-Preserving Memory for Multi-Agent Systems
comment: Code and supplementary materials available at: https://github.com/nZiben/statefuse
summary:
Agent systems accumulate conflicting observations across branches, retries, and replicas, yet many practical memory layers still collapse disagreement behind overwrite rules that are difficult to inspect or correct. We present StateFuse, a conflict-aware replicated memory contract built on standard OpSet/CRDT merge. StateFuse does not introduce a new join algebra; it defines an agent-facing semantics layer with immutable history, explicit conflict objects, exact and semantic correction handles (claim_id / claim_ref), deterministic predicate contracts, and projection-time resolution that cannot rewrite replicated state.
  We evaluate StateFuse against flat multi-value, raw-log, provenance-style, and collapsed baselines under matched resolver and verification policies. On a 282-question official conflict-bearing MemoryAgentBench slice, the compared methods tie on answer accuracy, but conflict-preserving surfaces keep contradictions visible while collapsed surfaces do not. In a controlled agent loop with uniform verification, preserving ambiguity enables safer abstention and correction than early collapse. A correction-handle ablation further shows that semantic handles matter when exact prior identifiers are unavailable.
  The resulting claim is narrow: StateFuse is best supported as a safer public memory contract for contradiction surfacing, abstention, and auditable correction, not as a universal accuracy gain.

AI.tldr: StateFuse provides a conflict-aware replicated memory contract built on OpSet/CRDTs, introducing an agent-facing semantics layer with immutable history and explicit conflict and correction handles, enabling contradiction surfacing and auditable corrections without rewriting replicated state; it achieves parity with baselines on accuracy but offers safer abstention and clearer dispute visibility, thus is best as a memory contract for transparency rather than universal accuracy gain.
AI.motivation: Practical memory layers in replicated systems often obscure disagreements by overwriting; there is a need for transparent, verifiable support for contradictions and corrections to enable safer decision-making and auditing.
AI.method: Introduce StateFuse on top of standard OpSet/CRDT merge with an agent-facing semantics layer: immutable history, explicit conflict objects, correction handles (claim_id/claim_ref), deterministic predicate contracts, and projection-time resolution that cannot rewrite replicated state. Compare against flat multi-value, raw-log, provenance-style, and collapsed baselines under matched resolver and verification policies using a 282-question conflict-bearing MemoryAgentBench slice.
AI.result: StateFuse matches baseline methods on answer accuracy but preserves conflict information, making contradictions visible; in a controlled verification loop, preserving ambiguity enables safer abstention and correction; semantic correction handles matter when exact prior identifiers are unavailable.
AI.conclusion: StateFuse is best viewed as a safer public memory contract for contradiction surfacing, abstention, and auditable correction, rather than a universal accuracy improvement.

title: Intercepting an Agile Target with Net-Carrying Drones using Competitive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: This article presents a solution to intercept an agile drone by a team of agile drone carrying catching nets. We formulate the problem as a competitive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) task. To address the problem of nonstationarity and catastrophic forgetting of agents overfitting to the current opponent strategy, we train the pursuers and the evader using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) with Prioritized Fictitious Self Play (PFSP). We train the agents in a high-fidelity simulator using low-level control commands, collective thrust and body rates (CTBR), to achieve agile flights for both the pursuers and the evader. We compare the performance of the trained policies in terms of catch rate, time to catch and crash rates, against heuristic baselines and show that our solution outperforms them. Ablation studies show that PFSP lead to more robust policies that can adapt to different opponent strategies, and that a low-level control commands are crucial for learning performing strategies in the pursuit-evasion task. Finally, a qualitative analysis of the learned behaviours highlights the emergence of cooperative tactics among the pursuers.

AI.tldr: MAPPO with PFSP trained in a high-fidelity simulator to intercept agile drones using catching nets; low-level CTBR controls enable agile pursuit; PFSP yields robust policies and cooperative pursuer tactics, outperforming heuristics.
AI.motivation: Address nonstationarity and catastrophic forgetting in competitive MARL for pursuit-evasion with agile drones; obtain robust, transferable policies against varying opponent strategies.
AI.method: Train pursuers and evader with Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) augmented by Prioritized Fictitious Self Play (PFSP) in a high-fidelity simulator using low-level control commands (collective thrust and body rates). Compare against heuristic baselines and perform ablations to assess PFSP and low-level control importance. Analyze learned behaviors for cooperation.
AI.result: Pursuit policies achieve higher catch rates, faster catch times, and lower crash rates than baselines. PFSP improves robustness to opponent variability. Ablations show PFSP benefits and low-level CTBR controls are crucial for performance. Qualitative analysis reveals emergent cooperative tactics among pursuers.
AI.conclusion: PFSP with MAPPO produces robust, adaptive pursuit-evasion strategies in agile drone scenarios; low-level CTBR control is essential for learning effective behaviors; cooperative tactics emerge among pursuers, indicating coordinated multi-agent success.

title: $\mathbfλ$-VAE: Variance Equalization for Posterior Collapse
summary: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) frequently suffer from posterior collapse, a failure mode in which the approximate posterior converges to the prior, rendering the latent code uninformative. Despite extensive research, a unified account of why collapse occurs has remained an open question. We identify and formalize two logically independent but coupled causes. \emph{Gradient imbalance} occurs when the decoder's reconstruction signal vanishes faster than the $\mathbb{KL}$ regularization pressure as the posterior widens. \emph{Information gap} occurs when the stochastic sampling step discards a substantial fraction of the encoder's computed representation, attenuating decoder sensitivity and making collapse inexpensive. Both causes share the same collapse trajectory, and we show that the information gap is algebraically equivalent to mismatch between the aggregate posterior and the prior, unifying two pathologies. Subsequently, we introduce $λ$-VAE, which resolves both causes through a single modification to the reparameterization step: the sampling noise is scaled by per-dimension exponent, while the $\mathbb{KL}$ penalty retains the original posterior variance. This asymmetry shifts the stable training attractor away from the degenerate collapsed state, driving all latent dimensions toward the same equilibrium -- a mechanism we term \emph{variance equalization}. A closed-form optimal exponent per dimension follows from a net information gain objective, with a single hyperparameter controlling the reconstruction-generation tradeoff. We validate on standard benchmarks (Binary MNIST, Binary Omniglot, CIFAR-10, CelebA-64), showing consistent reductions in collapsed dimensions, information capacity gains of up to $2.8\times$ nats, and reconstruction quality improvements of up to $+0.33$ BPD.

AI.tldr: Two independent but coupled causes of posterior collapse in VAEs are identified: gradient imbalance and information gap. They are unified via a prior–posterior mismatch. A λ-VAE is proposed that scales per-dimension sampling noise to achieve variance equalization, improving latent utilization and reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Posterior collapse degrades the usefulness of latent codes in VAEs. Although many fixes exist, there is no unified account explaining why collapse occurs. Understanding the mechanisms and providing a principled remedy would advance VAE robustness and generative quality.
AI.method: Formal analysis showing two coupled causes: (i) gradient imbalance where decoder pressure outruns KL regularization as posterior widens, and (ii) information gap where sampling discards encoder information, reducing decoder sensitivity. Proposes λ-VAE: modify the reparameterization by scaling noise with a per-dimension exponent while keeping the KL term unchanged; derives a closed-form optimal exponent per dimension from a net information gain objective; single hyperparameter controls reconstruction-generation tradeoff.
AI.result: Empirical validation on Binary MNIST, Binary Omniglot, CIFAR-10, and CelebA-64 demonstrates reduced instances of collapsed latent dimensions, information capacity gains up to 2.8 nats, and reconstruction quality improvements up to +0.33 BPD.
AI.conclusion: Variance equalization via dimension-wise scaled sampling noise (λ-VAE) provides a unified explanation and practical remedy for posterior collapse. The optimal per-dimension exponents maximize information gain, yielding a stable training attractor that avoids collapse while enhancing latent capacity and reconstruction across standard benchmarks.

title: Recovering Cloud Microstructures with Cascaded Diffusion Inversion
summary: High-resolution satellite imagery is critical for observing fine-scale cloud structures that inform weather modification strategies like cloud seeding for rain-enhancement. However, the spatial resolution of current geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites is often insufficient for capturing small cloud features. Current super-resolution methodologies are suited for natural images and, therefore, struggle to generalize to satellite-captured spectral images of cloud cover. To address this, we propose a two-stage diffusion-based super-resolution framework to enhance the resolution of multi-spectral cloud microstructures by a factor of $4\times$. Specifically, we use inverse diffusion to recover the high resolution properties from low resolution. Stage 1 utilizes real-world paired data to learn robust degradation handling and inter-sensor alignment, while Stage 2 employs a self-supervised internal downgrading of high resolution data to refine structural learning and texture synthesis. Our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art transformer and diffusion-based baselines in both reconstruction accuracy and visual quality. We demonstrate that the two-stage method better captures fine cloud microstructures (e.g. convective turrets and cloud gaps) that are crucial for effective cloud seeding decisions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of the two stages: Stage 1 excels in coarse structural fidelity, while Stage 2 contributes enhanced detail and realism. These results highlight a practical path toward improving cloud microphysics analysis and as a step towards utilizing AI for climate and sustainability. Our code and models are publicly available at: https://github.com/hananshafi/superresolution-cloud-microphysics.

AI.tldr: A two-stage diffusion-based super-resolution method for 4x upscaling of multi-spectral cloud imagery, combining real paired-data degradation learning (Stage 1) with self-supervised internal downgrading (Stage 2) to improve fine cloud microstructures; outperforms state-of-the-art baselines; code released.
AI.motivation: High-resolution cloud imagery is essential for observing fine-scale cloud features relevant to weather modification. Current satellite resolutions (geostationary/polar-orbiting) are often insufficient, and existing super-resolution methods struggle to generalize to satellite spectral images of clouds.
AI.method: Stage 1 uses inverse diffusion with real-world paired data to learn robust degradation handling and inter-sensor alignment. Stage 2 uses self-supervised internal downgrading of high-resolution data to refine structural learning and texture synthesis. The framework achieves 4x SR of multi-spectral cloud microstructures.
AI.result: The approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer and diffusion-based baselines in reconstruction accuracy and visual quality, better capturing fine microstructures such as convective turrets and cloud gaps. Ablation shows Stage 1 excels at coarse structural fidelity while Stage 2 adds detail and realism.
AI.conclusion: This two-stage diffusion-based SR framework provides a practical path toward improved cloud microphysics analysis and contributes toward AI-enabled climate and sustainability research. The authors release code and models publicly.

title: Uncovering Latent Depression Severity for Binary Depression Detection via Advantage-weighting Ranking
summary: Automatic depression detection using audio-visual data faces significant challenges, particularly in disentangling overlapping feature distributions and establishing robust decision boundaries. To address this, we propose a fine-grained multimodal framework featuring a temporal encoder and a mutual transformer to facilitate deep cross-modal fusion. Our core contribution is the Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss, which optimizes the latent space distribution through two complementary mechanisms: Advantage-weighted Separation, which mines hard pairs by computing a pairwise prediction difference matrix and dynamically weighting them based on their difficulty; and Advantage-weighted Compactness, which minimizes intra-class variance to force features to cluster around their respective class centers. Extensive experiments on D-vlog and LMVD demonstrate that our model reconstructs the latent ordinal structure by prioritizing hard pairs, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss within a fine-grained multimodal framework for depression detection, achieving SOTA on D-vlog and LMVD by emphasizing hard pair discrimination and compactness.
AI.motivation: Address challenges of overlapping feature distributions and fragile decision boundaries in audio-visual depression detection; need for precise cross-modal fusion to reveal latent ordinal structure.
AI.method: Proposes a temporal encoder and mutual transformer for cross-modal fusion; introduces Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss with two components: Advantage-weighted Separation (hard-pair mining via a pairwise prediction difference matrix with dynamic difficulty weighting) and Advantage-weighted Compactness (minimize intra-class variance toward class centers).
AI.result: Empirical results on D-vlog and LMVD show better latent ordinal structure reconstruction by prioritizing hard pairs and achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: The approach improves robustness and performance of automatic depression detection by combining a deep fusion architecture with a loss that selectively emphasizes hard comparisons and tight class clustering.

title: Delay-Aware Active Triangulation with Uncertainty-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Counter-UAS
summary: Multi-agent active visual triangulation enables precise 3D localization of aerial targets by coordinating mobile observers with controllable cameras. However, existing methods assume instantaneous state feedback, ignoring cumulative latency from detection, communication, and decision propagation. We present a delay-aware, uncertainty-driven multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for target localization in Counter-UAS applications. Our contributions are: (1) a Dec-POMDP formulation with Age-of-Information (AoI) augmented observations enabling delay-aware coordination -- AoI improves triangulation validity by 10.6 percentage points; (2) a controlled comparison showing that perception-consistent rewards outperform privileged clean-state rewards (0.547 m vs.0.633 m RMSE, 27% fewer track losses) -- both policies are trained through identical observation noise but differ in what they are optimized for, producing a stability-robustness tradeoff; and (3) multi-source analytical covariance propagation incorporating pixel, pose, gimbal, and intrinsics uncertainties -- restricting to angular noise alone causes 2.8-fold RMSE degradation. Experiments with MAPPO in 4096 parallel environments achieve 0.547 +- 0.217 m RMSE with 78.1% triangulation validity, while MLP policies achieve near-zero validity (0.7%), confirming recurrent memory as essential for delay compensation.

AI.tldr: Delay-aware, uncertainty-driven multi-agent RL for 3D localization under latency; AoI-augmented Dec-POMDP with MAPPO achieves ~0.547 m RMSE and 78% triangulation validity; perception-consistent rewards outperform clean-state rewards; angular noise dominates covariance effects; recurrence memory is essential for delay compensation.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent triangulation methods assume instantaneous feedback, neglectting cumulative latency from sensing, communication, and decision propagation, which degrades localization accuracy.
AI.method: Formulate a Dec-POMDP with Age-of-Information augmented observations. Compare perception-consistent rewards vs privileged clean-state rewards under identical observation noise. Develop multi-source analytical covariance propagation (pixel, pose, gimbal, intrinsics). Evaluate with MAPPO in 4096 parallel environments and contrast with MLP policies to assess memory impact.
AI.result: AoI augmentation improves triangulation validity by 10.6 percentage points. Perception-consistent rewards yield 0.547 m RMSE vs 0.633 m (27% fewer track losses). Covariance propagation shows angular noise dominates a 2.8x RMSE degradation. MAPPO (4096 envs) achieves 0.547±0.217 m RMSE with 78.1% validity; MLP policies yield ~0.7% validity, highlighting recurrence memory as essential for delay compensation.
AI.conclusion: Delay-aware, uncertainty-driven Dec-POMDP with AoI and multi-source covariance yields robust multi-agent triangulation under latency. Perception-aligned rewards improve accuracy and stability, while recurrent memory is crucial for maintaining triangulation validity under delays.

title: Self-Review Reinforcement Learning (SRRL) with Cross-Episode Memory and Policy Distillation
summary: Reinforcement Learning is commonly used to train large language models using environmental feedback. In applied settings, the environment usually provides sparse or delayed feedback. This makes it difficult for the model to pinpoint which actions in its reasoning led to success or failure. So, learning effectively from these signals is hard because the model must determine how each failure should inform meaningful behavioral corrections in subsequent iterations. We introduce a training framework, Self-Review Reinforcement Learning, that embeds an explicit self-review step into each RL episode. When a first-pass response fails, the model generates a self-review to identify what went wrong, which conditions an improved second attempt. Unlike inference-time reflection approaches, such as Reflexion, the framework optimizes self-review with policy gradients and internalizes improvements into the base policy via selective distillation, ensuring they persist across future episodes. A cross-episode memory keeps successful self-reviews for reuse when encountering similar tasks in future episodes during training. We evaluate SRRL against a standard RLVR baseline using the GRPO optimizer across two language models, Qwen 3-4B and OLMo-3- 7B, on GSM8K benchmark. SRRL consistently outperforms the RLVR in final reward performance and achieves greater learning efficiency by successfully transforming feedback into behavioral improvement.

AI.tldr: SRRL introduces a self-review loop inside each RL episode for LLM training, with policy-gradient optimization of the self-review, selective distillation into the base policy, and cross-episode memory, yielding better final rewards and learning efficiency than RLVR on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: Sparse or delayed feedback from the environment makes it difficult to identify which reasoning actions lead to success or failure, hindering effective learning of corrective behavior.
AI.method: Embed an explicit self-review step in each RL episode. When a first-pass response fails, the model generates a self-review to diagnose errors, which conditions an improved second attempt. The self-review is optimized via policy gradients and improvements are internalized into the base policy through selective distillation. A cross-episode memory stores successful self-reviews for reuse in similar tasks during training.
AI.result: SRRL consistently outperforms a standard RLVR baseline using the GRPO optimizer across two LLMs (Qwen 3-4B and OLMo-3-7B) on GSM8K, achieving higher final rewards and faster learning (better sample efficiency).
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit self-review and selective distillation yields persistent improvements in performance and learning efficiency for LLM reinforcement learning under sparse feedback, with demonstrated gains across model sizes and the GSM8K benchmark.

title: VEIL: How Visual Encoding Hijacking Induces Bias In Vision Models
summary: Rendering time series as chart images for CNN-based classification has become increasingly common in time-series classification (TSC). However, it remains unclear whether models learn underlying temporal patterns or rely on encoding-specific visual cues introduced by chart design. We present VEIL: a systematic study examining how chart encodings influence learned representations through complementary analyses of similarity, transferability, and attribution. Attention-guided training appears to mitigate this effect when encoding sensitivity is consistently identified across diagnostics, but provides limited or negative benefit when such signals are absent. These findings position VEIL within the broader question of how machines perceive visualizations -- extending graphical perception from human readers to vision models -- and show that visualization design choices shape learned representations in ways that warrant treating chart-based TSC as a representation and measurement problem rather than a simple modeling decision.

AI.tldr: Chart encodings affect learned representations in time-series classification; attention-guided training can mitigate encoding sensitivity when detectable, but may not help otherwise.
AI.motivation: To determine whether CNNs trained on rendered time-series charts learn actual temporal patterns or exploit encoding-specific visual cues, and to quantify how chart design shapes learned representations.
AI.method: VEIL conducts complementary analyses of similarity, transferability, and attribution to study the influence of chart encodings on learned representations, and evaluates attention-guided training as a mitigation strategy when encoding sensitivity is present.
AI.result: Attention-guided training reduces encoding sensitivity and improves robustness when encoding-specific cues are identifiable across diagnostics; when such cues are absent, attention guidance offers limited or negative benefits.
AI.conclusion: Visualization design choices fundamentally shape learned representations in chart-based time-series classification; chart-based TSC should be treated as a representation and measurement problem, extending graphical perception considerations from humans to vision models.

title: PCBWorld: A Benchmark Environment for Engine-Grounded PCB Design Automation
comment: Accepted to the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI (non-archival). Main text with appendix
summary: PCB routing is the task of connecting the nets of a board with copper traces under strict design rules, yet learning-based methods still lag behind rule-based routers. We introduce PCBWorld, an open-source engine-grounded PCB routing environment built on the KiCad EDA engine. As a human engineer does, agents in PCBWorld interactively route a board through the engine's native operations, using its Design Rule Check (DRC) feedback to keep the routing within the design rules. The environment supports both RL policies and tool-using LLM agents. Alongside the environment, PCBWorld-Bench provides three dataset families in KiCad's native board format (.kicad_pcb), covering two types of controllable synthetic instances and 679 real open-source boards. It scores any completed board with eight engine-checked evaluation metrics, regardless of the routing method. In our experiments, agents in PCBWorld consistently outperformed grid-action RL policies and open-loop LLM baselines, and an RL policy trained only on synthetic boards transferred zero-shot to real boards, approaching rule-based routers. These results position the engine-grounded, interactive approach of PCBWorld as a promising foundation for advancing the routing ability of both RL and LLM agents.

AI.tldr: Open-source, KiCad-based PCB routing environment (PCBWorld) enabling interactive, rule-consistent routing with RL and tool-using LLMs; includes datasets (PCBWorld-Bench) and eight evaluation metrics; shows improved performance and zero-shot transfer from synthetic to real boards, approaching rule-based routers.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between traditional rule-based PCB routers and learning-based methods by providing an engine-grounded, interactive environment that enforces design rules via DRC and supports RL and LLM tool usage. Enable standardized evaluation with KiCad boards and real-world datasets.
AI.method: Integrates KiCad as the execution engine; agents issue native operations to route boards with feedback from Design Rule Check (DRC). Provides PCBWorld-Bench with three KiCad-format dataset families (synthetic controllable instances and 679 real boards). Evaluates with eight engine-checked metrics. Compares RL policies, grid-action baselines, and open-loop LLMs; tests transfer from synthetic to realboards.
AI.result: Agents in PCBWorld outperform grid-action RL policies and open-loop LLM baselines. An RL policy trained solely on synthetic boards transfers zero-shot to real boards, approaching the performance of rule-based routers.
AI.conclusion: Engine-grounded, interactive routing with rule feedback is a promising foundation for advancing RL and LLM-based PCB routing, supported by standardized datasets and comprehensive evaluation.

title: Imagined Rollouts are Kinematic, Not Dynamic: A Diagnosis of Long-Horizon World-Model Failure
comment: 9 Pages Workshop Paper accepted at RSS Robot World Model Workshop 2026
summary: Long-horizon failure in world models is conventionally attributed to compounding error, a generic framing that does not distinguish what kind of error compounds. We propose a kinematic-vs-dynamic reframing: world models tend to imagine kinematically rather than dynamically. We operationalize this as the imagined Kinematic-Consistency Error, a per-step diagnostic that measures how far a rollout departs from a closed-form kinematic null, paired with a perturbation protocol that tests whether iKCE responds when physical conditions cross a regime boundary. We instantiate the diagnostic on a released DreamerV3 checkpoint trained on DMC walker-walk, where imagined iKCE runs roughly two orders of magnitude above that of matched real-physics rollouts. Across a friction sweep that crosses the gait-collapse boundary, the model's iKCE stays statistically flat even as the trained policy's reward collapses through the same range, providing the kinematic-not-dynamic signature. The diagnostic distinguishes kinematic from dynamic imagination at horizons longer than the embodiment's gait period.

AI.tldr: Proposes a kinematic-vs-dynamic framing for long-horizon failures in world models and introduces iKCE, a per-step diagnostic that measures distance from a closed-form kinematic null, coupled with a regime-boundary perturbation test. On DreamerV3/DMC walker-walk, iKCE is ~100x higher than real-physics rollouts and remains flat across a friction-induced gait-collapse boundary, indicating a kinematic rather than dynamic imagination at horizons beyond the gait period.
AI.motivation: To disentangle sources of long-horizon errors in world models by distinguishing kinematic imagination (deviations from a kinematic null) from dynamic imagination, challenging the generic compounding-error framing.
AI.method: Define imagined Kinematic-Consistency Error (iKCE) as a per-step metric measuring rollout deviation from a closed-form kinematic null; pair with a perturbation protocol that probes iKCE response when physical conditions cross a regime boundary; instantiate on a released DreamerV3 checkpoint trained on DMC walker-walk; perform a friction sweep across the gait-collapse boundary and compare iKCE with real-physics rollouts.
AI.result: iKCE for the model runs about two orders of magnitude higher than matched real-physics rollouts; across the friction sweep, iKCE remains statistically flat even as the policy reward collapses, signaling a kinematic-imagination signature rather than a dynamic one.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic can distinguish kinematic from dynamic imagination at horizons longer than the gait period, supporting a kinematic-not-dynamic explanation for long-horizon failures in this setting and offering a practical tool for diagnosing world-model biases and their regime-dependent behavior.

title: Federated Physics-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Distributed Stability Control in Smart Grids
comment: Accepted at IEEE SmartGridComm 2026. This is the accepted manuscript version. The final published version will appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Transient stability control in smart grids requires rapid post-fault damping of generator frequency and rotor angle deviations to prevent cascading failures. This paper proposes FedPPO-PG, a Federated Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization framework with Physics-Grounded neighborhoods, which reformulates transient stability control as a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning problem optimized directly against closed-loop stability objectives. Each generator hosts an independent local actor augmented with the frequency deviations of its two most strongly coupled electrical neighbors, identified from the post-fault Kron-reduced susceptance matrix. A guided policy initialization phase warm-starts all actors from the classical decentralized controller, while a centralized critic guides advantage estimation under the centralized training--decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm. Evaluated on a simulation of the IEEE 39-bus benchmark system across five training and three unseen fault contingencies, FedPPO-PG achieves 100% stabilization in all 24 trials, reduces mean stability time by 72.4%, and cuts the control power by 7-14 times compared to the centralized baseline. Each actor executes independently with no central coordinator at deployment, and the per-actor inference latency satisfies the IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018 real-time reporting requirements.

AI.tldr: A federated multi-agent PPO for transient stability in grids, FedPPO-PG, uses physics-grounded neighbor info and centralized training with a shared critic. It achieves full stabilization on IEEE-39 with substantial reductions in stabilization time and control power, and scales to decentralized execution with real-time latency compliance.
AI.motivation: Transient stability control requires fast damping of frequency and rotor-angle deviations; centralized controllers can be slow and fragile to single points of failure. A distributed, communication-efficient, physics-informed RL approach could provide rapid, scalable stabilization.
AI.method: Each generator hosts a local actor augmented with the frequency deviations of its two strongest neighboring generators, identified from the post-fault Kron-reduced susceptance matrix. Training uses a CTDE framework with a centralized critic guiding advantage estimation; actors are initialized from a classical decentralized controller. The federation (FedPPO-PG) optimizes a cooperative multi-agent PPO objective with neighborhood information and no central coordinator at deployment.
AI.result: On IEEE 39-bus simulations across five training and three unseen fault contingencies, the method achieves 100% stabilization in all 24 trials, reduces mean stabilization time by 72.4%, and cuts control power by 7–14x compared to a centralized baseline. Inference latency per actor meets IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018 real-time requirements, and no centralized controller is needed during deployment.
AI.conclusion: The FedPPO-PG framework with physics-grounded neighborhoods and CTDE demonstrates effective, scalable, decentralized transient stability control with strong performance gains over centralized baselines and compatibility with real-time operation.

title: REVIVE: A Multi-Modal Framework for Vandalism Detection and Recovery in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) face increasing threats from vandalism-induced occlusion attacks (VOAs) that compromise camera-based perception. While detection frameworks can identify vandalized images, restoring camera-stream utility after physical occlusion remains underexplored. This paper presents present the Recovery and Enhancement of Vandalized Images for Vision Excellence (REVIVE) framework, a vandalism recovery pipeline integrating: (1) binary VOA detection, (2) multi-class VOA pattern identification, (3) EfficientNet-based U-Net segmentation, and (4) type-aware recovery using Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training (BLIP)-guided Stable Diffusion inpainting, direct pixel replacement, or adaptive median filtering. Stable Diffusion shows variable reconstruction performance (per-pattern SSIM 0.667-0.867, PSNR 15.4-26.7dB) across VOA patterns, while aligned direct pixel replacement achieves near-identical reconstruction under the aligned-reference condition. On 500 tracked clean/vandalized image pairs, unrecovered VOAs reduce YOLOv8l object-detection recall to 0.588, while direct pixel replacement restores recall to 0.967 and F1-score to 0.970 under that aligned-reference condition. LaMa, Telea, and Navier-Stokes baselines improve image similarity but provide more limited downstream detection recovery, and Stable Diffusion is treated as an asynchronous recovery branch subject to a quality gate rather than a blocking real-time perception step. We evaluate a reference-available quality gate that filters recovered candidates before downstream use: without it, type-aware routing degrades per-image recall to 0.304, whereas with it, recall returns to 0.608, at or above the unrecovered baseline, ensuring the forwarded stream is never worse than the unrecovered frame. REVIVE therefore, provides a structured recovery framework from VOAs in AVs.

AI.tldr: REVIVE is a framework for detecting and recovering vandalized camera frames in autonomous vehicles, combining VOA detection, pattern identification, EfficientNet-U-Net segmentation, and type-aware recovery via BLIP-guided Stable Diffusion inpainting, direct pixel replacement, or adaptive median filtering to restore downstream perception.
AI.motivation: Vandalism-induced occlusion degrades camera-based perception in AVs; current detection methods do not fully restore utility, risking perception performance and safety.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline: (1) binary VOA detection, (2) multi-class VOA pattern identification, (3) EfficientNet-based U-Net segmentation, (4) type-aware recovery using BLIP-guided Stable Diffusion inpainting, direct pixel replacement, or adaptive median filtering. Includes a reference-available quality gate to filter recovered outputs for downstream use; compares Stable Diffusion, direct replacement, and baselines like LaMa, Telea, Navier-Stokes.
AI.result: Stable Diffusion reconstruction yields per-pattern SSIM 0.667–0.867 and PSNR 15.4–26.7 dB; aligned-reference direct pixel replacement achieves near-identical reconstruction. On 500 tracked image pairs, unrecovered VOAs reduce YOLOv8l recall to 0.588; direct pixel replacement restores recall to 0.967 and F1 to 0.970 under aligned-reference. Baselines improve image similarity but offer limited downstream detection recovery; stable diffusion treated as asynchronous with a quality gate. Without the gate, per-image recall drops to 0.304; with the gate, recall increases to 0.608, at or above the unrecovered baseline.
AI.conclusion: REVIVE offers a structured end-to-end recovery framework for VOAs in AVs, enabling significant restoration of downstream detection performance and a gating mechanism to ensure recovered frames do not underperform unrecovered frames.

title: SearchEyes: Towards Frontier Multimodal Deep Search Intelligence via Search World Simulation
summary: Training multimodal search agents to perform multi-hop reasoning remains challenging due to a fundamental structural disconnect: existing pipelines construct training data, search environments, and reward signals independently, causing synthesized structural metadata to be discarded, environments to rely on irreproducible external engines, and RL rewards to remain sparse at the trajectory level. We present \textbf{SearchEyes}, which uses a typed knowledge graph as the backbone of a \emph{simulated search world} that unifies all three components. We propose \textbf{Perception-Knowledge Chains (PKC)} to sample constrained multi-hop paths over the visual-knowledge intersection of Wikidata5M, retaining hop-level entity metadata that simultaneously defines a self-contained search world and step-level reward anchors. We further propose \textbf{Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization (HaPO)}, which reuses these anchors for step-level credit assignment without a separately trained process reward model. Experiments on six multimodal knowledge-intensive benchmarks show that SearchEyes achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source multimodal search agents, with SearchEyes-27B improving over the strongest open-source baseline by 6.2 points on average.%

AI.tldr: We present SearchEyes, a unified simulated search world built on a typed knowledge graph to enable end-to-end multi-hop multimodal reasoning; via Perception-Knowledge Chains sampling constrained hops over Wikidata5M's visual-knowledge intersection and Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization for step-level credit assignment, achieving state-of-the-art open-source multimodal search performance (SearchEyes-27B +6.2 points).
AI.motivation: Structural disconnect in existing multimodal search pipelines: training data, search environments, and reward signals are constructed independently, causing loss of hop-level metadata, reliance on external engines, and sparse, trajectory-level rewards. A unified framework can preserve hop-level metadata, provide self-contained environments, and enable dense, step-level supervision.
AI.method: Use a typed knowledge graph as the backbone to create a simulated search world. Perception-Knowledge Chains (PKC) sample constrained multi-hop paths over the visual-knowledge intersection of Wikidata5M, retaining hop-level entity metadata to define a self-contained search world and step-level reward anchors. Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization (HaPO) reuses these anchors for step-level credit assignment without a separately trained process reward model.
AI.result: Experiments on six multimodal knowledge-intensive benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance among open-source multimodal search agents. The 27B variant (SearchEyes-27B) improves over the strongest open-source baseline by 6.2 points on average.
AI.conclusion: The unified SearchEyes framework addresses the structural disconnect in current pipelines by integrating data, environment, and reward signals into a single, self-contained system. This enhances multi-hop reasoning and reproducibility, with strong empirical gains; the approach may generalize to other knowledge-intensive multimodal tasks.

title: RoboTALES: Learning Reasoning-Guided Robot Policies via Task-Aligned Simulated Futures
summary: Pretrained video generative models are promising backbones for visuomotor control, but their imagined futures often drift from task intent and are not reliably action-conditional. As a result, these models can be difficult to use for planning or policy extraction. To address these limitations, we propose RoboTALES, a single-stage framework that learns task-aligned simulated futures and uses them to train robot policies. Our approach introduces two key innovations: (1) a hierarchical LLM-based planner that breaks complex tasks into a sequence of subgoals to guide the model's imagination; and (2) a VLM-based critic that evaluates these ``imagined'' futures and uses reward-based feedback to keep the model's internal representations focused on the goal. By anchoring the video generator in abstract reasoning, we produce temporally consistent rollouts and more coherent actions. We evaluate RoboTALES on diverse manipulation tasks from RoboCasa and LIBERO10, and show that our method consistently outperforms existing methods, especially in long-horizon tasks. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/hananshafi/RoboTALES.

AI.tldr: RoboTALES uses a hierarchical LLM planner and a VLM critic to generate task-aligned, temporally consistent imagined futures from pretrained video generators, enabling effective single-stage policy learning and outperforming baselines on RoboCasa and LIBERO10; code released.
AI.motivation: Pretrained video generative models for visuomotor control often drift from task intent and are not reliably action-conditional, making planning and policy extraction difficult.
AI.method: A single-stage framework featuring (1) a hierarchical LLM-based planner that decomposes tasks into subgoals to guide the model's imagination, and (2) a VLM-based critic that evaluates imagined futures and provides reward-based feedback to keep representations aligned with the goal; a video generator anchored by abstract reasoning yields temporally consistent rollouts and coherent actions; policies are trained from these imagined futures; evaluated on RoboCasa and LIBERO10.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms existing approaches, with especially strong gains on long-horizon tasks across diverse manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring imagined futures to task goals via a planner and a critic enables reliable policy learning from video-based simulators, improving temporal coherence and goal alignment; code is publicly available.

title: EquiFiLM: Charge-Conditioned Equivariant Force Fields via Feature-wise Linear Modulation
summary: Foundation machine learning force fields (MLFFs) such as MACE-MP-0 and UMA cover broad chemical space at near density functional theory (DFT) accuracy. However, they assume equilibrium ground-state physics and do not natively handle externally induced changes to the electronic state, such as charging, applied fields, or electronic excitation, which limits their use for driven processes such as photoexcitation and charge injection. We propose EquiFiLM, a lightweight extension that adds continuous external conditioning to any equivariant foundation MLFF via a per-layer Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) block, learning externally driven changes to the potential energy surface from minimal training data. The block modulates only scalar channels and preserves E(3)-equivariance exactly. We demonstrate the recipe on charged liquid water with the foundation model MACE-MatPES as the backbone, yielding E-MACE. On the four training charges, E-MACE delivers a $3.1\times$ reduction in force RMSE ($21.3$ to $6.96$ meV/$\mathring{A}$) and a $61\times$ reduction in per-atom energy RMSE ($6.1$ to $0.1$ meV/atom) over a baseline without EquiFiLM trained on the same data, at indistinguishable inference cost. Across seven held-out interpolation and extrapolation charges, force RMSE stays within $18-61$ meV/$\mathring{A}$ and energy RMSE within $0.7-5.4$ meV/atom. The model runs stable molecular dynamics across the full range tested and predicts the charge-dependent first-shell response of the reduced pair distribution function probed by ultrafast electron diffraction. Adding this conditioning axis to the foundation requires only a few thousand DFT-labeled frames, against the $\approx 10^8$ structures of a charge-aware foundation trained from scratch. The recipe is backbone- and conditioning-agnostic: it applies without architectural change to any equivariant MLFF with scalar interaction-layer channels.

AI.tldr: EquiFiLM adds lightweight external conditioning to equivariant foundation ML force fields via per-layer FiLM blocks, enabling accurate, data-efficient modeling of externally induced electronic changes (charging, fields, excitations) while preserving E(3) equivariance; demonstrated on charged water with MACE-MatPES backbone (E-MACE) with substantial RMSE reductions, stable MD, and minimal training data; architecture-agnostic plug-in for scalar channels.
AI.motivation: Foundation MLFFs currently assume equilibrium ground-state physics and struggle with externally driven electronic changes (e.g., charging, fields, excitations). This limits modeling of driven processes like photoexcitation and charge injection. A lightweight conditioning mechanism that extends existing backbones without large data or architectural changes is needed.
AI.method: Introduce EquiFiLM, a per-layer Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) block that modulates only scalar channels to inject external conditioning while preserving exact E(3)-equivariance. The conditioning axis is backbone- and conditioning-agnostic and does not require architectural changes beyond adding FiLM layers. Demonstrated on charged liquid water using MACE-MatPES as backbone (resulting in E-MACE). Training uses only a few thousand DFT-labeled frames; inference cost remains unchanged. The model is evaluated on both in-distribution training charges and seven held-out interpolation/extrapolation charges; assesses force and energy RMSE, MD stability, and charge-dependent structural signals (reduced RDF).
AI.result: For four training charges, force RMSE improves from 21.3 to 6.96 meV/Å (3.1×) and energy RMSE from 6.1 to 0.1 meV/atom (61×) over a baseline without EquiFiLM. Across seven held-out charges, force RMSE remains in 18–61 meV/Å and energy RMSE 0.7–5.4 meV/atom. MD simulations remain stable across the tested range; the model captures charge-dependent first-shell RDF changes probed by ultrafast electron diffraction. EquiFiLM requires only a few thousand DFT frames, vs ~10^8 structures for a charge-aware model trained from scratch. The recipe is applicable to any equivariant MLFF with scalar interaction channels.
AI.conclusion: EquiFiLM provides a lightweight, data-efficient, and architecture-agnostic method to extend foundation MLFFs to externally driven electronic states, enabling accurate modeling of charging, external fields, and excitations without increasing inference cost. It broadens the applicability of equivariant MLFFs to driven processes and can be readily applied to other backbones and conditioning signals.

title: Clustered Codebook Quantization for 2D Gaussian-based Image Compression
comment: 3 pages. Accepted to ACM SIGGRAPH 2026 Poster Track. Code available at https://github.com/complight/Cluster_Guided_Vector_Quantization
summary: Gaussian-based image representations effectively model image content using compact parametric primitives while preserving high visual fidelity, yet storing a large number of floating-point parameters per primitive degrades rate-distortion efficiency at higher fidelity targets. To improve the rate-distortion performance in Gaussian representation, we present our Cluster-Guided Vector Quantization (CGVQ), a Gaussian primitive based image compression method. Our key idea is to partition Gaussian parameters further into homogeneous groups prior to quantization, enabling higher compression efficiency and accurate parameter reconstruction. In practice, our extensive experiments show that CGVQ decreases the bpp by 20% with respect to our baseline, while maintaining on-par visual quality

AI.tldr: CGVQ uses cluster-guided vector quantization to group Gaussian parameters into homogeneous clusters before quantization, improving rate-distortion efficiency by reducing bpp while preserving visual quality.
AI.motivation: Gaussian-based image representations store many floating-point parameters per primitive, which degrades rate-distortion efficiency at high fidelity targets; reducing bitrate without sacrificing fidelity is desirable.
AI.method: Partition Gaussian parameters into homogeneous groups (clusters) prior to quantization and apply vector quantization within each group, enabling more efficient parameter reconstruction.
AI.result: CGVQ achieves about a 20% reduction in bits-per-pixel (bpp) compared to the baseline, while maintaining equivalent visual quality.
AI.conclusion: The cluster-guided approach improves rate-distortion performance for Gaussian primitive-based image compression, delivering meaningful bitrate savings without sacrificing perceptual fidelity.

title: Integrating knowledge graphs and multilingual scholarly corpora for domain-adaptive LLMs in SSH
comment: 8 pages, 4 tables, workshop LLMs4SSH of LREC 2026 conference
summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into scientific research workflows, particularly for bibliographic discovery and literature synthesis, raises significant methodological, epistemic and regulatory challenges for the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH), especially with regard to disciplinary diversity, multilingual access to sources and the evaluation of results. This paper presents an on-going use case developed within the European project LLMs4EU and the ALT-EDIC infrastructure, aimed at adapting foundation models to SSH research practices and supporting tasks such as question answering, comparative document analysis and literature review. The evaluation framework follows the LLMs4EU protocol and encompasses both independent quantitative benchmarking (retrieval, summarisation, traceability and hallucination detection) and a qualitative assessment involving a panel of Digital Humanities experts. By embedding model adaptation within research infrastructures and a structured legal and ethical compliance framework, the use case explores how domain-sensitive and regulation-aware generative AI can support SSH scholarship while preserving reliability and epistemic responsibility.

AI.tldr: An ongoing use case integrating LLMs into SSH research workflows via LLMs4EU/ALT-EDIC, combining a mixed evaluation framework with regulatory-compliant infrastructure adaptation to enable reliability and epistemic responsibility.
AI.motivation: Address methodological, epistemic, and regulatory challenges of applying LLMs to Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH), including disciplinary diversity, multilingual access to sources, and robust evaluation.
AI.method: Develop an SSH-focused use case within the LLMs4EU and ALT-EDIC infrastructure; adapt foundation models for SSH tasks (question answering, comparative document analysis, literature reviews); follow the LLMs4EU evaluation protocol with both quantitative benchmarks (retrieval, summarisation, traceability, hallucination detection) and qualitative assessment by Digital Humanities experts; embed model adaptation within research infrastructures and a formal legal/ethical compliance framework.
AI.result: Ongoing effort presenting a use case and an evaluation framework; final results not yet reported; aims to demonstrate feasibility and establish metrics for reliable, epistemically responsible AI-assisted SSH research.
AI.conclusion: Indicates that domain-sensitive and regulation-aware generative AI can support SSH scholarship when integrated into proper infrastructures and governance; the approach shows promise for reliability, traceability, and epistemic responsibility in AI-assisted SSH research.

title: ThorArena: Benchmarking Humanoid Physical Interaction with Human Motion-Force Demonstrations
summary:
Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to perform contact-rich tasks that require not only accurate whole-body motion but also robust physical interaction with surrounding objects and humans. Although recent advances in humanoid motion imitation and whole-body control have achieved remarkable tracking performance, existing datasets and benchmarks primarily focus on kinematic motion while largely overlooking synchronized interaction forces. As a result, current evaluations fail to capture how external interaction forces affect tracking accuracy, stability, and control robustness.
  In this paper, we present ThorArena, a benchmark for evaluating force-aware humanoid interaction based on human demonstrations with synchronized motion and force measurements. We collect a real-world interaction dataset that simultaneously captures whole-body human motion and forces exerted by both hands across six representative physical interaction tasks. Based on these demonstrations, we propose force-aware evaluation metrics that jointly assess whole-body tracking accuracy, robustness under different force levels, control effort, and episode survival through the Force-Aware Tracking Score (FATS) and complementary diagnostic metrics. We further establish a unified benchmark protocol that replays recorded interaction forces in simulation and provides a standardized evaluation interface for different humanoid control policies.
  Experiments on representative whole-body control policies demonstrate that force-aware evaluation reveals substantial performance differences that remain largely hidden under conventional no-force evaluation. ThorArena provides a practical and reproducible framework for studying force-aware humanoid interaction and offers a new benchmark for evaluating contact-rich humanoid behaviors.

AI.tldr: ThorArena is a force-aware humanoid-robot benchmark built from real-world demonstrations that pairs motion with hand-originating interaction forces across six tasks, introducing FATS and a protocol to replay forces in simulation for evaluating force-sensitive performance of humanoid controllers.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks emphasize kinematic motion and neglect synchronized interaction forces, hindering evaluation of tracking, stability, and robustness under contact-rich manipulation.
AI.method: Collect real-world data of whole-body human motion with synchronized forces from both hands across six interaction tasks; define Force-Aware Tracking Score (FATS) and complementary metrics; develop a unified protocol to replay recorded forces in simulation and provide a standardized evaluation interface for various policies.
AI.result: Force-aware evaluation reveals substantial performance differences among control policies that are not captured by traditional no-force evaluation; ThorArena enables reproducible, force-sensitive benchmarking of contact-rich humanoid behavior.
AI.conclusion: ThorArena offers a practical framework for studying force-aware humanoid interaction and serves as a new benchmark for evaluating contact-rich humanoid control policies.

title: SafeImpute: Reliable Clinical Data Imputation via Conformal Selection
comment: Accepted at KDD 2026. Author accepted manuscript
summary: Clinical care often relies on key laboratory indicators, yet real-world patient visits are sparse and tests are ordered irregularly, leading to pervasive missingness. While many imputation methods improve average accuracy, they provide limited guidance on which imputed values are reliable enough for high-stakes downstream use. In this work, we study reliable clinical imputation, aiming to produce accurate imputations while selectively releasing the reliable results, with statistical control over clinically unacceptable errors. To achieve this goal, we propose SafeImpute, a reliable imputation framework for irregular and sparse clinical longitudinal records. SafeImpute constructs an event graph that captures both intra-patient temporal trajectories and inter-patient clinical similarity, and learns imputations with a two-relation GNN and adaptive fusion, regularized by an auxiliary masked reconstruction objective. For reliability guarantees, SafeImpute converts a proxy risk score into conformal p-values and applies the Benjamini--Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of unacceptable errors among released imputations at a user-specified tolerance. Experiments on our Mayo Clinic data, the public MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets show that SafeImpute achieves strong imputation accuracy while providing reliable error control, outperforming diverse baselines in both standard imputation evaluation and FDR-controlled selective-release evaluation.

AI.tldr: SafeImpute is a reliability-aware imputation framework for irregular, sparse clinical longitudinal data that delivers accurate imputations while selectively releasing only reliable values. It uses a two-relation GNN on an event graph combining intra-patient trajectories and inter-patient similarity, with adaptive fusion and an auxiliary masked reconstruction objective, and provides FDR-controlled selective release by converting a proxy risk score to conformal p-values and applying Benjamini–Hochberg. Evaluated on Mayo Clinic data and MIMIC-III/IV, it achieves strong accuracy and reliable error control, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Clinical lab data are sparsely observed and irregular; missing values threaten high-stakes decision making. While many imputation methods improve average accuracy, there is a need to quantify and control the risk of clinically unacceptable errors to guide selective release of imputations.
AI.method: Construct an event graph capturing intra-patient temporal trajectories and inter-patient clinical similarity. Learn imputations with a two-relation GNN and adaptive fusion, regularized by an auxiliary masked reconstruction objective. For reliability, convert a proxy risk score into conformal p-values and apply Benjamini–Hochberg to control FDR of unacceptable errors among released imputations at a user-specified tolerance.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on Mayo Clinic data and publicly available MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets shows that SafeImpute achieves strong imputation accuracy while providing reliable error control, outperforming diverse baselines in both standard imputation evaluation and FDR-controlled selective-release evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SafeImpute provides a practical framework for reliable clinical imputation, delivering accurate imputations with quantified control over the rate of unacceptable errors during selective release. It demonstrates the feasibility of reliability-guaranteed imputation for irregular, sparse longitudinal clinical data and can guide high-stakes downstream use.

title: Robust Face Super-Resolution and Recognition Through Multi-Feature Aggregation in Diffusion Models
summary: Images acquired in surveillance environments often suffer from conditions such as low resolution, variations in pose, irregular illumination, and occlusions. Due to the low quality of these images, face recognition algorithms often struggle. This major limitation can be addressed by employing super-resolution techniques that enhance the details of the image. However, due to the high degree of difficulty of the problem, most super-resolution algorithms tend to cause distortions in the image and in the individual's identity. Thus, additional information must be incorporated into the processing to improve recognition robustness. In this regard, surveillance cameras can capture multiple images, even at low quality, and the data extracted from these images, such as consecutive video frames, can significantly enhance both super-resolution and facial recognition. In this work, we introduce FASR++, a diffusion-model-based super-resolution algorithm. It leverages a reference low-resolution image and features extracted from multiple auxiliary low-quality images to generate a super-resolved output, minimizing distortions in the individual's identity. Our approach recovers facial features without explicitly providing soft attributes or computing a function gradient to guide the reconstruction process. FASR++ generates high-quality images that can considerably improve performance in face recognition tasks when used as a pre-processing step. We validate our approach on two standard face recognition datasets and attain state-of-the-art results for verification, face recognition, and image quality metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-based super-resolution (FASR++) for surveillance faces using a reference LR image and multi-frame information to preserve identity; achieves state-of-the-art results on two datasets for verification, recognition, and IQ metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS).
AI.motivation: Overcome SR-induced identity distortions in low-quality surveillance facial data by exploiting multi-frame context and diffusion-based reconstruction to enhance recognition robustness.
