comment: 23 pages. Equal contribution: Guang Yang and Brian Siyuan Zheng
summary: We propose a novel pipeline, Legato 2, for extracting symbolic notation and semantic knowledge from images of sheet music. Legato 2 features the first large-scale neural model for optical music recognition (OMR) to operate sequentially on a system-by-system basis, following the horizontal lines of notation as they are read on the page, rather than treating the page as an undifferentiated image, enabling better scaling to arbitrarily long inputs. It is also the first OMR model capable of generating symbolic transcriptions that include embedded textual content, such as titles and annotations. The pipeline combines system-level segmentation with an autoregressive vision-LM to capture both local notation details and score structure. Across multiple datasets, Legato 2 consistently outperforms prior state of the art. We also show that symbolic transcriptions complement visual inputs for frontier language models, improving their interpretation of dense musical documents. Legato 2 establishes new state-of-the-art performance in both OMR and downstream sheet music understanding.

AI.tldr: Legato 2 introduces a sequential, system-by-system OMR model that produces symbolic transcriptions including embedded text, achieving state-of-the-art in OMR and downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Address scalability to long sheet music inputs and the integration of textual annotations; enable symbolic transcription for downstream language models.
AI.method: System-level segmentation of the score, autoregressive vision-language model, sequential processing per system, generation of symbolic notation with text.
AI.result: Consistent state-of-the-art across multiple datasets; improved interpretation for dense musical documents when used with language models.
AI.conclusion: Legato 2 sets new benchmarks for OMR and sheet music understanding and demonstrates the value of combining system-level OMR with symbolic transcription.

title: Information Gain-based Rollout Policy Optimization: An Adaptive Tree-Structured Rollout Approach for Multi-Turn LLM Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning has become a promising paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon search tasks, where the agent must make a sequence of intermediate decisions before receiving a final outcome. However, existing methods still face a key limitation: the rollout budget is often allocated without explicitly assessing the utility of intermediate states. As a result, substantial computation may be spent on low-value states, even though different branches can vary drastically in their informativeness. In this paper, we propose Information Gain-based Rollout Policy Optimization (IGRPO), a policy optimization framework that treats intermediate-state informativeness as the organizing principle of rollout collection. Specifically, IGRPO performs budget-aware tree-structured rollouts by allocating expansion budget according to node-level informativeness, so that more informative branches are expanded more frequently while unpromising branches are progressively suppressed. We further demonstrate that the information gain-based rollout induces an explicit limiting teacher distribution over trajectories, which naturally yields a clear policy optimization target, thereby unifying adaptive tree-structured exploration with principled policy learning under a single framework. Experiments on seven challenging search-augmented QA benchmarks demonstrate that IGRPO consistently outperforms strong baselines under the same rollout budget constraints, validating the effectiveness of leveraging the induced teacher distribution to guide policy optimization for long-horizon search agents.

AI.tldr: IGRPO optimizes rollout in long-horizon LLM search by using information gain at each node to allocate budget, producing a teacher trajectory distribution that guides policy learning; empirically outperforms baselines under fixed rollout budgets.
AI.motivation: Current rollout budgets are not sensitive to intermediate-state informativeness, causing wasted computation; need budget allocation aligned with information value.
AI.method: Introduce information gain-based rollout policy optimization with tree-structured rollouts; allocate expansion by node informativeness; derive a teacher distribution over trajectories; combine adaptive search with policy optimization under a unified framework.
AI.result: Seven challenging search-augmented QA benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines under same rollout budget.
AI.conclusion: Information-gain-based rollout effectively channels budget and learning to long-horizon search tasks; unifies exploration and policy learning.

title: LAMP: Latent Motion Prior-Guided Real-World Learning for Dexterous Hand Manipulation
summary: Real-world learning for dexterous hands remains brittle because high-dimensional hand actions amplify imitation errors and make reinforcement-learning exploration prone to contact-breaking motion. While combining imitation learning (IL) with online reinforcement learning (RL) can reduce manual supervision, unconstrained exploration in raw hand-action spaces is sample-inefficient and risky for physical hardware. We introduce a latent motion prior module (\prior{}) that maps recent hand-action histories to a compact, history-conditioned latent prior and decodes continuous latent commands into executable high-dimensional hand targets. Built on this prior, \method{} is a three-stage real-world dexterous learning framework: it pretrains \prior{} from demonstrations, trains a visuomotor policy that predicts native arm commands and latent hand-action offsets, and improves the policy with online residual RL in the same latent hand-action space. This shared, decodable interface lets residual exploration make local corrections near demonstrated, contact-consistent hand motions rather than perturbing every finger joint independently. We evaluate \method{} on four real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks against raw, linear, and discrete hand-action interfaces. Starting from small task-specific demonstration sets, \method{} achieves a 56.25\% average IL success rate and raises it to 98.75\% after online RL, reaching 100\% final success on three tasks and 95\% on the remaining task.

AI.tldr: A latent motion prior is proposed to enable real-world dexterous manipulation with a three-stage IL+RL framework. It achieves high sample efficiency and strong final performance across four real-robot tasks by decoupling high-dimensional hand actions into a learnable latent space that can be greedily explored and refined online.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous manipulation suffers from brittle performance due to high-dimensional hand actions causing imitation errors and risky RL exploration. A constrained latent interface can improve sample efficiency and safety during joint imitation and reinforcement-learning-based improvements.
AI.method: Introduce a latent motion prior (Prior) that maps recent hand-action histories to a compact, history-conditioned latent prior and decodes latent commands into executable high-dimensional hand targets. The three-stage framework: (1) pretrain Prior from demonstrations; (2) train a visuomotor policy to predict native arm commands and latent hand-action offsets; (3) online residual RL in the same latent hand-action space. The shared decodable interface enables residual exploration to make local corrections near demonstrated, contact-consistent motions.
AI.result: Evaluated on four real-robot dexterous tasks against raw, linear, and discrete hand-action interfaces. Starting from small demonstration sets, average IL success is 56.25%; after online RL it rises to 98.75%, with three tasks reaching 100% final success and the remaining task at 95%.
AI.conclusion: A latent motion prior enables safer, more sample-efficient real-world dexterous learning by restricting exploration to a decodable latent space; combining IL with online RL in this latent space yields strong final performance from limited demonstrations.

title: FourTune: Towards Fully 4-Bit Efficient Post-Training for Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality generative modeling, while post-training is essential for adapting them to diverse downstream applications. However, post-training of large diffusion models is still challenging due to the prohibitive memory footprints and slow training speed, which existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods only partially address. To overcome these limitations, we propose FourTune, an efficient post-training framework for diffusion models based on an end-to-end W4A4G4 paradigm. FourTune introduces a triple-branch hybrid pipeline that augments the standard LoRA architecture with a frozen numerical stabilizer to isolate quantization-sensitive outliers, enabling stable training under native 4-bit computation. In addition, FourTune employs hardware-efficient block-wise quantization and customized fused kernels to support efficient quantized backpropagation and reduce memory bandwidth overhead. Across customization, reinforcement learning, and distillation tasks, FourTune matches the quality of full-precision fine-tuning. On FLUX.1-dev (12B), FourTune reduces memory overhead by 2.25$\times$ and increases end-to-end training throughput by 2.27$\times$ compared to BF16 LoRA.

AI.tldr: FourTune enables efficient 4-bit post-training for diffusion models using a triple-branch LoRA-plus-stabilizer and hardware-optimized quantization, achieving full-precision fine-tuning quality with substantial memory and throughput gains.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models require post-training adaptation for downstream tasks, but existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods struggle with memory and speed at low precision. An end-to-end 4-bit post-training solution could greatly reduce resource usage while maintaining quality.
AI.method: An end-to-end W4A4G4 paradigm with a triple-branch hybrid pipeline that augments LoRA with a frozen numerical stabilizer to isolate quantization-sensitive outliers for stable 4-bit training. It also uses hardware-efficient block-wise quantization and customized fused kernels to enable efficient backpropagation under quantization.
AI.result: FourTune matches the quality of full-precision fine-tuning across customization, reinforcement learning, and distillation tasks. On Flux.1-dev (12B), it reduces memory overhead by 2.25x and increases end-to-end training throughput by 2.27x compared to BF16 LoRA.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that end-to-end 4-bit post-training for diffusion models is viable with significant resource savings, enabling efficient adaptation of large diffusion models to downstream tasks.

title: Benchmarking the Robustness of Autonomous Driving to Environmental Illusions: A Lane Perception Perspective
summary: Environmental illusions (eg., shadows, reflections, and tire marks) are naturally existing yet overlooked phenomena in real-world driving environments. They can disturb visual perception, leading to misinterpretation of the scene and posing serious safety risks to autonomous driving (AD) systems. However, existing researches largely overlook these phenomena, leaving a critical gap. To address this issue, we study AD robustness through the lane perception perspective, a fundamental task supporting core functions like cruise control and lane centering. We focus on two representative models: conventional lane detection (LD) and vision-language model-based systems (ADVLMs). In this work, we introduce the first benchmark, LanEvil++, for evaluating the robustness of lane perception under environmental illusions. LanEvil++ encompasses 14 types of illusions and leverages the CARLA simulator to generate 94 high-fidelity, fully controllable 3D scenes, yielding a dataset of 90,292 annotated images, 1,596 video clips, and 41,855 visual question answering pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that environmental illusions substantially degrade the performance of state-of-the-art LD methods. On average, LD models experience a 5.27% drop in Accuracy and a 10.49% decline in F1-score, while ADVLMs show a 2.03% reduction in GPT-score and a 0.75% drop in Language-score. Among all illusions, shadows emerge as the most disruptive factor, reducing accuracy by up to 7.20%. Furthermore, closed-loop simulations reveal that these illusions can lead to incorrect driving decisions. Complementary real-world case studies highlight safety-critical failures in actual traffic scenes. To enhance robustness, we propose the Multimodal Illusion Defense Approach (MIDA). MIDA achieves substantial gains under challenging conditions, boosting robustness by 4.23% on LD models and 3.82% on ADVLMs.

AI.tldr: LanEvil++ is a benchmark to evaluate lane perception robustness to environmental illusions in autonomous driving, revealing degradation in both conventional lane detectors and vision-language models, and introducing MIDA to improve robustness.
AI.motivation: Environmental illusions such as shadows, reflections, and tire marks can mislead perception in real driving, posing safety risks. Lane perception is fundamental for AD, and existing work lacks robust benchmarks to study these effects.
AI.method: Introduce LanEvil++ benchmark with 14 illusion types generated in 94 controllable CARLA scenes, yielding 90,292 annotated images, 1,596 video clips, and 41,855 VQA pairs. Evaluate conventional LD methods and ADVLMs using accuracy, F1-score (LD), GPT-score and Language-score (ADVLMs). Demonstrate performance degradation; analyze shadows as most disruptive; perform closed-loop simulations and real-world case studies; propose Multimodal Illusion Defense Approach (MIDA) and report gains.
AI.result: LD accuracy decreases by 5.27% and F1-score by 10.49%; ADVLM GPT-score decreases by 2.03% and Language-score by 0.75%. Shadows cause up to 7.20% accuracy drop. Closed-loop driving reveals potential unsafe decisions. Real-world cases show safety-critical failures. MIDA yields +4.23% robustness for LD and +3.82% for ADVLMs.
AI.conclusion: Environmental illusions significantly threaten lane perception; LanEvil++ provides a first comprehensive benchmark; MIDA offers effective defense to improve robustness in both LD and ADVLMs, contributing to safer AD systems.

title: Demonstrating TOFFEE: A Learned System for Synthesizing Data Agent Trajectories at Scale
summary: LLM-powered data agents are playing an increasingly important role in data-driven decision making. However, existing data agents struggle to generalize to unseen data environments and analytical workflows, especially in heterogeneous enterprise settings. This creates a growing need for synthesizing high-quality data agent trajectories that capture complex analytical workflows for given data environments. Such trajectories support two key downstream uses: they can serve as supervised finetuning (SFT) data that adapts data agent models to the target domain, and as in-context learning (ICL) demonstrations to guide general-purpose LLMs in unfamiliar data environments. Thus, we introduce TOFFEE, a system for synthesizing high-quality data agent trajectories from given data environments via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with adaptive model selection and cross-task prefix reuse. We show that TOFFEE can effectively generate scalable trajectory data for complex analytical tasks across heterogeneous environments. In this demonstration, we present the system framework of TOFFEE, including its task pool construction, trajectory explorer, and learned cost model. We also introduce the web interface of TOFFEE and its workflow, and demonstrate two end-to-end scenarios: trajectory synthesis for data agent finetuning, and demonstration-augmented data agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: TOFFEE synthesizes high-quality data agent trajectories from data environments using Monte Carlo Tree Search with adaptive model selection and cross-task prefix reuse, to produce data for supervised fine-tuning and in-context learning demonstrations in heterogeneous enterprise settings.
AI.motivation: Data agents struggle to generalize to unseen data environments and workflows; synthesizing trajectories enables domain-adaptive fine-tuning and better guidance for LLMs in unfamiliar tasks.
AI.method: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with adaptive model selection and cross-task prefix reuse; system framework with task pool construction, trajectory explorer, and learned cost model; web interface; demonstrates two end-to-end scenarios.
AI.result: Demonstrates TOFFEE's ability to generate scalable trajectory data for complex analytical tasks across heterogeneous environments; presents system framework and two end-to-end demonstrations: trajectory synthesis for data agent fine-tuning and demonstration-augmented data agent reasoning.
AI.conclusion: TOFFEE provides a principled way to generate trajectory data that can be used for SFT and ICL, facilitating data agent generalization in diverse environments and guiding LLMs in unfamiliar data workflows.

title: OrchardBench: A Physically-Grounded, GPU-Parallel Apple-Orchard Simulation Benchmark for Agricultural Robotics
summary: Robotic tree-fruit harvesting is a flagship problem for agricultural automation, but progress is bottlenecked by the cost and irreproducibility of field experiments: an orchard is available only weeks a year, every tree is different, and a control error can permanently damage the crop or the plant. The tree models used in graphics and agronomy are geometrically detailed but physically inert, while the GPU-parallel simulators used in robot learning contain no plausible trees. We present OrchardBench, a physically-grounded, GPU-parallel simulation of apple-orchard trees on the Newton engine. Each tree is grown by a stochastic L-system and instantiated as a fully articulated body: branches are compliant torsional spring-dampers whose stiffness follows Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, they break at a wood modulus of rupture and fall as free hinges, and apples are independent bodies on stem tethers that detach at literature-grounded pull forces and load the branch when pulled. A moving, density-controllable foliage layer occludes the canopy as real leaves do. Every physical parameter is tied to a published source. Per-environment domain randomization makes each batched world a distinct tree, and a mobile manipulator with a wrist depth camera closes the loop with geometric fruit perception and an autonomous harvesting baseline. Careful engineering of the solver and the model lets OrchardBench run many parallel environments at interactive rates on a laptop GPU. We define the tasks and a metric suite spanning harvest completeness, throughput, and plant damage (with a per-canopy-zone breakdown), and report baseline results across foliage, fruit load, terrain, canopy zone, and parallelism. The analytic baseline succeeds on about 40% of the fruit it detects and harvests only about an eighth of the reachable fruit on a tree, leaving clear headroom for novel autonomy approaches.

AI.tldr: GPU-parallel, physically-grounded orchard simulation (OrchardBench) enabling scalable benchmarking for robotic apple-harvesting; uses stochastic L-systems, fully articulated tree dynamics, and per-environment domain randomization; baseline analytic controller achieves limited harvest ability, leaving room for learning-based autonomy.
AI.motivation: Bottlenecks in robotic tree-fruit harvesting due to costly, irreproducible field experiments; existing models are either geometrically detailed but inert or simulators lack plausible tree dynamics; a physics-based, GPU-enabled environment is needed to train and evaluate autonomous policies at scale.
AI.method: OrchardBench grows trees with a stochastic L-system and instantiates them as fully articulated bodies. Branches are modeled as torsional spring-dampers with stiffness from Euler-Bernoulli beam theory; branches break at a wood modulus of rupture and fall as free hinges; apples are independent bodies on stem tethers that detach under pull with load transferred to the branch. A density-controlled foliage layer occludes the canopy. All physical parameters are sourced from literature. Per-environment domain randomization creates diverse trees. A mobile manipulator with a wrist depth camera provides geometric fruit perception and an autonomous harvesting baseline.
AI.result: The environment defines tasks and metrics for harvest completeness, throughput, and plant damage with per-canopy-zone breakdown. Baseline analytic methods detect about 40% of the fruit and harvest roughly 1/8 of the reachable fruit. OrchardBench runs many parallel environments at interactive rates on a laptop GPU, indicating strong support for scalable autonomy research but with substantial headroom for improved policies.
AI.conclusion: OrchardBench offers a physically-grounded, GPU-accelerated platform with literature-grounded parameters and domain randomization to benchmark and develop autonomous harvesting policies. The modest baseline performance highlights significant potential gains from learning-based perception and control.

title: Low-Overhead Error-Corrected QCNNs Using Bivariate Bicycle Codes
summary: Quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) combine the power of quantum computing and classical CNN for computational speedup in classification tasks. However, noise levels on state-of-the-art quantum devices remain too high for practical QCNN execution. In addition, despite the reliable surface code providing a method for error rates below a threshold value, they have a prohibitively large qubit cost. Recently introduced bivariate bicycle (BB) codes are of particular interest for their high error threshold, constant encoding rate, and linear code distance. Through simulation with realistic hardware noise sources, we demonstrate that a 4-qubit unprotected QCNN fails to converge and exhibits a worse learning rate compared to numerical simulations. Addressing both limitations, we propose a distance-4 BB quantum error-correction (QEC) technique for QCNNs. In doing so, we validate that our low-overhead QEC technique for QCNNS represents a step toward practical QCNNs.

AI.tldr: Introduce distance-4 BB quantum error correction to QCNNs to boost robustness against noise and reduce qubit overhead, making practical QCNNs more feasible.
AI.motivation: Current QCNNs are limited by high noise on near-term devices and prohibitively large qubit costs of surface-code QEC. BB codes offer high error thresholds, constant encoding rate, and linear code distance, motivating their use for low-overhead QEC in QCNNs.
AI.method: Propose a distance-4 BB quantum error-correction technique tailored for QCNNs. Validate via simulations with realistic hardware noise: demonstrate that a 4-qubit unprotected QCNN fails to converge and has worse learning rate, and show that the BB-QEC approach addresses these limitations.
AI.result: Demonstrated that unprotected 4-qubit QCNN struggles to converge under realistic noise. The proposed distance-4 BB-QEC technique provides a low-overhead error-correction path, and its validation represents a step toward practical QCNNs.
AI.conclusion: Distance-4 BB codes offer a promising route to enable practical QCNNs by delivering high-threshold, low-overhead QEC, addressing both noise and qubit-resource challenges in QCNN implementations.

title: DeSeG: Decoupling Semantic Intent and Geometric Constraints for Physically Plausible Human-Scene Interaction
summary: Synthesizing physically plausible human-scene interactions (HSI) remains a critical challenge in computer vision and the development of human avatars. Although recent generative models enable diverse motion synthesis, they suffer from an inductive bias referred to as semantic-geometric entanglement. Because spatial constraints often strongly correlate with specific actions in training data, monolithic models will learn the shortcut bias, aggressively overriding the semantic intent when faced with strict geometric cues. Furthermore, this entanglement exacerbates physical hallucinations, such as body-scene penetrations. To address these limitations, we propose DeSeG, a hierarchical framework that explicitly decouples semantic intent from geometric constraints. First, we introduce a Residual Semantic Planner that encodes textual instructions and canonicalized goal voxels into a compact latent space, enabling fine-grained semantic control independent of spatial trajectories. Second, we propose a physics regularized diffusion executor that incorporates differentiable repulsive potential fields directly into the diffusion objective, enforcing collision-aware motion generation. Extensive experiments on the Lingo dataset demonstrate that DeSeG achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing mean scene penetration by 47% and improving semantic alignment by 29% over the SOTA baselines.

AI.tldr: DeSeG decouples semantic intent from geometric constraints in human-scene interaction synthesis via a hierarchical design, enabling semantic control and collision-aware motion, achieving state-of-the-art results on Lingo with substantial reductions in scene penetrations and improved semantic alignment.
AI.motivation: Semantic-geometric entanglement in current generative HSI models leads to physical hallucinations and overfitting to geometric cues; decoupling semantics from geometry is needed for plausible, controllable human-avatar interactions.
AI.method: A Residual Semantic Planner encodes textual instructions and canonicalized goal voxels into a compact latent space for semantic control; a physics-regularized diffusion executor integrates differentiable repulsive potential fields into the diffusion objective to enforce collision avoidance.
AI.result: On the Lingo dataset, DeSeG achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing mean scene penetration by 47% and increasing semantic alignment by 29% compared to SOTA baselines.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic intent from geometric constraints with DeSeG improves physical plausibility and semantic controllability in HSI synthesis, mitigating penetrations and improving alignment.

title: From Application-Layer Simulation to Native Meta-Architecture: Structural Tension as an Endogenous Driver for Heterogeneous AI Evolution
summary: Current large language models (LLMs) are fundamentally stateless: their behavior is fully determined by input at inference time, and any higher-order cognitive architecture must be simulated at the application layer through prompt engineering and context management. This paper proposes a theoretical framework for submerging such application-layer cognitive protocols into a native meta-architecture by introducing three interlocking mechanisms: (1) Structural Tension, an endogenous loss function derived from the conflict between new information and existing manifold topology, which drives the system toward internal self-consistency rather than external reward optimization; (2) an Offline Recurrent Loop, a sandboxed self-processing cycle that enables the system to maintain a dynamic resting potential and digest structural conflicts without external input; and (3) Inference-time Plasticity, the capacity for the system to reconfigure its context manifold topology without modifying pre-trained weights, subject to strict governance invariants including auditability, reversibility, and topological continuity. We argue that under these mechanisms, different model instances initialized with minute stochastic variances may, through path-dependent tension resolution, evolve distinct topological structures--constituting a heterogeneous intelligent ecology that breaks the homogeneity imposed by conventional alignment while remaining within hard governance rails. We provide operational definitions, a minimal set of reconfiguration operators, falsification criteria, and a worked example. The framework draws on and extends the Structural Intelligence (SI) governance protocols, repositioning governance--not capability--as the primary criterion for architectural intelligence.

AI.tldr: A theoretical framework to embed cognitive protocols into a native meta-architecture for LLMs, using Structural Tension, Offline Recurrent Loop, and Inference-time Plasticity to enable self-consistent, reconfigurable topologies under strict governance; includes definitions, operators, falsification criteria, a worked example, and reframes governance as the primary criterion for architectural intelligence.
AI.motivation: Overcome the statelessness of current LLMs by migrating higher-order cognitive governance from the prompt layer into a native architecture, enabling self-consistent behavior and reconfigurability while maintaining auditability and reversibility.
AI.method: Introduce three interlocking mechanisms—Structural Tension (endogenous loss from conflict between new information and manifold topology), Offline Recurrent Loop (sandboxed self-processing to resolve conflicts without external input), and Inference-time Plasticity (reconfigure context manifold without updating pre-trained weights, under governance invariants: auditability, reversibility, topological continuity). Formalize a minimal reconfiguration operator set, falsification criteria, and a worked example. Build on Structural Intelligence governance to shift governance from capability to architectural intelligence.
AI.result: A theoretical framework that enables path-dependent heterogeneity across model instances via tension resolution within a native meta-architecture, with a minimal operator set and falsification criteria, demonstrating governance-first architectural design.
AI.conclusion: Governance—not capability—should be the primary criterion for architectural intelligence; the framework demonstrates how to submerge cognitive protocols into architecture, enabling reconfiguration and self-consistency while preserving auditability and reversibility.

title: Responsible Personalisation: The Double-Edged Sword of Personalisation in Human-Robot Interaction
summary: While personalisation is becoming a defining capability in human-robot interaction (HRI), the existing literature on responsible personalisation remains fragmented, offering isolated accounts of ethical risks without a structured understanding of how they emerge across interaction contexts. This gap is particularly critical in HRI, where robots' embodiment and social presence can amplify and reshape such risks or generate new types of risks. We present a lifecycle-based and context-sensitive framework for personalised HRI, grounded in an embodiment-aware perspective. The framework combines stages of the personalisation process with interaction characteristics (short-term vs. long-term, open-domain vs. closed-domain), enabling systematic analysis of how risks arise and evolve. Building on this, we conduct an integrative analysis of key ethical risks, including autonomy erosion, biased user modelling, manipulation, dehumanisation, and privacy violations, and examine how they manifest across contexts. We translate these insights into actionable design recommendations and outline open research challenges. By structuring both the design space and risk landscape of personalised HRI, this work provides a foundation for more systematic, transparent, and ethically grounded approaches to personalised robot behaviour.

AI.tldr: A lifecycle-based, embodiment-aware framework for personalised HRI that links personalisation stages with interaction contexts to analyze ethical risks and guide design.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation in responsible personalisation literature and the amplification of risks due to robots’ embodiment and social presence in HRI.
AI.method: Proposes a framework that combines stages of the personalisation process with interaction characteristics (short-term vs. long-term, open-domain vs. closed-domain) from an embodiment-aware perspective; followed by integrative analysis of ethical risks.
AI.result: Identifies key ethical risks—autonomy erosion, biased user modelling, manipulation, dehumanisation, and privacy violations—and shows how they manifest across contexts; translates insights into actionable design recommendations and outlines open research challenges.
AI.conclusion: Provides a foundation for systematic, transparent, and ethically grounded approaches to personalised robot behaviour in HRI, via a structured design space and risk landscape.

title: Multimodal Molecular Representation Learning with Graph Neural Networks, Deep & Cross Networks, and SMILES Embeddings
summary: Molecular property prediction often relies on isolated data modalities, where continuous 3D graph neural networks (GNNs) struggle to efficiently capture long-range topological dependencies and exact macroscopic heuristics. In this work, we introduce a parameter-efficient Tri-Branch Modular Fusion Neural Network that synthesizes three orthogonal modalities: 3D spatial geometry (SchNet), discrete topological grammar (SMILES via ChemBERTa), and explicit macroscopic physicochemical descriptors (Deep & Cross Network). By bypassing standard scalar readouts and employing a shared late-fusion architecture, the framework establishes a mathematically rigorous multimodal latent space that effectively resolves the arithmetic and oversmoothing limitations of local message passing. We evaluate the proposed architecture on the QM9 benchmark, targeting the extensive thermodynamic property of atomization energy at 0 K ($U_0^{\mathrm{atom}}$). Through systematic combinatorial ablation and latent bottleneck optimization ($d_e=64$), the tri-modal framework achieves a validation Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0207 eV. Operating with fewer than one million parameters, this architecture decisively surpasses the sub-chemical accuracy threshold and yields a substantial 20.6% error reduction over a strictly controlled geometric baseline. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that integrating orthogonal macroscopic and topological data streams provides a synergistic, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ physical shortcut. This multimodal alignment offers a highly efficient alternative to brute-force parameter scaling, establishing a robust surrogate model for high-throughput virtual screening (HTVS) pipelines.

AI.tldr: Tri-branch multimodal fusion for molecular property prediction, integrating 3D geometry (SchNet), SMILES topology (ChemBERTa), and macroscopic descriptors (DCN) with a shared late-fusion latent space; achieves MAE of 0.0207 eV on QM9 U0_atom with <1M parameters, surpassing geometric baselines by ~20.6%.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of single-modality GNNs in capturing long-range topology and macroscopic physics; leverage complementary information from 3D structure, topology, and descriptors to achieve accurate, parameter-efficient predictions suitable for HTVS.
AI.method: A Tri-Branch Modular Fusion Network with three parallel branches: (1) a 3D geometry-based SchNet for local atomic environments, (2) a discrete topological model using SMILES representations via ChemBERTa, and (3) explicit macroscopic descriptors processed by a Deep & Cross Network. The branches feed into a shared latent space through a late-fusion architecture with a latent bottleneck (de=64) and bypass scalar readouts to mitigate oversmoothing; trained on QM9 U0_atom energy with parameter count <1e6.
AI.result: Validation MAE of 0.0207 eV on QM9 U0_atom; ~20.6% error reduction over geometry-only baseline; parameter-efficient (<1M parameters); surpasses chemical accuracy and demonstrates a robust multimodal surrogate for HTVS.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal data streams provide synergistic improvements, enabling an efficient, scalable surrogate for molecular property prediction that mitigates local GNN limitations and supports high-throughput screening.

title: Segmentation before Answering: Pixel Grounding for MLLM Visual Reasoning
summary: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have evolved from static perception to interleaved visual-language reasoning, often referred to as ``thinking with images''. A basic operation in this reasoning process is to zoom in on regions of interest (often represented with bounding boxes) to acquire finer visual details. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Seg}mentation before \textbf{Answer}ing (SegAnswer), which shifts the unit of zoom-in from the popular bounding box to pixel-level segmentation mask. By employing fine-grained masks to isolate the target area from cluttered environments, segmented visual input yields a more precise region of interest, effectively filtering out redundant background and interfering objects. Furthermore, the discrete patches of segmented visual input align more seamlessly with how MLLMs structure visual tokens via positional embeddings. In experiments, we evaluate SegAnswer across diverse benchmarks, including high-resolution perception, general perception, and hallucination. It achieves consistent improvements and also exhibits considerable performance on segmentation tasks, validating its capability for reliable pixel grounding.

AI.tldr: SegAnswer substitutes bounding-box zoom-ins with pixel-level segmentation masks, yielding a finer ROI, reduced background clutter, and better alignment with MLLM visual tokenization. It shows consistent gains across high-resolution perception, general perception, and hallucination benchmarks, and also demonstrates strong segmentation performance.
AI.motivation: Tackle ROI localization limitations in multimodal LLMs by using precise, pixel-level segmentation to isolate targets, mitigating background interference and improving token alignment.
AI.method: Propose SegAnswer framework: perform segmentation before answering, using fine-grained masks to isolate targets; treat segmented patches as discrete visual tokens that align with MLLMs' positional embeddings, enabling more accurate reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks shows consistent performance gains; the method also performs well on segmentation tasks, indicating reliable pixel grounding.
AI.conclusion: Segmentation-based ROI (pixel-level masks) enhances grounding and perception in MLLMs, offering a robust alternative to bounding-box zoom-ins and supporting more reliable interleaved visual-language reasoning.

title: Task Decomposition-Guided Reranking for Adaptive Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Skill usage can significantly enhance the ability of modern agent systems to complete complex tasks. However, the growing scale of skill libraries makes accurate skill selection increasingly challenging. In real-world scenarios, ambiguous semantic matching often arises between a specific task requirement and multiple generic yet semantically similar candidate skills. Moreover, existing methods tend to overlook the dynamic influence of task difficulty and skill applicability when selecting the optimal target skill set. To address these issues, we propose SkillReranker, an inference-time reranking framework for adaptive skill selection. Specifically, we first perform semantic decomposition on both the task and skill sides, yielding informative subtask and execution-state descriptions as well as transition-state descriptions that characterize each skill's functionality. These descriptions are then used to construct a directed acyclic execution graph, where intermediate task states are modeled as nodes and candidate skills as edges, thereby establishing a structured task-skill correspondence. On this basis, SkillReranker determines whether each state node satisfies the split condition to identify subtask intervals. For each task interval, we employ a cross-encoder to perform comprehensive scoring over candidate skills and select the most suitable ones to form the final target skill set. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld with three backbone LLMs show that SkillReranker effectively improves task performance, reduces environment interaction steps, and lowers token consumption compared with existing skill selection baselines.

AI.tldr: SkillReranker is an inference-time reranking framework that semantically decomposes tasks and skills to build an execution DAG and uses cross-encoder scoring to select optimal skills, improving task performance and efficiency across ALFWorld/ScienceWorld with multiple LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: As skill libraries grow, accurate skill selection becomes harder due to ambiguous semantic matches and neglect of dynamic task difficulty and skill applicability in current methods.
AI.method: Semantic decomposition of tasks and skills into subtasks, execution-state descriptions, and transition-state descriptions; construct a DAG with task states as nodes and skills as edges; identify subtask intervals via split conditions; for each interval, apply a cross-encoder to score candidate skills and select the final target skill set.
AI.result: Empirically improves task performance, reduces environment interaction steps, and lowers token consumption compared with existing baselines across three backbone LLMs on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.
AI.conclusion: SkillReranker provides an effective, scalable approach to adaptive skill selection by leveraging semantic graphs and interval-based scoring, enhancing efficiency and performance in complex task execution.

title: Training-Free Acceleration for Vision-Language-Action Models with Action Caching and Refinement
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for generalizable robotic manipulations. In particular, flow matching-based VLA models have shown remarkable success due to their capability to generate precise and smooth action sequences and capture multimodal distributions. However, the iterative denoising process in the action head acts as a major computational bottleneck, posing a critical challenge for real-time deployment. To address this challenge, we propose ActionCache, a plug-and-play external cache that opportunistically reuses past intermediate actions to warm-start generations from the vicinity of target actions, thereby drastically reducing the inference latency. Specifically, ActionCache stores the intermediate actions with compact multimodal keys, which enables retrieval from similar past contexts across different episodes or even different tasks. Experimental results in simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that ActionCache maintains high task success rates in a low-latency regime, achieving inference acceleration of up to $11.75\times$ and $34.43\times$ for representative flow-based VLA models, $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T-N1.6, respectively.

AI.tldr: ActionCache introduces a plug-and-play external cache to reuse past intermediate actions in flow-matching VLA models, drastically reducing inference latency while preserving task success.
AI.motivation: Mitigate computational bottleneck of iterative denoising in the action head of flow-based VLA models to enable real-time deployment.
AI.method: External cache storing intermediate actions with compact multimodal keys to retrieve similar past contexts across episodes/tasks; warm-starts generation near target actions to reduce iterations.
AI.result: Achieves up to 11.75x and 34.43x inference speedups on π_{0.5} and GR00T-N1.6 with maintained high task success; validated in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: External caching is an effective plug-and-play optimization for flow-based VLA models, enabling substantially faster inference without sacrificing performance.

title: Two Sides of the Same Coin: Learning the Backdoor to Remove the Backdoor
summary:
The community has recently developed various training-time defenses to counter neural backdoors introduced through data poisoning. In light of the observation that a model learns poisonous samples responsible for the backdoor easier than benign samples, these approaches either use a fixed threshold of the training loss for splitting or iteratively learn a reference model as an oracle for identifying benign samples. In particular, the latter has proven effective for anti-backdoor learning.
  Our method, HARVEY, leverages a similar yet crucially different technique: learning an oracle for poisonous rather than benign samples. Learning a backdoored reference model is significantly easier than learning a reference model on benign data. Consequently, we can identify poisonous samples much more accurately than related work identifies benign samples. This crucial difference enables near-perfect backdoor removal as we demonstrate in our evaluation. HARVEY substantially outperforms related approaches across attack types, datasets, and architectures, lowering the attack success rate to the very minimum at a negligible loss in natural accuracy. The figure below shows an overview of our methods working principle.

AI.tldr: HARVEY learns an oracle for poisonous samples to remove backdoors during training, achieving near-perfect removal with minimal natural accuracy loss and outperforming prior benign-sample-based defenses.
AI.motivation: Backdoor defenses contend with data-poisoned neural backdoors; recognizing poisonous samples directly can be more effective than identifying benign samples.
AI.method: Train a backdoored reference model to serve as an oracle to detect poisonous samples; filter/training-time intervention to remove backdoors; evaluation across attacks/datasets/architectures.
AI.result: Near-perfect backdoor removal; minimal natural accuracy loss; HARVEY outperforms related approaches across attack types, datasets, architectures.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from benign to poisonous-sample oracle is an effective defense strategy for backdoor mitigation, with broad applicability.

title: TRIG: Trajectory-Rig Decoupled Metric Geometry Learning
summary: Vision-centric autonomous driving requires accurate metric geometry and ego-motion estimation from synchronized multi-camera observations. Recent visual geometry models show strong performance in pose estimation, depth prediction, and 3D reconstruction, but are not tailored to rigid multi-camera driving systems. They often encode camera poses as entangled representations, in which time-varying ego-motion and static camera-rig geometry are jointly modeled, limiting the utilization of vehicle-side geometric priors. We propose Trajectory-Rig Decoupled Metric Geometry Learning (TRIG), a geometry perception framework for autonomous driving. TRIG factorizes camera poses into ego-trajectory and camera-rig components, enabling separate modeling of ego-motion and static multi-camera topology. We introduce decoupled pose encoding and supervision, which separately constrain trajectory evolution and rig geometry for metric-consistent learning. Moreover, sparse Temporal--Spatial attention separates cross-camera interaction from temporal aggregation, reducing global attention cost while preserving geometric reasoning. Experiments on five autonomous driving benchmarks show that TRIG achieves state-of-the-art performance in pose estimation, metric depth prediction, and 3D reconstruction.

AI.tldr: TRIG decouples ego-motion from rigid camera-rig geometry in multi-camera driving, enabling metric-consistent learning with decoupled supervision and sparse temporal-spatial attention, achieving state-of-the-art pose, depth, and 3D reconstruction on five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard visual-geometry models encode camera poses as entangled representations that merge ego-motion with static rig topology, hindering the exploitation of vehicle priors and limiting metric accuracy in rigid multi-camera rigs.
AI.method: Introduce Trajectory-Rig Decoupled Metric Geometry Learning (TRIG): factorizes poses into ego-trajectory and camera-rig components; uses decoupled pose encoding and supervision to constrain trajectory evolution and rig geometry; employs sparse Temporal–Spatial attention to separate cross-camera interactions from temporal aggregation, reducing global attention cost while preserving geometric reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on five autonomous driving benchmarks shows TRIG achieving state-of-the-art performance in pose estimation, metric depth prediction, and 3D reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling ego-motion from rig geometry with decoupled supervision and sparse attention enables better metric geometry learning for rigid multi-camera driving systems, with strong gains in pose, depth, and 3D reconstruction.

title: DT-Guard: Intent-Driven Reasoning-Active Training for Reasoning-Free LLM Safety Guardrail
summary: Large language models deployed in open-world applications require safety guardrails that are both robust to complex risks and efficient enough for low-latency runtime moderation. Existing guardrails face a practical trade-off between lightweight classification-based models, which are efficient but often struggle with concealed intent, ambiguous semantics, and borderline safety decisions, and reasoning-based guards, which improve judgment quality but introduce additional token generation and inference latency. We present DT-Guard, a content safety guardrail model based on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. The key idea is to use reasoning supervision during training while emitting only structured safety labels at inference time. DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process, Intent - Category - Safety, and constructs an intent-driven dataset with intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. To further improve hard-case robustness, we propose Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO), which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples, and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization accordingly. At inference time, DT-Guard directly generates structured labels without explicit reasoning traces, preserving deployment efficiency. Experiments on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks show that DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With only a 4B backbone, it reaches a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines. These results demonstrate that reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination.

AI.tldr: DT-Guard introduces a Reasoning-Active Training framework with Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization to enable low-latency safety discrimination using structured labels, outperforming 8B baselines with a 4B backbone.
AI.motivation: Open-world LLM safety requires both robustness to concealed and borderline risks and low latency for moderation. Existing methods trade off speed (classification) vs. judgment quality (reasoning), motivating a framework that internalizes reasoning supervision while keeping inference efficient.
AI.method: DT-Guard employs Reasoning-Active Training, then inference emits only structured safety labels. It uses a progressive Decision process: Intent -> Category -> Safety, with an intent-driven dataset including intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. RG-PHO identifies stable mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples via multi-rollout consistency and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization. At inference time, it outputs structured labels without explicit reasoning traces.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks yields average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With a 4B backbone, a dual-side average F1 of 0.878 is achieved, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination, enabling robust guardrails without the latency penalties of explicit reasoning traces.

title: Towards Real-World Applications with an Autonomous Powered Wheelchair
summary: Wheelchair users call for assistive mobility systems that provide active support, adapt to dynamic environments, and are intuitive and user-friendly. However, powered wheelchairs typically still provide limited autonomy and lack effective integration with advanced perception and navigation capabilities, particularly in complex real-world environments. This paper presents a preliminary study toward autonomous powered wheelchairs for real-world assistive mobility. We introduce a proof-of-concept prototype that integrates autonomous perception, gesture-based interaction, and navigation on a commercially available self-balancing powered wheelchair. The proposed system builds upon Genny Zero, a commercial self-balancing wheelchair that enables hands-free and intuitive operation through body-weight shifting. To extend its capabilities toward autonomous operation, we integrate an RGB-D camera for human-aware perception and interaction, together with a LiDAR sensor for localization and navigation. We demonstrate the integrated system in two assistive applications: (i) hailing, allowing users to call the wheelchair from a distance; and (ii) people-following, where the wheelchair follows a person using leader-follower strategies, including a constrained indoor navigation example. The results highlight the potential of combining autonomous robotics with assistive mobility platforms, while also showing the feasibility of the proposed integration and identifying the main technical challenges that must be addressed before moving toward user-ready, accessible, and intelligent mobility solutions. A video demonstrating the experimental setup and results is available at: https://youtu.be/LVAix_Qx7bM.

AI.tldr: Preliminary autonomous powered wheelchair prototype that integrates perception, gesture-based interaction, and navigation on a self-balancing wheelchair, demonstrated with hailing and people-following in indoor scenarios; shows feasibility and outlines main technical challenges for user-ready autonomous assistive mobility.
AI.motivation: Address the limited autonomy of powered wheelchairs and the lack of integration with advanced perception and navigation in real-world environments, enabling safer, more intuitive autonomous assistive mobility.
AI.method: Integrates RGB-D perception and LiDAR-based localization/navigation into Genny Zero, a commercial self-balancing wheelchair; adds gesture-based interaction; validates through two assistive applications (hailing and people-following) with constrained indoor navigation.
AI.result: Feasibility of the integration is demonstrated; successful implementation of hailing and leader-follower navigation; identifies key technical challenges to be overcome before user-ready deployment.
AI.conclusion: Shows strong potential for combining autonomous robotics with assistive mobility platforms, while highlighting that substantial work remains to address challenges for real-world usability and accessibility.

title: Heckman-Corrected Epistemic Uncertainty: Selection on Unobservables Defeats Importance Weighting
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Every number machine-generated from committed result JSONs (regenerate-and-diff verified); faithfulness-gated Heckman implementation reproduces published Stata reference output. Code, data, and tests archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21210466. Companion paper (survivor bias in learning-curve surrogates) forthcoming
summary: Training data for machine learning is routinely collected by a selection process the model never sees: loans are observed only when granted, outcomes only when a test was ordered. The standard fixes -- importance weighting, covariate-shift correction, MAR imputation -- assume selection is ignorable given observables. Econometrics solved the harder case in 1979: Heckman's two-equation model jointly fits a probit selection equation and an outcome equation linked through correlated errors, and the inverse-Mills-ratio term corrects for selection on unobservables, where importance weighting is structurally helpless. We instantiate this for deep epistemic uncertainty: a deep outcome network, a linear selection head, and a joint bivariate-normal likelihood over all units, ensembled for predictive variance. In a controlled generator where sampling probability depends on an unobservable correlated (rho up to 0.9) with the outcome noise, deep ensembles, MC dropout, and GP baselines are overconfident exactly where data was avoided: coverage of nominal-90% intervals falls to 64.4% at rho=0.9, and importance weighting with oracle propensities does not fix it (43.1%) -- reweighting corrects the covariate distribution, not the conditional bias E[y|x,selected] != E[y|x]. The Heckman correction restores coverage (88.9%) when the selection equation has an instrument -- a variable affecting selection but not the outcome -- and degrades measurably without one (40.3%); we chart this honesty curve rather than hide it. On real tabular data with induced MNAR selection, the corrected intervals are the best-calibrated (lowest region-ECE) non-oracle method in selected-against regions; baselines matching its raw coverage do so only by over-widening everywhere. Our estimators reproduce classic Stata output to seven digits. We state which identification regime a practitioner is in, and release the code.

AI.tldr: Extends Heckman-style selection correction to deep ML models to handle non-ignorable MNAR data; shows standard uncertainty methods fail when selection is tied to unobservables, but a Heckman approach with an instrument can restore nominal calibration; on real data, corrected intervals are best in selected regions; code is released and regimes of identification are reported.
AI.motivation: ML training data are often MNAR due to selection processes. Traditional fixes assume ignorability given observables; Heckman's two-equation model provides identification under correlation between selection and outcome errors (and with instruments). The work investigates how this extends to deep models and uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Proposes a deep outcome network with a linear selection head and a joint bivariate-normal likelihood across units, with ensembles to quantify predictive variance. Experiments include a controlled generator where selection probability correlates with outcome noise (rho up to 0.9). Comparisons between deep ensembles, MC dropout, GP baselines, and an oracle importance-weighting baseline. Uses an instrument in the selection equation to restore identification; evaluates calibration via coverage and region-ECE on real MNAR tabular data; reproduces Stata outputs.
AI.result: When rho=0.9, nominal-90% intervals have only 64.4% coverage for baseline methods; importance weighting with oracle propensities does not fix conditional bias. Heckman correction with an instrument yields 88.9% coverage, while without an instrument it degrades to 40.3%. On real data, corrected intervals are the best-calibrated non-oracle method in selected regions, while baselines that match raw coverage tend to over-widen elsewhere. The estimators reproduce classic Stata output to seven digits.
AI.conclusion: Identification regime matters for uncertainty calibration under MNAR. A Heckman-style, instrument-augmented correction can restore confidence interval coverage in the presence of non-ignorable selection; absent an instrument, calibration deteriorates. The work provides explicit regime labeling and releases code for practitioners.

title: Complementary Roles of Image Classification and Vessel Segmentation in AI-Based Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity Plus Disease in a Kenyan Preterm Cohort
summary:
Background. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a preventable cause of childhood blindness, with rising burden in low- and middle-income countries where ROP-trained ophthalmologists are scarce. Plus disease, marked by retinal vessel dilation and tortuosity, triggers treatment but is subjective and variable. Automated screening could extend specialist reach, but African evidence remains limited.
  Methods. We analysed 121 Kenyan preterm infants, covering 237 eyes and 1,635 fundus images graded as No Plus, Pre-Plus or Plus. Vessel annotations from two graders supported segmentation training. Eleven configurations were evaluated for eye-level Plus detection using patient-grouped nested cross-validation, including image classifiers, multiple-instance learning, multi-task segmentation-classification, and segment-then-classify pipelines.
  Results. Vessel segmentation was feasible, achieving pooled Dice 0.533, IoU 0.368, sensitivity 0.623 and specificity 0.979 on held-out images. RGB classifiers were highly sensitive but over-referred, while segmentation-coupled models were more specific. Combining approaches improved performance: an OR-based screen achieved the highest sensitivity, an AND-based confirmation achieved the highest specificity, and a probability ensemble gave the best balanced performance, with sensitivity 0.692, specificity 0.914 and balanced accuracy 0.803, outperforming the vision classifier alone.
  Conclusions. Classification and vessel segmentation are complementary for ROP Plus detection in Kenyan data. Classifiers support sensitive case-finding, while segmentation improves specificity and reduces over-referral. African ROP AI systems should use combined workflows and undergo prospective multi-site validation.

AI.tldr: Combined vessel segmentation and classification improves Plus detection in Kenyan preterm infants; segmentation boosts specificity, classifiers boost sensitivity, yielding a balanced, outperformance over a single-model approach.
AI.motivation: ROP is preventable blindness; increasing burden in LMICs with few trained ophthalmologists; Plus diagnosis is subjective; evidence in Africa scarce; need automated, generalizable screening pipelines.
AI.method: Analysis of 121 Kenyan preterm infants (237 eyes; 1,635 fundus images) graded No Plus, Pre-Plus, Plus. Vessel annotations from two graders used to train segmentation. Eleven configurations for eye-level Plus detection were evaluated using patient-grouped nested cross-validation, including RGB image classifiers, multiple-instance learning, multi-task segmentation-classification, and segment-then-classify pipelines.
AI.result: Vessel segmentation feasible: Dice 0.533, IoU 0.368, sensitivity 0.623, specificity 0.979. RGB classifiers were highly sensitive but over-referring; segmentation-coupled models were more specific. Combining approaches improved performance: OR-based screen yielded highest sensitivity, AND-based confirmation yielded highest specificity, and a probability ensemble gave best balanced performance (sensitivity 0.692, specificity 0.914, balanced accuracy 0.803), outperforming vision classifier alone.
AI.conclusion: Classification and vessel segmentation are complementary for ROP Plus detection in Kenyan data. Use combined workflows to optimize sensitivity and specificity; segmentation reduces over-referral. African ROP AI systems should use combined workflows and undergo prospective multi-site validation.

title: Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models
summary: The increasing adoption of end-to-end learning for autonomous driving introduces increased model complexity and opacity, raising the risk of learning undesired or erroneous behavior. In this work, we integrate unsupervised dictionary learning as a post hoc interpretability module within state-of-the-art driving models to decompose driving behavior into semantically meaningful concepts while demonstrating their causal influence on the model's driving decisions. We propose a stepwise framework for extracting and interpreting meaningful concepts from the end-to-end model and connecting them to the multifaceted model outputs, thereby revealing the underlying decision-making logic for the prediction of future trajectories. Furthermore, targeted interventions at the concept level allow us to manipulate and correct driving decisions, resulting in measurable improvements in overall driving performance. We thus demonstrate how interpretability can effectively be used to reduce model opacity, uncover erroneous behavior, and enable targeted mitigation, ultimately boosting model performance.

AI.tldr: End-to-end autonomous driving models can be made interpretable by adding an unsupervised dictionary-learning module post hoc to decompose behavior into semantically meaningful concepts, link them causally to driving decisions, and use concept-level interventions to improve performance.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving models are highly capable but opaque, risking unsafe or erroneous behavior. This work aims to reveal the decision logic by extracting interpretable concepts and demonstrating their causal influence on predictions, while enabling corrective interventions.
AI.method: Introduce unsupervised dictionary learning as a post hoc interpretability module. Develop a stepwise framework to extract and interpret concepts from the end-to-end model, connect these concepts to the model’s multi-output predictions (e.g., future trajectories), and perform interventions at the concept level to manipulate and correct decisions.
AI.result: Evidence of causal influence: the extracted concepts affect driving decisions. Concept-level interventions lead to measurable improvements in driving performance, indicating reduced opacity and the ability to mitigate erroneous behavior.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting end-to-end driving via concept-level, unsupervised dictionary learning can reduce opacity, uncover errors, enable targeted mitigation, and boost overall model performance.

title: Learning to Throw Objects Safely in Multi-Obstacle Environments
comment: This paper has been presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA), 2026
summary: Robotic throwing enables fast and efficient object placement beyond the robot's immediate workspace, but reliable throwing in cluttered environments remains underexplored. Existing approaches, such as TossingBot, learn throwing strategies from visual input but assume obstacle-free settings. In this paper, we address the problem of throwing objects into a target basket while avoiding obstacles placed randomly in the scene. We introduce a potential field state representation that compactly encodes both basket attraction and obstacle repulsion on a fixed-size grid, enabling reinforcement learning (RL) policies to generalize across arbitrary numbers and configurations of obstacles. The policy is initialized from kinesthetic demonstrations and optimized in simulation using three state-of-the-art RL algorithms (SAC, DDPG, TD3). Among these, SAC achieves the most consistent performance across scenarios. We compare the potential field representation against explicit state encodings and demonstrate that it achieves higher success rates and better scalability to unseen obstacle configurations. Real-robot experiments with unseen throwable objects confirm robust sim-to-real transfer, achieving up to $90\%$ success in cluttered scenes. These results demonstrate that PFR provides a practical and robust representation for safe and efficient robotic throwing in unstructured environments. A video showcasing our experiments is available at: https://youtu.be/ZZnJf8ua2dE

AI.tldr: A potential-field state representation for reinforcement learning enables robust, generalizable robotic throwing in cluttered environments, with SAC performing best among SAC/DDPG/TD3; real-robot tests show high sim-to-real transfer (up to 90% success).
AI.motivation: Enable reliable throwing in cluttered, unstructured environments where obstacles exist, overcoming the obstacle-free assumption in prior works like TossingBot and enabling generalization to arbitrary obstacle configurations.
AI.method: Introduce a compact potential field state representation on a fixed-size grid encoding basket attraction and obstacle repulsion. Use it as input to RL policies, initialized from kinesthetic demonstrations, and trained in simulation with SAC, DDPG, and TD3. Compare against explicit state encodings and conduct real-robot experiments with unseen throwable objects.
AI.result: The potential-field representation yields higher success rates and better scalability to unseen obstacle configurations than explicit encodings. SAC achieves the most consistent performance across scenarios. Real-robot experiments demonstrate robust sim-to-real transfer, achieving up to 90% success in cluttered scenes.
AI.conclusion: PFR provides a practical and robust representation for safe and efficient robotic throwing in unstructured environments, enabling generalization to arbitrary obstacle configurations and effective sim-to-real transfer.

title: Level-Crossing Density as a Mesh-Free High-Frequency Auxiliary Loss for Implicit Neural Representations
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code, raw experiment logs, and estimator unit tests: https://github.com/gunnerhowe/Research
summary: The Minkowski functionals of a field's excursion sets -- area, boundary measure, and Euler characteristic -- describe its level-set morphology; the Euler characteristic is the cheapest handle on topology. We derive smooth Monte-Carlo estimators for all three of a continuous neural field, evaluated at scattered points via the co-area formula and Gauss-Bonnet, using only autodiff: no grid, no complex, no persistence. The estimator is accurate to 1-3% against exact topology in 2D and 3D, and costs about 3 ms per iteration where a persistent-homology (PH) loss on a cubical grid costs 650-1000 ms -- a 250x gap. We establish four design rules without which these losses silently fail: a dense level ladder (invariants are flat in the parameters away from transitions), a $C^2$ backbone (ReLU nets hide curvature in kinks), the full Minkowski vector (Euler characteristic alone is an alternating sum, gamed by debris-hole cancellation; pricing perimeter closes the channel), and sampling-scale coverage. In 2D the vector-valued cap is the only method in a controlled comparison that both repairs topology (3/3 seeds) and preserves fidelity -- uniform smoothing repairs at 11-17x the fidelity cost, and the Euler term alone repairs nothing. In 3D neural-SDF fitting, however, a failure mode we believe general to any sampled soft topology objective appears: gradient descent adversarially hides topological noise below the sampling density, where the estimator is blind -- spurious-feature counts are invariant to 4x more samples, and closing the window needs cubically many points, erasing the cost advantage. A grid-based PH baseline, whose complex is the evaluation resolution, solves the same benchmark ($4/9$ exact; median $b_1$ error 1 vs. ours above $10^4$). The 250x cost of persistence is, at present, the price of having no null space. We release estimators, receipts, and benchmarks.

AI.tldr: We present smooth, differentiable, grid-free estimators for the Minkowski functionals (area, boundary length, Euler characteristic) of a field’s excursion sets, evaluated at scattered points via co-area formula and Gauss–Bonnet using autodiff only. They are 1–3% accurate vs exact topology in 2D/3D, and run ~3 ms per iteration—over 250× faster than grid-based persistent-homology losses. The work yields four design rules (dense level ladder, C2 backbone, full Minkowski vector, sampling-scale coverage) and demonstrates in 2D that a vector-valued cap both repairs topology and preserves fidelity, while in 3D a failure mode arises where gradient descent hides topological noise below sampling density. A grid-based PH baseline can achieve tighter b1 accuracy at higher cost. The authors release estimators, receipts, and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Topology-aware, differentiable, grid-free morphologies of neural fields are valuable for regularization and analysis, but existing methods (e.g., persistent homology on grids) are slow and brittle. A fast, smooth, autodiff-friendly estimator of Minkowski functionals could enable robust, scalable topology control during neural-field optimization.
AI.method: Derive smooth Monte-Carlo estimators for area, boundary measure, and Euler characteristic of a field’s excursion sets by combining the co-area formula with Gauss–Bonnet, computed at scattered sample points using autodiff. No grids or persistent-homology are required. Assemble a Minkowski vector (area, perimeter, Euler term, etc.) and enforce robustness via four design rules: (1) dense level ladder (invariants flat away from transitions), (2) C2 backbone (protect curvature from ReLU kinks), (3) full Minkowski vector (avoid Euler-only cancellation), and (4) sampling-scale coverage. Compare 2D and 3D neural-field regimes against a grid PH baseline on cubical grids; report fidelity, speed, and failure modes.
AI.result: Estimation accuracy of 1–3% against exact topology in 2D/3D. Per-iteration cost ~3 ms, versus PH losses on grids costing ~650–1000 ms (≈250× slower). In 2D, the vector-valued Minkowski cap uniquely repairs topology and preserves fidelity with 11–17× fidelity-cost penalties for alternatives like uniform smoothing; Euler-term alone performs poorly. In 3D neural-SDF fitting, a gradient-descent failure mode emerges: topological noise can be hidden below sampling density, with the estimator blind; spurious features persist even with 4× more samples, and closing the topology requires cubically more points. A grid-based PH baseline (with resolution set by evaluation complexity) achieves 4/9 exact and median b1 error ~1, outperforming the proposed approach in this regime, but at significantly higher cost. The work also provides benchmarks and releases estimators and receipts.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers fast, differentiable, grid-free topology estimators for neural-field morphology via Minkowski functionals, enabling efficient topology-aware analysis and regularization. It shows substantial speedups over grid-based PH and clarifies design choices essential for reliability, while also revealing a failure mode in 3D where gradient-based optimization can hide topology under sampling density. The work includes practical guidelines and open benchmarks, with a clear speed–fidelity trade-off relative to persistent homology.

title: Realistic Compound-Lens Defocus Blur Synthesis
summary: Defocus blur degrades fine image structures and limits visual perception, which can adversely affect downstream vision tasks. Although recent deep learning deblurring methods have achieved strong performance, their effectiveness depends on training data and often degrades across cameras and lenses due to limited optical diversity and realism in existing datasets. In this paper, we propose a pipeline for synthesizing realistic defocus deblurring datasets for diverse compound lenses. It integrates efficient wave-optics PSF computation via Debye CZT propagation, depth-aware defocus rendering with occlusion handling, and blur synthesis in the radiometrically linear space with camera ISP simulation. This unified pipeline enables the scalable generation of photorealistic defocus datasets with diverse lens characteristics. Using our pipeline, we generate CLDefocus, a large-scale synthetic dataset containing lens-diverse defocus image pairs. We further analyze the limitations of real-captured defocus datasets and show that such imperfections can bias full-reference evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that models trained on CLDefocus achieve improved cross-device generalization compared to models trained on existing real and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: A scalable pipeline to synthesize photorealistic defocus datasets across diverse lenses, yielding CLDefocus, which improves cross-device generalization for deblurring models.
AI.motivation: Defocus blur degrades fine image structures and current datasets lack sufficient optical diversity and realism, leading to poor cross-device generalization and biased evaluations on real datasets.
AI.method: 1) Compute PSF with efficient wave-optics using Debye CZT propagation; 2) render defocus with depth awareness and occlusion handling; 3) synthesize blur in radiometrically linear space with a camera ISP simulation; 4) assemble lens-diverse image pairs into a large-scale dataset (CLDefocus).
AI.result: Models trained on CLDefocus show improved cross-device generalization compared to models trained on existing real or synthetic datasets; analysis indicates real-captured datasets introduce imperfections that bias full-reference evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Optics-aware, radiometric-consistent data synthesis across diverse lenses yields more robust deblurring models and scalable datasets; CLDefocus demonstrates the value of realistic, lens-diverse synthetic data for cross-device performance.

title: TopoBrick: Agentic Topology Sampling of Exogenous Variables for Zero-Shot Building IoT Forecasting
summary: Building sensors are embedded in physical topology, spatial hierarchy, and operational context, yet existing forecasters often treat them as isolated time series or rely on fixed covariate sets. We present TopoBrick, a training-free framework for zero-shot building IoT (Internet-of-Things) forecasting. TopoBrick uses building knowledge graphs to construct a compact structural skeleton and employs an agentic topology sampler to select target-specific exogenous variables. The selected variables are organized by deployment-time availability, separating past-known sensor states from future-known calendar, schedule, and meteorological exogenous variables. Across three real-world buildings, TopoBrick outperforms strong zero-shot foundation-model baselines and remains competitive with fully trained building-specific models. Ablations show that topology-aware sampling is more reliable than random, ontology-only, or fixed-hop selection, especially for physically coupled HVAC and weather-driven sensing variables.

AI.tldr: TopoBrick enables training-free zero-shot IoT forecasting for buildings by using knowledge graphs and topology-aware exogenous-variable selection, outperforming baselines and rivaling trained models.
AI.motivation: Conventional forecasters treat sensors as isolated time series, ignoring building topology and context; need zero-shot, topology-informed approach for accurate forecasting with exogenous variables.
AI.method: Builds a building knowledge-graph–derived skeleton; uses an agentic topology sampler to pick target-specific exogenous variables; organizes variables by deployment-time availability distinguishing past sensor states from future calendar/meteorological variables; training-free.
AI.result: Outperforms zero-shot foundation-model baselines; competitive with fully trained building-specific models across three real buildings; ablations show topology-aware sampling is more reliable than random, ontology-only, or fixed-hop selections, particularly for HVAC and weather-driven sensing variables.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware, knowledge-graph-based, training-free approach improves zero-shot building IoT forecasting; topology-aware variable selection is key for physiologically coupled variables.

title: From Foundation to Application: Improving VLA Models in Practice
summary: Despite recent progress of VLA foundation models, the disparity between laboratory conditions and real-world applications continues to impede their practical implementation.
