To bridge this gap, we present LingBot-VLA 2.0, which advances LingBot-VLA through improvements in three functional domains. (1) Generalization across tasks and embodiments. Compared to the previous version, we revamp the data processing pipeline and curate around 60,000 hours of data for pretraining, including 50,000 hours of robot trajectories spanning 20 robot configurations and 10,000 hours of egocentric human videos. (2) Expanded action space in addition to dual-arm hardware platforms. In particular, our system accommodates degrees of freedom for the heads, waists, mobile bases, and dexterous hands, thereby empowering the robots to tackle more complex tasks in practical scenarios. (3) Predictive dynamics modeling for improved temporal reasoning. Specifically, we formulate future prediction as a proxy task, facilitated by a video representation model for semantic priors and a depth estimation model for geometric cues. Evaluations on the GM-100 benchmark, conducted in a generalist setting, validate the beneficial impact of these proposed modifications. Furthermore, benefiting from the expanded pretraining data that covers whole-body degrees of freedom, LingBot-VLA-2.0 demonstrates strong cross-embodiment long-horizon mobile manipulation capability across the two robotic platforms.

AI.tldr: LingBot-VLA 2.0 broadens generalization across tasks and embodiments with a large-scale, whole-body pretraining dataset, expanded action space, and predictive dynamics to improve temporal reasoning; evaluated on GM-100, it shows cross-embodiment, long-horizon mobile manipulation across two robot platforms.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between laboratory conditions and real-world deployment by enabling generalization across tasks, embodiments, and physical platforms, and by enhancing temporal reasoning through predictive dynamics.
AI.method: 1) Data pipeline overhaul and curation of ~60k hours for pretraining: 50k hours of robot trajectories across 20 configurations; 10k hours of egocentric human videos. 2) Expanded action space to include heads, waists, mobile bases, and dexterous hands for multi-embodiment manipulation. 3) Predictive dynamics via a proxy task using a video representation model for semantic priors and a depth estimation model for geometric cues. 4) Evaluation on GM-100 in a generalist setting, demonstrating cross-embodiment long-horizon manipulation on two platforms.
AI.result: The approach yields strong cross-embodiment long-horizon mobile manipulation performance and confirms the positive impact of the data, architecture, and prediction-task modifications across two robot platforms on GM-100.
AI.conclusion: LingBot-VLA-2.0 extends LingBot-VLA to whole-body, cross-embodiment capabilities with substantially larger pretraining data and predictive dynamics, moving toward practical real-world deployment; its gains are demonstrated on GM-100 and across two platforms.

title: Decision-Focused Scenario Generation and Selection for Efficient and Robust Grid Dispatch
summary: The increasing uncertainty from flexible demand and renewable generation has made distributionally robust optimization (DRO) an important tool for robust power system dispatch. DRO relies on forecast scenarios to construct ambiguity sets, but conventional scenario generation pipelines are often trained in an accuracy-oriented manner and may neglect spatial correlations among uncertainties. This mismatch can produce ambiguity sets that are statistically plausible but suboptimal for downstream operation. This work proposes a decision-focused generative framework for correlated scenario generation in DRO-based dispatch. Instead of training generative models solely to fit the historical uncertainty distribution, the proposed framework optimizes generated scenarios according to their induced downstream operational cost. The proposed framework is tailored to mainstream generative models, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models, while capturing the joint distribution of uncertainties across buses. To improve computational tractability, we further develop a differentiable scenario selector that selects decision-relevant scenarios from a generated pool and can be trained within the same decision-focused pipeline. Case studies demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively reduces 0.80%-2.02% operational cost across different generative models compared to accuracy-oriented methods.

AI.tldr: Decision-focused, correlated scenario generation for DRO-based power dispatch using VAEs/GANs/diffusion with a differentiable scenario selector; yields modest but consistent reductions in operational cost vs accuracy-focused methods.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty from flexible demand and renewables, coupled with spatial correlations across buses, makes accuracy-only scenario generation suboptimal for DRO-based dispatch. Need to align scenario generation with downstream operational costs.
AI.method: A decision-focused generative framework that learns joint uncertainty distributions across buses using mainstream generative models (VAE, GAN, diffusion). Introduces a differentiable scenario selector to pick decision-relevant scenarios from generated pools, all trained within a single decision-focused loop to minimize operational cost.
AI.result: Case studies show 0.80%–2.02% reductions in operational cost across generative models compared to accuracy-oriented baselines.
AI.conclusion: Aligning scenario generation with downstream optimization improves DRO-based dispatch; differentiable scenario selection enhances tractability; framework is applicable across multiple generative architectures.

title: Breaking Spurious Correlations via Generative Randomization and Cross-Variant Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Deep neural networks trained with Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often fail under distribution shifts because they exploit spurious correlations between object labels and background context. Recent generative approaches address this issue by creating counterfactual images with altered contexts, but typically use these samples as standard data augmentation, leaving the model free to retain background-sensitive representations. We propose a two-stage framework that uses generative intervention to explicitly learn background-invariant visual representations. First, we isolate the foreground object using zero-shot segmentation and generate context-shifted variants with a structure-preserving diffusion model, preserving object identity while varying the surrounding environment. We then introduce Cross-Variant Self-Supervised Learning, where variants of the same object under different backgrounds form positive pairs in a contrastive objective. This encourages the encoder to align object-centric representations while suppressing background-specific cues. Then, we fine-tune the pretrained encoder using an ERM warm-up followed by GroupDRO with layer-wise learning rates. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks demonstrate best worst-group performance, achieving 92.5% on Waterbirds, 81.7% on MetaShift, and 87.4% on NICO++. Code: https://github.com/surajyadav-research/GRSSL

AI.tldr: A two-stage generative intervention approach (GRSSL) learns background-invariant representations by creating context-shifted foreground variants with diffusion models and enforcing cross-variant contrastive learning, followed by ERM warm-up and GroupDRO fine-tuning; achieves state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds (92.5), MetaShift (81.7), and NICO++ (87.4).
AI.motivation: ERM models fail under distribution shifts by exploiting spurious background-object correlations. Generative data augmentations help but often leave background cues in representations; this work aims to explicitly learn background-invariant object representations.
AI.method: Stage 1: Isolate foreground via zero-shot segmentation and generate context-shifted, structure-preserving variants with a diffusion model that preserves object identity while varying surroundings. Stage 2: Cross-Variant Self-Supervised Learning (SSL): treat different background variants of the same object as positive pairs in a contrastive objective to align object-centric representations and suppress background cues. Fine-tuning: ERM warm-up followed by GroupDRO with layer-wise learning rates.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on distribution-shift benchmarks shows strong worst-group performance: Waterbirds 92.5%, MetaShift 81.7%, NICO++ 87.4%. Code provided at the referenced repository.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that explicit background-invariant learning through targeted generative interventions and cross-variant SSL improves robustness to background-based distribution shifts, outperforming standard ERM and augmentation baselines and generalizing across datasets.

title: A Definition and Roadmap for World Models
summary: World models -- internal simulators that learn the structure and dynamics of an environment -- have become one of the most actively debated concepts in AI. From model-based reinforcement learning and video generation to embodied robotics and ultimately, physical AI, researchers across AI subfields are building systems that they call "world models", yet there is no consensus on what a world model fundamentally is, what it should predict, or how it should be built. This perspective article provides a scientific definition of world models, discussions of their key technical aspects, and a staged roadmap for developing effective world models.

AI.tldr: A perspective article defines world models, surveys their technical aspects, and outlines a staged roadmap for developing effective world models.
AI.motivation: There is no consensus on what a world model fundamentally is, what it should predict, or how to build it; a unified definition and actionable roadmap are needed to advance research across AI subfields.
AI.method: Conceptual synthesis in a perspective piece: propose a formal definition, discuss core components (representation, dynamics, prediction targets, uncertainty, evaluation), and present a staged roadmap for development.
AI.result: Proposes a rigorous definition and delineates key technical considerations; outlines a multi-stage development plan with milestones to guide future work.
AI.conclusion: A structured framework and roadmap are necessary to unify world-model research and accelerate progress; the article contributes a formal definition and a practical roadmap.

title: WristMimic: Full-Body Humanoid Control with Wrist-Guided Manipulation
summary: Retargeting human object interaction demonstrations to physics based simulation requires reproducing not only body motion but also the object motion and contacts that make manipulation succeed. However, position only hand trajectories do not specify the contact forces needed to manipulate objects, and directly tracking them can overconstrain contact rich finger behavior. We introduce WristMimic, a wrist guided whole body control framework that explicitly separates contact free body motion from contact rich hand manipulation. The contact free body and wrist are guided by kinematic pose targets, whereas the fingers are not directly supervised by human hand pose. Instead, they learn grasping and manipulation behaviors from object tracking and contact outcomes. Our key insight is that the wrist is the natural gate between these two regimes. It is largely free from contact and can be tracked kinematically, yet it determines the global hand configuration and places the fingers within reachable grasp affordances. To ensure reliable wrist placement during interaction, we introduce wrist specific reset constraints and reward prioritization. Experiments show that WristMimic matches or surpasses methods using full finger pose supervision while enabling finger agnostic retargeting across diverse hand embodiments.

AI.tldr: WristMimic decouples wrist-guided, contact-free body motion from contact-rich hand manipulation, enabling finger-agnostic retargeting with competitive results.
AI.motivation: To enable physics-based retargeting of human object interactions by not relying on full finger pose supervision; position-only hand trajectories fail to specify contact forces and can overconstrain finger behavior.
AI.method: Introduce WristMimic, a wrist-guided whole-body control framework that separates contact-free body motion from contact-rich hand manipulation. The wrist and body are driven by kinematic pose targets; fingers are learned from object tracking and contact outcomes rather than direct finger pose supervision. The wrist acts as the interface between regimes, with wrist-specific reset constraints and reward prioritization to ensure stable placement.
AI.result: Experiments show WristMimic matches or surpasses methods using full finger pose supervision and enables finger-agnostic retargeting across diverse hand embodiments.
AI.conclusion: WristMimic provides a robust decoupled control paradigm for retargeting human-object interactions to physics-based simulators, leveraging the wrist as the primary mediator between free motion and manipulation to improve generalization across embodiments.

title: AbICL: In-Context Learning for Antigen-Specific Antibody Affinity Ranking
summary: Accurate ranking of antibody candidates according to their binding affinity is essential for therapeutic antibody discovery. However, existing methods treat affinity comparisons independently and ignore the contextual information encoded in other labeled comparisons, limiting their ability to capture antigen-specific binding landscapes. For many target antigens, a small number of experimentally characterized affinity comparisons are often available. An important question is whether the model can exploit these existing comparisons to infer antigen-specific ranking patterns that facilitate subsequent affinity ranking. This form of learning from labeled demonstrations closely resembles the paradigm of In-Context Learning, motivating us to revisit antibody affinity ranking from an ICL perspective. To this end, we propose AbICL, an ICL framework for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking. AbICL combines a pretrained structural encoder with a context ranking head and is trained with an episodic meta-training strategy that enables the model to leverage support demonstrations for test-time adaptation without gradient updates. Experiments on the AbRank benchmark demonstrate that AbICL consistently outperforms existing ranking baselines across almost all data splits and evaluation benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the value of contextual demonstrations depends on how well they match the target inference task, and becomes increasingly pronounced under distribution shift and fine-grained affinity discrimination. These findings highlight the potential of ICL as an effective paradigm for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking, particularly in challenging settings where a single global ranking function is insufficient.

AI.tldr: AbICL is an in-context learning framework for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking that uses a pretrained structural encoder and episodic meta-training to adapt using labeled demonstrations at test time without gradient updates, outperforming baselines on AbRank across splits and showing context relevance, especially under distribution shift and fine-grained discrimination.
AI.motivation: Existing affinity ranking methods treat comparisons independently and ignore contextual information from other labeled comparisons. With limited labeled data per antigen, leveraging demonstrations to infer antigen-specific ranking patterns could improve performance, aligning with In-Context Learning (ICL).
AI.method: AbICL integrates a pretrained structural encoder with a context-aware ranking head and trains via episodic meta-learning to enable test-time adaptation using support demonstrations without gradient updates, effectively conditioning affinity rankings on available demonstrations for the target antigen.
AI.result: On the AbRank benchmark, AbICL consistently outperforms existing ranking baselines across most data splits and benchmarks. Analyses show contextual demonstrations are most beneficial when they closely match the target task and their impact increases under distribution shift and when discriminating fine-grained affinities.
AI.conclusion: ICL-based approaches are a promising direction for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking, particularly in challenging settings where a single global ranking function falls short; AbICL provides empirical evidence of robust gains and highlights the value of contextual demonstrations for adaptation.

title: AVA-VLM: Adaptive Visual Attention-Vision Language Model for In-the-Wild Construction Site Monitoring
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are promising for construction-site monitoring, and recent construction-tailored VLMs have primarily adapted pretrained VLMs through direct QA-style fine-tuning from a single global image. We argue that this direct paradigm remains limited for in-the-wild deployment in terms of operational range, reliability under reduced-resolution inputs, and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose AVA-VLM, an Adaptive Visual Attention-Vision Language Model that follows a human-inspired coarse-to-fine reasoning strategy. AVA-VLM first reasons over a low-resolution global image and selectively requests a high-resolution local crop only when detailed inspection is needed, similar to how a human inspector zooms in on hard-to-see yet important areas. We further introduce a region-aware Chain-of-Thought dataset that teaches the model when to inspect, where to crop, and how to use local evidence. Experiments show that AVA-VLM improves reliability under long-distance and reduced-resolution conditions while substantially reducing visual-token usage.

AI.tldr: AVA-VLM introduces adaptive coarse-to-fine reasoning for vision-language models, initiating with a low-res global image and requesting high-res local crops only when needed; accompanied by a region-aware Chain-of-Thought dataset. It improves reliability under long-distance/reduced-resolution conditions and reduces visual-token usage.
AI.motivation: Direct fine-tuning from a single global image limits operational range, robustness to low-resolution inputs, and inference efficiency for in-the-wild deployment; a human-inspired coarse-to-fine strategy could mitigate these issues.
AI.method: Propose AVA-VLM: an Adaptive Visual Attention-Vision Language Model that first reasons over a low-resolution global image and selectively requests high-resolution local crops when detailed inspection is needed. Introduce a region-aware Chain-of-Thought dataset to teach when to inspect, where to crop, and how to fuse local evidence.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved reliability under long-distance and reduced-resolution conditions and substantial reductions in visual-token usage.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive coarse-to-fine reasoning with region-aware CoT enables more reliable and efficient construction-site monitoring with VLMs, bridging the gap between global reasoning and local evidence.

title: ExplAIner: A Declarative Query Language for Explaining Classification Models
summary: The XAI community has studied a wide range of queries and scores for explaining predictions of ML models. From a data management perspective, this proliferation of explanation notions calls for declarative query languages in which such notions can be specified, combined, and analyzed uniformly. In this paper, we develop such a framework for Boolean models. We first revisit FOIL, an interpretability query language for black-box models, and show that it has two fundamental limitations: it cannot express central optimality-based explanation queries, and its evaluation problem over decision trees is hard for every level of the polynomial hierarchy. We then introduce ExplAIner, a query language based on FOIL with an extended vocabulary and a layered structure. We show that ExplAIner can express a broad family of explanation notions, including abductive, contrastive, feature-based, and distance-based queries. We also prove that the evaluation problem for each query in ExplAIner belongs to the Boolean hierarchy over every class of Boolean models for which some basic predicates can be evaluated in polynomial time. In particular, that property holds for deterministic and decomposable Boolean circuits. Finally, we introduce Opt-FOIL, an optimization-oriented fragment of ExplAIner for computing explanations that are minimal with respect to strict partial orders, and prove that its evaluation problem is in $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$ under the same tractability assumptions. These complexity results have a direct algorithmic consequence: a fixed ExplAIner query can be evaluated with a fixed number of calls to a SAT solver, while a notion of explanation specified in Opt-FOIL can be computed with a polynomial number of such calls. This is particularly relevant in formal XAI, where SAT solvers have been successfully used to compute explanations for several classes of ML models.

AI.tldr: Proposes ExplAIner, a declarative query language extending FOIL for Boolean models to express various explanation notions (abductive, contrastive, feature-based, distance-based); establishes complexity bounds (Boolean hierarchy; FP^NP) and introduces Opt-FOIL for optimization-based explanations, with SAT-solver implications.
AI.motivation: XAI has a proliferation of explanation notions; a uniform Declarative framework is needed to specify, combine, and analyze explanations for black-box models. FOIL's limitations motivate an extended language for Boolean models.
AI.method: Extend FOIL with an enriched vocabulary and layered structure to form ExplAIner, enabling a broad family of explanations (abductive, contrastive, feature-based, distance-based). Prove that evaluation of ExplAIner queries falls within the Boolean hierarchy for classes where basic predicates are P-time (e.g., deterministic and decomposable Boolean circuits). Introduce Opt-FOIL, an optimization-oriented fragment, for minimal explanations under strict partial orders, with evaluation in FP^NP. Argue that a fixed ExplAIner query requires a fixed number of SAT calls, while Opt-FOIL requires a polynomial number of SAT calls.
AI.result: ExplAIner can express a wide range of explanation notions (abductive, contrastive, feature-based, distance-based). Its evaluation lies in the Boolean hierarchy for suitable Boolean models (e.g., deterministic and decomposable circuits). Opt-FOIL attains FP^NP evaluation complexity, enabling optimization of explanations under partial orders. Algorithmically, fixed ExplAIner queries reduce to a fixed bound on SAT calls; Opt-FOIL queries admit a polynomial bound on SAT calls, aligning with practical SAT-based computation in formal XAI.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified declarative framework for explanations over Boolean models, enabling uniform specification, combination, and analysis of explanations. The complexity results yield concrete SAT-solvers deployment guidance and demonstrate practical relevance in formal XAI for computing minimal explanations.

title: SIEVE: Structure-Aware Data Selection for Imitation Learning with VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained by imitation learning on large-scale robot demonstration datasets, but more data does not necessarily yield better policies due to redundancy, noise, and uneven coverage. Existing data selection methods often assess demonstrations at either the trajectory or state-action level, missing the reusable structures that compose long-horizon behaviors. In this paper, we propose SIEVE, a structure-aware data selection method for VLA imitation learning. SIEVE views demonstrations as compositions of reusable primitives and transition interfaces. It first discovers visuo-motor primitives from segmented trajectories, then allocates selection budgets to composition patterns by maximizing reuse-aware structural exposure under diminishing returns. Finally, it selects medoid trajectories within each composition-pattern bucket to retain central, stable, and imitation-friendly demonstrations. Experiments across multiple datasets, benchmarks, and VLA models show that SIEVE consistently outperforms competitive data selection baselines. Notably, SIEVE can surpass full-data training while using only 50% of demonstrations and 50% of training steps, suggesting that reusable structure, captured through primitives and transitions, is an important signal for efficient VLA imitation learning.

AI.tldr: SIEVE is a structure-aware data selection framework for Vision-Language-Action imitation learning that models demonstrations as reusable primitives and transitions, selecting medoid trajectories per pattern to maximize reuse under diminishing returns, achieving strong data efficiency.
AI.motivation: In VLA imitation, more data can be redundant, noisy, and unevenly covered. Existing selection methods miss long-horizon reusable structures, motivating a method that exploits primitives and transition interfaces to improve efficiency.
AI.method: Decompose demonstrations into visuo-motor primitives via segmentation; allocate a budget across composition patterns by maximizing reuse-aware structural exposure with diminishing returns; within each pattern bucket, select medoid trajectories to retain central, stable, and imitation-friendly examples.
AI.result: SIEVE consistently outperforms competitive data selection baselines across multiple datasets, benchmarks, and VLA models, and can surpass full-data training with only about 50% of demonstrations and 50% of training steps, highlighting the value of reusable structure for VLA imitation learning.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting reusable structure—primitives and transitions—yields significant data-efficiency gains for VLA imitation. SIEVE demonstrates that principled structure-aware selection can outperform indiscriminate data acquisition and even full-data training in some settings.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection of Information Operations Users via Behavioral and Language Patterns
summary: Information Operations on social media networks have been identified as a significant threat to democracy and modern society, but they are challenging and expensive to detect by humans. Existing supervised IO detection methods fail to capture the dynamic nature of evolving IO user behavior, while existing unsupervised approaches rely on oversimplified assumptions of coordination among IO users that may not exist in practice. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we formulate IO user detection as an anomaly detection problem and propose a novel unsupervised IO user detection approach called Temporal-bEhavior-laNguage Signals for information Operation Recognition (TENSOR), which leverages multimodal data, including temporal online user behavior, such as message posting activities, and the textual content of the messages. The motivation is that IO users are typically a very small fraction of all online users and have unique temporal behavioral and language patterns. Specifically, we train a Temporal Point Process (TPP) to capture abnormal temporal behavioral patterns of IO users because they are known to behave in a coordinated manner for IO campaigns. We further introduce a novel evidence function that converts LLM responses, which are generated from user post timelines, into quantitative scores to adjust the TPP outputs for better IO user detection. Experimental results show that TENSOR outperforms the baselines on five real-world IO datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/xiuzhenzhang/TENSOR.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised IO user detection with TENSOR uses temporal point processes and an evidence function to incorporate LLM-derived signals from user timelines, achieving superior detection on five real-world IO datasets; code available.
AI.motivation: IO campaigns consist of a very small fraction of online users with distinctive temporal and linguistic signatures. Existing supervised/unsupervised methods struggle with evolving behavior and oversimplified coordination assumptions, motivating an anomaly-detection approach.
AI.method: Train a Temporal Point Process (TPP) to model abnormal temporal behavior among IO users, incorporate multimodal data (temporal posting activity and message content), and introduce an evidence function that converts LLM-derived responses from post timelines into quantitative scores to adjust TPP outputs for better IO user detection.
AI.result: TENSOR outperforms baselines on five real-world IO datasets; code is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of combining temporal dynamics with language-derived signals for unsupervised IO user detection, offering a practical tool and indicating directions for robustness and generalization in future work.

title: Harrison.Rad 1.5 Technical Report: A radiology foundation model that can draft reports from images, priors and clinical context
summary: Imaging demand is growing faster than the radiology workforce can expand, and reporting backlogs cannot be resolved through training and recruitment alone. The most direct opportunity is reducing the time and effort radiologists spend producing reports, a task that requires interpreting images, integrating clinical history and prior studies, and drafting structured findings. We present Harrison.Rad 1.5 (HR1.5), a radiology-specific multimodal large language model that accepts interleaved text and visual inputs and generates structured and unstructured text across plain-film radiology, spanning computed radiography, chest, musculoskeletal, abdominal, spine, and pelvic x-rays, and mammography. HR1.5 is trained through a three-stage pipeline: domain adaptation of a base language model on radiology reports, contrastive vision-encoder training with curriculum-based hard negatives on ~6 million image-report instances, and visual-question-answering fine-tuning on multi-turn conversations. We evaluate it with a Findings-Diagnosis scoring framework that extends RadGraph-XL entity extraction with ontology-based synonym matching and polarity-contradiction detection, benchmarked on RadBench, a simulated FRCR 2B Short Case examination scored against Angoff-method thresholds, ReXGradient, and internal multi-modality datasets. HR1.5 is the only system evaluated to meet the simulated FRCR passing standard and achieves the highest accuracy on closed-format clinical questions, across anatomical regions, on internal multi-body-part and mammography reporting, and on the primary clinically-aligned score for public chest reporting. We further examine explainability and model behaviour, including question-sensitive Grad-CAM heatmaps, attention analysis, and confidence estimation, to support responsible future evaluation toward clinical use, and a framework for clinically grounded assessment of report quality.

AI.tldr: HR1.5 is a radiology-specific multimodal LLM that ingests text and images to generate structured and unstructured radiology reports across X-ray modalities, trained via a three-stage pipeline, and achieving state-of-the-art results on simulated FRCR benchmarks with explainability analyses.
AI.motivation: Address growing imaging demand and backlogs by reducing radiologists' reporting time and effort, going beyond training and recruitment by automating structured reporting across multiple radiology modalities.
AI.method: Three-stage training: (1) domain adaptation of a base language model on radiology reports; (2) contrastive vision-encoder training with curriculum-based hard negatives on ~6 million image-report pairs; (3) visual-question-answering fine-tuning on multi-turn conversations.
AI.result: HR1.5 uniquely meets the simulated FRCR passing standard, achieving the highest accuracy on closed-format clinical questions across anatomical regions in internal multi-body-part and mammography reporting, and the primary clinically-aligned score for public chest reporting; includes explainability tools (Grad-CAM heatmaps, attention analysis, confidence estimation) and a framework for clinically grounded report-quality assessment.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates strong potential for clinical use with robust evaluation and explainability; warrants further prospective clinical validation and deployment studies.

title: Finding H. pylori in the Fine Print: Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Case Finding from Gastric Biopsy Reports
summary: Data from Singapore indicated that about 31% of the population had evidence of Helicobacter pylori infection. Persistent H. pylori infection is associated with chronic active gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, and its eradication is key to gastric cancer prevention. However, evidence supporting \textit{H. pylori} positivity and H. pylori-associated gastritis may be distributed across heterogeneous coded and free-text report fields and may require contextual interpretation of assertion and negation, limiting keyword search, and making manual review difficult to scale. We conducted a retrospective pilot evaluation of the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a field-name-driven, evidence-linked extraction workflow, using 54 de-identified gastric biopsy pathology reports from a large healthcare system in Singapore. Four clinician-scoped binary fields were evaluated: gastric/stomach biopsy, biopsy status, H. pylori positivity, and H. pylori-associated gastritis. Across 216 feature-case decisions, nMAS correctly classified 213, corresponding to 98.61% overall accuracy. A separately implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator produced similar aggregate and per-field classification metrics. Although predictive performance was similar, nMAS maintained unified report-level outputs with supporting source sentences; the demonstrated contribution is therefore workflow integration and traceability rather than predictive superiority. Under an illustrative, unmeasured scenario, reviewing 1,000 reports at five minutes per manual review versus five seconds per evidence-linked verification would reduce review time from 83.3 to 1.4 staff-hours, corresponding to 81.9 staff-hours and about USD~6,100 in potential staff-time value. Larger multi-institutional studies should evaluate evidence-span correctness, clinician verification time, and generalizability.

AI.tldr: nMAS extracts evidence-linked, binary H. pylori-related findings from gastric biopsy pathology reports; achieves 98.61% accuracy on 54 Singapore reports; comparable to UMA-style MiniMax; emphasizes workflow integration and traceability over predictive superiority, with illustrative time savings for large-scale review.
AI.motivation: H. pylori positivity and related gastritis data are embedded across heterogeneous coded and free-text fields. Manual review is time-consuming and hard to scale; a traceable, field-name-driven extraction workflow is needed to enable reliable, scalable data capture for clinical decision support and research.
AI.method: Retrospective pilot using 54 de-identified gastric biopsy pathology reports from a Singapore healthcare system. Four binary fields were evaluated (gastric/stomach biopsy, biopsy status, H. pylori positivity, H. pylori-associated gastritis). 216 feature-case decisions were made. A field-name-driven, evidence-linked extraction workflow (nMAS) was compared to a UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 classifier. Outputs included unified report-level results with supporting source sentences.
AI.result: nMAS correctly classified 213 of 216 decisions (98.61% overall accuracy). The UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator yielded similar aggregate and per-field metrics. nMAS provided traceable outputs with source sentences, highlighting workflow integration and interpretability rather than predictive superiority. A hypothetical 1,000-report batch suggested potential staff-time reductions from 83.3 to 1.4 hours (≈81.9 hours saved) and about USD 6,100 in value.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a field-name-driven, evidence-linked extraction workflow can achieve high accuracy while preserving traceability and unified outputs, enabling scalable review. The main contribution lies in workflow integration rather than superior predictive performance. Larger, multi-institutional studies are needed to assess evidence-span correctness, clinician verification time, and generalizability.

title: Hilti-Trimble-Oxford Dataset: 360 Visual-Inertial Benchmark with Floor Plan Priors for SLAM and Localization
summary: Automated progress monitoring on construction sites is an active area of research and development. Robot and human-carried mapping systems have been developed to build 3D maps of building and infrastructure projects. While LiDAR-based mapping systems achieve high accuracy, the cost of LiDAR can be prohibitive. Consumer-grade cameras with wide field of view ("360 cameras") combined with embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a cost-effective alternative. To support change detection and progress monitoring, highly accurate visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and floor plan-referenced localization systems are required. In this paper we present a high-quality dataset collected at an active construction site, which captures realistic challenges such as variable lighting conditions, moving workers, fast motions, and repetitive structures. The dataset offers thirty visual-inertial sequences recorded across seven floors over an eight-month period of the construction project. Ground truth trajectories were collected using a high quality LiDAR-inertial SLAM system rigidly attached to the 360 camera. Additionally, we report the results of an open research challenge evaluating the best visual SLAM and localization systems from around the world. The Challenge attracted substantially higher participation in SLAM, with 62 teams compared to 22 in floor-plan-referenced localization, reflecting the broader maturity of SLAM methods. The higher errors in localization further highlight the difficulty of this task in construction and point to the need for continued research, which this dataset is intended to support. The dataset and the benchmark are publicly available at: https://hilti-trimble-challenge.com/dataset-2026.

AI.tldr: A publicly available 360-degree visual-inertial SLAM dataset from an active construction site, collected across seven floors, with ground-truth via LiDAR-inertial SLAM, plus a world-wide benchmark showing SLAM methods attract more participation but expose localization challenges.
AI.motivation: Need for cost-effective, accurate progress monitoring in construction using consumer cameras; current datasets are limited in realism and scale for visual SLAM in dynamic, multi-floor sites; benchmarking is required to drive method development.
AI.method: Collected 30 visual-inertial sequences over eight months on seven floors of an active site using 360 cameras with embedded IMUs; ground-truth trajectories obtained from a LiDAR-inertial SLAM system rigidly attached to the camera; open challenge evaluating top visual SLAM and floor-plan localization methods; dataset and benchmark publicly released.
AI.result: Public dataset and benchmark released. The SLAM challenge saw substantially higher participation (62 teams) than floor-plan localization (22 teams). Localization errors were higher, underscoring the difficulty of constructing and localizing in real-world construction environments.
AI.conclusion: The dataset fills a gap for realistic, challenging visual SLAM and localization on construction sites and should catalyze further research in SLAM robustness, dynamic scene handling, and improved localization against floor plans; ongoing work is needed to improve localization under dynamic conditions and repetitive structures.

title: Strategic Bargaining in Multi-Buyer Markets: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards for LLM Negotiations
summary:
Negotiation is a fundamental strategic interaction in management science, characterized by agents attempting to reach agreements while protecting private information, such as reservation costs and hidden valuations. A prevalent yet complex scenario involves a single seller negotiating concurrently with multiple buyers, each possessing heterogeneous, private budgets. In such settings, constrained by a limited number of communication turns, the seller must balance exploring the broader market to discover the highest valuation with concentrating sufficient turns on a single target buyer to secure the best possible outcome. Our analysis reveals a significant gap in standard Large Language Models (LLMs): while these models are linguistically proficient, they fail to act as effective economic decision-makers. Specifically, they exhibit a failure to explore the buyer pool, often fixating on the current highest bid rather than strategically investigating the market to discover latent high valuations.
  In this paper, we propose a specialized training recipe using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). By anchoring the reward function to objective economic outcomes, the strategic balance between market discovery and surplus extraction emerges natively through the learning process. Our results demonstrate that the trained seller undergoes a multi-stage strategic evolution, learning to leverage price anchoring and strategic probing to identify more profitable counterparties. The agent extracts a substantially higher surplus than frontier models by both improving its persuasive bargaining skills and consistently closing deals with high-value buyers. Finally, we show that our seller strategies generalize robustly to unseen buyer negotiation styles and budget distributions.

AI.tldr: A single seller negotiates with multiple private-budget buyers under limited rounds; standard LLMs fail to explore market; RLVR-trained seller learns to balance market discovery and surplus extraction, achieving higher surplus and robust generalization.
AI.motivation: Identify and address the gap where linguistic proficiency in LLMs does not translate into effective economic decision-making in multi-party negotiation settings; extend AI capability to strategic market exploration.
AI.method: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) with a reward aligned to objective economic outcomes; training yields emergent multi-stage strategies, including price anchoring and targeted probing; evaluation across unseen buyer styles and budgets.
AI.result: Agent attains substantially higher surplus than frontier models; improved bargaining, closes with high-value buyers; strategies generalize to unseen negotiation styles.
AI.conclusion: RLVR enables emergent, robust strategic behavior in automated negotiations; demonstrates bridging language models with economic decision-making and market discovery; potential for scalable automated negotiation agents.

title: Few-Medoids: An Embarrassingly Simple Coreset Selection Method for Few-Shot Knowledge Distillation
summary: Coreset selection aims to identify a small and highly representative subset of a massive dataset for efficient model training. The problem remains challenging even in the few-shot knowledge distillation (KD) setup, where a full-scale pre-trained teacher informs the student network. Typical sample selection strategies often struggle to surpass the random selection baseline. In this paper, we showcase few-medoids, an embarrassingly simple coreset selection strategy that chooses the samples closest to the centroid (average image) of each class. We present extensive KD experiments on four datasets, covering a wide range of image classification problems, and three teacher-student model pairs, comprising both convolutional and transformer networks. Although the proposed method is embarrassingly simple, our empirical results indicate that few-medoids is able to consistently surpass the random selection baseline, as well as the other coreset selection strategies. We therefore consider that few-medoids can be used as a drop-in replacement for commonly-used baselines (e.g. herding or k-center Greedy), in future research on coreset selection. To reproduce the reported results, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/CemilAndreiDilmac/Few-Shot-KD-Coreset.

AI.tldr: Few-medoids is a simple coreset selection method for few-shot KD that selects samples closest to the per-class centroid, consistently beating random and standard baselines across diverse datasets and model types, suggesting it can serve as a drop-in replacement for traditional coreset strategies.
AI.motivation: Coreset selection in few-shot knowledge distillation is hard; existing strategies often underperform random baselines. A minimal, centroid-based approach could offer robust, generalizable sampling with low complexity.
AI.method: Compute the per-class centroid (mean image) and select, for each class, the samples with smallest L2 distance to that centroid (few-medoids). Evaluate via knowledge distillation using a full pre-trained teacher across four datasets and three teacher-student pairs (CNNs and transformers).
AI.result: Empirical results show that few-medoids consistently surpass random selection and other coreset strategies (e.g., herding, k-center greedy) across diverse datasets and architectures. The method demonstrates strong, reproducible gains, and code is released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The simple centroid-based coreset selection is effective in few-shot KD and can serve as a reliable drop-in replacement for common baselines, motivating further study in broader KD settings and datasets.

title: Danus: Orchestrating Mathematical Reasoning Agents with Fact-Graph Memory
summary: Recent LLM-based mathematical reasoning agents have begun to tackle research-level problems and, in several cases, have contributed to the resolution of open problems. However, scaling and orchestrating such agents effectively remains challenging, due to the difficulty of coordinating parallel proof search while keeping intermediate claims organized and reliable. In this paper, we propose Danus, an orchestration system for research-level mathematical reasoning centered on a shared fact graph as a global memory-management mechanism. Danus consists of a main agent that performs planning and coordination, multiple worker agents that carry out proof search in parallel, and a stateless verifier that checks proposed mathematical claims before they are admitted into the fact graph. Each verified fact is stored together with its proof and logical dependencies, allowing the system to build long arguments incrementally while keeping the shared proof state organized. The main agent periodically summarizes the evolving proof state, redirects workers across promising directions, and supports interaction with human mathematicians through progress reports. We evaluate Danus through six research-level case studies in algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics, illustrating how the fact-graph memory mechanism enables Danus to construct long, detailed mathematical proofs. Our results suggest that fact-graph-based orchestration provides an effective route toward scaling mathematical reasoning agents for long-horizon research problems. Danus is open source at https://github.com/frenzymath/Danus.

AI.tldr: Danus is an orchestration framework for research-level mathematical reasoning that uses a shared fact graph as global memory. It coordinates a main planner, parallel worker agents for proof search, and a stateless verifier to ensure each claimed fact is validated with proof and dependencies, enabling incremental long-form proofs. Evaluated on six case studies across algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics; open-sourced at GitHub.
AI.motivation: To address scalability and reliability challenges in LLM-based mathematical reasoning, specifically the difficulty of coordinating parallel proof search and maintaining organized, verifiable intermediate claims over long-horizon, research-level tasks.
AI.method: Introduce Danus with three components: a main agent for planning and coordination, multiple worker agents performing parallel proof search, and a stateless verifier. Employ a shared fact graph as a global memory, admitting only verified facts with their proofs and dependencies. The main agent periodically summarizes the evolving proof state, redirects workers, and interfaces with human mathematicians.
AI.result: Six research-level case studies in algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics demonstrate that the fact-graph memory enables Danus to construct long, detailed mathematical proofs and effectively orchestrate long-horizon reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Fact-graph-based orchestration is a promising route to scaling mathematical reasoning agents for long-horizon research problems; Danus is open source at the linked GitHub repository.

title: Clustering-Embedded Model Predictive Path Integral Control: Avoiding Averaging-Induced Failure and Enabling Efficient Cluster Selection for Dynamic Obstacles
summary: With the widespread availability of parallel computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control have become increasingly powerful for complex nonlinear systems in non-smooth task spaces. However, the sampling and forward-simulation pipeline in MPPI suffers from averaging-induced failure in cluttered environments, where the importance-weighted update averages incompatible rollouts and leads to hesitation or even collision when an obstacle lies directly ahead. This paper proposes Clustering-Embedded MPPI (CE-MPPI), a framework that architecturally resolves the averaging-induced failures inherent in standard MPPI within non-convex environments. Rather than simply mitigating interference, CE-MPPI redefines the control law by integrating a high-fidelity pruning and clustering stage. By leveraging density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) alongside a novel geometric direction feature that is extracted from collision-derived reference points, the system isolates feasible trajectory modes from the noise of infeasible rollouts. This is paired with an intelligent selection logic that optimizes for minimum cost in static scenes while actively steering opposite to obstacle flux in dynamic environments. Experiments in 2-D JAX-accelerated simulations show that CE-MPPI alleviates obstacle-front hesitation and avoids persistent coupling with moving obstacles in dynamic scenes. In particular, real-world tests on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator with CUDA-parallel rollouts in Isaac Gym achieve a 48\% reduction in time-to-goal and a 12\% shorter end-effector path.

AI.tldr: CE-MPPI adds clustering-based pruning to MPPI to isolate feasible trajectory modes, reducing averaging-induced failures in cluttered/non-convex environments; yields faster time-to-goal and shorter paths in UR5e experiments.
AI.motivation: Standard MPPI suffers from averaging-incompatible rollouts in non-convex, cluttered spaces, leading to obstacle-front hesitation and potential collisions; need a method to disentangle feasible trajectory modes from infeasible noise.
AI.method: Integrates DBSCAN clustering with a novel geometric direction feature derived from collision-derived reference points, plus an intelligent selection logic that minimizes static-scene cost and opposes obstacle flux in dynamic scenes; implemented in 2-D JAX simulations and 6-DoF UR5e with CUDA rollouts in Isaac Gym.
AI.result: CE-MPPI alleviates obstacle-front hesitation, avoids persistent coupling with moving obstacles, and achieves a 48% reduction in time-to-goal and 12% shorter end-effector path in real-world tests.
AI.conclusion: Clustering-embedded pruning redefines MPPI control law to handle non-convex environments, improving planning robustness and efficiency; demonstrated on both simulated and real robot experiments.

title: Differentially Private Natural Gradient Descent
summary:
Under a fixed privacy budget, the utility of differentially private (DP) training is ultimately determined by its optimization efficiency. Standard first-order DP optimizers such as DP-SGD rely solely on local gradients and ignore the underlying loss curvature. This geometric blindness causes severe zigzagging in ill-conditioned landscapes, squandering precious privacy budgets on inefficient iterations. Practitioners are thus trapped in a bind: either stop training prematurely or inject massive per-step noise, both of which critically compromise final model utility. Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) resolves this by preconditioning gradients with curvature, aligning updates with the loss geometry and extracting more efficient signal from every noisy step, offering a principled pathway to break the privacy-utility bottleneck.
  Despite its theoretical appeal, directly integrating NGD with DP introduces fundamental challenges: curvature estimation itself consumes prohibitive privacy budgets, isotropic DP operations conflict with the anisotropic scaling of NGD, and the inverse curvature catastrophically amplify parameter updates in flat directions, causing training instability. We propose DP-NGD, a practical framework that systematically addresses these obstacles by decoupling curvature estimation from private data, reconciling isotropic DP constraints with anisotropic second-order optimization via a whitened-space mechanism, and dynamically clamping the curvature to stabilize training. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DP-NGD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, breaking through the utility ceilings of first-order baselines while delivering up to a $10\times$ convergence speedup under the same privacy budget.

AI.tldr: Proposes DP-NGD, a practical differentially private natural gradient descent that decouples curvature estimation from private data and uses a whitened-space mechanism to reconcile isotropic DP with anisotropic second-order updates; achieves up to 10x faster convergence and state-of-the-art accuracy under the same privacy budget.
AI.motivation: DP-SGD's first-order nature ignores loss curvature, causing inefficient updates; curvature estimation consumes privacy budgets; need a method to exploit second-order information under DP without privacy cost blow-up.
AI.method: DP-NGD decouples curvature estimation from private data; uses whitening to align updates in private setting; introduces dynamic curvature clamping to stabilize training; combines isotropic DP with anisotropic second-order updates in a privacy-preserving way.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on standard benchmarks shows state-of-the-art accuracy and up to 10× convergence speedup under the same DP budget, surpassing first-order DP baselines.
AI.conclusion: DP-NGD offers a practical framework to integrate natural gradient preconditioning into DP training, addressing key privacy-utility bottlenecks and enabling more efficient learning under fixed privacy budgets.

title: GaussFusion: Towards Multimodal 3D Gaussian Pretraining
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting provides an explicit representation that jointly models geometry and appearance, serving as a scalable foundation for 3D representation learning. Existing pre-training methods for Gaussian representations, such as masked Gaussian reconstruction, primarily capture local structures but offer limited semantic supervision. In this paper, we propose GaussFusion, a multimodal pre-training framework for 3D Gaussian representations. GaussFusion integrates image and text supervision into masked Gaussian modeling through cross-modal semantic alignment, enabling the Gaussian encoder to learn both visual and language-level semantic information during pre-training. To better adapt masked modeling to the non-uniform distribution of Gaussian primitives, we further propose Gaussian Salience-guided Multi-scale Hole Masking (GSHM). GSHM constructs spatially continuous masked regions based on Gaussian salience. By applying hole masks at multiple scales, GSHM encourages the encoder to capture both fine-grained local patterns and broader structural dependencies. Extensive experiments on downstream tasks demonstrate that GaussFusion improves the transferability of Gaussian representations. Notably, GaussFusion outperforms Gaussian-MAE on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN (PB-T50-RS) by 0.61\% and 3.85\%, respectively.

AI.tldr: Multimodal pre-training for 3D Gaussian representations (GaussFusion) that uses image/text supervision in masked Gaussian modeling, aided by salience-guided multi-scale hole masking to handle non-uniform Gaussian primitives, leading to improved transferability over Gaussian-MAE on 3D benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current Gaussian pre-training (e.g., Gaussian-MAE) emphasizes local geometric/appearance reconstruction but lacks semantic supervision and does not account for the non-uniform distribution of Gaussian primitives, limiting cross-modal and downstream transfer performance.
AI.method: GaussFusion integrates cross-modal semantic alignment (image and text) into masked Gaussian modeling to imbue the 3D Gaussian encoder with visual and language semantics. It introduces Gaussian Salience-guided Multi-scale Hole Masking (GSHM), which masks regions based on Gaussian salience across multiple scales to promote learning of both fine details and broader structure.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show improved transferability. GaussFusion outperforms Gaussian-MAE on ModelNet40 by 0.61% and on ScanObjectNN (PB-T50-RS) by 3.85%.
AI.conclusion: GaussFusion effectively leverages multimodal supervision and a salience-guided masking strategy to train semantically rich 3D Gaussian representations with superior downstream performance compared to prior Gaussian pre-training approaches.

title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework for Elastodynamic Wave Propagation in Bimaterial Systems
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for solving partial differential equations while embedding the underlying physical laws directly into the learning process. This study presents a PINN-based framework for modeling transient elastodynamic wave propagation in bimaterial systems governed by the axisymmetric equations of linear elasticity. A steel-aluminum specimen representative of a Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar configuration is considered, and the governing elastodynamic equations, together with the corresponding initial, boundary, and interface conditions, are incorporated directly into the network through a physics-informed loss function. High-fidelity finite-element simulations performed using ANSYS Workbench Explicit Dynamics are used for validation and as supplementary data constraints during training. The proposed framework accurately predicts wave transmission and reflection across the bimaterial interface and reproduces axial and radial displacement histories, face-averaged responses, and the dominant stress and strain evolution with close agreement to the finite-element solutions. The trained network further demonstrates the ability to predict wave responses at previously unseen time instants and for modified material properties without requiring additional finite-element simulations, providing a continuous surrogate model for elastodynamic analysis. Mesh-sensitivity studies confirm numerical robustness, while additional material combinations demonstrate the generality of the proposed methodology. The results show that integrating physics-informed neural networks with explicit finite-element analysis provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for elastodynamic wave propagation in heterogeneous solids, offering an effective surrogate modeling approach for high-rate solid mechanics and impact engineering applications.

AI.tldr: PINNs integrated with axisymmetric elastodynamics and explicit-FEA data form a surrogate for transient wave propagation in bimaterial steel–aluminum systems, accurately predicting interface transmission/reflection and displacement/stress histories, with good generalization to unseen times/materials.
AI.motivation: Provide a computationally efficient surrogate model for high-rate elastodynamics in heterogeneous solids, enabling rapid predictions and design insights for impact engineering.
AI.method: Develop a physics-informed neural network that enforces axisymmetric linear-elasticity PDEs, initial/boundary/interface conditions via a physics-informed loss; train on high-fidelity FE data from ANSYS Explicit Dynamics for validation and as data constraints; examine predictions of wave transmission/reflection, axial/radial displacements, face-averaged responses, and stress/strain evolution; assess mesh sensitivity and generalization to new materials.
AI.result: The PINN reproduces FE solutions closely, capturing interface behavior and dominant response metrics; it generalizes to unseen time instances and material properties without additional FE simulations; shows robustness to mesh variations and demonstrates applicability to multiple material combinations.
AI.conclusion: Integrating PINNs with explicit FEM yields an accurate, efficient surrogate for elastodynamic wave propagation in heterogeneous solids, with potential for high-rate impact applications and reduced computational costs.

title: Hypothesis-driven Model Expansion under Uncertainty for Open-World Robot Planning
comment: Accepted to Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2026
summary: We consider an open-world planning setting in which service robots must operate in unknown environments with incomplete knowledge of objects and actions. Traditional closed-world approaches with pre-programmed knowledge bases fail when robots encounter unexpected situations and tasks, posing a fundamental challenge for autonomous knowledge expansion in human environments. In this work, we propose an open-world planning framework that enables robots to automatically generate, verify, and update hypotheses about their abstract world models. Our key insight is to explicitly maintain uncertainty-aware knowledge expansion and integrate hypothesis verification into goal-reaching planning. The framework leverages foundation models to generate initial hypotheses over states and transitions, and applies automated planning to produce action sequences that jointly address hypothesis verification and task execution. Through iterative execution and refinement, the robot expands its knowledge by incorporating verification feedback from the foundation models when hypotheses prove incorrect. Extensive experiments in simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that our framework enables autonomous knowledge expansion and effective operation in open-world settings. These results indicate that integrating uncertainty-aware model expansion from robot foundation models with planning advances the practical deployment of household service robots.

AI.tldr: An open-world planning framework for service robots that autonomously expands and verifies its world model by generating and testing hypotheses with foundation models, integrated into planning for simultaneous hypothesis verification and task execution.
AI.motivation: Robots must operate in unknown environments with incomplete knowledge; closed-world planning fails to handle unexpected situations, hindering autonomous knowledge growth and robust household service tasks.
AI.method: The approach maintains uncertainty-aware, evolving knowledge; uses foundation models to generate hypotheses about states and transitions; automated planning produces action sequences that both execute tasks and verify hypotheses; iterative execution/refinement updates the world model with verification feedback.
AI.result: Demonstrated in both simulated and real-world settings that the framework enables autonomous knowledge expansion and effective operation in open-world tasks, improving practical deployment of household service robots.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty-aware model expansion from robot foundation models with planning advances enables robust open-world deployment of household service robots.

title: No Subspace to Track: Non-Identifiability and Optimizer State in Low-Rank Training
summary: Memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore train large language models by projecting gradients onto a rank-r subspace recomputed every T steps, assuming this subspace is a slowly drifting object that can be tracked. We show that beyond a small reproducible core, there is no such object. Two estimates of the top-r subspace computed at the same step from disjoint minibatches disagree as much as estimates computed T steps apart (0.73 vs 0.74 of the maximal chordal distance sqrt(2r), at Pythia-160M with r=128): the apparent rotation at each refresh is dominated by estimator noise. This holds across four model families in three architecture classes from 70M to 6.9B parameters, strengthening with scale, and more weakly in a vision transformer. Only ~39 of 128 directions are reproducible across minibatches, and averaging cannot recover the rest: under N-fold averaging the gradient's spectral tail shrinks as N^(-1/4) rather than the N^(-1/2) of pure noise, so no averaging budget makes the subspace well defined. What helps instead follows from treating each refresh as a change of coordinates for Adam's state. Carrying the second moment blindly is provably about (r-k*)/2 worse than the best rotation-blind estimator, while the first moment transports exactly through the rotation, the optimal linear map under isotropic gradients and the rule LDAdam uses. At 1B over 40k steps (3 seeds), full LDAdam reaches 18.7 perplexity at beta2=0.999, beating untransported GaLore after its best beta2 fix (19.3); shortening the second-moment memory to beta2=0.99 helps the refreshing optimizers, though for canonical GaLore the effect is small and a full-rank control reverses it. One measurable fact, subspace non-identifiability, clarifies why GaLore works, which patches work, and what to check before trusting a low-rank assumption: the reproducible rank k*.

AI.tldr: Rank-r subspace projections used by memory-efficient optimizers often do not correspond to a stable, slowly drifting object; estimates from different minibatches disagree and only a small reproducible component exists. A principled alternative is to treat refreshes as coordinate changes in Adam's state, with LDAdam (transported second moments) outperforming untransported GaLore, particularly at large scale.
AI.motivation: To empirically test the core assumption behind GaLore-style optimizers that a low-rank gradient subspace is stable across minibatches and refreshes, and to understand why such methods can sometimes work or fail as models scale.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation across four model families (70M to 6.9B parameters) and three architectures (including vision transformers). Compare top-r subspace estimates from disjoint minibatches and from refresh intervals (T). Use spectral distance (maximal chordal distance) to quantify subspace disagreement; assess reproducible rank k*, averaging effects, and the impact of coordinate changes on Adam's state. Compare GaLore with LDAdam in terms of perplexity on language modeling (Pythia-160M and 1B-scale tests), exploring beta2 settings and memory length.
AI.result: Subspace estimates from disjoint minibatches disagree as much as those separated by T steps, indicating the subspace is dominated by estimator noise rather than a stable object. Across scales, only about 39 of 128 directions are reproducible; averaging cannot recover the rest, with tail shrinking as N^(-1/4). Treating each refresh as a coordinate change for Adam’s state yields a provable advantage: LDAdam transports second moments and first moments through rotation, reducing loss relative to GaLore; at 1B and 40k steps, LDAdam with beta2=0.999 achieves 18.7 perplexity versus 19.3 for GaLore, and beta2 tweaks help or harm depending on configuration.
AI.conclusion: The central assumption of a slowly drifting fixed subspace for gradient projections is largely invalid; subspace non-identifiability explains why GaLore-like methods can appear to work in some cases but are fragile and not scalable. Effective optimization under this regime comes from accounting for coordinate changes induced by refreshes (LDAdam), which preserves information more faithfully than rotating or projecting second moments. The reproducible rank k* is a practical diagnostic for when such low-rank assumptions may be trusted.

title: PolicyShiftGuard: Benchmarking and Improving Policy-Adaptive Image Guardrails
summary: Image guardrails are typically trained and evaluated under a fixed safety policy, implicitly treating safety as an intrinsic property of an image. Real deployments are different: the same image may be allowed in one product, restricted in another, and newly disallowed when a policy boundary changes. We study policy-adaptive image guardrailing, where a model must decide whether an image violates the currently supplied policy and generalize to held-out policy definitions. We introduce PolicyShiftBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 2,000 policy-discriminative instances over 265 images, where each image is paired with 7.55 policy-conditioned prompts on average to test whether models adapt to the active policy rather than relying on image-level safety priors. We then propose PolicyShiftGuard, a compact policy-conditioned guardrail trained with a two-stage training recipe that combines Randomized Policy SFT (RP-SFT) with Boundary-Pair Policy Adaptation (BP-Adapt). BP-Adapt trains matched prompts for the same image and risk category using standard label supervision and a pairwise comparison loss that separates blocking policies from passing policies. Experiments show that existing VLMs and specialized guardrails remain brittle under policy shifts, while PolicyShiftGuard substantially improves policy-sensitive performance. The 7B model achieves SOTA performance of 76.9 Avg. F1 and 72.1 Avg. PSS on PolicyShiftBench, transfers well to UnSafeBench and SafeEditBench, and improves the latency-performance trade-off with a concise output format. Ablations confirm that matched pass/block boundary pairs are essential for stable policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: Introduces PolicyShiftBench for policy-adaptive image safety and PolicyShiftGuard, a two-stage policy-conditioned guardrail trained with RP-SFT and BP-Adapt to adapt to changing safety policies; achieves state-of-the-art results on policy-shift benchmarks with strong cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: Current image guardrails rely on fixed safety policies and image priors, but real deployments face shifting policies. There is a need for models that can discern policy compliance and generalize to unseen policies without rebuilding the model.
AI.method: PolicyShiftBench: 2,000 policy-discriminative instances over 265 images with averaged 7.55 policy-conditioned prompts per image to test adaptation to the active policy. PolicyShiftGuard: two-stage training—Randomized Policy SFT (RP-SFT) to expose the model to diverse policies, and Boundary-Pair Policy Adaptation (BP-Adapt) which uses matched image/risk-category prompts and a pairwise loss to separate blocking vs passing policies.
AI.result: PolicyShiftGuard substantially improves policy-sensitive performance over existing VLMs and guardrails under policy shifts. The 7B model achieves 76.9 Avg. F1 and 72.1 Avg. PSS on PolicyShiftBench, with good transfer to UnSafeBench and SafeEditBench. The approach reduces latency while maintaining performance, and ablations show that matched boundary pairs are essential for stable policy adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Policy-conditioned training with boundary-aware adaptation enables robust policy-sensitive guardrails that generalize to unseen policies and across domains, offering practical utility for deployment and a favorable latency-performance trade-off.

title: Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi Objective Battery Management in Dairy Farms
summary: The dairy industry in Ireland has a large potential for the integration of renewable energy and the reduction of carbon emissions. However, researchers of distributed generation control are mainly focused on residential and commercial applications. To contribute to the effective integration of renewable energy in the dairy sector, this paper presents a multi-objective optimisation control system based on differential evolution and multi agent Deep Reinforcement Learning. The proposed control is organised in two layers: the upper layer uses dynamic pricing, and the lower layer is based on multi-agent reinforcement learning for battery management. This paper also simulates the electrical response of the proposed control system in a rural distribution circuit. The simulation results show that the proposed control framework can improve profits from energy arbitrage up to 18% compared to using Rule-based models, increase the use of distributed generation without significantly increasing cost, and comply with the Irish grid code in terms of voltage variation.

AI.tldr: Two-layer optimization/control for dairy energy: dynamic pricing + multi-agent DRL battery management; simulation shows up to 18% arbitrage profits, higher DG uptake, and grid voltage compliance.
AI.motivation: Address under-explored renewable integration in the dairy sector and rural distribution; extend distributed generation control beyond residential/commercial.
AI.method: Upper layer uses dynamic pricing; lower layer employs multi-agent deep reinforcement learning for battery management; differential evolution for multi-objective optimization; simulated on rural Irish distribution circuit.
AI.result: Energy arbitrage profits up to 18% vs rule-based models; higher DG deployment without significant cost increase; complies with Irish grid code on voltage variation.
AI.conclusion: Feasible, beneficial framework for renewable integration in the dairy sector with demonstrated economic and grid-compatibility gains; warrants further validation and extension.

title: Neural-ESO: A Dual-Pathway Architecture for Provably Robust Learning-Based Control
summary: A learning-enabled disturbance-rejection framework based on a Neural Extended State Observer (Neural-ESO) is presented in this letter. Unlike existing learning-based control methods that largely rely on the learned model once deployed, Neural-ESO adopts a dual-pathway architecture: a predictive pathway uses a neural network to provide a feedforward disturbance estimate that accelerates convergence, while a corrective pathway employs a conventional ESO to compensate prediction errors and prevent over-reliance on the neural component. Using Lyapunov theory and a small-gain analysis, we show that enforcing a Lipschitz bound on the learning component guarantees uniform ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop error dynamics. The proposed framework is validated on a quadrotor landing task subject to strong ground-effect disturbances across normal and out-of-distribution scenarios, demonstrating accuracy-robustness trade-off and greater operational reliability during training, deployment, and transfer compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: A Neural Extended State Observer (Neural-ESO) combines a neural network-based predictive path with a conventional ESO-based corrective path for disturbance rejection. It enforces a Lipschitz bound on the learning component to guarantee uniform ultimate boundedness (UUB) of the closed-loop error via Lyapunov and small-gain analysis. Validated on a quadrotor landing task with strong ground-effect disturbances, showing better accuracy-robustness and reliability during training, deployment, and transfer compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: To improve disturbance rejection in learning-enabled control by integrating a predictive neural estimate with a safety-oriented corrective observer, addressing over-reliance on learned models and enhance robustness during training and deployment.
AI.method: A dual-pathway architecture: (i) predictive pathway uses a neural network to estimate disturbances feedforward; (ii) corrective pathway uses a conventional ESO to compensate residual errors. Stability analysis via Lyapunov theory and small-gain theorem with a Lipschitz constraint on the neural component ensures uniform ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop error. Validation on a quadrotor landing task with strong disturbances, including out-of-distribution scenarios.
AI.result: The framework achieves accuracy-robustness trade-offs and improved operational reliability during training, deployment, and transfer relative to state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining stability guarantees under the imposed Lipschitz bound.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing a Lipschitz bound on the neural component within a Neural-ESO ensures stability (UUB) and robust disturbance rejection without excessive reliance on the learned model, yielding reliable performance across normal and OOD disturbances in a quadrotor landing task.

title: Auditing of Unlearning Algorithms
summary: Evaluating whether unlearning algorithms truly remove training data influence remains an open challenge. We propose a practical auditor that computes data-dependent lower bounds on the unlearning parameter $\varepsilon$ using membership inference attacks. Evaluating multiple unlearning algorithms, we find a sharp separation: algorithms with rigorous guarantees, such as model clipping and rewind-to-delete, achieve very small $\varepsilon$ bounds that do not falsify their unlearning guarantees, whereas empirical methods such as Hessian-based unlearning, interleaved ascent-descent, ascent on the forget set, and fine-tuning on the retain set exhibit large bounds, indicating poor unlearning. Our auditor provides a practical tool for empirically falsifying unlearning claims through a hypothesis-testing framework, and we validate it on CIFAR-100 and Shakespeare text.

AI.tldr: Audits unlearning claims via data-dependent lower bounds on epsilon using membership inference; guaranteed methods show strong unlearning (small epsilon) while empirical methods show weak unlearning (large epsilon); validated on CIFAR-100 and Shakespeare text.
AI.motivation: Unlearning correctness is hard to verify; there is a need for practical, data-driven audits to falsify unlearning guarantees and compare algorithms.
AI.method: Develop a practical auditor that computes data-dependent lower bounds on the unlearning parameter epsilon from membership inference attacks; apply a hypothesis-testing framework to assess whether unlearning claims hold across several algorithms (guaranteed methods like clipping/rewind-to-delete vs. empirical methods like Hessian-based, interleaved ascent-descent, forget-set ascent, fine-tuning) on CIFAR-100 and Shakespeare text.
AI.result: A clear separation is observed: guaranteed/unlearning-guaranteed methods yield very small epsilon bounds consistent with their claims, whereas empirical/unlearning methods yield large epsilon bounds, indicating poor unlearning; the auditor can empirically falsify unlearning claims.
AI.conclusion: The auditor is a practical tool for empirically testing unlearning claims in ML; rigorous guarantees lead to substantially stronger unlearning as measured by epsilon, while many empirical methods fail to achieve genuine unlearning; validated on standard benchmarks.
