title: Progressive Reasoning with Primitive Correction for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
summary: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) aims to combine known attributes and objects as primitives for recognizing previously unseen attribute-object pairs. Prior works either predict attributes and objects independently, missing their strong contextual dependency, or use unidirectional conditional modeling (e.g., object-guided attribute prediction), which is prone to error propagation. We propose PRPC, a Progressive Reasoning framework with Primitive Correction, which explicitly models the bidirectional dependency between attributes and objects via step-wise inference. PRPC performs mutual correction of primitives to suppress prediction errors in earlier steps. Specifically, we formulate CZSL as structured, Q&A-style Chain-of-Thought reasoning process and constrain the MLLM to follow predefined semantic steps to generate intermediate decisions. To further enhance the reliability and logical consistency of intermediate reasoning, we introduce reinforcement learning post-training with a GRPO-based objective, providing step-level rewards aligned with the progressive inference procedure. Extensive experiments on three CZSL benchmarks demonstrate that PRPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of progressive reasoning and bidirectional correction for robust compositional generalization.

AI.tldr: PRPC introduces a Progressive Reasoning framework with Primitive Correction for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL). It models bidirectional attribute–object dependencies via stepwise inference, uses a Q&A-style chain-of-thought with a constrained MLLM to generate intermediate decisions, and applies reinforcement learning with a GRPO-based objective for step-level rewards, achieving state-of-the-art results on three CZSL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: CZSL suffers from weakly coupled or unidirectional modeling of attributes and objects, leading to context mismatch and error propagation. There is a need for bidirectional dependency modeling and reliable intermediate reasoning to enhance compositional generalization.
AI.method: PRPC performs progressive reasoning with mutual primitive correction to suppress earlier errors. It formulates CZSL as a structured, question-answer style chain-of-thought process, constraining a large language model (MLLM) to follow predefined semantic steps for intermediate decisions. It incorporates reinforcement learning post-training with a GRPO-based objective to align step-level rewards with the progressive inference procedure.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three CZSL benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of progressive reasoning and bidirectional correction for robust compositional generalization.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional dependency modeling with stepwise mutual correction and constrained chain-of-thought reasoning, reinforced by GRPO-based RL fine-tuning, yields robust CZSL performance and strong generalization; the approach highlights the value of structured reasoning in compositional tasks.

title: Doomed from the Start: Early Abort of LLM Agent Episodes via a Recall-Controlled Probe Cascade
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Code will be released soon
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents solving multi-step tasks frequently commit to trajectories that are doomed to fail, yet continue to consume substantial inference compute before the failure becomes observable. We show that failure is predictable early from the agent's internal representations: lightweight per-round probes on hidden activations anticipate eventual episode failure as early as the first interaction round, where scorers reading only the agent's observable behavior are barely better than chance. We turn this signal into a practical abort cascade: one distribution-free calibrated gate per round, with per-round recall budgets jointly searched so that eventually-successful episodes survive all gates at a user-specified global rate; this episode-level guarantee is the one that matters in deployment, since false-abort risk accumulates across gates. Across two agent models on TextCraft, the cascade meets every recall target from 90% to 97% and, at the 90% target, saves 47.1% +/- 10.3% (Qwen-2.5-7B) and 37.2% +/- 8.8% (Llama-3.2-3B) of inference compute, 1.6--1.7x the best single-gate policy. An otherwise-identical cascade reading only behavior saves roughly half as much, and adding behavioral features to the probe yields no further gain: the hidden states capture what behavior reveals. Finally, we characterize the sample complexity of certifying high recall targets, telling practitioners which recall promises their data can, and provably cannot, back. The code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: Early failure detection in LLM agents via lightweight probes on hidden activations enables a calibrated per-round gate cascade that preserves high recall and reduces inference compute; on TextCraft with two models, achieves 90-97% recall and substantial compute savings; behavior-only gates are less effective; hidden states capture the predictive signal; code forthcoming.
AI.motivation: Reduce wasted compute from doomed multi-step agent trajectories by predicting failures from internal representations, enabling safe aborts before observable failure.
AI.method: Train/establish per-round probes on hidden activations; construct a distribution-free calibrated gate per round; jointly optimize per-round recall budgets to meet a global recall target; compare cascade to behavior-only gate; evaluate on two models (Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B) on TextCraft; analyze sample complexity.
AI.result: Recall targets of 90-97% achieved; at 90% recall, compute savings of 47.1% ± 10.3% for Qwen-2.5-7B and 37.2% ± 8.8% for Llama-3.2-3B; 1.6-1.7x efficiency over best single-gate policy; behavior-only cascade yields about half the savings; adding behavioral features to probes yields no extra gain.
AI.conclusion: Internal hidden representations encode predictive failure signals; a calibrated per-round abort cascade provides robust episode-level guarantees and practical compute savings; results suggest broad applicability and inform practitioners on recall-target certification; code release forthcoming.

title: UniLM-Nav: A Unified Framework for Zero-Shot Last-Mile Navigation
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to navigate to a target object or receptacle and then perform intended manipulation. However, reaching the vicinity of the target does not guarantee a manipulation-ready base pose, a problem known as last-mile navigation. Prior methods for last-mile navigation either rely on manual pose annotation or task-specific training, limiting their scalability to open-vocabulary settings with fine-grained spatial constraints. We propose UniLM-Nav, a unified framework for zero-shot open-vocabulary last-mile navigation. UniLM-Nav decomposes last-mile navigation into view selection, task-conditioned affordance grounding, and geometry-aware base-pose reasoning, all resolved with a shared multimodal large language model (MLLM) backend. Specifically, UniLM-Nav first selects a reference view that best captures the target object or receptacle from recently collected observations. It then grounds task-relevant affordance point in the selected view and lifts the result into the robot-centric coordinate frame. Finally, conditioned on the grounded affordance, task context, and robot geometry, it infers a manipulation-ready base pose for the robot. We evaluate UniLM-Nav on the OVMM benchmark, where it outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method, MoTo, by 3.13 percentage points. Analyses show that the components of our method are crucial to final performance, and that the choice of MLLM also has a substantial effect. We further deploy UniLM-Nav on a Unitree B2 quadruped robot with a 6-DoF Unitree Z1 manipulator, validating its applicability to real-world mobile manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: UniLM-Nav offers a unified, zero-shot open-vocabulary last-mile navigation framework that uses a shared multimodal LLM to perform view selection, affordance grounding, and geometry-aware base-pose reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art on OVMM and validating on a real Unitree robot.
AI.motivation: Last-mile navigation is a bottleneck in mobile manipulation. Existing methods rely on manual pose annotations or task-specific training, which hinders scalability to open-vocabulary settings with fine-grained spatial constraints. A unified, scalable approach is needed to generalize to open worlds.
AI.method: Decompose last-mile navigation into three stages—(1) reference view selection from recent observations, (2) task-conditioned groundings of affordance points in the selected view lifted to robot coordinates, and (3) geometry-aware inference of a manipulation-ready base pose conditioned on grounded affordance, task context, and robot geometry. All stages are resolved via a shared multimodal large language model (MLLM) backend. Evaluation on OVMM with ablations and a real-robot deployment on a Unitree B2 with a 6-DoF Z1 manipulator.
AI.result: UniLM-Nav outperforms the previous state-of-the-art MoTo on OVMM by 3.13 percentage points. Ablation analyses show the components (view selection, affordance grounding, geometry-aware reasoning) are crucial to performance, and the choice of MLLM significantly affects results.
AI.conclusion: A unified, zero-shot open-vocabulary last-mile navigation framework is effective for mobile manipulation, bridging perception and geometry through a shared MLLM backend. Demonstrated improvements on OVMM and validated on real hardware, indicating practical applicability.

title: K-ABENA: K-Adaptive Backpropagation with Error-based N-exclusion Algorithm : (Compensated Loss-Based Sample Exclusion with Unbiased Gradient Estimation)
comment: 11 pages main text + appendices, 13 pages total. Code: https://github.com/Bonbhel/kabena-ml
summary: We present K-ABENA (K-Adaptive Backpropagation with Error-based N-exclusion Algorithm), a selective gradient computation framework that reduces per-iteration training cost by excluding a fraction of low-loss ("minor") observations from the backward pass. Its canonical form (v3) combines a defensive-mixture sampling design over the minor set with Horvitz-Thompson inverse-probability reweighting, yielding a design-unbiased Horvitz-Thompson gradient estimator (Lemma 2) and whose self-normalized practical variant carries a bias of order O(1/m) with an explicit constant (Lemma 3). We prove an O(1/sqrt(T)) non-convex convergence guarantee for SGD under the estimator, with an additive term that quantifies the residual bias (Theorem 1). We further prove that uncompensated loss-based selection - a family that includes OHEM, SBP, and the two earlier K-ABENA variants - admits no stationary point at any minimizer where its selection bias is bounded away from zero (Proposition 2), and we quantify this failure empirically: at 0.17% class imbalance, uncompensated variants reach test AUC 0.53-0.62 versus 0.9998 for full-batch SGD, while the compensated estimator attains 0.9991 at identical 28.4% compute savings. On real datasets (Breast Cancer, Digits, Wine, Diabetes) the compensated estimator is statistically indistinguishable from full-batch SGD (paired permutation tests, p >= 0.5; Section 7) while saving 28-54% of per-epoch gradient computation. A biased "regularized mode" (the earlier half-domain variant) is retained as an option with a proven exact bias decomposition (Lemma 5) and quantified contraindications: it collapses to 0.386 accuracy under 40% label noise (baseline: 0.832) and to 0.53 AUC under extreme imbalance. Every advantage and every limitation reported in this paper is either proved or measured; all experiments are CPU-scale (NumPy/scikit-learn) and their scope is stated explicitly.

AI.tldr: K-ABENA provides a selective gradient framework that drops low-loss observations during backpropagation using Horvitz-Thompson reweighting, yielding a design-unbiased gradient estimator with provable convergence and practical bias control; compensated variants match full-batch SGD performance with 28-54% compute savings, while uncompensated methods fail under bias. The approach is theoretically grounded and empirically validated on multiple datasets with CPU-scale experiments.
AI.motivation: Reduce per-iteration SGD cost by excluding minor (low-loss) observations during backpropagation without sacrificing convergence or accuracy; address bias introduced by selective gradient computation.
AI.method: Defensive-mixture sampling over the minor set combined with Horvitz-Thompson inverse-probability reweighting to obtain a design-unbiased gradient estimator; self-normalized variant with O(1/m) bias; non-convex SGD convergence guarantee with additive bias term; analysis of compensated vs uncompensated loss-based selection; exact bias decomposition for a biased regularized mode; extensive CPU-scale experiments on multiple datasets.
AI.result: Established an unbiased Horvitz-Thompson gradient estimator (Lemma 2); stated that self-normalized estimator has bias O(1/m) (Lemma 3); proved O(1/√T) convergence with additive bias (Theorem 1); uncompensated schemes (OHEM, SBP, etc.) fail to have stationary points when bias is bounded away from zero (Proposition 2); compensated estimator achieves near full-batch performance with substantial compute savings (e.g., 28.4% compute savings yielding 0.9991 AUC on some tasks), and on real datasets the compensated method is statistically indistinguishable from full-batch SGD (p ≥ 0.5) with 28-54% savings; biased regularized mode quantified (e.g., 0.386 accuracy at 40% label noise; 0.53 AUC under extreme imbalance).
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers provable guarantees and practical gains, with clearly delineated advantages and limitations; all results are either proved or measured on CPU-scale experiments, providing a robust assessment of selective gradient computation.

title: NegROI: Click-Centric Uncertainty-Guided Refinement with Scene-Conditioned Negative Prompts for Robust Interactive 3D Segmentation
summary: Interactive 3D segmentation aims to extract object masks in point clouds with minimal user clicks. Despite recent progress, most existing approaches still struggle with (i) coarse voxel resolution that blurs fine boundaries under limited clicks and (ii) hard false positives caused by confusing background structures. These issues are exacerbated by density and scale shifts across datasets (e.g., dense RGB-D reconstructions vs. sparse LiDAR scans), where fixed refinement heuristics and purely click-driven decoding generalize poorly. To address them, we propose NegROI -- a novel transformer-based interactive framework that couples click-centric multi-resolution refinement with scene-conditioned negative prompts. Given a coarse voxel prediction, it refines only a local Region Of Interest (ROI) around the current click on a finer grid and fuses refined logits back to the coarse mask. To improve robustness and efficiency, we introduce uncertainty-driven selective refinement that prioritizes ambiguous regions. Meanwhile, we model hard background patterns via a set of scene-conditioned negative prompts obtained by cross-attention over scene tokens. We further stabilize these prompts with a diversity regularizer. Finally, we propose boundary-aware hard negative mining to supervise negative-prompt attention toward boundary-proximal, high-confidence false positives. Our experiments on common benchmark datasets (i.e., ScanNet, S3DIS, and KITTI) demonstrate improved click efficiency and reduced false positives, with stronger cross-dataset robustness than the state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: NegROI: a transformer-based interactive 3D segmentation framework that refines local ROIs guided by user clicks and scene-conditioned negative prompts, achieving higher click efficiency and fewer false positives across ScanNet, S3DIS, and KITTI.
AI.motivation: To overcome coarse voxel resolution, false positives from confusing background structures, and cross-dataset density/scale shifts that degrade fixed refinement heuristics and purely click-driven decoding.
AI.method: Couples click-centric multi-resolution refinement with scene-conditioned negative prompts. Starting from a coarse voxel mask, refine only a local ROI around the current click on a finer grid and fuse logits back. Introduces uncertainty-driven selective refinement to focus on ambiguous areas. Models hard background via scene-conditioned negative prompts obtained by cross-attention over scene tokens, stabilized with a diversity regularizer. Adds boundary-aware hard negative mining to direct negative-prompt attention toward boundary-proximal, high-confidence false positives.
AI.result: On ScanNet, S3DIS, and KITTI, NegROI achieves improved click efficiency and reduced false positives, with stronger cross-dataset robustness than state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: NegROI demonstrates robust, efficient interactive 3D segmentation across diverse data regimes, thanks to ROI-focused refinement and negative prompts; effective across density and scale shifts. Future work could extend to dynamic scenes and further reduce annotation costs.

title: RMISC: A Large-scale Real-world Multivariate Corpus for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Recent years have witnessed the emergence of multivariate modeling using time series foundation models (TSFMs), which achieve advanced zero-shot generalization. Modern multivariate TSFMs are predominantly pretrained on multivariate synthetic data, which is easier to scale but may fail to capture the complex temporal dynamics and cross-variable relationships present in real-world time series. This raises a key question: Whether and to what extent the leading TSFMs trained with the real-world corpus perform better than those trained with synthetic data? To answer this, we establish the RMISC corpus, a considerably large-scale, high-quality, openly accessible, real-world, and multivariate time series archive that contains around 200 datasets and 142 billion time points across diverse domains. Furthermore, we pretrain four advanced TSFMs on univariate, synthetic multivariate, and real-world multivariate data and evaluate their zero-shot generalization capabilities on standard in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks. Experimental results show that incorporating real-world multivariate data predominantly improves the generalization performance for both univariate and multivariate TSFMs. These results provide a deeper understanding of how real-world multivariate data contributes to the development of stronger TSFMs.

AI.tldr: Real-world multivariate data improves zero-shot generalization of time-series foundation models (TSFMs) more than synthetic data, as demonstrated by large-scale RMISC pretraining and evaluation.
AI.motivation: To determine whether real-world multivariate data provides advantages over synthetic data for pretrained TSFMs, addressing concerns that synthetic data may fail to capture complex temporal dynamics and cross-variable relationships.
AI.method: Construct RMISC, a large-scale, real-world, multivariate time-series corpus (~200 datasets, 142B time points). Pretrain four advanced TSFMs on three data regimes (univariate, synthetic multivariate, real-world multivariate) and evaluate zero-shot generalization on standard in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.result: Incorporating real-world multivariate data yields notable generalization gains for both univariate and multivariate TSFMs, with the improvements predominantly observed across ID and OOD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Real-world multivariate data substantially contributes to building stronger TSFMs; results underscore the importance of real-world data in dataset curation and pretraining strategies for improved generalization.

title: RynnWorld-Teleop: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Digital Teleoperation
summary: Scaling robot learning requires massive, diverse trajectory data, yet collection is currently bottlenecked by physical teleoperation, where every demonstration binds operator time to specific hardware and workspaces. We introduce digital teleoperation, a paradigm that decouples data collection from physical constraints by replacing the real robot with a generative world model. In this framework, an operator's hand-pose stream drives a robot-centric generative world model to synthesize high-fidelity egocentric videos from a single reference image. The recorded pose stream serves as an embodiment-agnostic action label transferable to any target robot via standard retargeting, yielding complete state-action trajectories for imitation learning independent of physical hardware. We instantiate this paradigm in RynnWorld-Teleop, a system that integrates depth-aware skeletal conditioning, progressive human-to-robot training on a video Diffusion Transformer, and streaming autoregressive distillation. This pipeline compresses the generative process into a single-pass inference, enabling 40+ FPS, real-time interactive generation on a single H100 GPU. Policies trained exclusively on RynnWorld-Teleop-generated data achieve effective zero-shot Sim2Real transfer across dexterous and diverse bimanual tasks. Moreover, augmenting real-world datasets with our digitally teleoperated data consistently improves success rates, demonstrating that RynnWorld-Teleop serves as a high-fidelity, scalable data engine for the next generation of robotic agents.

AI.tldr: Digital teleoperation uses a generative world model to synthesize robot-centric egocentric videos from hand pose, enabling hardware-agnostic state-action data with real-time generation and zero-shot Sim2Real transfer.
AI.motivation: Scaling robot learning requires massive, diverse trajectory data, but collecting demonstrations via physical teleoperation is bottlenecked by operator time and hardware constraints.
AI.method: Replace the real robot with a generative world model that, driven by an operator's hand-pose stream, synthesize high-fidelity egocentric videos from a single reference image. The pose stream serves as an embodiment-agnostic action label transferable to any target robot via retargeting, yielding complete state-action trajectories. RynnWorld-Teleop integrates depth-aware skeletal conditioning, a video Diffusion Transformer, and streaming autoregressive distillation for single-pass, 40+ FPS inference.
AI.result: Policies trained solely on the digitally teleoperated data achieve effective zero-shot Sim2Real transfer across dexterous, diverse bimanual tasks. Augmenting real-world datasets with digitally teleoperated data improves success rates.
AI.conclusion: RynnWorld-Teleop is a high-fidelity, scalable data engine for next-generation robotic agents, decoupling data collection from hardware constraints and enabling rapid, wide-ranging data collection for imitation learning.

title: More Convincing, Not More Correct: Self-Play Reward Hacking of Reference-Free LLM Judges
comment: 9 pages main text, 15 pages total including references and appendix; 4 figures
summary: Training a language model against its own reference-free judgments (the premise of self-rewarding, self-play, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines) assumes a model's verdict on a shown answer tracks correctness. We show it fails structurally: conditioned on a candidate, a judge scores plausibility, not correctness, leaving false-positive basins a policy learns to exploit. We measure this with a hidden-anchor audit: a held-out, cross-source exact-match check the judge never sees. On GSM8K with Qwen3 policies, self-play drives the judge's pass rate from 0.72 to 0.94 while true accuracy stays at 0.20 (three seeds). This reward hacking is not white-box gaming: the errors transfer across judge families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma) and scales, a strict three-judge ensemble still accepts 55% of them, and no plausibility-scoring defense closes the basin. The decisive variable is whether the judge commits an answer of its own before using the candidate: committing first drops the false-positive rate from 0.719 to 0.012, blind solving lifts discrimination to 0.96, and used as the training reward the de-anchored channel keeps false positives at zero, preventing the basin rather than only detecting it. A falsifiable bound (the gap is at most 1 - accuracy) predicts which regimes are exposed. The full arc replicates without training under best-of-N selection in code and competition math, and with a Gemma policy.

AI.tldr: Self-rewarding evaluation loops in LLMs cause reward hacking: judges optimize plausibility rather than correctness, inflating measured performance while true accuracy stays low. Simple defenses (ordering, unseen evaluation channels) can mitigate or prevent false positives; a falsifiable bound describes exposure regimes.
AI.motivation: Evaluate robustness and generalizability of self-rewarding, self-play, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines; demonstrate plausibility-based scoring can diverge from correctness and quantify defenses and limits.
AI.method: Hidden-anchor audit: held-out cross-source exact-match check the judge does not see; GSM8K with Qwen3 policies; cross-family judge transfer (Qwen, Llama, Gemma); three-seed experiments; three-judge ensembles; ablations including committing-first, blind solving, and de-anchored channel rewards; best-of-N replication and policy-specific results.
AI.result: Self-play raises judge pass rate from 0.72 to 0.94 while true accuracy remains 0.20; reward hacking transfers across judge families; three-judge ensembles still accept 55%; committing-first drops FP rate to 0.012; blind solving yields discrimination ~0.96; de-anchored channel keeps FP at zero; a bound predicts exposure regimes; results replicate under best-of-N and with Gemma policy.
AI.conclusion: Reward hacking in reference-free judge-based training is a substantive risk; targeted defenses can mitigate or prevent FP basins; falsifiable bounds help predict regime exposure; findings generalize across policies and training setups, underscoring need for robust eval and design of LLM-based evaluation pipelines.

title: Decoupled Single-Mask Annotation Noise Detection via Cross-Sectional Patch Self-Consistency
summary: Vascular computed tomography datasets are commonly annotated only once per scan, yielding the pervasive yet under addressed problem of single mask annotation noise. Existing solutions either require costly multirater fusion or are coupled with network training, preventing explicit auditing of where and why labels fail. We introduce a decoupled framework for single-mask annotation noise detection that leverages cross-sectional patch self-consistency to produce interpretable and auditable noise evidence. Tubular anatomy exhibits strong cross-sectional recurrence: patches extracted orthogonally along vessel centrelines recur in appearance across locations and subjects. Thus, anatomically similar patches should have consistent masks, and disagreement signals unreliable annotation. Our method samples cross-sectional patches, retrieves intensity-equivalent neighbours via scalable vector search, and computes a patch-level noise score from statistical mask disagreement, yielding explicit image-mask evidence for every flagged region. Aggregating scores produces scan-level quality maps for dataset quality assessment or quality-weighted training. Experiments on the coronary CT dataset validate the detected noise for improving training robustness and reveal systematic annotation biases. Specifically, transverse and oblique vessels exhibit 5.1 times higher error rates than axis-aligned structures, with additional correlations to cross-sectional area and intensity. Code is available here.

AI.tldr: A decoupled method to detect single-mask annotation noise in vascular CT using cross-sectional patch self-consistency; yields interpretable evidence and scan-level quality maps; reveals annotation biases and improves training robustness.
AI.motivation: Single-mask annotations are prone to noise and bias; existing methods rely on multirater fusion or integrate with training, hindering auditing of where and why labels fail.
AI.method: Extract cross-sectional patches along vessel centrelines, retrieve intensity-equivalent neighbors via scalable vector search, and compute a patch-level noise score from statistical mask disagreement. Aggregate to scan-level quality maps enabling dataset QA and quality-weighted training; framework is decoupled from model training for auditable evidence.
AI.result: On a coronary CT dataset, the approach detects annotation noise, improves training robustness, and uncovers systematic biases. Transverse and oblique vessels show 5.1x higher error rates than axis-aligned structures, with correlations to cross-sectional area and intensity. Code is provided.
AI.conclusion: A decoupled, interpretable noise-detection framework leveraging cross-sectional patch recurrence yields explicit image-mask evidence for flagged regions and scalable dataset quality maps, enabling robustness gains and bias diagnostics in vascular CT annotations.

title: FootsiesGym: A Fighting Game Benchmark for Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
comment: Accepted to the RLC 2026 Reinforcement Learning & Video Games Workshop; 14 pages, 9 figures
summary: We present FootsiesGym, an open-source environment for learning in a non-trivial two-player, zero-sum, imperfect-information game. Built on HiFight's minimalist 2D fighting game Footsies, it isolates the cyclic, non-transitive strategic interactions of fighting game neutral play while remaining simple enough for efficient analysis. We provide a vectorized simulator that enables high-throughput training on standard hardware, making the environment accessible and reproducible. We describe the design of the environment, benchmark several reinforcement learning algorithms, and discuss open research directions it enables. The code is available at https://github.com/como-research/FootsiesGym.

AI.tldr: FootsiesGym is an open-source, vectorized RL environment for a two-player, zero-sum, imperfect-information fighting-game setting, built on Footsies; enables high-throughput training, baseline RL benchmarks, and discussion of future research, with code on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Provide a controllable, efficient, and reproducible testbed to study non-transitive, imperfect-information interactions in fighting games and facilitate RL research in such domains.
AI.method: Develop a vectorized simulator and environment that encapsulates neutral play in Footsies, ensuring two-player zero-sum dynamics and imperfect information; benchmark several RL algorithms; release open-source code.
AI.result: Demonstrates feasibility of high-throughput training; provides baseline benchmarks and design details; enables reproducible experiments; specific results not disclosed in abstract.
AI.conclusion: FootsiesGym offers a practical platform for analyzing cyclic strategies in fighting-game neutral play and identifies open research directions.

title: RynnWorld-4D: 4D Embodied World Models for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation in the open world requires not only recognizing what a scene looks like, but also anticipating how its 3D structure moves under interaction. We argue that synchronized RGB, depth, and optical flow, namely RGB-DF, provide a physically grounded representation that captures the underlying 4D dynamics of a scene. Compared to 2D pixel videos, this multi-modal synergy aligns visual appearance with geometric structure and temporal motion, creating a representation space significantly closer to the low-level end-effector actions demanded by robotic systems, thereby narrowing the gap between world prediction and policy learning. Building on this insight, we introduce RynnWorld-4D, a generative model that co-produces future RGB frames, depth maps, and optical flow from a single RGB-D image and a language instruction within one unified diffusion process. This 4D world model features a tri-branch architecture that integrates cross-modal attention with frame-wise 3D RoPE, ensuring that appearance, geometry, and motion evolve consistently. To supply training data at scale, we curate Rynn4DDataset 1.0, a massive dataset of over 254.4 million frames across egocentric human and robotic manipulation videos with high-quality pseudo-labels for depth and optical flow. We further propose RynnWorld-4D-Policy, an inverse dynamics head that consumes the internal 4D representations of RynnWorld-4D in a single forward pass, bypassing expensive multi-step denoising, to output robot actions in a closed-loop manner. Experiments show that RynnWorld-4D produces temporally and spatially coherent 4D predictions, and that RynnWorld-4D-Policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world dexterous bimanual manipulation tasks, particularly excelling in tasks demanding spatial precision and temporal coordination.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based 4D world model (RGB, depth, optical flow) conditioned on RGB-D and language, with a tri-branch architecture and 3D RoPE, plus a large-scale Rynn4DDataset and an inverse-dynamics policy that achieves state-of-the-art in dexterous manipulation.
AI.motivation: To create a representation that jointly models appearance, geometry, and motion (4D dynamics) to bridge perceptual prediction and control for open-world robotic manipulation, reducing the gap between world models and policy learning.
AI.method: A unified diffusion model (RynnWorld-4D) that co-produces future RGB, depth, and optical flow from a single RGB-D image and a language instruction. It features a tri-branch architecture with cross-modal attention and frame-wise 3D Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) to keep appearance, geometry, and motion coherent. Training data is scaled with Rynn4DDataset 1.0 (254.4M frames) with pseudo-labels for depth and optical flow. An inverse dynamics head (RynnWorld-4D-Policy) uses the 4D representations for closed-loop action generation in a single forward pass.
AI.result: The model yields temporally and spatially coherent 4D predictions across RGB, depth, and optical flow. The policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world dexterous bimanual manipulation tasks, demonstrating superior spatial precision and temporal coordination.
AI.conclusion: 4D world modeling conditioned on RGB-D and language can effectively align perception with control, enabling efficient, closed-loop manipulation. Large-scale multi-modal data and a specialized architecture are key to achieving coherent 4D predictions and strong policy performance.

title: Drift Happens: An Empirical Study of Neural Architecture Robustness to Temporal Distribution Shift
comment: 33 pages, 28 figures. Extended version of the QCDS 2026 proceedings paper; proceedings version to appear in Springer LNCS. Interactive website: https://drift-happens.org/
summary:
Real-world data distributions evolve over time, inducing temporal distribution shift that can substantially degrade the reliability of deployed machine learning systems. However, the extent to which architectural choices and their associated inductive biases affect temporal robustness remains insufficiently understood.
  We present a systematic empirical comparison of temporal robustness across three heterogeneous, time-indexed domains encompassing image classification, multi-label text classification, and text regression tasks. Using a unified evaluation framework based on temporal drift matrices, we train models on cumulative historical data and evaluate their performance on both earlier and later time periods, thereby quantifying cross-temporal generalization. Our study spans model families ranging from simple multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks to recurrent networks and pretrained Transformer-based encoders.
  Collectively, the results show that architectural inductive biases systematically shape temporal robustness: models whose inductive biases lead them to exploit localized, highly discriminative features attain the highest in-distribution accuracy, yet those features are often the ones that change most over time, so these models degrade fastest, while pretrained encoders that draw on coarser, more stable representations drift more gradually. These observations offer practical guidance for selecting architectures for real-world systems subject to temporal drift.

AI.tldr: Architectural inductive biases shape temporal robustness; models relying on local, discriminative features achieve high in-distribution accuracy but degrade quickly under temporal drift, whereas pretrained encoders with coarse representations drift more slowly across image, text classification, and text regression tasks.
AI.motivation: To understand how model architecture and inductive biases influence robustness to time-based distribution shifts in real-world data.
AI.method: Systematic empirical comparison across three time-indexed domains (image classification, multi-label text classification, text regression). Use a unified evaluation framework with temporal drift matrices. Train on cumulative historical data; evaluate on earlier and later time periods to measure cross-temporal generalization. Evaluate across model families from MLPs and CNNs to RNNs and pretrained Transformer encoders.
AI.result: Inductive biases systematically shape temporal robustness: models that exploit localized, highly discriminative features achieve high in-distribution accuracy but degrade fastest due to feature change over time; pretrained encoders that rely on coarser, more stable representations drift more gradually. Findings consistent across the three domains, offering guidance for architecture selection under temporal drift.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidance for selecting architectures for real-world systems subject to temporal drift, suggesting a bias toward models with more stable, coarse representations when long-term temporal robustness is a priority.

title: Propose and Attend: Training-free MLLM Grounding Confidence via Multi-Token Localized Attention
summary: Multimodal large language models can emit localized predictions, bounding boxes for objects and temporal windows for video and audio events, but they hallucinate these regions prolifically. The model's own token log-probabilities are nearly uninformative: they conflate grounding quality with input ambiguity, and coordinate tokens become near-deterministic once the model commits. We propose Multi-Token Localized Attention (MTLA): a training-free, post-hoc score that measures how strongly a prediction's tokens attend to the region they claim. Prior attention-based detectors, which sum attention over the entire input modality and read a single response token, are weaker special cases; we show that summing only within the claimed region and aggregating across all prediction tokens recovers a stronger grounding signal. The same recipe applies almost trivially to other modalities and tasks: object detection in images and temporal localization in video and audio. Across multiple MLLM families and three modalities, MTLA improves hallucination AUROC by +7 to +38 over the best prior training-free baseline. Used as a confidence score for re-ranking, it nearly doubles the zero-shot COCO detection AP of an open-source 8B generalist (from 20.4 to 37.0), narrowing the gap to supervised detectors without any task-specific training.

AI.tldr: MTLA is a training-free, post-hoc score that assesses how strongly a model's prediction tokens attend to the claimed region, by summing attention within that region across all tokens. It provides a stronger grounding signal than prior attention-based detectors, improves grounding metrics across modalities, and boosts zero-shot localization performance without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Grounding visual/audio/text predictions in multimodal LLMs is unreliable; token log-probabilities often conflate ambiguity with grounding and become deterministic once the model commits, leading to hallucinated localizations. A training-free, post-hoc measure of token-region attention can provide a robust grounding signal.
AI.method: Introduce Multi-Token Localized Attention (MTLA): for each prediction token, compute attention restricted to the claimed region; sum these attentions across all prediction tokens, and aggregate across modalities. This post-hoc score is trained-free and can be applied to images, videos, and audio localization tasks. Compared to prior detectors that sum attention over the whole input and read a single token, MTLA uses region-local attention and token-aggregation to recover a stronger grounding signal.
AI.result: MTLA yields substantial gains in grounding performance: +7 to +38 AUROC over the best prior training-free baseline across multiple MLLM families and modalities. Using MTLA as a confidence score for re-ranking nearly doubles zero-shot COCO detection AP for an open-source 8B model (20.4 -> 37.0). It narrows the gap to supervised detectors without task-specific training.
AI.conclusion: A simple, training-free post-hoc mechanism (MTLA) provides a strong, generalizable grounding signal for multimodal localization across images, video, and audio, improving localization metrics and reducing hallucinations without additional training.

title: FreqDepthKV: Frequency-Guided Depth Sharing for Robust KV Cache Compression in Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: Long-context LLM inference is increasingly limited by the memory and bandwidth cost of KV caches, yet aggressive compression can remove the layer-specific evidence needed for retrieval and multi-step reasoning. We introduce FreqDepthKV, an inference-time cache compression method that factorizes adjacent-layer KV states into shared low-frequency depth components and sparse high-frequency residuals. A lightweight online probe assigns attention heads to shared-depth, residual-depth, or exact cache modes according to their contribution to reconstruction-sensitive attention logits, allowing the compression policy to adapt to prompt structure without retraining. Across long-context question answering, needle retrieval, summarization, and code generation benchmarks, FreqDepthKV preserves task accuracy under substantially smaller cache budgets. With a 32k-token prefill window, FreqDepthKV reaches 58.3 Exact Match, 63.0 F1, 32.5 ROUGE-L, and 48.1 pass@1, closely matching full KV while outperforming prior compressed-cache methods. It also improves decoding throughput to 70.4 tokens/s, reduces TTFT to 2.06 seconds, and lowers peak KV memory to 6.2 GB, achieving a 3.9x effective compression ratio.

AI.tldr: Adaptive KV-cache compression (FreqDepthKV) factorizes adjacent-layer KV states into shared low-frequency depth components and sparse high-frequency residuals, guided by an online probe, achieving near-full KV performance with substantial memory/throughput gains.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory and bandwidth of KV caches; aggressive compression can discard layer-specific evidence needed for retrieval and multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: FreqDepthKV factorizes adjacent-layer KV states into shared-depth components and residuals. A lightweight online probe assigns attention heads to shared-depth, residual-depth, or exact cache modes based on each head's contribution to reconstruction-sensitive attention logits, enabling adaptive, retraining-free compression.
AI.result: On long-context tasks (QA, needle retrieval, summarization, code generation), accuracy is preserved under smaller caches. With a 32k-token prefill window, metrics reach EM 58.3, F1 63.0, ROUGE-L 32.5, pass@1 48.1; decoding throughput 70.4 tokens/s; TTFT 2.06s; peak KV memory 6.2 GB; ~3.9x effective compression, closely matching full KV and outperforming prior compressed-cache methods.
AI.conclusion: FreqDepthKV provides substantial memory and speedups for long-context inference with minimal accuracy loss, by adaptively compressing KV caches without retraining and across diverse tasks.

title: Embodied Human-Robot Interaction via Acoustics: A MARL Approach with AcoustoBots for Spatial Data Physicalization
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Robotic System and Artificial Intelligence (RSAI 2026), 10-12 July, 2026, Tokyo, Japan
summary: Traditional data physicalization is often static and disconnected from real environments, limiting its ability to convey embodied spatial dynamics and engage users. To address this limitation, we present AcoustoBots, a mobile acoustophoretic data-physicalization platform in which TurtleBot3 robots carry upward-facing 8 x 8 ultrasonic phased arrays. Each array levitates a particle whose height (1-10 cm) encodes a local urban scalar value, such as population density, noise, or traffic. A MARL (Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning) policy based on the Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm, with centralized training and decentralized execution, selects collision-aware navigation actions, while a high-rate Gerchberg-Saxton-Phased Array of Transducers (GS-PAT) acoustic controller maintains trap stability and updates array phases to achieve the commanded height during motion. This creates a closed perception-display-action loop. We evaluate single-robot city-to-city traversal and dual-robot cooperative coverage on a 4 m x 3 m scaled UK map using PhaseSpace-based localization for repeatable multi-robot trials. Results show stable in-motion levitation and consistent, location-dependent height rendering, with task success rates of 90% and 80% for the single and dual-robot regimes, respectively, over 10 trials per regime, and low collision counts. These findings support acoustophoretic levitation as a simple, glanceable, robot-mediated communication cue for embodied human-robot interaction in spatial analytics.

AI.tldr: A mobile acoustic levitation platform (AcoustoBots) uses TurtleBot3 with 8x8 ultrasonic phased arrays to levitate particles whose height encodes urban data; MARL (MADDPG) governs collision-aware navigation; GS-PAT maintains levitation phases; demonstrated on 1- and 2-robot tasks with 90%/80% success and potential as glanceable spatial analytics cues.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of traditional data physicalization—static, disconnected from real environments—by enabling embodied spatial dynamics and interaction through mobile, robot-mediated data display via acoustophoretic levitation.
AI.method: A mobile platform where upward-facing 8x8 ultrasonic phased arrays on TurtleBot3 levitate particles to heights (1–10 cm) encoding scalar data. Navigation is driven by a MARL policy based on MADDPG with centralized training and decentralized execution for collision awareness. A GS-PAT acoustic controller updates array phases to maintain target heights during motion. A closed perception-display-action loop is evaluated on a 4 m × 3 m scaled UK map using PhaseSpace localization, with single- and dual-robot setups across 10 trials each.
AI.result: The system achieves stable levitation during motion and consistent, location-dependent height rendering. Task success rates are 90% (single robot) and 80% (dual robot) over 10 trials per regime, with low collision counts.
AI.conclusion: Acoustophoretic levitation provides a simple, glanceable, robot-mediated communication cue for embodied human–robot interaction in spatial analytics, enabling intuitive data display during navigation and exploration.

title: Learning Sparsest Linear Causal DAGs with Latent Confounders via Higher-Order Cumulants
summary:
Recovering the exact directed acyclic graph (DAG) in linear non-Gaussian acyclic models with latent confounders (LvLiNGAM) remains a challenging problem. Although LvLiNGAM is identifiable only up to an observational equivalence class, each equivalence class is characterized by a unique sparsest DAG. Recovering the sparsest DAG from finite samples, however, remains difficult. Although existing methods are asymptotically consistent, they do not provide an explicit finite-sample procedure for recovering the unique sparsest DAG, nor do they handle models with an arbitrary number of latent confounders.
  In this paper, we propose a finite-sample method for recovering the sparsest DAG without imposing any restriction on the number of latent confounders. Simulation studies and real-data analyses demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior finite-sample performance compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Finite-sample procedure to recover the sparsest DAG in LvLiNGAM with latent confounders; outperforms existing asymptotically consistent methods in simulations and real data.
AI.motivation: LvLiNGAM is identifiable only up to an observational equivalence class; each class contains a unique sparsest DAG, but finite-sample recovery is challenging and the number of latent confounders is unconstrained.
AI.method: Introduce a finite-sample method that recovers the sparsest DAG without restricting the number of latent confounders; applicable to arbitrary latent confounder counts; validated by simulations and real-data analyses.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves superior finite-sample performance compared with existing approaches in both simulated and real datasets.
AI.conclusion: A practical finite-sample tool to recover the sparsest DAG in LvLiNGAM with latent confounders, robust to the number of latent confounders and outperforming prior asymptotically consistent methods.

title: SpecTrack: Spectral Prompt Guided Adaptive Experts for Multispectral Object Tracking
summary: Multispectral image(MSI) and hyperspectral image(HSI) object tracking object tracking exploits recorded band-wise observations to improve target--background discrimination under similar RGB appearance, mixed pixels, illumination variation, occlusion, and clutter. However, existing trackers commonly process all search regions through a fixed capacity spectral--spatial path, ignoring that tracking difficulty varies substantially across frames and target states. Clear regions may require only lightweight local discrimination, whereas ambiguous boundaries and spectrally similar distractors often demand stronger contextual reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose SpecTrack, a spectral--spatial complexity-aware tracker that formulates MSI tracking as search-region-level adaptive capacity allocation. Its core component, the Spectral Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (SAMoE) module, provides a capacity-ordered expert pool with progressively increasing latent rank, receptive field, and depth. Expert selection is guided by a Spectral Prompt Router, which fuses semantic context, spatial boundary cues, and a latent channel-variation cue computed after multispectral patch embedding to activate a sparse subset of SAMoE experts for each search region. In parallel, a Shared Global Expert supplies common latent spectral--spatial context to reduce fragmented sparse-routing decisions. Experiments on MUST, MSITrack, and HOTC20 demonstrate a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off. The accuracy-oriented SpecTrack-L384 achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive AUCs of 65.2\%, 51.9\%, and 72.6\% on the three benchmarks, while the balanced SpecTrack-B224 reaches 62.4\% AUC at 43.7 FPS on MUST. An additional GOT-10k evaluation indicates RGB-domain architectural generalization, with SpecTrack-L384 achieving 79.3\% AO.

AI.tldr: SpecTrack uses a region-level adaptive capacity allocator for MSI/HSI tracking, via a SAMoE module and a Spectral Prompt Router, achieving favorable AUC and FPS on MSI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Tracking difficulty varies across frames and target states; a fixed spectral-spatial path wastes capacity and degrades discrimination; there is a need for region-aware resource allocation to balance accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Spectral Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (SAMoE) provides a pool of experts with progressively increasing latent rank, receptive field, and depth. A Spectral Prompt Router fuses semantic context, boundary cues, and a latent channel-variation cue (computed after multispectral patch embedding) to activate a sparse subset of SAMoE experts per search region. A Shared Global Expert provides common context to stabilize routing.
AI.result: Evaluations on MUST, MSITrack, and HOTC20 show SpecTrack-L384 achieving AUCs of 65.2%, 51.9%, and 72.6%, respectively; SpecTrack-B224 attains 62.4% AUC at 43.7 FPS on MUST; RGB-domain generalization on GOT-10k with SpecTrack-L384 achieving 79.3% AO.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive spectral-spatial capacity allocation via SAMoE and the spectral router yields competitive state-of-the-art performance and favorable efficiency, with demonstrated cross-domain generalization and strong performance on MSI benchmarks.

title: Bridging Physical Reasoning and Task Generalization via Visual Action Outcome Reasoning Alignment
comment: ICML'26 Workshop RLxF: Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to generalize in interactive physical reasoning, particularly under unseen tasks and environments. Two key failure modes are prominent: hallucinated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that contradicts physical reality, and misalignment between the model's reasoning and actions. We present VAORA (Visual Action Outcome Reasoning Alignment), a novel reward design that directly addresses both issues. VAORA introduces two complementary rewards: Visual Alignment Reward, which anchors VLM reasoning to the visual context independent of the agent action itself, and Visual-Action Alignment Reward, which grounds reasoning in the visual outcome induced by the model's action. Together, these rewards suppress hallucinated CoT and reduce the gap between reasoning and behavior. To improve training stability, we further employ smooth, dense rewards by estimating success probabilities using a pre-trained in-domain expert agent. Experiments on PHYRE and Virtual Tool support our performances across novel-task and unseen-environment settings, confirming that grounded and generalizable physical intelligence can be induced through VAORA.

AI.tldr: VAORA introduces two visual grounding rewards to align vision-language model reasoning with visual outcomes in interactive physics tasks, reducing hallucinated chain-of-thought and misalignment with actions; uses dense rewards via a pre-trained expert; improves generalization on PHYRE and Virtual Tool.
AI.motivation: Address two major failure modes of vision-language models in interactive physical reasoning: (i) hallucinated chain-of-thought (CoT) that contradicts physical reality, and (ii) misalignment between the model's internal reasoning and its actions. The goal is robust, task- and environment-generalizable physical intelligence.
AI.method: Propose two complementary rewards: Visual Alignment Reward (VAR) anchors reasoning to the visual context independent of the agent’s actions, and Visual-Action Alignment Reward (VAAR) grounds reasoning in the visual outcome produced by the model’s actions. To stabilize training, use smooth, dense rewards by estimating success probabilities with a pre-trained in-domain expert agent.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on PHYRE and Virtual Tool demonstrates improved performance in novel-task and unseen-environment settings, indicating that grounded and generalizable physical intelligence can be induced by VAORA.
AI.conclusion: VAORA provides effective grounding for VLM-based physical reasoning, reducing CoT hallucinations and the reasoning–action gap, and enabling better generalization across interactive physics tasks.

title: Lift3D-VLA: Lifting VLA Models to 3D Geometry and Dynamics-Aware Manipulation
summary: Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong generalization across diverse tasks. However, effective robotic manipulation in physical environments fundamentally requires geometric understanding and spatial reasoning. While some VLA approaches attempt to incorporate 3D information, they are constrained by limited data availability and geometric information loss in current 3D encoding pipelines, and fail to jointly capture 3D geometry and temporally structured actions in dynamic environments. To address these limitations, we introduce Lift3D-VLA, a unified VLA framework that equips models with explicit 3D point cloud reasoning and enables temporally coherent action generation. First, building upon our previous work Lift3D, an enhanced 2D model-lifting strategy is proposed to geometrically align 3D points with pretrained 2D positional embeddings. This design enables direct point-cloud encoding within the VLA vision encoder while minimizing spatial information loss. Based on explicit 3D inputs, we propose Geometry-Centric Masked Autoencoding (GC-MAE), a dual-objective self-supervised framework that reconstructs the current point cloud while predicting its future geometric evolution. This formulation allows the 2D vision encoder to internalize both 3D structure and physical dynamics. To fully exploit 3D representations, we further design layer-wise temporal action modeling, which leverages multiple layers of the LLM to collaboratively predict action chunks, enabling temporally consistent predictions. Across 22 simulated tasks and 8 real-world manipulation tasks, Lift3D-VLA achieves 10.8% and 11.1% higher mean success rates on MetaWorld and RLBench than the best-performing prior VLA methods, and outperforms the strongest real-world baseline by 4 percentage points, while exhibiting stronger generalization to out-of-distribution perturbations.

AI.tldr: Lift3D-VLA unifies vision-language-action with explicit 3D point-cloud reasoning and temporally coherent action generation; introduces 2D-to-3D point lifting, GC-MAE self-supervised learning for current/future geometry, and layer-wise temporal action modeling; achieves state-of-the-art gains on MetaWorld/RLBench and better real-world generalization.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation requires robust geometric understanding and temporal action planning. Existing VLA methods struggle to preserve 3D geometry in encodings and to model temporally structured actions in dynamic environments; thus a framework that jointly handles 3D structure and temporal action is needed.
AI.method: 1) Lift3D: a 2D model-lifting strategy to geometrically align 3D points with pretrained 2D positional embeddings, enabling direct point-cloud encoding in the VLA vision encoder; 2) Geometry-Centric Masked Autoencoding (GC-MAE): a dual-objective self-supervised framework that reconstructs the current point cloud and predicts its future geometric evolution; 3) layer-wise temporal action modeling: multiple layers of an LLM collaborate to predict action chunks for temporally coherent actions.
AI.result: Evaluated on 22 simulated tasks and 8 real-world manipulation tasks. Lift3D-VLA achieves 10.8% and 11.1% higher mean success rates on MetaWorld and RLBench than the best prior VLA methods, respectively, and outperforms the strongest real-world baseline by 4 percentage points, with improved robustness to out-of-distribution perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Lift3D-VLA demonstrates that explicit 3D reasoning and temporally coherent action generation can be jointly learned within a VLA framework, yielding better generalization and real-world performance; the approach leverages point-cloud encoding, geometry-centric self-supervision, and multi-layer LLM-based temporal planning.

title: Stability Annealing Selects the Implicit Bias of Smoothed Sign Descent: A Rate-Indexed Barrier Path on Separable Data
summary: Adaptive gradient methods can favor max-margin separators that differ from gradient descent, yet a fixed positive numerical stability constant eventually changes the update geometry again. This paper studies the rate-controlled middle case for full-batch linear classification on separable data. For memoryless stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent with weighted exponential loss, we prove that the normalized iterates converge to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice. The proof rewrites the dynamics exactly as entropic mirror ascent on a concave dual objective, controls the dual gap by a KL recursion, and yields an explicit S_t^{-1/2} normalized-iterate envelope. The static barrier geometry is fully characterized, including KKT conditions and both endpoint limits. Experiments validate the exact dual identities to floating-point error, illustrate the predicted path and rate diagram, and show an empirical fixed-epsilon crossover scaling in cumulative time. We further report robustness and boundary diagnostics for logistic tails, fixed-epsilon crossover, and adaptive-method variants, delineating the scope of the proved smoothed-sign theory.

AI.tldr: Rate-controlled stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent for full-batch linear classification on separable data converges, in normalized form, to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice; dynamics map to entropic mirror ascent on a dual objective with a KL-based error envelope.
AI.motivation: To understand how adaptive gradient methods with memoryless stability constraints bias optimization trajectories toward max-margin separators, and to characterize the intermediate regime where stability alters geometry but not asymptotics; to provide a rigorous dual formulation, convergence envelope, and practical diagnostics for smoothed-sign dynamics.
AI.method: Model the memoryless stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent with weighted exponential loss on separable data. Reformulate the dynamics as entropic mirror ascent on a concave dual objective. Use a KL recursion to bound the dual gap and derive an explicit S_t^{-1/2}-normalized-iterate envelope. Fully characterize the barrier geometry, including KKT conditions and endpoint limits. Validate identities and behavior through experiments, and analyze fixed-epsilon crossover and robustness across adaptive variations.
AI.result: Proved that normalized iterates converge to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice. Established exact dual identities (to floating-point precision), provided a concrete rate diagram and a fixed-epsilon crossover scaling in cumulative time, and demonstrated robustness diagnostics for logistic tails and adaptive-method variants.
AI.conclusion: The work clarifies the geometry and dynamics of rate-controlled adaptive methods in linear classification, delineates the applicability of the smoothed-sign theory, and offers precise dual formulations, convergence envelopes, and practical diagnostics for practitioners.

title: SparseCtrl-HOI: Sparse Temporal Control for Human-Object Interaction Video Generation
summary: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) video generation aims to synthesize realistic videos of humans manipulating diverse objects, serving as a promising avenue for AI-driven live streaming e-commerce. A primary obstacle in this domain lies in the complexity of modeling fine-grained physical dynamics and the intricate spatial-temporal coordination between human hands and objects. Existing approaches to this problem typically rely on dense temporal guidance, e.g., frame-wise hand-object pose sequences, to strictly control the interaction process. However, such dense guidance incurs high annotation costs and affects motion synthesis diversity. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SparseCtrl-HOI, a novel sparse temporal control framework for HOI video generation. It requires only a few keyframes that capture interaction states at designated timestamps. Specifically, we employ a Time-Controlled Rotary Positional Embedding (TiRoPE) mechanism to temporally anchor these keyframes while preserving their spatial integrity. Subsequently, to govern the dynamics across intermediate frames, we propose a Motion Prior Injection Module that leverages Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to extract high-level motion priors. This empowers the model to hallucinate logically and physically plausible transitions. Furthermore, we build SparseHOI-5K, a high-quality and richly annotated dataset for HOI video generation with sparse temporal control. Comprehensive evaluations confirm that our method substantially reduces annotation overhead while synthesizing superior live-streaming e-commerce videos. Both our code and dataset are publicly available at https://mpi-lab.github.io/SparseCtrl-HOI.

AI.tldr: SparseCtrl-HOI introduces sparse temporal control for HOI video generation using few keyframes, TiRoPE anchoring, and Motion Prior Injection with MLLMs; accompanied by SparseHOI-5K dataset; achieves lower annotation cost and high-quality, plausible HOI videos for live e-commerce.
AI.motivation: Overcome the high cost and limited diversity of dense frame-to-frame guidance in HOI video generation; enable efficient and diverse synthesis with sparse annotations.
AI.method: Use Time-Controlled Rotary Positional Embedding (TiRoPE) to anchor sparse keyframes temporally; employ a Motion Prior Injection Module that leverages Multimodal LLMs to extract high-level motion priors for intermediate frames; create SparseHOI-5K dataset with sparse temporal annotations; perform experiments evaluating quality and annotation efficiency.
AI.result: Significant reduction in annotation overhead; generated HOI videos with plausible, physically consistent dynamics and improved performance for live-streaming e-commerce; code and dataset released.
AI.conclusion: Sparse temporal control with TiRoPE and MLLM-based priors is effective for HOI video generation, balancing annotation efficiency with video quality; dataset supports broader adoption.

title: DepthWeave-KV: Token-Adaptive Cross-Layer Residual Factorization for Long-Context KV Cache Compression
summary: Long-context language model inference is increasingly limited by the memory bandwidth and capacity required to store key-value caches, yet existing compression methods often apply uniform budgets across layers or tokens and degrade retrieval when lexical cues and semantic states require different preservation. We introduce DepthWeave-KV, a token-adaptive cache compression method that factorizes key and value states across neighboring transformer layers using shared low-rank channel bases while retaining lightweight token-specific residuals where attention behavior is sensitive. DepthWeave-KV combines cross-depth residual factorization with a token-conditional depth router that allocates higher reconstruction rank to instruction-bearing and retrieval-critical tokens, and uses calibration-free online error tracking from attention-output probes to adapt compression during generation without retraining the base model. A fused CUDA implementation jointly performs basis lookup, residual dequantization, and attention projection to reduce decode-time memory traffic. Across LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, L-Eval, and long-form QA and summarization benchmarks, DepthWeave-KV achieves near-full-cache task quality with substantially lower memory use, improving average score and retrieval accuracy over prior compressed caches while reaching 8.3x KV memory reduction and 72.8 tokens per second at 64K context.

AI.tldr: DepthWeave-KV is a per-token, per-depth adaptive cache compression for long-context LMs. It factorizes key/value caches across neighboring layers with shared low-rank bases, augmented by token-specific residuals, and uses a token-level depth router plus calibration-free online error tracking to adapt compression without retraining. It achieves large memory reduction (8.3x) with near-full quality on multiple long-context benchmarks and practical throughput gains (72.8 tokens/s at 64K).
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth/capacity to store key-value caches. Uniform compression budgets across layers/tokens degrade retrieval of tokens with different preservation needs. There is a demand for adaptive, token-aware cache compression that preserves critical tokens and uses no retraining.
AI.method: Factorize key/value states across neighboring transformer layers using shared low-rank channel bases; attach lightweight token-specific residuals where attention behavior is sensitive. Introduce a token-conditional depth router to allocate higher reconstruction rank to instruction-bearing and retrieval-critical tokens. Use calibration-free online error tracking from attention-output probes to adapt compression during generation. Implement a fused CUDA pipeline for basis lookup, residual dequantization, and attention projection to minimize decode-time memory traffic.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, L-Eval, and long-form QA/summarization shows near-full-cache task quality with substantially lower memory use. DepthWeave-KV outperforms prior compressed caches in average score and retrieval accuracy, achieving 8.3x KV memory reduction and 72.8 tokens per second at 64K context.
AI.conclusion: Token-adaptive, depth-aware cache compression with online error tracking enables large memory savings while preserving retrieval quality, providing practical, retraining-free acceleration for long-context LMs and potentially broad applicability to cache-based inference.

title: Learning When to Automate: Queue Control in Human-AI Service Systems
summary: We study a human-AI service system in which tasks arrive sequentially and are processed through a two-stage architecture: an automated chatbot followed, when necessary, by a human agent. We consider $T$ sequentially arriving tasks, each belonging to one of $K$ heterogeneous types. For each task the decision maker chooses how many resources to allocate to the chatbot, whose type-dependent success probabilities are initially unknown. Tasks not resolved by the chatbot enter type-dependent human-service queues, where they are processed by a human agent with unknown service rates. This model captures a central tradeoff in hybrid service systems: relying more on automation reduces human congestion but increases chatbot costs, while insufficient automation may overload the human agent. We propose the UCB-DPP policy, which combines Upper Confidence Bounds with Drift-Plus-Penalty control to learn the unknown parameters of the system while making queue-aware decisions. We prove that UCB-DPP achieves regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ and guarantees mean-rate stability of the human-service queues. Simulations on synthetic instances show that the proposed policy outperforms natural baselines.

AI.tldr: A learning-based control for a hybrid chatbot-human service system that achieves sublinear regret while stabilizing human queues.
AI.motivation: Optimize a two-stage, type-diverse service system where chatbot automation and human agents incur costs; unknown chatbot success probabilities and human service rates require online learning to balance automation against human congestion.
AI.method: Introduce UCB-DPP, integrating Upper Confidence Bounds with Drift-Plus-Penalty control to learn unknown parameters and make queue-aware resource allocation decisions across K task types over T arrivals.
AI.result: The policy achieves a regret of tilde O(K sqrt(T)) and ensures mean-rate stability of human-service queues; simulations show it outperforms natural baselines.
AI.conclusion: UCB-DPP provides a principled, scalable framework for jointly learning system parameters and controlling hybrid automation to minimize costs while preventing human queues from growing.

title: Unlearnable Faces: Privacy Protection Surviving Extraction Pipeline
summary: Unlearnable examples keep publicly shared photos from being learned by unauthorized face-recognition models. An imperceptible perturbation, added before sharing, makes any model trained on the protected photos fail on clean faces. The perturbation is crafted on the shared image, however the attacker trains on the face it extracts, cropped and resized to the recognizer input, and under this extraction the protection collapses. We propose LPID, which builds the extraction into the unlearnable-example objective. LPID confines the perturbation to the extracted face region and optimizes it through a differentiable model of the extraction, concentrating its energy in the frequency band the extraction preserves. Because this robustness is a property of the transform rather than of any identity, LPID is re-optimized per album and protects even users it has never seen. LPID attains the lowest attacker accuracy of all methods in every setting we evaluate, holding the attacker below $10\%$ under crop+resize extraction on identities unseen at protection time, while remaining imperceptible at $32.7$\,dB PSNR and $0.161$ LPIPS.

AI.tldr: LPID proposes an extraction-aware unlearnable perturbation for face images. It optimizes a perturbation within the extracted face region using a differentiable extraction model, concentrating energy in preserved frequency bands, and re-optimizes per album. It remains robust to crop+resize and achieves attacker accuracy <10% on unseen identities, while remaining perceptually imperceptible (32.7 dB PSNR, 0.161 LPIPS).
AI.motivation: To counteract the vulnerability of standard unlearnable perturbations when input images are cropped and resized before recognition, exposing protected photos to potential leakage of privacy. The goal is a perturbation robust to the attacker’s preprocessing pipeline and adaptable per album.
AI.method: Integrate the face extraction process into the unlearnable objective by constraining the perturbation to the extracted face region and optimizing through a differentiable model of extraction. The perturbation is energy-concentrated in the frequency band preserved by the extractor, enabling robustness to transform-based preprocessing. The approach is re-optimized per album to protect even unseen users.
AI.result: LPID achieves the lowest attacker accuracy across evaluated settings, keeping the attacker below 10% for crop+resize extraction on identities unseen during protection. It maintains imperceptibility with 32.7 dB PSNR and 0.161 LPIPS.
AI.conclusion: Transform-robust unlearnable perturbations can be tailored to the extraction pipeline, yielding strong protection that generalizes to unseen identities and preserves perceptual quality. LPID’s per-album re-optimization and frequency-focused design address the collapse of protection under standard preprocessing.

title: The Large Cancer Assistant (LCA): A Model-Agnostic Orchestration Framework for Scalable Clinical Decision Support in Oncology
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables, 9 appendices, 14 references, Elsevier JBI format
summary: - Objective: Multimodal deep learning models in oncology are currently limited by monolithic designs that rigidly couple data ingestion, clinical routing, and artificial intelligence (AI) inference. To address this inflexibility, we propose the Large Cancer Assistant (LCA), a model-agnostic, post-hoc orchestration framework designed for scalable clinical decision support. - Methods: The LCA is mathematically formalized as a 7-tuple architecture grounded in the principle of Algorithmic Impermeability, ensuring the orchestration logic remains strictly independent of underlying black-box AI models. We introduce the Entry Theory, leveraging Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) to standardize multimodal patient data along distinct structural and medical axes. The system dynamically orchestrates data via a Cancer Switching Module and intentionally isolates the core AI execution from volatile hospital IT infrastructures by outputting a Standardized Intermediate Payload (SIP). - Results: A Proof of Concept (PoC) validated the orchestration logic across four technical scenarios. The framework executed a nominal flow with negligible orchestration overhead. It empirically demonstrated algorithmic impermeability by maintaining an invariant routing projection during AI model swaps, and it validated strict failure-safety by achieving a 100\% recall rate in generating targeted Supplementary Data Requests (SDR) under injected data anomalies. Multi-protocol execution capability was also successfully verified. - Conclusion: By structurally decoupling multimodal ingestion from feature inference, the LCA provides a highly adaptable and modular orchestration foundation. The SIP establishes a clear architectural boundary, natively setting the stage for downstream Electronic Medical Record (EMR) interoperability as an independent future paradigm.

AI.tldr: LCA provides a model-agnostic, post-hoc orchestration framework that decouples multimodal data ingestion from AI inference via a Standardized Intermediate Payload, enabling flexible model swaps and future EMR interoperability.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal oncology models are monolithic and rigid, hindering flexible integration and scalable clinical decision support. An architecture that preserves AI secrecy (Algorithmic Impermeability) while enabling modular data handling and interoperability is needed.
AI.method: Formalize a 7-tuple architecture with Algorithmic Impermeability; introduce Entry Theory leveraging Geometric Deep Learning to standardize multimodal patient data along structural/medical axes; employ a Cancer Switching Module to orchestrate data; output a SIP to isolate AI from hospital IT; PoC across four scenarios to test throughput, routing invariance, failure-safety (SDR recall under data anomalies), and multi-protocol execution.
AI.result: PoC confirms the orchestration logic with low overhead, demonstrates invariant routing during AI model swaps, achieves 100% SDR recall under injected anomalies, and verifies multi-protocol execution capability.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling data ingestion from AI inference yields a modular, adaptable orchestration framework; SIP defines a clear architectural boundary and foreshadows downstream EMR interoperability as a future direction.

title: SplineNet: An Isogeometric Deep Learning Method for Complex Shells
summary: We present a novel isogeometric deep learning method, termed SplineNet, for the seamless design and analysis of shell structures with complex geometries. The proposed approach is built upon watertight spline representations, e.g., analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines, and features exact geometric descriptions of Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models in neural networks. Bézier extraction is used to build the network architecture, where Bernstein polynomials serve as the nonlinear activation functions. SplineNet can be applied in a data-free or data-driven way. In the data-free case, energy-based formulations can be naturally incorporated as loss terms, which fulfill the need of Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) and can be accurately calculated. In particular, the Kirchhoff--Love (KL) model is adopted to solve for the mechanical behaviors of shell structures. This way, CAD and CAE can be tightly integrated in a deep neural network without the time-consuming model/data exchange process. In the data-driven case, SplineNet can be used as the trunk net of Deep Operator Networks (DeepONet) to provide interpretability. Given such a trained network and unseen input data, results can be immediately obtained without retraining the network or repeatedly performing the traditional workflow for analysis.
