In the end, a variety of numerical examples are studied to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, especially when real-world complex geometries are involved.

AI.tldr: SplineNet isogeometric DL for CAD/CAE-integrated shell analysis using watertight splines, Bézier extraction, and Bernstein activations; supports energy-based data-free loss (Kirchhoff-Love) and data-driven DeepONet trunk for fast inference on complex geometries.
AI.motivation: Bridge CAD and CAE with deep learning while preserving exact geometry and enabling efficient, physics-consistent shell analysis of complex geometries.
AI.method: Represent geometry with analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines (watertight). Build NN via Bézier extraction; use Bernstein polynomial activations; energy-based losses for KL shell in data-free mode; optionally act as trunk for DeepONet in data-driven mode; enables CAD-CAE integration without data exchange; applies to both data-free and data-driven regimes.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness on complex real-world geometries, showing that SplineNet can yield accurate, geometry-exact predictions and rapid inference once trained, with seamless CAD/CAE integration.
AI.conclusion: SplineNet provides a geometry-exact, physics-informed DL framework for shell analysis, achieving seamless CAD/CAE integration, interpretable data-driven options, and fast predictive capability for complex geometries.

title: OBBSeg: Irregular Lesion Segmentation under Oriented Bounding Box Annotations
summary: Pixel-level annotation remains a major bottleneck in medical image segmentation, making weak supervision an attractive yet under-constrained alternative. We propose OBBSeg, an intermediate supervision paradigm guided by Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) that bridges the gap between full and weak supervision. By jointly encoding spatial extent and orientation, OBBs provide compact geometric supervision that better aligns with elongated or anisotropic lesions, reducing the ambiguity of coarse box annotations. To mitigate the inherent rectangular bias of OBBs, we introduce a Mask-to-OBB loss, a differentiable formulation that enforces geometric consistency between predicted masks and OBB regions. Furthermore, we incorporate prompt-driven semantic guidance through two complementary modules-PAFE and DBFE-which enhance foreground representation and suppress background interference. Extensive experiments on 13 datasets across 5 imaging modalities show that OBBSeg not only outperforms existing weakly supervised methods but also achieves performance comparable to fully supervised approaches, demonstrating its potential for efficient and scalable medical image segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/StarLxc3/OBBSeg.

AI.tldr: Leverages Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) as intermediate supervision for medical image segmentation; introduces a differentiable Mask-to-OBB loss and prompt-driven modules (PAFE, DBFE) to improve weakly supervised performance, achieving results near fully supervised methods across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Pixel-level annotations for medical segmentation are expensive and time-consuming. Weak supervision via coarse boxes is under-constrained and error-prone. OBBs capture elongated or anisotropic lesions more effectively than axis-aligned boxes, reducing annotation ambiguity and offering scalable supervision.
AI.method: Proposes OBBSeg, which jointly encodes spatial extent and orientation via OBBs as intermediate supervision. Introduces a differentiable Mask-to-OBB loss to enforce geometric consistency between predicted masks and OBB regions, mitigating the rectangular bias of OBBs. Adds two prompt-driven modules, PAFE and DBFE, to provide foreground enhancement and background suppression, guided by prompts.
AI.result: Across 13 datasets and 5 imaging modalities, OBBSeg outperforms existing weakly supervised methods and achieves performance comparable to fully supervised approaches, indicating strong potential for efficient, scalable medical image segmentation.
AI.conclusion: OBBSeg demonstrates that OBB-guided intermediate supervision, coupled with geometric consistency loss and prompt-driven semantic guidance, can bridge the gap between weak and full supervision, enabling competitive segmentation performance with reduced annotation burden; code is available publicly.

title: Rethinking Indic AI from a Lens of Cultural Heritage Preservation
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) makes inroads into different parts of the Indian subcontinent, there is significant interest in studying how AI impacts the linguistic and cultural foundations of this civilization. AI is seen as a ''double-edged sword'' where on the one hand, it can enable access and inclusion for a large population, on the other, it can homogenize worldviews and exclude underrepresented languages and worldviews. In this paper, we try to characterize this problem by addressing the extensive characteristic nature of Indian linguistics and the way they closely connect to cultural practices and worldview. We then perform a longitudinal survey of how Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques have evolved in this space, tracing the historical development of Indic NLP, covering key milestones, methodological shifts, and resource creation efforts. In addition, the paper also examines the structural and sociolinguistic characteristics of Indian languages, such as rich morphology, complex scripts and grammar rules, diglossia, and large dialectal variation, and explains how these create unique challenges for building AI foundation models. We then discuss the growing role of Indic foundation models and analyze how these models address these long-standing resource and representation gaps. Finally, we propose a research direction called 'Culture Sensing', which re-imagines AI based on hermeneutic reasoning. Culture Sensing aims to address open problems such as ensuring equitable performance across low-resource languages and producing outputs that are culturally meaningful. By bringing together past work, current techniques, and emerging trends, this paper outlines research directions that can guide the next phase of Indic NLP and contribute to the development of more robust and inclusive Indic foundation models.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal survey of Indic NLP, its cultural-linguistic foundations, challenges in morphology/scripts/diglossia/dialectal variation, and a Culture Sensing direction leveraging Indic foundation models to ensure equitable and culturally meaningful outputs.
AI.motivation: To understand AI's impact on India's linguistic-cultural ecology and guide inclusive development of NLP and foundation models.
AI.method: Comprehensive literature review and historical analysis of Indic NLP, structural and sociolinguistic characterization, assessment of current AI foundation models, and proposal of Culture Sensing as a research agenda.
AI.result: Identified resource and representation gaps, mapped milestones in Indic NLP, and outlined how foundation models can address challenges; proposed Culture Sensing as a hermeneutic AI approach.
AI.conclusion: Advocates culture-aware, equitable Indic NLP via robust foundation models and an interpretive research direction; emphasizes preserving linguistic diversity and cultural meaning.

title: Scalable Perturbation Learning for Online Self-Supervised Echo State Networks
summary:
Intelligent systems should not only solve tasks but also adapt under real-world constraints. Autonomous adaptation via self-supervised learning, sequential adaptation via online learning, and memory-efficient implementation via perturbation-based learning are important requirements for such systems. However, these requirements are generally in tension for high-dimensional systems, because perturbation-based learning suffers from variance that grows with the dimension of the perturbed variables.
  In this study, we focus on echo state networks (ESNs), where this tension naturally arises in large reservoirs. We propose a perturbation-based learning rule for online self-supervised learning in ESNs. The proposed rule is derived from an orthogonal decomposition of the self-supervised learning cost, which separates an input-dependent component from a redundant component determined by the fixed ESN parameters. By perturbing only the input-dependent component, the effective perturbation dimension is reduced from the reservoir dimension to the input dimension.
  Thus, the proposed method preserves self-supervised adaptation, online learning, and scalar-feedback perturbation learning, while avoiding reservoir-size-dependent variance growth. This suggests a design principle for scalable and hardware-compatible learning: online learning should be restricted to the dynamically necessary low-dimensional component of the objective.

AI.tldr: Perturbation-based online self-supervised learning for ESNs reduces perturbation dimensionality from reservoir size to input size via an orthogonal decomposition, enabling scalable, hardware-friendly online adaptation with scalar feedback.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional reservoirs in ESNs create a tension between online adaptation and variance-limited perturbation methods. Real-world intelligent systems require self-supervised, online, memory-efficient learning.
AI.method: Decompose the SSL cost orthogonally into an input-dependent component and a redundant component tied to fixed ESN parameters. Perturbation is applied only to the input-dependent part, shrinking the effective perturbation dimension to the input dimension.
AI.result: Preserves self-supervised adaptation, online learning, and scalar-feedback perturbation learning while avoiding variance growth tied to reservoir size; proposes a design principle to limit online learning to dynamically necessary low-dimensional objective components.
AI.conclusion: Provides a scalable, hardware-compatible learning strategy for ESNs and offers a general design principle for perturbation-based learning in high-dimensional systems; potential impact on online, memory-efficient AI.

title: Structured Data Extraction from Real Estate Documents using Clustering, Classification, and Large Language Models
summary: Real estate property listings expose structured metadata through the API. Still, the richest property-level information (i.e., legal status, structural condition, utility supplies, heating systems) sits in attached questionnaire documents that no automated system currently processes at scale. These documents are heterogeneous. Some are digitally generated with selectable text, others are scanned physical forms. There are even more complex layouts that contain checkbox annotations that defeat conventional text extraction. In this paper, we present an end-to-end pipeline for acquiring, classifying, and extracting structured data from selectable text documents. The pipeline was applied to 3965 questionnaire documents collected from a live property platform via reverse-engineered REST APIs. First, we classified each document into one of three structural categories (text_only, scanned, and special_char), then extracted 35 predefined property attributes from eligible documents using DeepSeek R1 as the Large Language Model, prompted to return a structured JSON object. All 2781 submitted documents were processed successfully, producing a final dataset of 2766 unique property records. Downstream validation confirmed the data quality. Cosine similarity matching achieves a Jaccard consistency score of 0.82, and K-Means clustering produces interpretable market segments with a silhouette score of 0.2088. Results show that the proposed extraction from each property document is both feasible and reliable at this scale.

AI.tldr: End-to-end LLM-based pipeline extracts 35 property attributes from heterogeneous questionnaire documents; processed 2,781 of 3,965 docs, yielding 2,766 unique property records; clustering identifies market segments; validation shows data quality (Jaccard 0.82) and reasonable clustering (silhouette 0.2088).
AI.motivation: Rich property-level metadata lives in attached questionnaire documents that are heterogeneous (text, scanned, special_char layouts) and not processed at scale by automated systems; need automated classification and extraction to build structured data for analytics.
AI.method: Collect 3,965 questionnaire documents from a live platform via reverse-engineered REST APIs; classify each document into text_only, scanned, or special_char; extract 35 predefined property attributes from eligible documents using DeepSeek R1 LLM, prompted to return a structured JSON object; compile final dataset, then perform downstream validation using cosine similarity/Jaccard consistency and K-means clustering for market segmentation.
AI.result: All 2,781 submitted documents were processed; final dataset contains 2,766 unique property records; cosine similarity with Jaccard consistency score of 0.82; K-means clustering yields interpretable market segments with a silhouette score of 0.2088; demonstrates feasibility and reliability of extraction at scale.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline effectively handles heterogeneous document formats, enabling scalable extraction of structured property data and downstream analytics; appropriate for real estate domains and potentially adaptable to other domains with mixed document layouts.

title: KVpop -- Key-Value Cache Compression with Predictive Online Pruning
summary: Key-value (KV) cache growth is a major bottleneck in autoregressive decoding, as memory and bandwidth scale linearly with context length. Existing KV eviction methods often rely on static heuristics or proxy scores, which poorly track future token utility and cause brittle eviction as relevance shifts. To address this, we introduce KVpop, which learns a fixed-budget KV eviction policy by directly supervising the keep-or-drop decision. The scorer is trained against a novel future-attention target, computed efficiently without materializing dense attention maps. We further introduce a delayed memory-based scorer that, uniquely among learned eviction methods, defers scoring for a fixed number of steps to exploit near-future context. On AIME and HMMT mathematical reasoning, KVpop retains 98% of full-attention performance on Qwen3-4B at 75% KV cache compression and 97% at 88% compression, consistently outperforming established eviction baselines. Qwen3-8B shows even stronger results, reaching near-full teacher performance. These results show that supervising eviction with future-attention signals cuts memory costs while maintaining quality.

AI.tldr: KVpop learns a fixed-budget key-value cache eviction policy by supervising keep-or-drop decisions with future-attention signals and a delayed scoring mechanism, yielding near-full-attention quality at high compression on Qwen models and outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: KV cache growth is a major bottleneck in autoregressive decoding; memory and bandwidth scale with context length, and existing eviction heuristics fail to track evolving token utility, leading to brittle performance as relevance shifts.
AI.method: A learned eviction policy (KVpop) trained to maximize keep/drop decisions under a fixed budget, using a future-attention target as supervision. The scorer avoids materializing dense attention maps and includes a delayed memory-based variant that defers scoring for several steps to leverage near-future context.
AI.result: KVpop achieves high retention of full-attention quality under heavy KV compression: 98% on Qwen3-4B at 75% KV compression and 97% at 88% compression on AIME/HMMT tasks; Qwen3-8B approaches near-full teacher performance, consistently outperforming eviction baselines.
AI.conclusion: Supervising eviction with future-attention signals and employing delayed scoring yields substantial memory savings without sacrificing model quality, making learned eviction practical for large-scale autoregressive decoding.

title: Why does Deep Learning Improve Visual SLAM?
summary: Visual SLAM is a well-established technology utilized in a wide range of real-world applications. However, its performance still degrades under challenging visual conditions, such as low texture, severe motion blur, and poor illumination. Systems based on deep learning outperform classical geometry-based ones and achieve state-of-the-art results by combining learned 2D data association and uncertainty with differentiable geometric optimization in recurrent architectures. Still, it remains unclear exactly which components are fundamentally responsible for this success. In this paper, we ask: Is the superior performance of deep learning-based systems driven primarily by learned 2D data association, the combination of learned 2D data association and uncertainty, or the recurrent architecture itself? We investigate this question empirically by conducting a controlled study. Our findings reveal that the success of DL-based V-SLAM systems hinges on learned 2D data association and uncertainty rather than their recurrent architecture, underscoring the necessity of learning-based paradigms for the design of these components. Upon acceptance, the code will be released as open source.

AI.tldr: DL-based V-SLAM's advantage stems mainly from learned 2D data association and uncertainty, not from the recurrent architecture; emphasizes learning these components for performance gains.
AI.motivation: Unclear which components of DL V-SLAM drive performance gains; need to disentangle the roles of learned 2D data association, uncertainty modeling, and recurrence.
AI.method: Controlled empirical ablation study comparing DL V-SLAM variants with/without learned 2D data association, with/without uncertainty modeling, and with/without recurrence; evaluated under challenging visual conditions to identify primary performance drivers.
AI.result: Performance gains are primarily due to learned 2D data association and uncertainty; the recurrent architecture contributes less to overall performance.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based design of 2D data association and uncertainty is essential for DL V-SLAM; recurrence is not the main driver; code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Modeling Normal Is All You Need: Joint Latent Clustering for Anomaly Detection in Multimodal Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Faults on a cyber-physical system (CPS) are too rare and unrepresentative to characterise, or even to select a model on, so detection must instead model normal behaviour; the standard point-adjusted evaluation, however, rewards detectors that never do. CPS normal behaviour is the union of many imbalanced, curved, thin-fringed operating regimes rather than a single blob; we state this structure as ten assumptions (A1-A10), abbreviated Massive, Implicit, Imbalanced Multimodality (MIIM). We model the normal law with a jointly learned latent representation plus explicit Gaussian-mixture mode clustering, scored in the latent rather than by a global density or a reconstruction residual, and evaluate under a deliberately fair protocol: raw point-wise metrics with no point adjustment, a trivial-detector difficulty split, prevalence-matched F1, and train-normal-only calibration. On three real CPS datasets (WADI, HAI, SKAB), the detector wins both the combined column and the difficult correlation/dynamics-fault column on all three, reaching difficult-subset AUROC 0.831 on HAI, 0.726 on WADI, and 0.610 on SKAB. The margin is largest on the two multimodal datasets the MIIM assumptions target and slimmest on the near-unimodal one, tracking multimodality as the thesis predicts, and it holds against three deep detectors (USAD, TranAD, GDN) re-computed with the same raw metrics, all of which collapse on the difficult subset. The methodological contributions are the MIIM assumption set, the difficulty-stratified fair protocol, and a latent-only score that drops reconstruction because a flexible decoder rebuilds the hard faults faithfully.

AI.tldr: A CPS anomaly detector tailored for Normal-behavior modeling under Massive, Implicit, Imbalanced Multimodality (MIIM); uses latent representation with Gaussian-mixture mode clustering and a latent-only score to handle multimodal, skewed CPS data. Evaluated with a fair protocol on WADI, HAI, SKAB, achieving AUROC gains over deep detectors and across difficult subsets.
AI.motivation: Faults in CPS are rare, making fault-based modeling impractical. CPS operates in diverse, imbalanced, multimodal regimes; existing point-adjusted evaluations reward detectors that never trigger, obscuring useful detection performance. A method that explicitly models normal multimodal behavior and uses fair evaluation aims to improve detection realism and robustness.
AI.method: Joint latent representation learning with explicit Gaussian-mixture mode clustering to capture multiple normal regimes; scoring in latent space rather than global density or reconstruction residual; avoids reconstruction-based metrics; evaluation under a fair protocol with raw point-wise metrics, difficulty-stratified splits, prevalence-matched F1, and train-normal-only calibration.
AI.result: On three CPS datasets (WADI, HAI, SKAB) the detector outperforms baselines on both the combined and difficult columns, achieving AUROC 0.831 (HAI), 0.726 (WADI), 0.610 (SKAB) on difficult subsets; outperforms deep detectors USAD, TranAD, GDN when re-evaluated with the same raw metrics; performance correlates with multimodality (largest gains on multimodal datasets, smallest on near-unimodal).
AI.conclusion: MIIM provides a principled set of assumptions for CPS normal behavior, a difficulty-stratified fair evaluation protocol, and a latent-only scoring approach that avoids reconstruction pitfalls, yielding robust detection across multimodal operational regimes.

title: KOAL: Knowledge-Driven Prostate Cancer Grading with Ordinal-Aware Learning
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at MICCAI 2026. This is the submitted version prior to peer review. The final authenticated version will be available on SpringerLink
summary: Non-invasive prediction of Gleason Grade Group (GGG) in prostate cancer using multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) is clinically vital for reducing unnecessary biopsies. Existing GGG prediction methods face two major limitations. First, they often overlook non-image information critical for GGG prediction, including age, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), and expert priors embedded in radiology reports. Second, they tend to oversimplify GGG as flat categorical labels, failing to account for its intrinsic hierarchy of primary and secondary Gleason patterns. To this end, we propose a novel Knowledge-Driven Ordinal-Aware Learning (KOAL) framework with three synergistic modules. Specifically, the Clinical-Context Modulation (CCM) module uses clinical variables (e.g., age and PSA) to dynamically modulate discriminative image representations. The Knowledge-Guided Prototype Alignment (KGPA) module leverages an LLM to extract group-specific expert knowledge from training radiology reports and clinical guidelines, producing offline semantic anchors describing grade-specific radiological findings without requiring patient-specific reports at inference. Through prototype contrastive alignment, patient-specific mpMRI representations are matched with these anchors to promote pathology-aligned representation learning. The Hierarchical Ordinal-aware Constraints (HOC) module decouples primary and secondary Gleason pattern prediction and maps their probabilistic outputs to GGG via a Differentiable Bio-logic Mapping Layer (DBML), ensuring pathological grading consistency. Experiments on public PI-CAI and in-house datasets demonstrate that KOAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/Gother-GZ/KOAL.

AI.tldr: A knowledge-driven, ordinal-aware framework (KOAL) enhances non-invasive Gleason Grade Group prediction from mpMRI by integrating clinical context, expert knowledge anchors from radiology reports with an LLM, and hierarchical ordinal constraints to map primary/secondary Gleason patterns to final grades; it outperforms state-of-the-art and provides code.
AI.motivation: GGG prediction from mpMRI benefits from non-imaging data (age, PSA, radiology priors) and must respect the hierarchical, ordinal nature of Gleason patterns. Existing methods largely ignore these aspects, leading to suboptimal, potentially inconsistent predictions.
AI.method: KOAL comprises three components: (1) Clinical-Context Modulation (CCM) to fuse age/PSA into image representations; (2) Knowledge-Guided Prototype Alignment (KGPA) that uses an LLM to extract group-specific expert knowledge from training radiology reports and guidelines to create offline semantic anchors; patient mpMRI is aligned with these anchors via prototype contrastive learning; (3) Hierarchical Ordinal-aware Constraints (HOC) with a Differentiable Bio-logic Mapping Layer (DBML) to decouple primary/secondary Gleason predictions and map them to the GGG scale.
AI.result: KOAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods on public PI-CAI and in-house datasets, indicating that incorporating clinical context, expert knowledge anchors, and hierarchical ordinal constraints improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Integrating clinical context, structured expert knowledge anchors, and hierarchy-aware loss/mapping yields more accurate and consistent non-invasive GGG predictions from mpMRI; code is publicly available for reproducibility.

title: x-Prediction Is All You Need:Training-Free Accelerated Generation via Endpoint Decodability
summary: Diffusion and flow matching models generate high-quality samples, but their ODE samplers often need tens to hundreds of neural function evaluations (NFEs). This remains a practical challenge for released checkpoints, since many accelerators require additional design choices and training cost through retraining, distillation, or trajectory redesign. We investigate a different route based on $x$-prediction. During sampling, standard affine probability paths already expose $x_0$ information: an intermediate state and its path velocity determine a principled estimate of the clean sample. We formalize this property as \textbf{endpoint decodability} and show that the decoder is the minimum-MSE estimator $\mathbb{E}[x_0\mid x_t]$ under the usual $\ell_2$ objective. This yields \textbf{Truncated Jump Sampling} (TJS): stop the ODE at an early-exit time $t^*$ and return the decoded $x_0$. TJS requires no retraining, distillation, or architecture change. Across SDXL, SD3.5M, Z-Image-Turbo, and three class-conditional benchmarks, it reduces NFEs by 20--70\% with near-matched quality. The analysis also shows why endpoint prediction can work without straightening the trajectory, providing inference acceleration without trajectory redesign.

AI.tldr: Introduce Truncated Jump Sampling (TJS) that leverages endpoint decodability in x-prediction diffusion models to decode x0 from x_t and its velocity, enabling early exit of the ODE solver to reduce NFEs by 20–70% with minimal quality loss; no retraining or architecture changes required.
AI.motivation: Reduce sampling cost of diffusion models using existing checkpoints by exploiting information available along the sampling trajectory rather than redesigning models or retraining.
AI.method: Formalize endpoint decodability as the minimum-MSE estimator E[x0 | x_t] under L2, and implement Truncated Jump Sampling: stop the ODE at an early time t* and decode x0 from the intermediate state and its path velocity; no training changes.
AI.result: Significant inference-time speedups (20–70% fewer NFEs) with near-parity image/text quality across SDXL, SD3.5M, Z-Image-Turbo, and three class-conditional benchmarks; provides theoretical insight on why endpoint prediction works without trajectory straightening.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint decodability enables practical, training-free acceleration for diffusion samplers via early-exit decoding; the approach does not require retraining, distillation, or trajectory redesign and generalizes across multiple models and tasks.

title: Self-Supervised Implicit CEST Reconstruction via Physics-Informed Lorentz Encoding
summary: Multi-Pool Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) MRI provides valuable metabolic information but is clinically limited by long acquisition times. Although sparse sampling reduces scanning time, reconstructing high-resolution Z-spectra from limited data remains an ill-posed inverse problem. Conventional interpolation and generic Implicit Neural Rep-resentations (INRs) often lack physical constraints, leading to spectral artifacts and physically invalid signals. To address this, we propose Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed framework that formulates CEST reconstruction as a self-supervised reconstruction task via implicit continuous coordinate learning. Unlike generic positional encodings, LE regularizes the continuous spectral mapping by projecting sparse coordinates into a physically constrained space governed by a combination of parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions. This mechanism effectively reduces noise and enforces consistency with physical models. Experiments on in vivo human brain data demonstrate that LE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, under a 39-point sampling strategy, LE achieves a PSNR of 57.58 dB and an SSIM of 0.9994. Furthermore, the learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically ordered trajectory in the latent space, ensuring accurate quantitative metabo-lite mapping (APT, NOE, MT).

AI.tldr: Introduces Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed, self-supervised implicit neural representation framework for reconstructing high-resolution CEST Z-spectra from sparse data by embedding the spectrum in a Lorentzian-parametric space with learnable bases; yields strong artifact suppression and accurate metabolite mapping.
AI.motivation: CEST MRI suffers from long acquisition times and ill-posed reconstruction under sparse sampling; conventional interpolation and generic INRs struggle to enforce physical constraints, leading to artifacts and physiologically implausible signals.
AI.method: LE maps sparse frequency-offset coordinates into a constrained spectral manifold defined by parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions, implemented as an implicit continuous-coordinate model trained in a self-supervised fashion to enforce physical consistency across the Z-spectrum.
AI.result: On in vivo brain data with 39-point sampling, LE achieves PSNR 57.58 dB and SSIM 0.9994, outperforming state-of-the-art methods; the learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically ordered latent trajectory that supports accurate quantitative metabolite mapping (APT, NOE, MT).
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed, Lorentz-based encodings reduce noise, enforce physical plausibility, and enable high-quality, quantitative multi-pool CEST reconstructions from sparse data.

title: MSA-DCNN: A Data-Efficient Multi-Scale Deformable CNN for Medical Image Classification
summary: Existing deep learning methods perform well in medical image classification but struggle with multi-scale morphology and limited annotations due to fixed sampling and data-hungry training. Existing approaches address these challenges in isolation: DCN-based models provide adaptive sampling but lack explicit multi-scale attention fusion and label-efficient regularisation; multi-scale architectures typically rely on static fusion; and semi-supervised methods target label scarcity without jointly modelling adaptive cross-scale representations. We propose MSA-DCNN, a scale-consistent deformable attention learning framework that introduces adaptive multi-scale sampling, within-scale saliency refinement, learned cross-scale fusion, and auxiliary self-distillation within a unified optimisation scheme, with potential to generalise to structurally heterogeneous anatomy. We evaluate on three public benchmarks and an external hold-out set for leukaemia. MSA-DCNN demonstrates competitive and often better performance against ViT baselines, CNN baselines, and a MICCAI semi-supervised baseline under distribution shift and label scarcity in accuracy, F1, and AUC (binary), while using fewer parameters. Ablations confirm complementary component contributions, supporting MSA-DCNN as a practical foundation for data-efficient medical image classification.

AI.tldr: MSA-DCNN: a scale-consistent deformable attention framework for data-efficient medical image classification with adaptive multi-scale sampling, within-scale saliency refinement, cross-scale fusion, and self-distillation.
AI.motivation: Address multi-scale morphology and data scarcity in medical image classification by integrating adaptive sampling, multi-scale fusion, and label-efficient regularisation within a single unified model.
AI.method: MSA-DCNN introduces adaptive multi-scale sampling via deformable attention, within-scale saliency refinement, learned cross-scale fusion, and auxiliary self-distillation within a unified optimisation scheme, aiming to handle structurally heterogeneous anatomy.
AI.result: Evaluated on three public benchmarks and an external hold-out set for leukaemia; achieves competitive or superior accuracy, F1, and AUC (binary) versus ViT baselines, CNN baselines, and MICCAI semi-supervised baselines under distribution shift and label scarcity, with fewer parameters; ablations show complementary contributions.
AI.conclusion: MSA-DCNN is a practical, data-efficient foundation for medical image classification that generalises to structurally heterogeneous anatomy, thanks to integrated adaptive sampling, refined cross-scale fusion, and self-distillation.

title: Leveraging Extragradient for Effective Sharpness-Aware Minimization in Deep Learning
summary: Generalization remains a pivotal challenge in deep learning, where traditional optimizers like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) often converge to sharp minima, leading to overfitting and reduced performance on unseen data. Building on Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), for seeking flat minima associated with improved generalization, we propose the Extragradient-Inspired Sharpness-Aware Minimization (EISAM), a novel optimizer that enhances generalization via the extragradient technique. EISAM uses a two-step update process: a prediction step investigating the geometry of the loss landscape and a perturbation step that refines updates with a base optimizer. This approach achieves better generalization performance than SAM. Crucially, EISAM reduces sensitivity to the perturbation radius, enhancing robustness, and simplifying the tuning across diverse settings. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that EISAM consistently outperforms SGD, Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), and SAM in test accuracy and training efficiency across various architectures. Theoretical analysis further confirms that EISAM tightens the generalization bound by steering parameters toward flatter minima with reduced curvature. Accompanied by a thorough hyperparameter analysis, EISAM offers practical tuning guidance, establishing it as a robust, scalable, and broadly applicable optimization solution that advances both the theory and practice in deep learning.

AI.tldr: EISAM is an extragradient-based variant of SAM that alternates a prediction step with a perturbation step to seek flatter minima, yielding stronger generalization and robustness with less hyperparameter sensitivity, outperforming SGD, Adam, and SAM in accuracy and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Generalization gaps in deep learning arise from sharp minima; while SAM promotes flat minima, it has sensitivity to perturbation radius and tuning. EISAM aims to improve generalization further using extragradient ideas to stabilize updates and reduce parameter sensitivity.
AI.method: Two-step optimization inspired by the extragradient method: (1) a prediction step that probes the loss landscape geometry, and (2) a perturbation step that refines updates using a base optimizer. The perturbation radius is tuned to reduce sensitivity, and the base optimizer can be SGD/Adam. Theoretical analysis links updates to flatter minima with reduced curvature.
AI.result: Empirically, EISAM consistently outperforms SGD, Adam, and SAM in test accuracy and training efficiency across various architectures and datasets. It also exhibits reduced sensitivity to the perturbation radius. Theoretically, it tightens generalization bounds by steering parameters toward flatter minima with lower curvature. A comprehensive hyperparameter study provides practical tuning guidance.
AI.conclusion: EISAM is a robust, scalable, and broadly applicable optimization method that advances both theory and practice in deep learning by improving generalization through an extragradient-inspired approach with reduced hyperparameter sensitivity.

title: PVCap: Towards Accurate 3D Dense Captioning via PseudoCap and VoxelCapNet
summary: 3D dense captioning, an emerging vision-language task, aims to generate descriptive sentences for each object in the 3D scene. Despite the impressive results achieved by previous methods, they suffer from two limitations. First, current research often employs global rigid transformations, such as rotation, to augment scenes without changing their spatial layouts. However, diverse spatial layouts are crucial for training a 3D dense captioning model to describe spatial relations between objects. Second, previous works mainly focus on the design of the caption generation pipeline while utilizing a simple network architecture for other components, i.e., backbone and detection head, which is crucial for extracting rich semantic information for captioning. In this paper, we propose PVCap to alleviate the aforementioned problems. Our PVCap consists of PseudoCap and VoxelCapNet. Specifically, PseudoCap employs a random mixing technique on instances within the dataset, generating numerous pseudo frames with diverse spatial layouts at the instance level. By utilizing a teacher-student framework, PseudoCap obtains pseudo caption labels for these pseudo frames. This data augmentation approach significantly increases the number of training samples and enhances the model's ability to describe the environment effectively. Regarding VoxelCapNet, we introduce a robust caption network that utilizes voxel features and adapts the caption head to the voxel-based network architecture. Our VoxelCapNet can serve as a competitive baseline for future research on 3D dense captioning. Extensive experiments are conducted on two prevalent benchmarks, i.e., ScanRefer and Nr3D. Notably, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art by 11.41% and 13.99% in CIDEr@0.5IoU, respectively. Codes will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: PVCap introduces two components for 3D dense captioning: (1) PseudoCap for data-augmentation via pseudo frames with diverse spatial layouts using a teacher-student framework to generate pseudo captions; (2) VoxelCapNet, a voxel-based caption network that strengthens the backbone/caption head for improved semantic feature extraction. It achieves state-of-the-art CIDEr@0.5IoU on ScanRefer and Nr3D.
AI.motivation: Current 3D dense captioning methods limit spatial layout diversity by relying on global rigid transformations and use simple architectures for backbone/detection components. This reduces the model's ability to learn robust spatial relations and extract rich semantic cues needed for high-quality captions.
AI.method: PseudoCap creates numerous pseudo frames by randomly mixing instances within the dataset to diversify spatial layouts. A teacher-student framework is used to obtain pseudo caption labels for these pseudo frames, enabling strong data augmentation. VoxelCapNet introduces a voxel-based caption network that leverages voxel features and adapts the caption head to this architecture, providing a more consistent and robust pipeline for caption generation.
AI.result: Across ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks, PVCap surpasses current state-of-the-art by 11.41% and 13.99% in CIDEr@0.5IoU, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of the augmentation strategy and the voxel-based caption network.
AI.conclusion: PVCap provides a competitive, scalable baseline for 3D dense captioning, showing that combining instance-level pseudo-frame augmentation with voxel-based captioning yields significant performance gains. The authors also commit to releasing code.

title: X-FEMR: A Token-level Explainable Approach for Electronic Health Records Foundation Models using Transformer-based Models
comment: Accepted by IJCAI-ECAI 2026 AI and Health Track
summary: Foundation Models for Electronic Health Records (FEMRs) are pretrained on large-scale structured patient data, enabling them to convert longitudinal patient trajectories into generalizable representations for diverse clinical prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, FEMRs remain black-box models, raising concerns about bias, interpretability, and clinical trust. To address this, we propose the first token-level explainability approach for FEMRs. We train a Transformer-based surrogate model on input-output pairs from the FEMR across two prediction tasks, approximating its behavior while preserving temporal dynamics. We identify the most influential tokens, providing insights into how FEMRs leverage different aspects of patient history for predictions. To evaluate clinical relevance, we introduce a novel clinical alignment metric that quantifies the correspondence between the surrogate model's key tokens and clinically validated features. Our results demonstrate that the surrogate closely approximates FEMR predictions and that token-level explanations align well with clinical knowledge, offering a practical framework for interpretable and trustworthy clinical AI.

AI.tldr: Token-level explainability for foundation models in electronic health records using a Transformer surrogate, with a novel clinical alignment metric; surrogate closely matches FEMR outputs and highlights clinically meaningful token influences.
AI.motivation: Address opacity, bias, and trust concerns of FEMRs by providing interpretable, token-level explanations that align with clinical knowledge.
AI.method: Train a Transformer-based surrogate on input-output pairs from FEMRs across two prediction tasks, preserving temporal dynamics. Identify influential tokens and evaluate them with a new clinical alignment metric that measures their correspondence to clinically validated features.
AI.result: The surrogate closely approximates FEMR predictions and its token-level explanations align with clinical knowledge; the clinical alignment metric supports the relevance of the identified tokens.
AI.conclusion: This approach offers a practical, interpretable, and trustworthy framework for FEMRs, bridging the gap between high performance and clinical interpretability.

title: EcoVision: AI-Powered Drone Imaging for Salt Marsh Vegetation Monitoring and Dominance Mapping
summary: High-resolution RGB imagery acquired from low-altitude UAV surveys was processed through a modular pipeline incorporating transformer-based semantic segmentation, connected-component vegetation extraction, fine-grained species classification using a ConvNeXt architecture, and grid-based dominance scoring at 2x2m resolution. The framework targeted two ecologically significant halophytic grasses, Spartina maritima and Puccinellia maritima, and was trained using a curated and manually annotated UAV imagery, along with biodiversity imagery sourced from publicly accessible datasets. In order to identify these plants from the imagery, our segmentation yielded reliable species masks (mean IoU = 0.56; pixel-level accuracy = 0.96), while object-level classification achieved very good discrimination (F1 = 0.99). Dominance estimates closely matched quadrat-based field surveys, with mean absolute differences below 8%, preserving fine-scale spatial structure under realistic survey conditions. The developed system, named EcoVision, establishes a practical foundation for scalable, high-resolution salt marsh monitoring, demonstrating how AI-driven workflows can translate pixel-level predictions into ecologically interpretable metrics.

AI.tldr: Modular UAV-based pipeline EcoVision for high-resolution salt marsh vegetation: transformer segmentation, connected-component extraction, ConvNeXt fine-grained classification, and 2x2 m grid dominance scoring. Achieves IoU 0.56, pixel accuracy 0.96, F1 0.99; dominance MAE < 8% and strong quadrat agreement; supports scalable, ecologically interpretable monitoring.
AI.motivation: Need scalable, high-resolution, species-specific monitoring in salt marsh ecosystems and a pipeline that translates pixel-level predictions into field-relevant ecological metrics.
AI.method: A four-stage workflow: (1) transformer-based semantic segmentation to create species masks; (2) connected-component analysis to extract vegetation objects; (3) ConvNeXt-based fine-grained species classifier; (4) grid-based dominance scoring at 2x2 m resolution. Training used curated, manually annotated UAV imagery plus biodiversity imagery from public datasets.
AI.result: Mean IoU 0.56; pixel-level accuracy 0.96; object-level F1 0.99. Dominance estimates match quadrat surveys within 8% MAE. Spatial structure preserved under realistic survey conditions. EcoVision is a practical, scalable foundation for salt marsh monitoring.
AI.conclusion: AI-driven workflow translates pixel-level predictions into ecologically interpretable metrics, establishing EcoVision as a practical framework for scalable, high-resolution salt marsh monitoring and adaptable to other ecosystems.

title: Canopy: A Heterograph Foundation Model for Metabolic Engineering
summary: Designing microbial strains that produce high-value chemicals at commercially viable titers remains a central challenge in metabolic engineering. Existing computational approaches either rely on stoichiometric constraint-based models that cannot learn from experimental data, or apply tabular machine learning to hand-crafted features that discard the relational structure of biological knowledge. We present Canopy, a heterogeneous graph foundation model that integrates ten public and proprietary data sources into a unified knowledge graph (KG) of 6.9M nodes across 13 types and 34 edge types, covering genes, proteins, metabolites, reactions, pathways, strains, and fermentation experiments. Node features are encoded through domain-specific foundation models (ESM-2 for protein sequences, MoLFormer for chemical SMILES, and PubMedBERT for biomedical text), yielding a multi-modal representation within a single graph. We pretrain a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) augmented with SignNet positional encodings, Jumping Knowledge aggregation, and virtual nodes using four self-supervised objectives (link prediction, masked node modelling, distance prediction, and contrastive experiment clustering), balanced via learned homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. On the downstream task of fermentation titer prediction, frozen Canopy embeddings achieve $R^{2} = 0.41$ with a lightweight probe, outperforming tabular baselines (best $R^{2} = 0.24$) and homogeneous GNN variants.

AI.tldr: Canopy is a multi-modal heterogeneous graph foundation model that links 6.9M biological entities from 10 data sources into a knowledge graph, pretrains an Heterogeneous Graph Transformer with SSL losses, and yields improved fermentation titer predictions (R^2=0.41) over tabular baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing metabolic engineering approaches either rely on non-learnable stoichiometric models or on tabular ML with engineered features that ignore relational biological structure. There is a need to leverage relational knowledge and experimental data to predict titers and guide strain design.
AI.method: Construct a heterogeneous knowledge graph with 6.9M nodes (13 types) and 34 edge types from ten public/proprietary data sources. Encode node features with domain-specific foundation models (ESM-2 for proteins, MoLFormer for chemicals, PubMedBERT for text). Pretrain a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) with SignNet positional encodings, Jumping Knowledge, and virtual nodes using four self-supervised objectives: link prediction, masked node modelling, distance prediction, and contrastive experiment clustering, with losses balanced by learned homoscedastic uncertainty. Downstream task uses frozen Canopy embeddings in a lightweight probe for fermentation titer prediction.
AI.result: On fermentation titer prediction, Canopy embeddings achieve R^2 = 0.41, outperforming best tabular baselines (R^2 = 0.24) and homogeneous GNN variants.
AI.conclusion: Integrating a large, multi-modal knowledge graph with SSL-trained foundation representations yields superior predictive embeddings for metabolic engineering tasks, illustrating the value of graph-based foundation models for strain design and fermentation optimization.

title: RoME: Robust Mixture of Low-Rank Experts against Multiple Adversarial Perturbations
summary: Multi-perturbation adversarial training (MAT) aims to achieve robustness against multiple $\ell_p$ perturbations but suffers from robustness trade-offs between different threats. To address this, we employ a mixture of experts (MoE) to route different threats through distinct model pathways. However, naive application of MoE encounters two critical challenges: experts tend to overlook threat-specific features and redundantly capture features shared across threats, and gating networks suffer from threat-agnostic routing where they learn nearly identical routing patterns across threats, thus preventing the construction of threat-specific model pathways. To this end, we propose Robust Mixture of Low-Rank Experts (RoME), where each expert is a low-rank additive update to the shared backbone, allowing it to capture threat-common features while experts focus on threat-specific information. To address threat-agnostic routing, RoME introduces (i) dual-scale gating that exploits threat-discriminative signals from local and global level features, and (ii) threat-guided gating diversification that enforces diverse expert utilization across threats. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RoME outperforms existing state-of-the-art MAT in union robustness and natural accuracy and improves robustness against unseen threats. Codes are available at https://github.com/wkim97/RoME.

AI.tldr: RoME: a robust mixture of low-rank experts for multi-perturbation adversarial training using low-rank additive updates to a shared backbone, with dual-scale and threat-guided gating to create threat-specific pathways and improve union robustness and natural accuracy.
AI.motivation: MAT faces robustness trade-offs across multiple perturbation types and MoE gating can become threat-agnostic, causing redundant, non-discriminative routing.
AI.method: Introduce Robust Mixture of Low-Rank Experts (RoME): each expert is a low-rank additive update to the shared backbone; dual-scale gating leverages local and global features for threat-discriminative routing; threat-guided gating diversification enforces diverse expert utilization across threats.
AI.result: Empirical results show RoME outperforms state-of-the-art MAT in union robustness and natural accuracy and improves robustness against unseen threats; code is released.
AI.conclusion: RoME effectively decouples threat-common and threat-specific information through low-rank expert updates and enhanced gating, enabling threat-specific model pathways and improved robustness.

title: Quantitative Gaussian-Process limits of Tensor Programs
summary:
We study the infinite-width Gaussian-process limit of random neural networks
  through the lens of tensor programs, and we provide a quantitative convergence
  theory in Wasserstein distance.
  Our main result gives explicit finite-width error bounds, of order inverse square-root of the widths
  between finite-network executions and their
  Gaussian-process limits. The framework is architecture-agnostic and covers feed-forward models together
  with weight-sharing schemes relevant for recurrent and transformer-type
  architectures.

AI.tldr: Finite-width neural networks converge to their infinite-width Gaussian-process limit with explicit 1/√width error bounds, analyzed via tensor programs in a architecture-agnostic framework that covers feed-forward and weight-sharing networks (RNNs/transformers).
AI.motivation: To rigorously quantify how quickly neural networks converge to the GP limit as width grows, and to provide a general, architecture-agnostic framework for finite-width corrections across common architectures (including recurrent and transformer-type with weight sharing).
AI.method: Model the neural network computations as tensor programs and study their distributional convergence to a Gaussian process in the infinite-width limit; derive quantitative Wasserstein-distance bounds between finite networks and the GP limit, with explicit 1/√width rates; ensure the framework accommodates weight-sharing schemes.
AI.result: Establishes explicit finite-width error bounds of order O(1/√width) in Wasserstein distance between finite-network executions and their Gaussian-process limits; the analysis is architecture-agnostic and applies to feed-forward models and weight-sharing schemes relevant for recurrent and transformer-type architectures.
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian-process limit is approached at a quantifiable rate with a uniform, architecture-agnostic theory, enabling finite-width corrections to be understood in a single tensor-program-based framework, including recurrent and transformer-like networks.

title: WebRetriever: A Large-Scale Comprehensive Benchmark for Efficient Web Agent Evaluation
summary: As web agents increasingly demonstrate capabilities in automated task execution, the development of robust evaluation frameworks for assessing their navigation and task completion performance has emerged as a critical research priority. However, existing benchmarks exhibit fundamental limitations. First, they suffer from insufficient scale and limited domain diversity, constraining comprehensive evaluation of cross-domain generalization. Second, prevailing LLM-as-Judge evaluation methodologies inadequately capture fine-grained interaction semantics, particularly regarding precise query formulation and filtering operations. Third, current benchmarks predominantly emphasize navigation success metrics while neglecting critical requirements for real-world deployment scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce WebRetriever, a large-scale benchmark encompassing 800 websites and 1,550 tasks across diverse domains, including consumer, professional, and enterprise sectors, with comprehensive coverage of user intent patterns. We propose NavEval (Navigation Evaluation), a novel LLM-as-Judge framework that leverages rich interaction context beyond visual screenshots, achieving state-of-the-art alignment with human judgment across multiple evaluation datasets. Furthermore, we establish three complementary evaluation protocols that collectively provide holistic assessment of web agent capabilities: navigation proficiency, knowledge-assisted interaction, and end-to-end task completion with information extraction. Extensive experimental analysis reveals substantial performance disparities across evaluation protocols, demonstrating that navigation success alone is an insufficient predictor of real-world application effectiveness. WebRetriever delivers fine-grained diagnostic insights into agent capabilities and establishes a rigorous foundation for advancing web agent research and development.

AI.tldr: WebRetriever introduces a large-scale, cross-domain benchmark and a rich, context-aware LLM-as-Judge framework (NavEval) with three complementary evaluation protocols for holistic assessment of web agents, showing navigation alone is insufficient for real-world effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks are too small and domain-limited, provide shallow evaluation of interaction semantics, and focus on navigation success without deployment realism. There's a need for scalable, diverse datasets and evaluation methods that capture fine-grained query formulation, filtering, and end-to-end information extraction.
AI.method: 1) WebRetriever: a benchmark with 800 websites and 1,550 tasks across consumer, professional, and enterprise domains, designed to cover diverse user intent. 2) NavEval: an LLM-as-Judge leveraging rich interaction context beyond visual screenshots to align with human judgments. 3) Three evaluation protocols: (a) navigation proficiency, (b) knowledge-assisted interaction, (c) end-to-end task completion with information extraction.
AI.result: NavEval achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human judgment across multiple datasets; results show substantial performance gaps between evaluation protocols, indicating navigation success alone poorly predicts real-world effectiveness; WebRetriever provides fine-grained diagnostics and a robust foundation for advancing web agent research.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a holistic, scalable evaluation framework for web agents, combining a large diverse benchmark with a context-aware judging method and three complementary protocols to better predict deployment performance and diagnose capabilities.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Embeddings of PDE Solution Families
summary: We introduce a physics-informed framework for learning finite-dimensional embeddings of solution families of partial differential equations. The method uses a multihead Physics-Informed Neural Network in which a shared body learns a latent manifold representing the solution space, while linear heads reconstruct individual solutions associated with different initial conditions. A head-orthogonalization penalty removes degeneracies in the latent representation and stabilizes the principal-component spectrum across training realizations. Because the initial condition is built into the network output by construction, these principal components measure the additional variability the network learns on top of the initial profile, not the full solution itself. We apply the method to the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation, with the heat and wave equations as robustness checks. For a latent dimension $n_b=20$, the learned manifolds exhibit pronounced effective dimensional reduction: for Burgers dynamics, only $2$-$4$ principal components capture about $95\%$ of the latent-space variance, while $4$-$7$ capture about $99\%$, depending on the initial-condition family; the same qualitative compression holds for the heat and wave equations. We also split the wavenumber axis into bands (``Fourier shells'') and measure how much each band contributes to every principal component. The resulting frequency profile is invariant under the change-of-basis freedom that the orthogonalization penalty leaves in the latent space, and is therefore reproducible across independent training runs. More broadly, this establishes the learned spectral profiles and principal components as robust observables of solution-manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed, multihead PINN learns finite-dimensional embeddings of PDE solution families; with a head-orthogonalization penalty, it achieves robust, reproducible spectral characterizations and strong dimensionality reduction across Burgers, heat, and wave equations.
AI.motivation: To obtain compact, robust latent representations (manifolds) of PDE solution families that separate initial-condition effects from additional learned variability, enabling stable and informative observables of solution-manifold geometry.
AI.method: A multihead Physics-Informed Neural Network with a shared body learns a latent manifold; linear heads reconstruct solutions for different initial conditions. A head-orthogonalization penalty removes degeneracies and stabilizes the principal-component spectrum. The initial condition is encoded in the network output. The method analyzes spectral content by splitting the wavenumber axis into Fourier shells to quantify each shell's contribution to principal components. They test on 1D viscous Burgers equation, with heat and wave equations as robustness checks; latent dimension nb=20.
AI.result: For Burgers dynamics, only 2–4 principal components capture about 95% of latent-space variance, and 4–7 capture about 99% (dependence on initial-condition family). The same qualitative compression holds for heat and wave equations. The Fourier-shell analysis yields frequency profiles that are invariant to basis changes caused by the orthogonalization penalty and reproducible across independent training runs. Overall, learned spectral profiles and principal components emerge as robust observables of the solution-manifold geometry.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields effective dimensional reduction and robust, reproducible spectral characterizations of PDE solution manifolds, providing a practical framework for analyzing and comparing families of PDE solutions across different initial conditions.

title: AEGIS: A Mechanism-Guided Defense against Visual Synonym Jailbreaks in Text-to-Image Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models have achieved high visual fidelity and broad adoption, but remain vulnerable to safety violations when adversaries exploit them to synthesize illicit content. Existing alignment paradigms, from input sanitization to structural feature pruning, are largely organized around unsafe concepts explicitly exposed during filtering, editing, or localization. This leaves a blind spot for visual synonym attacks (VSA), a jailbreak where benign-looking prompts elicit prohibited imagery through implicit visual associations. As a result, current defenses face a safety-utility dilemma: they may either under-mitigate VSA threats or over-suppress visually similar benign concepts. The core challenge is that VSA hides the unsafe target at the textual surface while revealing it through generation-time visual-semantic convergence. In this work, we therefore shift from static suppression of pre-specified unsafe concepts to dynamic tracing of how unsafe semantics emerge during generation. Our mechanistic analysis shows that VSA and explicit unsafe prompts converge through sparse semantic-injecting attention heads, which serve as inference-time bottlenecks for prohibited visual semantics. Based on this insight, we propose AEGIS (Adaptive Evasion Guard via Identification and Steering), an inference-time defense that applies similarity-aware repulsion only at the identified vulnerable heads. Evaluated against 16 baselines, AEGIS improves both safety and utility. On SD 1.4, it reduces ASR to $\mathbf{0.00}/\mathbf{0.03}$ for in-domain violence/nudity VSA and achieves ASRs $\le \mathbf{0.09}$ on out-of-domain explicit and adversarial attacks. It preserves benign fidelity, avoids suppressing hard-negative concepts, and transfers to SD 2.1 and FLUX.1 after re-identifying the critical heads for each backbone.

AI.tldr: AEGIS is an inference-time defense for text-to-image diffusion that identifies sparse, generation-time attention heads responsible for unsafe semantics and applies similarity-aware repulsion only at those heads, improving safety against visual synonym attacks while preserving benign image fidelity and generalizing across backbones.
AI.motivation: VSA reveals unsafe targets via generation-time visual-semantic convergence, while static pre-filtering fails to address implicit associations; existing defenses trade off safety and utility.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis to locate sparse semantic-injecting attention heads that bridge unsafe prompts and prohibited imagery. Introduce AEGIS, which applies similarity-aware repulsion exclusively at identified vulnerable heads during generation-time, adapting to each backbone.
AI.result: On Stable Diffusion 1.4, AEGIS reduces in-domain violence/nudity VSA attack success rates to 0.00/0.03 and ≤0.09 for out-of-domain attacks, while preserving benign fidelity. It avoids over-suppressing hard negatives and transfers to SD 2.1 and FLUX.1 after re-identifying critical heads per backbone, outperforming 16 baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, head-level, generation-time mitigation can effectively curb Visual Synonym Attacks without sacrificing utility, and generalizes across model backbones with per-backbone head identification.

title: TILDE: TILt-based Distributional Erasure for Concept Unlearning
summary: Concept unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models is critical for safe and practical deployment: with rising privacy concerns, copyright disputes, trademark constraints, and safety regulations, deployed systems must be able to suppress unwanted concepts after training. Existing methods often remove the target concept effectively, but practical unlearning also requires an equally fundamental property: the unlearned model should retain quality, diversity, and semantic coverage on benign generation. The gold standard is a retain-only model trained from scratch without the unwanted data. However, common erasure objectives do not specify which post-unlearning distribution should approximate this reference, leaving retention as an implicit consequence of the update rule. We propose TILDE, TILt-based Distributional Erasure, which formulates concept unlearning as a distributional alignment problem: the desired target is the minimum-deviation conditional distribution from the pretrained model under a forgetting constraint. This energy-tilted, anchor-free target suppresses concept-expressing images while preserving benign relative mass for each prompt. We instantiate this principle with residual $\nabla$-GFlowNet training, which learns the score correction induced by the forget energy relative to the pretrained diffusion model. Across objects, artistic styles, and characters, TILDE achieves strong forgetting while improving retention and distributional fidelity over prior baselines.

AI.tldr: TILDE reframes text-to-image concept unlearning as distributional alignment, aiming to erase unwanted concepts while preserving benign generation by constructing a minimum-deviation conditional distribution from a pretrained model under a forgetting constraint. It uses energy-tilted targets and residual score corrections via ∇-GFlowNet training to achieve strong forgetting with improved retention and fidelity over baselines.
AI.motivation: Growing privacy concerns, copyright and trademark constraints, and safety regulations necessitate unlearning unwanted concepts from diffusion-based generators without sacrificing model quality, diversity, or coverage of benign outputs.
AI.method: Formulates unlearning as aligning the post-update distribution to a target that minimizes deviation from the pretrained distribution under a forgetting constraint (an energy-tilted, anchor-free target). Implements this via residual ∇-GFlowNet training to learn the score correction induced by the forget energy relative to the pretrained diffusion model.
AI.result: TILDE achieves strong forgetting across objects, styles, and characters while improving retention and distributional fidelity compared to prior baselines, indicating better preservation of benign generation while erasing targeted concepts.
AI.conclusion: A principled framework for concept unlearning that balances forgetting and retention by targeting a distributional objective; demonstrated effectiveness across diverse domains, with potential for broader applicability and further exploration of computational efficiency and evaluation metrics.

title: Tuning-Free Latent Diffusion Models for Ultrahigh-Resolution Image Editing
comment: 29 pages, 29 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
summary: Recent diffusion-based generative models have shown impressive performance in image generation and editing. However, due to memory limitations and the high cost of collecting high-resolution training images, existing methods are typically restricted to inputs with linear resolutions below 1K. In contrast, photos captured by modern mobile devices often reach linear resolutions up to 8K, revealing a significant gap between current capabilities and real-world demands. Simply upscaling low-resolution edited results often results in visually enlarged but blurry images that lack fine details. This paper introduces UltraDiffEdit, a novel, tuning-free image editing framework that extends off-the-shelf latent diffusion models (LDMs) to ultrahigh resolutions. UltraDiffEdit employs a multi-scale progressive editing strategy, iteratively blending high-resolution edited content with unedited areas in a coarse-to-fine manner. We employ multi-patch encoding to preserve both edited and unedited visual details within the latent space. To mitigate editing artifacts, our global-local consistency denoising technique consistently integrates edited and unedited latent features, ensuring smooth transition at editing boundaries from the latent representation to the final image. We also introduce a patch-based hybrid sampling approach that captures local, intermediate, and global features, ensuring semantic coherence and enhancing fine detail during denoising. We conduct extensive experiments demonstrating UltraDiffEdit's superior editing quality and flexibility: it can handle image resolutions up to 8K using only a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/LonglongaaaGo/UltraDiffEdit.

AI.tldr: A tuning-free framework, UltraDiffEdit, enables ultrahigh-resolution (up to 8K) image editing using off-the-shelf latent diffusion models via multi-scale progressive editing, multi-patch latent encoding, global-local denoising, and patch-based hybrid sampling, achieving high-quality edits on a single RTX 3090.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between current diffusion-based editing methods (restricted to sub-1K resolutions due to memory and data limitations) and real-world ultrahigh-resolution mobile-captured images (up to 8K), while avoiding tuning complexity.
AI.method: Extend latent diffusion models with a multi-scale progressive editing pipeline that blends edited and unedited content from coarse to fine scales; use multi-patch encoding to preserve both edited and unedited details in latent space; apply global-local consistency denoising to integrate edited/unedited latent features and smooth editing boundaries; employ a patch-based hybrid sampling strategy to capture local, intermediate, and global features during denoising; designed to be tuning-free and capable of handling 8K on a single RTX 3090; code available.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate superior editing quality and flexibility, with the framework handling resolutions up to 8K on a single RTX 3090; source code released at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: UltraDiffEdit provides a practical, tuning-free pathway for ultrahigh-resolution image editing by combining multi-scale, patch-based latent encoding, and consistency-denoising techniques to preserve details and semantic coherence during editing.

title: EntroPath: Maximum Entropy Path Ensemble Embedding for Manifold Learning
summary: We introduce EntroPath, a manifold learning method that recovers geodesic geometry from data graphs through ensembles of diffusion paths. Many existing graph-based embeddings rely either on locally normalised random walks or on shortest-path distances. The former can concentrate diffusion in densely sampled regions, while the latter are sensitive to spurious shortcut edges in the graph. EntroPath instead builds its dissimilarities from the maximum entropy random walk (MERW), which aggregates the full ensemble of k-step paths between points rather than relying on any single trajectory. We show that the resulting free-energy dissimilarity converges to squared geodesic distance in the short-time limit, via Varadhan's heat-kernel formula. The diffusion depth k interpolates smoothly between local neighbourhood structure and global manifold geometry, and the symmetrised kernel admits an exact Gram factorisation connecting EntroPath to kernel methods. We further provide scalable extensions via landmark projection and diffusion-potential pseudotime. Across synthetic manifolds and single-cell benchmarks, EntroPath consistently matches or outperforms diffusion- and shortest-path-based methods, while remaining competitive with neighbourhood-preserving embeddings (UMAP, t-SNE) on local-structure metrics. Its gains are most pronounced on manifolds with non-uniform sampling density and well-separated branching trajectories, where path-ensemble diffusion more faithfully preserves the underlying geodesic geometry.

AI.tldr: EntroPath uses maximum-entropy random walks to build a diffusion-based, geodesic-preserving dissimilarity that converges to squared geodesic distance; it bridges local and global geometry and admits a Gram factorization as a kernel method, with scalable extensions.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of local-normalized random walks (density concentration) and pure shortest-path metrics (shortcuts) in graph embeddings; goal is to faithfully recover underlying geodesic geometry from data graphs.
AI.method: Construct free-energy dissimilarities from the ensemble of k-step paths under maximum entropy random walk (MERW); show convergence to squared geodesic distance via Varadhan's heat-kernel formula in the short-time limit; use diffusion depth k to interpolate between local and global structure; employ a symmetrised kernel with an exact Gram factorisation linking to kernel methods; provide scalable extensions via landmark projection and diffusion-potential pseudotime.
AI.result: Theoretical convergence to squared geodesic distance; empirical results on synthetic manifolds and single-cell data show EntroPath matches or surpasses diffusion- and shortest-path-based methods and is competitive with UMAP/t-SNE on local structure metrics; gains are strongest for non-uniform sampling densities and well-separated branching trajectories.
AI.conclusion: EntroPath offers a geodesic-aware, tunable-diffusion embedding that unifies kernel and manifold learning perspectives, with scalable variants and robust performance across challenging graph geometries.

title: RFHNet: Relational and Frequency-Aware Hashing Network for Large-Scale Fine-Grained Food Image Retrieval
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Published in ACM ICMR 2026
summary: Fine-grained food image retrieval is a key task in computational gastronomy, with applications in food traceability, dietary monitoring, and smart catering systems. Although hashing-based retrieval is attractive for large-scale search due to its storage efficiency and fast Hamming-distance computation, existing methods often perform poorly in fine-grained food scenarios, where subtle local semantics and frequency-sensitive visual cues are essential. To address this challenge, we propose RFHNet, a cascaded hierarchical hashing network that captures both global structure and fine-grained local details through multi-level representations. RFHNet includes three components: (1) Fine-grained Relation Modeling (FRM) to capture subtle visual differences among similar food components; (2) Multi-Frequency Modulated Fusion (MFMF) to extract informative multi-frequency features; and (3) Hierarchical Semantic Synergy (HSS) to adaptively integrate multi-level representations and generate discriminative hash codes. Experiments on six food-specific benchmarks show that RFHNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art hashing methods, with mAP gains of 4.44\% to 17.20\% at 12 bits. These results validate the effectiveness of RFHNet for large-scale visual food retrieval and smart catering applications. The source code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: A cascaded hierarchical hashing network (RFHNet) for fine-grained food image retrieval, combining global and local representations via FRM, MFMF, and HSS to produce discriminative hash codes with improved mAP at 12 bits.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained food retrieval requires capturing subtle local cues and frequency-sensitive features; hashing methods trade off between efficiency and discriminative power, but existing methods underperform in fine-grained food domains.
AI.method: RFHNet architecture: (1) FRM for subtle visual differences among food components, (2) MFMF for extracting informative features across multiple frequencies, (3) HSS for adaptive integration of multi-level representations into hash codes in a cascaded, hierarchical fashion.
AI.result: Evaluations on six food benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art hashing methods, with mAP gains ranging from 4.44% to 17.20% at 12-bit codes.
AI.conclusion: RFHNet demonstrates effectiveness for large-scale visual food retrieval and smart catering; source code to be released, indicating reproducibility and practical deployment potential.

title: GraphBU: MILP Instance Generation with Graph-Native Block Units
summary: Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) instances used for solver development are hard to obtain when models come from private or application-specific pipelines. A generator must keep the structure that solvers and learned policies rely on. Existing general generators usually choose their generation unit from a formulation template, summary statistics, local graph edits, or blocks found after recombination. These units do not explicitly record how a local part of the MILP is coupled to the rest of the instance. We propose GraphBU, a graph-native generator whose basic unit is a local subproblem plus its interface. The method promotes coupling nodes into master constraints or boundary variables and uses the resulting block units for compatibility-checked replacement. The analysis focuses on the properties needed by this construction: promotion separates interfaces, replacement can preserve feasibility under an interface-slack condition, and the graph construction is invariant to row-column permutations. On MILP instances generation, this unit keeps graph statistics close to the source family, preserves feasibility on most datasets, and improves downstream Predict-and-Search training. Genrated by GraphBU, The average graph-statistical similarity was approximately 0.934, the average feasibility was approximately 96.7%, and the average increase in the main index of downstream PS was approximately 8.0%.

AI.tldr: GraphBU is a graph-native MILP instance generator using local subproblems with an interface as the basic unit, promoting coupling into master constraints to achieve permutation-invariant, feasibility-preserving generation that improves Predict-and-Search (PS) training.
AI.motivation: MILP generators struggle to preserve inter-part coupling and graph structure when generating instances, especially from private/app-specific pipelines. A generator that records local interfaces and maintains structural invariants is needed to produce realistic, solvable instances for solver development and learning-based methods.
AI.method: Units are local subproblems plus their interface. The method promotes coupling nodes into master constraints or boundary variables and uses the resulting blocks for compatible replacement.
