AI.result: Results show a clear performance gap; even top models struggle when moving from perceptual counting to analytical reasoning and under adverse conditions, highlighting the limits of current grounding and reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: HoloCount provides a systematic evaluation framework for grounded counting in MLLMs and offers a roadmap for developing more reliable systems; dataset available at the provided URL.

title: XRFormer: Multiscale Tokenization for XRF Representation Learning
summary: X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy is a key modality for material analysis in cultural heritage. However, automated learning from XRF spectra remains challenging: XRF spectra are complex one-dimensional signals composed of sharp elemental peaks, broader structures, and background variations that are not taken into account by existing learning-based models. This paper introduces XRFormer, a transformer architecture tailored to XRF spectra through a multiscale convolutional tokenizer that injects locality and multi-resolution inductive biases before global self-attention. The tokenizer progressively reduces spectral resolution while increasing embedding dimensionality, and the resulting token sequence is processed by a standard transformer encoder. We further investigate self-supervised pretraining for XRF representation learning using Masked Spectral modeling (MSM) and a physics-informed Peak Presence Prediction (PPP) objective. Experiments on the Pigments Checker STANDARD v.5 dataset for pigment identification and unmixing show that XRFormer consistently outperforms ViT, SpectralFormer (with and without CAF), and a 1D-CNN baseline for pigment identification. For pigment unmixing, XRFormer achieves robust abundance estimation while maintaining significantly higher parameter efficiency than SpectralFormer, operating at a lower token resolution (128 vs. 512 tokens) and with less than half the number of parameters (1.5M vs. 3.37M). MSM yields consistent gains across both tasks, while PPP further enhances performance for both identification and unmixing when tuned with an appropriate peak prominence. These results highlight multiscale, modality-aware tokenization as an effective and parameter efficient foundation for transformer-based XRF modeling under data-limited conditions. A GitHub repository is provided at https://github.com/sofiane1010/XRFormer.

AI.tldr: XRFormer introduces a multiscale convolutional tokenizer and transformer for XRF spectra, enabling efficient, accurate pigment identification and unmixing with self-supervised pretraining (MSM, PPP); achieves superior performance with fewer parameters and lower token counts than baselines.
AI.motivation: XRF spectra are complex 1D signals with sharp elemental peaks, broad background structures, and variable backgrounds. Existing learning models lack locality and multi-resolution inductive biases, limiting performance especially under data scarcity.
AI.method: Propose XRFormer: a multiscale convolutional tokenizer that injects locality and multi-resolution biases before a standard transformer encoder. The tokenizer progressively reduces spectral resolution while increasing embedding dimensionality. Use MSM (Masked Spectral Modeling) and PPP (Peak Presence Prediction) for self-supervised pretraining. Evaluate on Pigments Checker STANDARD v.5 for pigment identification and unmixing, comparing against ViT, SpectralFormer (with/without CAF), and 1D-CNN.
AI.result: XRFormer consistently outperforms baselines for pigment identification. For pigment unmixing, it yields robust abundance estimation with substantially higher parameter efficiency (1.5M vs 3.37M) and lower token count (128 vs 512). MSM provides performance gains across tasks; PPP yields further improvements when peak prominence is tuned.
AI.conclusion: Multiscale, modality-aware tokenization is an effective and parameter-efficient foundation for transformer-based XRF modeling under data-limited conditions, with public code available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: PIPBench: A Profile-Inclusive Framework for Personalized Image Generation Evaluation
summary: Recent text-to-image models such as DALLE-3 excel at following diverse prompts yet remain blind to individual aesthetic preferences. We study personalized image generation, where models must align outputs with a user's implicit visual preferences based on a few historically preferred images and a short prompt. To this end, we introduce PIPBench, the first profile-inclusive benchmark for evaluating personalized image generation. We further propose a novel data construction pipeline that leverages psychological and demographic profiling dimensions for both real-user data collection and scalable agent-based data generation. Using PIPBench, we conduct a thorough evaluation of representative line of methods. Our experiments reveal key limitations in existing methods, suggesting new challenges and opportunities for personalized text-to-image synthesis. Project page: https://wuyuhang05.github.io/PIPBench/

AI.tldr: Introduces PIPBench, a profile-inclusive benchmark for personalized image generation, and a data-construction pipeline that uses psychological and demographic profiling to collect real-user data and generate scalable agent data; evaluates existing methods and finds key limitations, outlining challenges and opportunities for personalized text-to-image synthesis.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where text-to-image models can follow prompts but fail to align with individual user aesthetics. Provide a benchmark and scalable data pipeline to support personalized image generation.
AI.method: Proposes PIPBench as a profile-inclusive benchmark. Develops a data-construction pipeline leveraging psychological and demographic profiling dimensions for real-user data collection and scalable agent-based data generation. Evaluates a representative set of personalization methods on PIPBench.
AI.result: Experiments reveal key limitations in existing personalization methods, highlighting challenges and opportunities for improving personalized T2I synthesis.
AI.conclusion: PIPBench establishes a foundation for evaluating personalized image generation and points to substantial future work needed to align outputs with individual aesthetics, with ethical and methodological considerations in data collection and modeling.

title: Analysis-by-Proxy: Localization Signals in VLMs Operating as Condition Encoders
comment: Accepted as a Spotlight at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly utilized as the conditioning backbone for diffusion-based image editing due to their remarkable multimodal reasoning capabilities. While standalone VLMs demonstrate strong localization capabilities, editing pipelines frequently struggle to maintain this accuracy, particularly in complex, multi-entity scenes. In this work, we investigate this performance gap, hypothesizing that it stems from treating the VLM as a condition encoder. In this role, the model is restricted to a single forward pass, preventing the autoregressive generation process for which it was optimized, thereby failing to fully expose its capabilities. To investigate whether this spatial understanding persists when the VLM is used as a condition encoder, we introduce Analysis-by-Proxy. In this framework, we train a lightweight, interpretable proxy model on the VLM's intermediate representations using an auxiliary localization task. By analyzing the VLM through this proxy, we uncover the specific VLM representations that encode localization information. Our findings expose a fundamental mismatch between how spatial knowledge is represented within a VLM condition encoder and how it is extracted by current editing pipelines. We reveal that under single-pass constraints, the localization signal does not reliably propagate to the predefined layer configurations commonly used for conditioning. Instead, this crucial signal remains hidden within intermediate representations, at locations that vary depending on the input prompt. Using our introduced Analysis-by-Proxy framework, we reveal the fundamental failures of existing condition extraction strategies in editing pipelines, opening the door to more principled design of conditioning architectures.

AI.tldr: Presents Analysis-by-Proxy to diagnose why VLMs fail to preserve localization in single-pass diffusion editing; shows localization cues live in prompt-dependent intermediate representations rather than fixed layers, revealing fundamental flaws in current conditioning strategies.
AI.motivation: Understand why a strong VLM's spatial localization does not reliably transfer to editing pipelines when used as a condition encoder, and whether the single-pass constraint undermines its capabilities.
AI.method: Introduce Analysis-by-Proxy: train a lightweight, interpretable proxy model on the VLM's intermediate representations using an auxiliary localization task to expose where localization information is encoded.
AI.result: Reveal that localization information is encoded in intermediate representations; there is a mismatch between spatial knowledge and how editors extract it; under single-pass constraints, localization signals do not propagate to common conditioning layers and remain hidden, varying with input prompts.
AI.conclusion: Current condition-extraction strategies are fundamentally flawed; to design better conditioning architectures, editors must account for prompt-dependent, mid-layer localization signals and leverage the ABP framework to identify where useful spatial information resides.

title: Andha-Dhun: A First Look at Audio Descriptions in Hindi
comment: Accepted to NCVPRIPG 2026, Download data at https://github.com/katha-ai/AndhaDhun-HindiAD
summary: Audio Descriptions (ADs) narrate visual content for Blind and Low Vision (BLV) audiences during gaps in audiovisual media. There is growing momentum around ADs in movies and TV shows, and with mandates from India's Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), there is a need to expand ADs beyond English. Yet, there is no work that generates ADs for any Indian language. To address this gap, we present the first systematic study of ADs in Hindi, contributing to aspects such as data, generation, and evaluation. We introduce Andha-Dhun, the first dataset of human-authored Hindi ADs collected from 8 full-length movies. We explore two approaches for generating ADs in Hindi: (i) directly from English dense video descriptions, and (ii) translating English ADs into Hindi. We evaluate these approaches using perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge metrics to assess fluency and quality respectively. We also analyze movies that have both English and Hindi human-authored ADs and find that naive translation introduces artifacts and narrows diversity compared to original Hindi ADs. Direct machine translation fails to adapt cultural references, while human-translated ADs do better but still fall short. Our findings emphasize that the purpose of Hindi ADs is accessibility for Indian BLV audiences, and that this requires adapting content for the audience more than strict fidelity to the source.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of Hindi audio descriptions (ADs) for blind/low-vision viewers, introducing Andha-Dhun—Hindi AD dataset from 8 films. Evaluates two generation routes (English-to-Hindi translation vs direct Hindi AD generation) and finds translation artifacts and reduced diversity; machine translation struggles with cultural adaptation, while human translations help but still fall short. Concludes that Hindi ADs require audience-adapted content, not mere fidelity.
AI.motivation: Expand ADs to Indian languages to meet accessibility needs and CBFC mandates; address the gap of Hindi AD generation, ensuring content is culturally accessible and diverse for Indian BLV audiences.
AI.method: 1) Create Andha-Dhun: a dataset of human-authored Hindi ADs from 8 full-length films. 2) Evaluate two generation approaches: (i) generate Hindi ADs directly from English dense video descriptions, (ii) translate English ADs into Hindi. 3) Assess fluency and quality using perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge; compare with movies that have both English and Hindi human-authored ADs to study artifacts and diversity.
AI.result: Naive translation introduces artifacts and narrows diversity compared to original Hindi ADs. Direct machine translation fails to adapt cultural references. Human-translated ADs perform better but still lag behind ideal adaptation. Overall, strict fidelity to English ADs is less effective than audience-adapted translation; content adaptation is crucial for accessibility.
AI.conclusion: Hindi ADs require audience-focused localization rather than strict translation. The work provides the first Hindi AD dataset and evaluation framework, highlighting the need for culturally-aware generation strategies to enhance accessibility for Indian BLV viewers.

title: Verification of Dynamic Holographic Behavior in Identity Documents
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR 2025)
summary: This paper addresses the remote verification of the authenticity of Optically Variable Devices (commonly known as holograms) on identity documents. Typically placed over the cardholder's photo, these devices provide strong and easily verifiable security for human inspection but pose challenges for automated verification. Existing approaches easily cover static frauds (e.g. paper photocopy) and can be evaluated for such, but their capacity to detect real, dynamic fraud cases (e.g. handcrafted hologram) has not been evaluated to date because of the lack of public datasets. Furthermore, they are usually trained to detect known attack types, and few of them can generalize to new, unseen attacks. This work features three contributions to address these limitations: 1) a new public dataset, MIDV-DynAttack, which extends the existing MIDV-Holo dataset with realistic, static and dynamic attacks against identity document specimens, tripling the number of attack samples compared to the original dataset, 2) a novel verification method which can assess the authenticity of a specific hologram thanks to the analysis of its dynamic behavior and appearance, can be trained without dynamic attack samples, and exhibits new state-of-the-art performance, 3) a benchmark of existing approaches which follows a clear evaluation protocol and emphasizes the inability of other approaches to deal with dynamic attacks, as well as new challenging attacks to deal with. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/EPITAResearchLab/pouliquen.25.icdar.

AI.tldr: Introduces MIDV-DynAttack dataset and a dynamic-analysis hologram verification method achieving SOTA, plus a reproducible benchmark of existing methods.
AI.motivation: Address major limitations in automated hologram verification: (i) lack of public datasets covering dynamic (attacked) holograms, (ii) poor generalization to unseen attacks, (iii) need for a protocol to benchmark different approaches.
AI.method: A new public dataset MIDV-DynAttack expanding MIDV-Holo with realistic static and dynamic attacks; a novel verification method analyzing hologram dynamics and appearance to assess authenticity, trainable without dynamic attack samples; and a benchmarking protocol evaluating existing approaches on dynamic attacks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art verification performance on authenticating holograms, with the dataset tripling attack samples and enabling robust testing against dynamic attacks; code and data are publicly available at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: The work advances automated hologram verification by providing a public dynamic-attack dataset, a dynamic-aware verifier with strong generalization, and a standardized benchmark to compare methods, promoting reproducibility and resilience against evolving spoofing tactics.

title: EgoPolice: A Benchmark for Egocentric Video Understanding in High-Stakes Police Body-Worn Camera Footage
summary: We introduce EgoPolice, a carefully curated dataset of real, egocentric police-civilian interactions, sourced from publicly available body-worn camera videos. We select police-civilian action labels that are critical for police behavioral research and annotate them at a second-by-second granularity. The videos feature rapid and irregular camera motion, dense human interactions, and rare high-stakes events, making the dataset a challenging benchmark for motion-robust and context-aware egocentric perception. We provide two different tasks, classification and multiple-choice question-answering, and benchmark both open-source and closed-source models. We find that even the best video models like Gemini 2.5 Pro still struggle to accurately predict high-risk actions such as "Weapon Out". Beyond serving as a benchmark, EgoPolice provides a foundation for developing models capable of identifying events of interest in large-scale body-worn camera video repositories, enabling more efficient downstream human review.

AI.tldr: EgoPolice is a new egocentric police–civilian dataset with second-by-second annotations for classification and QA tasks, benchmarked against contemporary models, revealing difficulty in detecting high-risk actions like weapon display; aimed at benchmarking motion-robust and context-aware perception and aiding efficient review of BWC footage.
AI.motivation: Address the need for robust, context-aware egocentric perception in high-stakes police footage and provide a dataset that supports behavioral research and efficient review of large BWC repositories.
AI.method: Curate real BWC videos, annotate police–civilian actions at 1 Hz granularity, define two tasks (action classification and multiple-choice QA), and benchmark both open-source and closed-source models on these tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art video models (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro) struggle to accurately predict high-risk actions (e.g., 'Weapon Out'), indicating the dataset's challenging nature and the gap in current models.
AI.conclusion: EgoPolice can serve as a benchmark and a foundation for developing models that identify events of interest in large-scale BWC video repositories, enabling more efficient downstream human review.

title: A VLM-Enhanced Framework for Comprehensive Traffic Sign Condition Assessment Integrating Daytime Visual Performance and Nighttime Retroreflectivity Evaluation
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Preprint. An earlier version of this work was presented at the 105th Annual Meeting of the Transportation Research Board (TRB), January 2026
summary: Traffic signs are crucial components of road safety, serving as visual tools under all lighting conditions. The Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) specifies daytime visual factors such as legibility and color contrast, and nighttime retroreflectivity requirements. Traditional assessment methods rely on manual inspections, which the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) notes are subjective, labor-intensive and pose safety concerns, while retroreflectometers are expensive and unaffordable for smaller agencies. Most existing studies focus on either daytime factors or nighttime retroreflectivity but rarely integrate both aspects comprehensively. This study develops a novel framework that systematically evaluates traffic signs through integrated daytime-nighttime assessment. The methodology employs three fine-tuned Vision Language Models (VLMs) for daytime visual performance assessment across four key factors: legibility, color, surface and shape integrity, and surrounding environment conditions. VLM predictions are converted to numerical scores through sentiment analysis and Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) scoring, while nighttime performance is assessed using LiDAR-derived retroreflectivity following established calibration procedures. The framework integrates these components into a comprehensive Sign Condition Index (SCI) for maintenance guidance. Evaluation results demonstrated that LLaVA and Qwen outperformed InternVL, achieving bidirectional cosine similarity scores of 0.67-0.76 across all factors. Among 462 validated traffic signs, 68 were flagged by the proposed framework as requiring immediate replacement due to inadequate retroreflectivity performance. This research provides a cost-effective alternative to traditional manual inspections for comprehensive traffic sign condition assessment.

AI.tldr: A framework for integrated daytime-nighttime traffic sign assessment using fine-tuned Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and LiDAR-derived retroreflectivity to produce a Sign Condition Index (SCI), addressing the gap between daytime legibility/color/surface/shape and nighttime retroreflectivity.
AI.motivation: To overcome subjectivity, labor-intensive manual inspections and the unaffordability of retroreflectometers, by providing a cost-effective, comprehensive method that combines daytime visual factors with nighttime reflectivity.
AI.method: Fine-tune three VLMs to assess daytime factors (legibility, color, surface/shape integrity, environment). Convert VLM outputs to numerical scores via sentiment analysis and CLIP scoring. Measure nighttime performance with LiDAR-derived retroreflectivity using established calibration. Integrate into a Sign Condition Index (SCI) for maintenance guidance.
AI.result: LLaVA and Qwen outperform InternVL, achieving bidirectional cosine similarity 0.67-0.76 across factors. Among 462 signs, 68 flagged for immediate replacement due to inadequate retroreflectivity.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a cost-effective, comprehensive alternative to manual inspections, enabling more systematic maintenance decisions by combining daytime and nighttime sign performance.

title: Prompt-Adapter Context Routing for Parameter-Efficient Multi-Shot Long Video Extrapolation
summary: We present PACR-Video, a parameter-efficient framework for multi-shot long video extrapolation that preserves recurring entities, scene structure, visual style, and causal progression without full generator fine-tuning. PACR-Video keeps a text-to-video diffusion transformer frozen and augments it with low-rank temporal adapters conditioned by learned shot-role prompt tokens. To maintain long-horizon coherence, it builds a recursive prompt bank that stores compact entity, location, action, and style prompts from previous shots, then routes them through adapter gates according to predicted narrative dependencies. A Shot-Local/Story-Global tuning objective combines next-shot reconstruction, cross-shot identity contrast, and prompt sparsity regularization, while an adapter composition schedule balances early-shot visual consistency with later-shot event progression and viewpoint change. Across six multi-shot and long-video benchmarks, PACR-Video outperforms text-to-video, tuning-based, memory-augmented, streaming, and recursive-context baselines on distributional quality, semantic alignment, identity consistency, temporal smoothness, motion stability, transition coherence, and human preference. These results show that compact prompt routing and lightweight temporal adaptation provide sufficient controllable capacity for stable long video extrapolation.

AI.tldr: PACR-Video is a parameter-efficient approach for multi-shot long video extrapolation that preserves recurring entities, scene structure, visual style, and causal progression without full generator fine-tuning. It freezes a text-to-video diffusion transformer and augments it with low-rank temporal adapters guided by learned shot-role prompts. It uses a recursive prompt bank to maintain coherence across shots, routing prompts via adapter gates based on predicted narrative dependencies. A Shot-Local/Story-Global objective combines next-shot reconstruction, cross-shot identity contrast, and prompt sparsity. An adapter composition schedule balances early-shot consistency with later-shot progression. Evaluations on six long-video benchmarks show PACR-Video outperforming various baselines on quality, alignment, identity, and temporal metrics, demonstrating that compact prompt routing and lightweight adaptation can enable stable long video extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon video extrapolation requires maintaining identity, scene structure, visual style, and causal progression over many shots without incurring expensive full fine-tuning of large diffusion models. Existing approaches struggle with coherence, efficiency, and controllability for multi-shot, long-video generation.
AI.method: Freeze the text-to-video diffusion transformer and augment it with low-rank temporal adapters conditioned on learned shot-role prompt tokens. Build a recursive prompt bank storing compact prompts (entities, locations, actions, style) from previous shots and route them through adapter gates according to predicted narrative dependencies. Train with a Shot-Local/Story-Global objective combining next-shot reconstruction, cross-shot identity contrast, and prompt sparsity regularization. Use an adapter composition schedule to balance early-shot visual consistency with later-shot event progression and viewpoint changes.
AI.result: On six multi-shot and long-video benchmarks, PACR-Video outperforms text-to-video, tuning-based, memory-augmented, streaming, and recursive-context baselines across metrics including distributional quality, semantic alignment, identity consistency, temporal smoothness, motion stability, transition coherence, and human preference.
AI.conclusion: Compact prompt routing and lightweight temporal adaptation provide sufficient controllable capacity for stable long video extrapolation, enabling effective long-horizon generation without full generator fine-tuning.

title: Mitigating Domain Shift in Conditioned Floor Plan Generation: Synthetic Pre-training for Data-Efficient Adaptation
summary: Robustness to domain shift is a key requirement for floor plan generative models to be applicable beyond the single dataset they were trained on, as floor plans vary widely across regions due to distinct architectural cultures, spatial constraints, and construction practices, while acquiring new annotated datasets remains costly and domain-specific. Yet, no prior work has studied this robustness in the context of conditioned floor plan generation. In this paper, we evaluate state-of-the-art models from two fundamentally different generative paradigms across three public datasets (RPLAN, MagicPlan and Swiss Dwellings) and show that they are highly sensitive to domain shift, with up to an order of magnitude performance degradation when transferred across domains. To mitigate this with minimal target-domain supervision, we introduce a procedural method to generate a large-scale synthetic training dataset that enforces strict physical constraints (non-overlapping rooms, valid door placement, graph consistency) while intentionally sacrificing architectural realism through highly irregular spatial arrangements and aggressive geometric perturbation of room shapes. We show that pre-training on this synthetic data considerably improves zero-shot cross-domain performance, outperforming in-domain training on MagicPlan. Furthermore, it provides a highly effective initialization for fine-tuning, accelerating target domain adaptation and outperforming real-world initialization baselines by up to 40% in a low-data regime.

AI.tldr: Synthetic predictive pre-training on a constrained procedural-floor-plan dataset improves cross-domain robustness for conditioned floor plan generation, enabling strong zero-shot transfer and data-efficient fine-tuning, outperforming in-domain training and real-world initializations.
AI.motivation: Floor plan generative models exhibit strong susceptibility to domain shift due to regional architectural diversity, spatial constraints, and construction practices; annotating new target-domain data is costly, motivating robust cross-domain transfer.
AI.method: Procedurally generate a large synthetic training dataset enforcing strict physical constraints (non-overlapping rooms, valid door placement, graph consistency) and introducing irregular layouts and aggressive geometric perturbations to room shapes; pre-train models on this data and evaluate zero-shot transfer and fine-tuning with limited target-domain data.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models from two generative paradigms show high sensitivity to domain shift, with up to ~10x performance degradation when transferred across domains; synthetic pre-training substantially improves zero-shot cross-domain performance, outperforms in-domain MagicPlan training, and provides a strong initialization that accelerates adaptation, outperforming real-world initializations by up to 40% in low-data settings.
AI.conclusion: Structured synthetic data with strict physical constraints can markedly improve cross-domain robustness and data-efficient adaptation for conditioned floor plan generation, offering a scalable pathway to robust cross-domain deployment.

title: AirflowAttack: Thermal-Airflow Adversarial Perturbations against Infrared Remote-Sensing Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed on infrared (IR) remote sensing imagery in security-critical settings, yet their adversarial robustness remains unexamined. We present AirflowAttack, to our knowledge the first adversarial attack for IR remote-sensing VLMs and the first to weaponize thermal-airflow turbulence as the perturbation prior. A lightweight generator synthesizes a single input-agnostic perturbation regularized toward physically plausible airflow patterns. Optimized on one surrogate CLIP model, it attains a mean zero-shot scene-classification attack success rate (ASR, the fraction of samples whose top-1 class changes) of 48.5% across five diverse CLIP backbones, far exceeding four IR-specific physical baselines (27.7--37.0%). Applied to six state-of-the-art VLMs, it cuts scene-classification accuracy by up to 38.2% relative, yet paradoxically makes some models more confident in their IR analysis, confabulating the perturbation as genuine thermal evidence such as temperature gradients and convection. Ablations show the airflow prior raises physical plausibility at no measurable cost to attack success. Together with a benchmark spanning eleven models and four tasks, these findings expose critical vulnerabilities in the rapidly expanding IR VLM ecosystem.

AI.tldr: AirflowAttack introduces the first physically plausible adversarial attack for infrared remote-sensing VLMs using thermal-airflow turbulence as a perturbation prior, achieving strong transferability and revealing vulnerabilities across multiple models.
AI.motivation: IR remote-sensing VLMs are increasingly deployed in security-critical contexts, but their adversarial robustness remains largely unexamined. This work proposes a physically grounded threat model by leveraging airflow turbulence, highlighting potential real-world risks and the need for defenses.
AI.method: A lightweight input-agnostic perturbation generator is optimized against one surrogate CLIP model and regularized toward physically plausible airflow patterns. The perturbation is single, input-agnostic, and crafted to cause zero-shot scene-classification misclassification. The approach leverages an airflow prior to improve physical plausibility without extra cost to attack performance, and is evaluated across six VLMs and across multiple backbones with ablations and a broader benchmark.
AI.result: Mean zero-shot scene-classification attack success rate (ASR) of 48.5% across five CLIP backbones, outperforming IR-specific baselines (27.7–37.0%). When applied to six state-of-the-art VLMs, the attack reduces scene-classification accuracy by up to 38.2% relative. Some models exhibit increased confidence in the perturbation, confabulating it as genuine thermal evidence. Ablations show the airflow prior enhances physical plausibility without reducing ASR. A broad benchmark spanning eleven models and four tasks underscores the vulnerability of IR VLMs to this threat.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals critical vulnerabilities in the IR VLM ecosystem, demonstrating that physically grounded perturbations based on airflow can effectively compromise scene understanding. It motivates the development of robust defenses and more physically aware training to mitigate such threats.

title: Point as Skeleton: Accumulated Point Cloud Enhanced Autoregressive Generation for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving Simulation
summary: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) remains challenging, as existing driving simulation methods often trade off closed-loop interactivity (e.g., CARLA) and real-world visual fidelity (e.g., nuScenes). We present \textbf{\emph{Point as Skeleton}}, a generative sensor simulation framework for state-updated autoregressive driving video generation, in which an autoregressive generator synthesizes visual observations from step-wise updated ego states, actor states, scene maps, and point-cloud skeleton conditions. To support closed-loop rollout, we introduce Reset-and-Roll, which adapts rolling diffusion inference to simulation by preventing future-conditioned latent states from being committed across simulation steps. To stabilize error accumulation during step-wise autoregressive rollout, we introduce point-cloud skeletons that decouple foreground and background assets and project them into camera-view painted-point and template-depth conditions, providing appearance and geometric cues. We further implement a nuPlan-based renderer-level closed-loop generative interface for evaluating generation under ego deviations from the original log. Experiments on nuScenes and nuPlan show that \textit{Point as Skeleton} improves autoregressive generation quality during closed-loop rollout, demonstrating its potential for visually faithful closed-loop driving simulation. The code is available at https://github.com/krauwu/point-as-skeleton.

AI.tldr: A generative sensor-simulation framework, Point as Skeleton, uses point-cloud skeletons to support stable, closed-loop autoregressive driving video generation with a Reset-and-Roll mechanism and a nuPlan-based renderer interface, achieving improved fidelity on nuScenes/nuPlan; code released.
AI.motivation: To overcome the trade-off between closed-loop interactivity and high visual fidelity in driving simulators and to stabilize long-horizon autoregressive generation under ego-driven variations.
AI.method: A step-wise autoregressive generator conditions on updated ego/actor states, scene maps, and point-cloud skeletons. Point-cloud skeletons decouple foreground/background assets and project into camera-view painted-point and template-depth cues. Reset-and-Roll adapts rolling diffusion inference to prevent future-conditioned latent leakage across steps. A nuPlan-based renderer-level interface enables evaluation under ego deviations. Evaluations are conducted on nuScenes and nuPlan; code is publicly available.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved autoregressive generation quality during closed-loop rollout and visually faithful closed-loop driving simulation.
AI.conclusion: Validates Point as Skeleton as a viable approach for high-fidelity, interactive E2E-AD simulation, with an open-source implementation to facilitate further evaluation and extension.

title: CAIRN: Cross-Room 3D Scene Understanding with Topology-Aware Large Multimodal Models
summary: Existing 3D scene-grounded Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) focus on answering questions grounded in simplified single-room 3D scenes, lacking the ability to reason over real-world household environments containing multiple interconnected rooms and diverse object categories. We introduce CAIRN, a topology-aware 3D-LLM for multi-room 3D scene understanding. CAIRN aligns transformer attention with scene hierarchy, giving the model explicit awareness of object-level relations and room-level connectivity. It enriches object tokens with room-local relational context via a graph neural network, introduces learned room tokens for room-level abstraction, and applies a hierarchical attention mask with geometric bias to route information according to scene topology. CAIRN is developed on CAIRN-MR, a benchmark we introduce on HM3D for multi-room 3D scene understanding, covering grounding, captioning, and four question-answering tasks that progressively evaluate from intra-room perception to cross-room reasoning. Experiments show that CAIRN outperforms prior 3D-LLMs by a large margin across all CAIRN-MR tasks while remaining competitive on five single-room benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CAIRN is a topology-aware 3D-LLM for multi-room scene understanding that aligns transformer attention with scene hierarchy, uses a GNN-augmented object representation and learned room tokens, evaluated on the CAIRN-MR benchmark; it substantially outperforms existing 3D-LLMs and stays competitive on single-room tasks.
AI.motivation: Current 3D-LLMs mainly handle simplified, single-room 3D scenes and struggle with real-world multi-room households that include interconnected rooms and diverse object categories; a topology-aware architecture could enable cross-room reasoning by encoding scene hierarchy and room-level connectivity.
AI.method: CAIRN aligns transformer attention with scene hierarchy; enriches object tokens with room-local relational context via a graph neural network; introduces learned room tokens for room-level abstraction; employs a hierarchical attention mask with geometric bias to route information per scene topology; trains/evaluates on CAIRN-MR, a HM3D-based benchmark for multi-room understanding including grounding, captioning, and four QA tasks; benchmarks cover intra-room perception to cross-room reasoning.
AI.result: CAIRN achieves a large margin of improvement over prior 3D-LLMs across all CAIRN-MR tasks and remains competitive on five single-room benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware sculpting of attention and explicit room-level abstractions enable effective cross-room 3D reasoning; CAIRN introduces a multi-room 3D-LLM framework and benchmark that advance realistic household understanding.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Calcification Classification in Mammography Across Multi-Site Datasets
summary: Deep learning-based computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems have shown strong performance in breast cancer diagnosis, particularly for classification tasks in mammography. However, domain shifts across multi-site datasets remain a challenge, especially when models are applied to unseen domains. In this work, we proposed a calcification classification framework to improve malignant versus benign breast disease classification across multi-site mammography datasets. The framework consisted of two components: (1) an unsupervised domain adaptation module based on style transfer models (AdaIN and CycleGAN) to generate vendor-specific and technique-specific training samples without additional annotations, and (2) a supervised classification module using Swin Transformer V2 as the backbone. We evaluated the proposed method on three datasets: cross-validation on OPTIMAM (National Health Service, United Kingdom; n=2994), followed by external validation on EMBED (Emory University; n=125), and Duke Calcification Dataset v1 (n=788). These datasets cover multiple vendors and include both full-field digital mammography and synthetic 2D images derived from digital breast tomosynthesis. The proposed framework improved cross-site performance for both EMBED (AUC 0.68 to 0.72) and the Duke Calcification Dataset (AUC 0.68 to 0.73). These findings indicate that domain adaptation can reduce domain shifts and improve the generalization for calcification classification across multi-site datasets.

AI.tldr: A two-component framework improves calcification-based breast cancer classification across multi-site mammography by combining unsupervised domain adaptation via style transfer (AdaIN and CycleGAN) with a Swin Transformer V2 classifier, showing improved cross-site AUC on EMBED and Duke datasets after cross-validation on OPTIMAM.
AI.motivation: Domain shifts across multi-site mammography datasets hinder generalization of deep learning CAD systems; calcification classification requires robust cross-site performance without additional annotations.
AI.method: (1) Unsupervised domain adaptation using style-transfer models AdaIN and CycleGAN to generate vendor- and technique-specific training samples without extra annotations. (2) Supervised classification with Swin Transformer V2 backbone. Evaluation on OPTIMAM (3-fold cross-validation), external validation on EMBED and Duke Calcification Dataset v1, including both FFDM and synthetic 2D images from DBT.
AI.result: Cross-site AUC improved: EMBED from 0.68 to 0.72; Duke Calcification Dataset from 0.68 to 0.73, in addition to the internal cross-validation on OPTIMAM.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised domain adaptation via style transfer can mitigate domain shifts and enhance generalization for calcification classification across multi-site mammography datasets.

title: MonoIR-RS: Infrared Remote Sensing Vision-Language Learning with CLIP and VLM Adaptation
summary: Infrared remote-sensing imagery captures intensity structure, object-background contrast, and illumination-invariant cues often invisible in RGB imagery. Yet, most remote-sensing vision-language resources and models focus on visible-band semantics, leaving infrared vision-language understanding underexplored. We introduce MonoIR-RS, a large-scale infrared remote-sensing vision-language dataset and benchmark that couples IR-aware data construction with CLIP-style contrastive adaptation and VLM instruction tuning. Built from the same source pool and split as FusionRS, MonoIR-RS retains the infrared image as the model-facing modality, yielding 600,000 synthesized infrared images and 59,032 retained IR-aware caption records. The model experiments use this retained language-supervision subset, whose captions rewrite supervision around grayscale structure and infrared-style contrast instead of RGB appearance. We show that the synthesized infrared imagery is markedly closer to real thermal imagery than a grayscale conversion on the AVIID benchmark. We fine-tune five CLIP backbones and six VLM backbones, and calibrate them against zero-shot behavior: IR-aware adaptation lifts CLIP mean recall by up to 12.8 points and drives VLM captioning IR-cue coverage to 100% while reducing residual RGB-color leakage to near zero. By isolating the infrared modality from RGB-IR dual-modal learning, MonoIR-RS offers a controlled, reproducible testbed for aligning infrared remote-sensing evidence with language.

AI.tldr: Presents MonoIR-RS: a large-scale infrared remote-sensing vision-language dataset and benchmark built to isolate IR modality and adapt CLIP/VLMs via IR-aware supervision; reports strong IR-specific improvements and 100% IR-cue captioning coverage.
AI.motivation: Address the underexploration of infrared future in vision-language understanding by providing an IR-focused dataset and evaluation framework that decouples IR from RGB-IR dual-modal learning and aligns infrared evidence with language.
AI.method: Data construction: from FusionRS with IR-facing modality, generating 600k synthesized infrared images and 59,032 IR-aware captions. Training: CLIP-style contrastive adaptation and VLM instruction tuning on the retained IR-supervision subset; evaluation against zero-shot baselines, IR-aware cloning to reduce RGB leakage. Backbones: five CLIP variants and six VLM variants fine-tuned.
AI.result: IR-aware adaptation boosts CLIP mean recall by up to 12.8 points; VLM captioning reaches 100% IR-cue coverage; RGB-color leakage reduced to near zero. Synthesized IR images align more with real thermal imagery than grayscale conversion on AVIID. Provides a controlled testbed for aligning IR evidence with language.
AI.conclusion: Isolating infrared modality from RGB-IR learning yields a reproducible framework for infrared remote-sensing language grounding. MonoIR-RS enables IR-focused evaluation and improves IR-cue usage while minimizing RGB leakage, supporting more faithful IR-language alignment.

title: From RGB Generation to Dense Field Readout: Pixel-Space Dense Prediction with Text-to-Image Models
summary: Large-scale text-to-image models are attractive backbones for dense prediction because RGB generation pretraining learns rich semantic, structural, and geometric priors. Existing generative and editing approaches reuse these priors by casting dense prediction as target generation: annotations such as depth, normals, alpha mattes, masks, and heatmaps are encoded into an RGB-trained VAE latent space and decoded back as image-like targets. We argue this inherits more of the generative output interface than dense prediction requires: unlike RGB synthesis, dense prediction asks for pixel-correct, task-native fields on the same image plane, not new RGB content to be rendered. Our key observation is that a pretrained DiT already organizes RGB inputs through a patch-to-token-to-patch lattice on the image plane, so each token indexes a fixed output patch whose channels can carry task-native quantities instead of RGB appearance. We instantiate this as ReChannel: we keep the VAE encoder for the DiT's input distribution but drop the target-side decoder, adapt the frozen DiT with task LoRA, and map each token to its p x p x K_t pixel-space patch through a shared token-local linear head--about 33K parameters, no spatial mixing. Using FLUX-Klein, we evaluate on six dense prediction tasks and over a dozen benchmarks. This minimal interface sets new state-of-the-art on trimap-free matting, KITTI depth, and referring segmentation, and stays competitive on normals, saliency, and pose. In a matched 4B setting it is more accurate and 2.48x faster than an edit-plus-latent-decode counterpart--dense perception can benefit from generative pretraining without inheriting its output interface.

AI.tldr: A minimal, patch-centric reinterpretation of DiT for dense prediction (ReChannel) achieves SOTA on several tasks with a tiny 33k-parameter task head, while keeping the DiT VAE encoder, dropping the target decoder, and mapping tokens to pixel-space patches—yielding faster, more accurate dense perception than RGB-generation-based edits.
AI.motivation: Dense prediction requires pixel-precise, task-native outputs. Prior work on reusing RGB-generation priors via latent decoders imposes an RGB output interface, which can misalign with dense prediction needs. The authors leverage DiT's patch-based token lattice to produce patch-wise, task-relevant channels directly.
AI.method: Use a pre-trained DiT with its VAE encoder; freeze DiT; remove the target-side decoder; apply task-specific LoRA adapters; map each DiT token to a p x p x K_t pixel-space patch via a shared token-local linear head (~33k parameters); no spatial mixing; train/evaluate with FLUX-Klein on six dense prediction tasks across 12+ benchmarks.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art on trimap-free matting, KITTI depth, and referring segmentation; competitive on normals, saliency, and pose; in a matched 4B-parameter setting, outperforms an edit-plus-latent-decode approach in accuracy and is 2.48x faster; demonstrates that dense perception can benefit from generative pretraining without inheriting its output interface.
AI.conclusion: Dense prediction can leverage generative priors by repurposing the DiT’s patch-based tokens for task-native outputs, enabling a compact, efficient interface (ReChannel) that preserves performance gains without generating RGB content.

title: ProxyPose: 6-DoF Pose Tracking via Video-to-Video Translation
summary: Tracking the six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose of objects and surfaces from monocular video is a long-standing problem in computer vision. To tackle this problem, existing methods require inputs beyond the video itself-such as 3D models, depth maps, object masks, or task-specific learned features-and they struggle with textureless, transparent, reflective, or deformable surfaces. Here, we introduce ProxyPose, which recasts 6-DoF pose tracking as video-to-video translation. Given only a video and a single marked pixel in the first frame, a fine-tuned video diffusion model translates the input into a proxy video-a synthetic video depicting a colored polyhedron undergoing the same local rigid-body motion as the surface region at the marked pixel. Because the proxy's geometry and appearance are known by construction, recovering its full 6-DoF trajectory reduces to classical pose estimation with off-the-shelf solvers. This formulation leverages large-scale video pre-training to absorb the hardest aspects of pose tracking-handling challenging materials, occlusions, and deformations-into the translation step, while operating at the pixel level with no assumptions about object identity, boundaries, or global rigidity. ProxyPose achieves state-of-the-art 6-DoF pose tracking accuracy without the additional inputs required by competing methods and after fine-tuning the video model only on synthetic data. We further demonstrate that ProxyPose extends to face tracking, camera pose estimation, and challenging in-the-wild scenes that are beyond the reach of existing approaches. Project page: https://ruihangzhang97.github.io/proxypose/.

AI.tldr: ProxyPose reframes 6-DoF pose tracking as video-to-video translation: a fine-tuned video diffusion model converts a monocular video (with one marked pixel) into a proxy video of a colored polyhedron undergoing the same local motion, after which standard pose solvers recover the full trajectory.
AI.motivation: Monocular 6-DoF tracking is brittle with textureless, transparent, reflective, or deformable surfaces and often requires extra inputs; leveraging large-scale video priors can absorb these challenges into a translation step.
AI.method: Fine-tune a video diffusion model on synthetic data to translate an input video (given a single marked pixel in the first frame) into a proxy video depicting a structured polyhedron undergoing the same local motion. The proxy’s geometry/appearance are known, so 6-DoF pose is recovered with classical solvers. Training relies on synthetic data; no extra per-sequence inputs are needed.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art 6-DoF pose tracking accuracy without additional inputs; demonstrates robustness to challenging materials, occlusions, and deformations; generalizes to face tracking, camera pose estimation, and in-the-wild scenes beyond prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: ProxyPose shows that large-scale video priors can be harnessed via video-to-video translation to simplify and robustify pose tracking, enabling reliable monocular 6-DoF tracking with minimal input and broad applicability.

title: Vision as Unified Multimodal Generation
summary: We formulate computer vision as unified multimodal generation, where heterogeneous visual tasks are expressed in the native text and image generation spaces of a unified multimodal model, without task-specific architectures. Under this formulation, SenseNova-Vision uses natural-language instructions and optional visual prompts to specify tasks, target regions or views, and decoding conventions, and generates responses as text for symbolic outputs, images for dense spatial predictions, or mixed text-and-image outputs for compositional tasks. To support large-scale training, we convert diverse computer vision annotations into instruction-response examples compatible with these generation spaces, resulting in the SenseNova-Vision Corpus, a computer-vision instruction-response corpus spanning text, image, and mixed targets. Starting from an off-the-shelf pretrained unified multimodal model, SenseNova-Vision is trained primarily on this corpus, with auxiliary multimodal data used as a capability-preserving mixture, and requires no task-specific prediction heads or architectural modifications. The resulting model covers a broad range of vision tasks, including detection, OCR, keypoint estimation, segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction, point maps, and camera pose estimation, while supporting language-defined variants that combine category, color, region, and other visual cues. Experiments show that a single unified model can match leading task-specialized systems across structured visual understanding, dense geometric prediction, segmentation, and multi-view visual geometry. These results suggest unified multimodal generation as a scalable route for integrating computer vision capabilities into general-purpose foundation models. The model and corpus are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Proposes SenseNova-Vision: a unified multimodal generation approach that treats heterogeneous vision tasks as text/image generation problems within a single foundation model, trained on an instruction-response corpus to cover multiple tasks without task-specific heads.
AI.motivation: To remove task-specific architectures and heads by expressing diverse vision tasks in a single unified generation space, enabling scalable integration of computer vision capabilities into general-purpose models.
AI.method: Convert diverse CV annotations into instruction-response examples compatible with text, image, and mixed generation targets; train a pretrained unified multimodal model on the SenseNova-Vision Corpus with auxiliary multimodal data; use natural-language instructions and optional visual prompts to define tasks, regions, and decoding conventions; no architectural changes.
AI.result: The model covers detection, OCR, keypoint estimation, segmentation, depth, surface normals, point maps, and camera pose, plus language-defined variants; experiments show a single model matches leading task-specific systems across structured vision, dense geometry, segmentation, and multi-view geometry.
AI.conclusion: Unified multimodal generation is a scalable route for integrating CV capabilities into foundation models; the SenseNova-Vision model and corpus are publicly available.
